grade9-biology.question: The circulatory system is made up of the blood, the blood vessels and:
grade9-biology.answer: The heart
grade9-biology.hint: It is the pump that drives the blood.
grade9-biology.explanation: Blood, blood vessels and the heart together make up the circulatory system.

grade9-biology.question: What is the main job of the heart?
options: To remove waste from the blood
To take oxygen out of the air
To pump blood around the body
To digest the food that is eaten
grade9-biology.answer: To pump blood around the body
acceptableAnswers: To pump blood around the body
grade9-biology.hint: It is a muscular pump.
grade9-biology.explanation: The heart is a muscular pump that keeps blood moving through the vessels.

grade9-biology.question: Which of these does the blood NOT transport?
options: Light from the eyes to the brain
Digested food to all of the body cells
grade9-biology.answer: Light from the eyes to the brain
acceptableAnswers: Light from the eyes to the brain
grade9-biology.hint: Three of these are really carried in the blood.
grade9-biology.explanation: Blood carries oxygen, dissolved food and carbon dioxide; light is not transported by blood at all.

grade9-biology.question: Which part of the blood is the pale yellow liquid?
grade9-biology.answer: Plasma
grade9-biology.hint: It is the liquid the other parts float in.
grade9-biology.explanation: Plasma is the straw-coloured liquid in which the cells and platelets are carried.

grade9-biology.question: Which part of the blood carries oxygen?
grade9-biology.answer: Red blood cells
grade9-biology.hint: They contain haemoglobin.
grade9-biology.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen and carries it to the body cells.

grade9-biology.question: What is the main job of the white blood cells?
options: To carry dissolved food to the cells
To help the blood to clot at a wound
To carry oxygen around the body
To defend the body against disease
grade9-biology.answer: To defend the body against disease
acceptableAnswers: To defend the body against disease
grade9-biology.hint: They are part of the body defences.
grade9-biology.explanation: White blood cells fight infection by engulfing microbes and producing antibodies.

grade9-biology.question: What is the main job of the platelets?
options: To fight microbes that enter the body
To help the blood clot when a vessel is cut
To carry hormones around the body
To carry oxygen from the lungs
grade9-biology.answer: To help the blood clot when a vessel is cut
acceptableAnswers: To help the blood clot when a vessel is cut
grade9-biology.hint: They act at a wound.
grade9-biology.explanation: Platelets help the blood to clot, which seals a wound and stops further blood loss.

grade9-biology.question: A person has too few red blood cells. Which symptom would you expect?
options: Blood that clots far too quickly
Tiredness, because less oxygen reaches the body cells
Frequent bleeding from a wound that will not stop
grade9-biology.answer: Tiredness, because less oxygen reaches the body cells
acceptableAnswers: Tiredness, because less oxygen reaches the body cells
grade9-biology.hint: Match the symptom to the job of the missing cells.
grade9-biology.explanation: Fewer red cells means less oxygen delivered, so the person tires easily - the condition called anaemia.

grade9-biology.question: Why does a red blood cell have no nucleus?
options: It allows the cell to divide more often
It helps the cell to fight infection
It makes the cell live much longer
It leaves more room to carry oxygen
grade9-biology.answer: It leaves more room to carry oxygen
acceptableAnswers: It leaves more room to carry oxygen
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what fills the cell instead.
grade9-biology.explanation: Losing the nucleus leaves more space for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen.

grade9-biology.question: Which vessel carries blood away from the heart?
grade9-biology.answer: An artery
grade9-biology.hint: The A goes away.
grade9-biology.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return it.

grade9-biology.question: Which vessel carries blood back towards the heart?
grade9-biology.answer: A vein
grade9-biology.hint: The opposite of an artery.
grade9-biology.explanation: Veins carry blood back towards the heart.

grade9-biology.question: The three vessels shown are drawn to the same scale. Which is the artery?
options: B, because it has the widest space inside
C, because it is the smallest of the three
A, because it has the thickest wall
None of them, because arteries have no wall
grade9-biology.answer: A, because it has the thickest wall
acceptableAnswers: A, because it has the thickest wall
grade9-biology.hint: An artery carries blood at high pressure.
grade9-biology.explanation: A has much the thickest, most muscular wall, which is what withstands the high pressure from the heart.

grade9-biology.question: The three vessels shown are drawn to the same scale. Which is the capillary?
options: C, because it is tiny with a very thin wall
B, because it has the widest space inside
None of them, because capillaries are not vessels
A, because it has the thickest wall
grade9-biology.answer: C, because it is tiny with a very thin wall
acceptableAnswers: C, because it is tiny with a very thin wall
grade9-biology.hint: A capillary wall is one cell thick.
grade9-biology.explanation: C is the smallest with the thinnest wall, which is what lets substances pass through it easily.

grade9-biology.question: Why is the wall of a capillary only one cell thick?
options: So the blood can be pumped at a much higher pressure
So oxygen and food can pass quickly into the cells around it
So the capillary can stretch to hold more blood
So the blood flows through it as fast as possible
grade9-biology.answer: So oxygen and food can pass quickly into the cells around it
acceptableAnswers: So oxygen and food can pass quickly into the cells around it
grade9-biology.hint: Exchange is what a capillary is for.
grade9-biology.explanation: A wall one cell thick gives a very short diffusion distance, so exchange with the surrounding tissue is fast.

grade9-biology.question: Why do veins contain valves while arteries do not?
options: The blood in veins is at higher pressure than in arteries
The blood in veins is at low pressure and could flow backwards
Veins carry blood that contains no oxygen at all
Veins are much closer to the heart than arteries
grade9-biology.answer: The blood in veins is at low pressure and could flow backwards
acceptableAnswers: The blood in veins is at low pressure and could flow backwards
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what stops the blood going the wrong way.
grade9-biology.explanation: Vein blood is at low pressure, so valves are needed to keep it flowing one way, back towards the heart.

grade9-biology.question: The drawing shown is 58 mm wide. The real cell is 0.0058 mm wide. What is the magnification?
grade9-biology.hint: Magnification = drawing size ÷ real size.
grade9-biology.explanation: 58 ÷ 0.0058 = 10 000. Magnification has no unit.

grade9-biology.question: Which formula gives the magnification of a drawing?
grade9-biology.answer: Magnification = drawing size ÷ real size
grade9-biology.hint: A bigger drawing of the same object means a bigger magnification.
grade9-biology.explanation: Magnification is how many times larger the drawing is: drawing size divided by real size.

grade9-biology.question: Why does a magnification have no unit?
options: It is measured in the same unit as the drawing
It is always a whole number
It is a length divided by a length, so the units cancel
It is always measured in millimetres
grade9-biology.answer: It is a length divided by a length, so the units cancel
acceptableAnswers: It is a length divided by a length, so the units cancel
grade9-biology.hint: Look at what is divided by what.
grade9-biology.explanation: Both quantities are lengths in the same unit, so the units cancel and the answer is a plain number.

grade9-biology.question: A cell is 0.02 mm across and is drawn 40 mm across. What must be done before dividing?
options: Both lengths must first be converted into centimetres
The drawing must be converted into micrometres
Nothing: both lengths are already in millimetres
The real size must be converted into metres
grade9-biology.answer: Nothing: both lengths are already in millimetres
acceptableAnswers: Nothing: both lengths are already in millimetres
grade9-biology.hint: Check the units of each measurement first.
grade9-biology.explanation: Both are in millimetres, so they can be divided directly: 40 ÷ 0.02 = 2000.

grade9-biology.question: What is a pulse?
options: The stretching of an artery each time the heart beats
The pressure of blood inside a vein
The amount of blood pumped in one minute
The sound the heart makes as it closes its valves
grade9-biology.answer: The stretching of an artery each time the heart beats
acceptableAnswers: The stretching of an artery each time the heart beats
grade9-biology.hint: It can be felt where an artery runs near the skin.
grade9-biology.explanation: Each heartbeat sends a surge of blood that stretches the artery wall - that stretch is the pulse.

grade9-biology.question: Where can a pulse most easily be felt?
options: At the wrist, where an artery runs near the skin
On the forehead, over the skull
On the back of the hand, directly over a large vein
On the knee, over the joint
grade9-biology.answer: At the wrist, where an artery runs near the skin
acceptableAnswers: At the wrist, where an artery runs near the skin
grade9-biology.hint: A pulse is felt over an artery, not a vein.
grade9-biology.explanation: The artery at the wrist runs close to the surface, so its stretch can be felt easily.

grade9-biology.question: What happens to the pulse rate during hard exercise?
options: It falls, because the body is saving its energy
It stops until the exercise is finished
It rises, because the muscles need more oxygen
It stays exactly the same throughout
grade9-biology.answer: It rises, because the muscles need more oxygen
acceptableAnswers: It rises, because the muscles need more oxygen
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what working muscles need more of.
grade9-biology.explanation: Exercising muscles need more oxygen and glucose, so the heart beats faster and the pulse rate rises.

grade9-biology.question: What happens during a heart attack?
options: The kidneys stop filtering the blood
The lungs fill with fluid and stop working
The blood supply to part of the heart muscle is blocked
The blood supply to part of the brain is blocked
grade9-biology.answer: The blood supply to part of the heart muscle is blocked
acceptableAnswers: The blood supply to part of the heart muscle is blocked
grade9-biology.hint: The name says which organ is affected.
grade9-biology.explanation: A blocked coronary artery starves part of the heart muscle of oxygen, which is a heart attack.

grade9-biology.question: What happens during a stroke?
options: The lungs take in too much oxygen at once
The blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted
The blood supply to part of the heart is interrupted
The blood becomes too thin to clot at a wound
grade9-biology.answer: The blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted
acceptableAnswers: The blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted
grade9-biology.hint: A stroke affects a different organ from a heart attack.
grade9-biology.explanation: A stroke happens when the blood supply to part of the brain is cut off or a vessel there bursts.

grade9-biology.question: Which of these increases the risk of cardiovascular disease?
grade9-biology.answer: Smoking
grade9-biology.hint: Three of these protect the heart.
grade9-biology.explanation: Smoking damages the blood vessels and raises the risk of heart attack and stroke.

grade9-biology.question: Which change would most reduce a person’s risk of a heart attack?
options: Drinking more sweet fizzy drinks each day
Taking regular exercise and eating less fatty food
Sleeping for an extra hour each afternoon
Watching less television in the evening
grade9-biology.answer: Taking regular exercise and eating less fatty food
acceptableAnswers: Taking regular exercise and eating less fatty food
grade9-biology.hint: Two changes act directly on the heart and vessels.
grade9-biology.explanation: Exercise strengthens the heart and a low-fat diet reduces the fatty deposits that block arteries.

grade9-biology.question: The graph shows deaths from heart disease against the amount of salt eaten. What does it show?
options: There is no pattern in the data at all
Deaths rise as salt intake rises
Deaths stay the same at every salt intake
Deaths fall as salt intake rises
grade9-biology.answer: Deaths rise as salt intake rises
acceptableAnswers: Deaths rise as salt intake rises
grade9-biology.hint: Follow the line from left to right.
grade9-biology.explanation: The line rises steadily from left to right, so a higher salt intake goes with more deaths.

grade9-biology.question: Reading the same graph, roughly how many deaths per 1000 occur at a salt intake of 6 g per day?
grade9-biology.hint: Go up from 6 on the horizontal axis to the line, then across.
grade9-biology.explanation: At 6 g the line is level with 30 on the vertical axis.

grade9-biology.question: The graph shows deaths rising with salt intake. What does that NOT prove on its own?
options: That the two measurements rise together
That the pattern is the same across the range
That the salt is what causes the deaths
That deaths are higher at 10 g than at 2 g
grade9-biology.answer: That the salt is what causes the deaths
acceptableAnswers: That the salt is what causes the deaths
grade9-biology.hint: Two things rising together is not the same as one causing the other.
grade9-biology.explanation: The graph shows a correlation; proving cause needs further evidence, because something else could explain both.

grade9-biology.question: A drawing of a cell is 60 mm wide. The real cell is 0.006 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.
grade9-biology.hint: Magnification = drawing size ÷ real size.

grade9-biology.question: A drawing of a cell is 40 mm wide. The real cell is 0.02 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.
grade9-biology.hint: Both lengths are already in millimetres.

grade9-biology.question: A cell 0.05 mm across is drawn at a magnification of 400. Calculate the width of the drawing, in mm.
grade9-biology.hint: Drawing size = real size × magnification.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil counts 18 pulse beats in 15 seconds. Calculate the pulse rate in beats per minute.
grade9-biology.hint: There are four lots of 15 seconds in a minute.
grade9-biology.explanation: 18 × 4 = 72 beats per minute.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil counts 35 beats in 30 seconds. Calculate the pulse rate in beats per minute.
grade9-biology.hint: Double the count for 30 seconds.
grade9-biology.explanation: 35 × 2 = 70 beats per minute.

grade9-biology.question: Name the liquid part of the blood.
grade9-biology.answer: Plasma
grade9-biology.hint: It is pale yellow.
grade9-biology.explanation: Plasma is the liquid part of the blood.

grade9-biology.question: Name the red pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
grade9-biology.answer: Haemoglobin
grade9-biology.hint: It gives blood its colour.
grade9-biology.explanation: Haemoglobin binds oxygen and carries it round the body.

grade9-biology.question: Name the type of blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
grade9-biology.answer: Artery
grade9-biology.hint: A for away.
grade9-biology.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

grade9-biology.question: Name the smallest blood vessels, whose walls are one cell thick.
grade9-biology.answer: Capillaries
grade9-biology.hint: Exchange happens across them.
grade9-biology.explanation: Capillaries are the tiniest vessels, where exchange with the tissues takes place.

grade9-biology.question: Write the formula used to calculate magnification.
grade9-biology.answer: Magnification = drawing size / real size
grade9-biology.hint: It is one length divided by another.
grade9-biology.explanation: Magnification = drawing (image) size divided by real (actual) size.

grade9-biology.question: State one lifestyle change that reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease.
grade9-biology.answer: Stop smoking
grade9-biology.hint: Think about smoking, diet or exercise.
grade9-biology.explanation: Not smoking, exercising regularly and eating less fat and salt all lower the risk.

grade9-biology.question: What are the three main parts of the human circulatory system?
options: The blood, the blood vessels and the heart
The oxygen, the red cells and the aorta
The blood, the lungs and the kidneys
The plasma, the arteries and the liver
grade9-biology.answer: The blood, the blood vessels and the heart
acceptableAnswers: The blood, the blood vessels and the heart
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what carries the blood, what moves it and where it travels.
grade9-biology.explanation: The circulatory system consists of the blood (the transport fluid), blood vessels (the pipes) and the heart (the pump).

grade9-biology.question: What term describes a circulation in which blood passes through the heart twice for every complete circuit of the body?
grade9-biology.answer: Double circulation
grade9-biology.hint: Blood travels to the lungs and back, then to the body and back — two loops.
grade9-biology.explanation: Humans have a double circulation: the pulmonary circuit goes to the lungs; the systemic circuit goes to the rest of the body.

grade9-biology.question: What is the name of the largest artery in the body, which leaves the left ventricle?
grade9-biology.answer: The aorta
grade9-biology.hint: It is the main vessel carrying oxygenated blood to the body.
grade9-biology.explanation: The aorta leaves the left ventricle and branches to carry oxygenated blood to all organs of the body except the lungs.

grade9-biology.question: Which side of the heart receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body?
options: The left side of the heart
The upper chambers of both sides
The right side of the heart
The lower chambers of both sides
grade9-biology.answer: The right side of the heart
acceptableAnswers: The right side of the heart
grade9-biology.hint: The right side handles blood coming back from the body.
grade9-biology.explanation: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood via the vena cava; the right ventricle then pumps it to the lungs through the pulmonary artery.

grade9-biology.question: Blood that has been oxygenated in the lungs returns to the heart through which vessel?
grade9-biology.answer: The pulmonary vein
grade9-biology.hint: The name contains the word "pulmonary" for lungs, and it is a vein (to the heart).
grade9-biology.explanation: The pulmonary vein carries freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

grade9-biology.question: What is the main function of the valves found between the chambers of the heart?
options: To control the amount of oxygen entering the red blood cells
To increase the speed of blood leaving the heart each beat
To prevent blood flowing backwards between the heart chambers
To pump blood from the atria into the ventricles by contracting
grade9-biology.answer: To prevent blood flowing backwards between the heart chambers
acceptableAnswers: To prevent blood flowing backwards between the heart chambers
grade9-biology.hint: They snap shut when pressure reverses.
grade9-biology.explanation: Valves (such as the bicuspid and tricuspid valves) open when blood moves forward and close to prevent backflow.

grade9-biology.question: What do the coronary arteries supply to the heart?
options: Oxygen and nutrients to the heart muscle itself
Blood to the kidneys for filtering waste products
Deoxygenated blood to the pulmonary circulation
Oxygenated blood to the lungs for gas exchange
grade9-biology.answer: Oxygen and nutrients to the heart muscle itself
acceptableAnswers: Oxygen and nutrients to the heart muscle itself
grade9-biology.hint: They wrap around the outside surface of the heart.
grade9-biology.explanation: The coronary arteries branch from the aorta and supply the heart muscle with oxygen and glucose; a blockage leads to a heart attack.

grade9-biology.question: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the whole body back to the right atrium?
grade9-biology.answer: The vena cava
grade9-biology.hint: There are two of them — superior and inferior.
grade9-biology.explanation: The vena cava (superior from the upper body, inferior from the lower body) returns deoxygenated blood to the right atrium.

grade9-biology.question: Why is the muscular wall of the left ventricle thicker than the wall of the right ventricle?
options: It contains more valves that need extra muscle to open and close
It receives more blood from the pulmonary vein than the right side
It must pump blood all the way around the body at high pressure
It must pump blood against gravity into the brain and upper body
grade9-biology.answer: It must pump blood all the way around the body at high pressure
acceptableAnswers: It must pump blood all the way around the body at high pressure
grade9-biology.hint: A greater distance requires greater force — and therefore a thicker wall.
grade9-biology.explanation: The left ventricle drives blood through the entire systemic circulation; the right ventricle only has to reach the nearby lungs, so needs far less pressure.

grade9-biology.question: A patient has a blockage in the coronary arteries. Which tissue is most immediately at risk?
options: Lung tissue, which will receive too little blood for gas exchange
Heart muscle, which will be starved of oxygen and glucose
The aorta wall, which will burst from a build-up of pressure
White blood cells, which will fail to reach infected tissues
grade9-biology.answer: Heart muscle, which will be starved of oxygen and glucose
acceptableAnswers: Heart muscle, which will be starved of oxygen and glucose
grade9-biology.hint: Consider which tissue those specific arteries supply.
grade9-biology.explanation: The coronary arteries supply only the heart muscle; a blockage causes cardiac cells to die from lack of oxygen — a myocardial infarction.

grade9-biology.question: What is the name of the upper chambers of the heart that receive incoming blood?
grade9-biology.answer: Atria (singular: atrium)
grade9-biology.hint: They are the collecting chambers before the blood moves downward.
grade9-biology.explanation: The left and right atria receive blood from the pulmonary vein and vena cava respectively; they then push it into the ventricles below.

grade9-biology.question: The pulmonary artery carries blood away from the heart. What makes it unusual compared with most other arteries?
options: It has thinner walls than any other artery in the body
It contains pocket valves unlike other arteries in the body
It flows towards the heart rather than away from the heart
It carries deoxygenated rather than oxygenated blood to the lungs
grade9-biology.answer: It carries deoxygenated rather than oxygenated blood to the lungs
acceptableAnswers: It carries deoxygenated rather than oxygenated blood to the lungs
grade9-biology.hint: Arteries generally carry oxygenated blood — the pulmonary artery is the exception.
grade9-biology.explanation: Most arteries carry oxygenated blood away from the heart; the pulmonary artery is unique in carrying deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

grade9-biology.question: In a double circulation, what is the purpose of the pulmonary circuit?
options: To carry oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to all body organs
To allow the right atrium to collect blood from the body organs
To pump deoxygenated blood directly into the coronary arteries
To carry blood to the lungs to gain oxygen and release carbon dioxide
grade9-biology.answer: To carry blood to the lungs to gain oxygen and release carbon dioxide
acceptableAnswers: To carry blood to the lungs to gain oxygen and release carbon dioxide
grade9-biology.hint: The pulmonary circuit is the loop between the heart and the lungs.
grade9-biology.explanation: In the pulmonary circuit, deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle is sent to the lungs, where CO₂ is removed and O₂ is absorbed before the blood returns to the left atrium.

grade9-biology.question: Which component of blood is the pale yellow liquid in which the blood cells are suspended?
grade9-biology.answer: Plasma
grade9-biology.hint: It is the liquid part — the "carrier" for everything else.
grade9-biology.explanation: Plasma is the straw-coloured liquid that makes up about 55% of blood volume; it carries dissolved nutrients, hormones, carbon dioxide and waste products.

grade9-biology.question: Which blood component is responsible for carrying oxygen from the lungs to the body tissues?
grade9-biology.answer: Red blood cells
grade9-biology.hint: They contain a special oxygen-carrying protein.
grade9-biology.explanation: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin and releases it at respiring body cells.

grade9-biology.question: What is the main role of white blood cells in the body?
options: To defend the body against infection by pathogens
To transport dissolved food from the gut to body cells
To seal wounds by forming clots at injury sites
To carry oxygen from the lungs to all body tissues
grade9-biology.answer: To defend the body against infection by pathogens
acceptableAnswers: To defend the body against infection by pathogens
grade9-biology.hint: They are part of the immune system.
grade9-biology.explanation: White blood cells fight infection by engulfing microbes (phagocytosis) and by producing antibodies that target specific pathogens.

grade9-biology.question: Why do red blood cells have a biconcave disc shape?
options: To increase the surface area for absorbing and releasing oxygen
To help cells clump together to form a clot at a wound site
To allow the cell to pass through heart valves more easily
To make the cell stronger so it can survive high blood pressure
grade9-biology.answer: To increase the surface area for absorbing and releasing oxygen
acceptableAnswers: To increase the surface area for absorbing and releasing oxygen
grade9-biology.hint: A larger surface area means more haemoglobin is close to the cell surface.
grade9-biology.explanation: The biconcave shape increases the surface area to volume ratio, allowing haemoglobin to load and unload oxygen more rapidly than a sphere of the same volume.

grade9-biology.question: Which protein in red blood cells combines with oxygen in the lungs?
options: Fibrinogen, which forms fibrin strands during blood clotting
Insulin, which is produced in the pancreas and enters the blood
Haemoglobin, which forms oxyhaemoglobin when oxygen binds
Antibodies, which bind to antigens on the surface of pathogens
grade9-biology.answer: Haemoglobin, which forms oxyhaemoglobin when oxygen binds
acceptableAnswers: Haemoglobin, which forms oxyhaemoglobin when oxygen binds
grade9-biology.hint: It is the iron-containing pigment that gives blood its red colour.
grade9-biology.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells combines reversibly with oxygen in the high-oxygen environment of the lungs; in tissues with low oxygen levels it releases it.

grade9-biology.question: Which type of white blood cell destroys bacteria by engulfing them in a process called phagocytosis?
grade9-biology.answer: Phagocytes
grade9-biology.hint: The name comes from the Greek for "eating cells".
grade9-biology.explanation: Phagocytes engulf and digest bacteria and other foreign particles; lymphocytes work differently by producing antibodies.

grade9-biology.question: Why do mature red blood cells have no nucleus?
options: To prevent the cell from dividing rapidly inside blood vessels
To allow the cell to survive much longer in the bloodstream
To reduce the mass of the cell so it flows faster through capillaries
To leave more space for haemoglobin to increase oxygen-carrying capacity
grade9-biology.answer: To leave more space for haemoglobin to increase oxygen-carrying capacity
acceptableAnswers: To leave more space for haemoglobin to increase oxygen-carrying capacity
grade9-biology.hint: More haemoglobin per cell means more oxygen delivered per trip.
grade9-biology.explanation: During maturation, the nucleus is ejected from the red blood cell, freeing up cytoplasm to be packed with haemoglobin; this is an adaptation for efficient oxygen transport.

grade9-biology.question: What is the role of platelets in the blood?
options: To produce antibodies that target and destroy specific pathogens
To transport carbon dioxide from body cells to the lungs
To clump together at a wound and trigger formation of a blood clot
To carry dissolved glucose from the gut to all body cells
grade9-biology.answer: To clump together at a wound and trigger formation of a blood clot
acceptableAnswers: To clump together at a wound and trigger formation of a blood clot
grade9-biology.hint: They act at injury sites to stop bleeding.
grade9-biology.explanation: Platelets are small cell fragments that aggregate at a damaged vessel wall and release chemicals that initiate the clotting cascade, forming a fibrin clot.

grade9-biology.question: A person has a very low platelet count. What complication is most likely?
options: High blood pressure because the blood becomes thicker than normal
Frequent bacterial infections because immunity is severely weakened
Slow clotting, so wounds bleed for an abnormally long time
Reduced oxygen supply, causing tiredness and breathlessness
grade9-biology.answer: Slow clotting, so wounds bleed for an abnormally long time
acceptableAnswers: Slow clotting, so wounds bleed for an abnormally long time
grade9-biology.hint: Match the complication to the job that platelets normally perform.
grade9-biology.explanation: Platelets initiate clotting; without enough of them (thrombocytopenia), even minor wounds bleed excessively and internal bleeding is hard to stop.

grade9-biology.question: What are the four main components of blood?
options: Arteries, veins, capillaries and valves working together
Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
Plasma, haemoglobin, antibodies and fibrinogen proteins
Water, oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide dissolved together
grade9-biology.answer: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
acceptableAnswers: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
grade9-biology.hint: Three of the four are cells (or cell fragments); one is the liquid.
grade9-biology.explanation: Blood is made up of plasma (the liquid), red blood cells (oxygen carriers), white blood cells (immune defenders) and platelets (clotting agents).

grade9-biology.question: Why do red blood cells contain no mitochondria?
options: So they do not consume the oxygen they are transporting to other cells
Because haemoglobin molecules take up all the space in the cell
Because mitochondria are found only in cells that also have a nucleus
To allow them to survive in the very low-oxygen conditions in veins
grade9-biology.answer: So they do not consume the oxygen they are transporting to other cells
acceptableAnswers: So they do not consume the oxygen they are transporting to other cells
grade9-biology.hint: If they used oxygen themselves, less would reach working muscle cells.
grade9-biology.explanation: Red blood cells respire anaerobically; lacking mitochondria means they do not use the oxygen they carry, so it is available for delivery to other tissues.

grade9-biology.question: Which type of blood vessel carries blood away from the heart?
grade9-biology.answer: Artery
grade9-biology.hint: Remember: A for Artery, A for Away.
grade9-biology.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; their thick muscular-elastic walls help them withstand each surge.

grade9-biology.question: In which type of blood vessel do substances pass between the blood and the body cells?
grade9-biology.answer: Capillary
grade9-biology.hint: They are the smallest and thinnest-walled vessels.
grade9-biology.explanation: Capillary walls are only one cell thick, allowing oxygen, glucose and other substances to diffuse freely between blood and surrounding cells.

grade9-biology.question: What structural feature allows arteries to withstand the high blood pressure generated by the heart?
options: A very wide lumen relative to wall thickness throughout the length
Thick muscular and elastic walls that stretch and recoil with each beat
A single-cell-thick wall that allows pressure to escape gradually
Numerous pocket valves evenly spaced along the entire artery
grade9-biology.answer: Thick muscular and elastic walls that stretch and recoil with each beat
acceptableAnswers: Thick muscular and elastic walls that stretch and recoil with each beat
grade9-biology.hint: The heart forces blood out at high pressure — the walls must resist this.
grade9-biology.explanation: Artery walls contain smooth muscle and elastic tissue; they stretch on each heartbeat and recoil between beats to maintain smooth blood flow.

grade9-biology.question: What is the function of the pocket valves found at intervals in veins?
options: To prevent blood flowing backwards as it returns to the heart
To stop oxygen escaping from the blood into surrounding tissue
To increase the speed of blood flowing towards the lungs
To control how much blood passes from veins into capillaries
grade9-biology.answer: To prevent blood flowing backwards as it returns to the heart
acceptableAnswers: To prevent blood flowing backwards as it returns to the heart
grade9-biology.hint: Blood in veins is at low pressure and could pool without these valves.
grade9-biology.explanation: Pocket valves open when blood moves toward the heart and snap shut if it begins to flow backwards, preventing back-flow especially in the limbs.

grade9-biology.question: Which type of blood vessel has walls only one cell thick?
grade9-biology.answer: Capillary
grade9-biology.hint: The thinner the wall, the easier diffusion becomes across it.
grade9-biology.explanation: Capillary walls consist of a single layer of endothelial cells; this minimises the diffusion distance between blood and tissues.

grade9-biology.question: Why are capillary walls only one cell thick?
options: To allow the capillary wall itself to absorb oxygen for energy
To withstand the high pressure of blood flowing from the arteries
To minimise the diffusion distance between blood and tissue cells
To provide space for the valves that prevent backflow in capillaries
grade9-biology.answer: To minimise the diffusion distance between blood and tissue cells
acceptableAnswers: To minimise the diffusion distance between blood and tissue cells
grade9-biology.hint: A shorter diffusion distance means a faster rate of exchange.
grade9-biology.explanation: Substances such as oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide cross the capillary wall by diffusion; a single-cell thickness gives the shortest possible diffusion path.

grade9-biology.question: A cross-section of a blood vessel shows a very thick wall with much elastic tissue and a narrow lumen relative to wall thickness. Which vessel type does this represent?
options: An artery, adapted to withstand high blood pressure from the heart
A vein, adapted to carry blood back to the heart at low pressure
A capillary, adapted for rapid exchange with surrounding body cells
A lymph vessel, adapted for collecting excess fluid from tissues
grade9-biology.answer: An artery, adapted to withstand high blood pressure from the heart
acceptableAnswers: An artery, adapted to withstand high blood pressure from the heart
grade9-biology.hint: Which vessel needs the strongest wall to resist the most pressure?
grade9-biology.explanation: Arteries have thick walls with much elastic and muscle tissue; their lumen appears narrow compared with the wall. Veins have thin walls and a wide lumen.

grade9-biology.question: Why do arteries not need valves, even though veins do?
options: The thick walls of arteries physically prevent any backflow of blood
Arteries are too close to the heart for backflow to become a problem
Blood in arteries is at high pressure and always flows away from the heart
Arteries carry oxygenated blood, which does not require valve control
grade9-biology.answer: Blood in arteries is at high pressure and always flows away from the heart
acceptableAnswers: Blood in arteries is at high pressure and always flows away from the heart
grade9-biology.hint: What is the relationship between pressure and direction of flow?
grade9-biology.explanation: The ventricles force blood into arteries at high pressure; this pressure is sustained between heartbeats by elastic walls, so blood always flows one way — valves are unnecessary.

grade9-biology.question: Why do veins generally have a wider lumen than arteries of the same external diameter?
options: Blood is at low pressure in veins, so a wide lumen reduces resistance to flow
The pocket valves in veins take up space, requiring a wider lumen
Veins must carry more dissolved oxygen than arteries at any given moment
Veins are compressed by surrounding muscles, so they need a wider space
grade9-biology.answer: Blood is at low pressure in veins, so a wide lumen reduces resistance to flow
acceptableAnswers: Blood is at low pressure in veins, so a wide lumen reduces resistance to flow
grade9-biology.hint: Low-pressure flow benefits from low resistance — wider = less resistance.
grade9-biology.explanation: Veins have thin walls that leave more of the vessel as lumen; the wide lumen reduces resistance and allows blood to return to the heart despite low driving pressure.

grade9-biology.question: The wall of a capillary is formed from a single layer of cells called the endothelium. Why is this an advantage for the capillary's function?
options: It enables the capillary to actively transport substances into the tissues
It creates the shortest possible diffusion distance between blood and tissue cells
It allows the capillary to stretch and recoil with each heartbeat easily
It provides a strong barrier preventing pathogens from entering blood
grade9-biology.answer: It creates the shortest possible diffusion distance between blood and tissue cells
acceptableAnswers: It creates the shortest possible diffusion distance between blood and tissue cells
grade9-biology.hint: The thinner the wall, the faster diffusion can occur across it.
grade9-biology.explanation: A single-cell-thick wall minimises the distance that oxygen and glucose must diffuse from blood to cells, and that carbon dioxide and waste must travel back.

grade9-biology.question: Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood directly from the lungs back to the left atrium?
grade9-biology.answer: The pulmonary vein
grade9-biology.hint: It is the vein that returns blood from the lungs.
grade9-biology.explanation: The four pulmonary veins carry freshly oxygenated blood from the alveolar capillaries to the left atrium; it is then pumped to the body via the left ventricle and aorta.

grade9-biology.question: During vigorous exercise, blood is redirected to skeletal muscles. What most likely happens to blood flow in the capillaries of the gut simultaneously?
options: Blood flow to the gut also increases to speed up digestion
Blood flow to the gut decreases as vessels there constrict
Blood flow to the gut remains exactly the same during exercise
Blood flow to the gut stops completely for the duration of exercise
grade9-biology.answer: Blood flow to the gut decreases as vessels there constrict
acceptableAnswers: Blood flow to the gut decreases as vessels there constrict
grade9-biology.hint: The body redirects a limited blood supply — more to muscles means less elsewhere.
grade9-biology.explanation: Arterioles supplying the gut constrict during exercise, redirecting blood to skeletal muscles; the gut's needs are temporarily sacrificed for the increased demand of working muscles.

grade9-biology.question: What is the correct formula for calculating the magnification of a biological drawing?
grade9-biology.answer: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size
grade9-biology.hint: You divide the big (drawn) length by the small (real) length.
grade9-biology.explanation: Magnification = image (drawing) size ÷ actual (real) size. Both must be in the same unit, and the result has no unit.

grade9-biology.question: What unit is written after the magnification number in a biological drawing?
options: No unit — magnification is a ratio and has no unit at all
Times (×) is written as a formal unit after the number
Millimetres (mm), because drawings are always measured in mm
Micrometres (μm), because cells are measured in μm
grade9-biology.answer: No unit — magnification is a ratio and has no unit at all
acceptableAnswers: No unit — magnification is a ratio and has no unit at all
grade9-biology.hint: It is a ratio — the same quantity divided by the same quantity cancels.
grade9-biology.explanation: Magnification is a dimensionless ratio: mm ÷ mm (or μm ÷ μm) leaves no unit. The × symbol is a prefix, not a unit.

grade9-biology.question: A drawing of a cell is 50 mm wide. The actual cell is 10 mm wide. What is the magnification?
grade9-biology.hint: Divide the drawing size by the real size.
grade9-biology.explanation: Magnification = 50 ÷ 10 = 5. Both sizes are in mm so no conversion is needed.

grade9-biology.question: A microscope image shows a red blood cell at ×500 magnification. The cell appears 40 mm wide in the image. What is the actual width of the cell?
grade9-biology.answer: 0.08 mm (or 80 μm)
grade9-biology.hint: Rearrange: actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
grade9-biology.explanation: Actual size = 40 ÷ 500 = 0.08 mm. Converting: 0.08 mm × 1000 = 80 μm.

grade9-biology.question: A student draws a capillary cross-section 45 mm in diameter. The actual capillary is 9 μm in diameter. Which is the correct magnification?
options: ×50 (because 45 mm rounded and then divided by 9 directly)
×0.0002 (because actual size divided by image size is inverted)
grade9-biology.hint: Convert 9 μm to mm first, then divide the image size by the actual size.
grade9-biology.explanation: 9 μm = 9 ÷ 1000 = 0.009 mm. Magnification = 45 ÷ 0.009 = 5000. No unit.

grade9-biology.question: A student calculates the magnification of a cell drawing as 36 mm ÷ 0.09 mm = 400, but the correct answer is 4000. What error did the student most likely make?
options: They divided image size by a number that was already correctly converted
They measured the image size in cm rather than mm on the ruler
They multiplied instead of dividing the two measurements together
They converted μm to mm incorrectly, getting 0.09 instead of 0.009
grade9-biology.answer: They converted μm to mm incorrectly, getting 0.09 instead of 0.009
acceptableAnswers: They converted μm to mm incorrectly, getting 0.09 instead of 0.009
grade9-biology.hint: Check the conversion: 1 μm = 0.001 mm (divide by 1000, not by 100).
grade9-biology.explanation: 1 μm = 0.001 mm, so 9 μm = 0.009 mm, not 0.09 mm. Using 0.09 gives 36 ÷ 0.09 = 400 instead of 36 ÷ 0.009 = 4000.

grade9-biology.question: What is a pulse?
options: The total volume of blood pumped by the left ventricle per minute
The electrical signal that the heart sends to surrounding body tissues
The number of times blood passes through the capillaries each minute
The rhythmic surge of pressure in an artery caused by each heartbeat
grade9-biology.answer: The rhythmic surge of pressure in an artery caused by each heartbeat
acceptableAnswers: The rhythmic surge of pressure in an artery caused by each heartbeat
grade9-biology.hint: It is felt as a rhythmic throbbing in an artery.
grade9-biology.explanation: Each time the heart contracts, it forces a surge of blood into the arteries; the elastic walls bulge outwards and this wave of pressure is the pulse.

grade9-biology.question: Where on the body can a pulse most easily be detected?
options: At the elbow (brachial pulse) or the shin (tibial pulse)
At the wrist (radial pulse) or the neck (carotid pulse)
At the chest (cardiac pulse) or the foot (dorsal pulse)
At the temple (temporal pulse) or the eardrum (tympanic pulse)
grade9-biology.answer: At the wrist (radial pulse) or the neck (carotid pulse)
acceptableAnswers: At the wrist (radial pulse) or the neck (carotid pulse)
grade9-biology.hint: Find a place where an artery passes close to the skin surface over a bone.
grade9-biology.explanation: The radial artery at the wrist and the carotid artery in the neck both pass close to the surface, where they can be compressed gently against underlying bone to feel the pulse.

grade9-biology.question: What causes the pulse that can be felt when pressing on an artery?
options: The opening and closing of valves inside the artery at each heartbeat
The elastic artery wall bulging outward with each surge of blood from the heart
The contraction of smooth muscle in the artery wall at regular intervals
White blood cells moving rapidly through the artery in distinct bursts
grade9-biology.answer: The elastic artery wall bulging outward with each surge of blood from the heart
acceptableAnswers: The elastic artery wall bulging outward with each surge of blood from the heart
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what happens to the artery wall when pressure rises suddenly.
grade9-biology.explanation: Each heartbeat forces a bolus of blood into the arteries; the elastic walls stretch and then recoil, producing a pressure wave that travels outward — this is the pulse.

grade9-biology.question: What is the normal resting pulse rate for a healthy adult?
grade9-biology.answer: Between 60 and 80 beats per minute
grade9-biology.hint: At rest the heart does not need to work very hard.
grade9-biology.explanation: A normal resting heart rate is 60–80 bpm; trained athletes may have rates as low as 40 bpm because their hearts pump more blood per beat.

grade9-biology.question: Why does the pulse rate increase during vigorous exercise?
options: The body produces less carbon dioxide, signalling the heart to work faster
White blood cells multiply during exercise, thickening the blood overall
Muscles need more oxygen, so the heart beats faster to deliver it
Blood pressure falls during exercise, so the heart compensates by speeding up
grade9-biology.answer: Muscles need more oxygen, so the heart beats faster to deliver it
acceptableAnswers: Muscles need more oxygen, so the heart beats faster to deliver it
grade9-biology.hint: Active muscles use more oxygen in respiration — how does the heart respond?
grade9-biology.explanation: During exercise, respiring muscles demand more oxygen and glucose; the heart increases its rate and stroke volume to supply this, raising the pulse rate.

grade9-biology.question: After running a race, a fit athlete's pulse rate returns to its resting level within 2 minutes. What does this indicate?
options: The athlete ran at such low intensity that the pulse barely increased
The athlete has high blood pressure that pushed more blood per beat
The athlete has an efficient cardiovascular system that recovers quickly
The athlete has an unusually slow resting pulse rate during exercise
grade9-biology.answer: The athlete has an efficient cardiovascular system that recovers quickly
acceptableAnswers: The athlete has an efficient cardiovascular system that recovers quickly
grade9-biology.hint: A faster return to resting heart rate is a sign of cardiovascular fitness.
grade9-biology.explanation: Recovery time — how quickly the pulse returns to resting after exercise — is a measure of cardiovascular fitness; a fit person recovers faster because their heart handles the demand more efficiently.

grade9-biology.question: Why is the pulse stronger and easier to feel in arteries than in veins?
options: Blood in arteries is at higher pressure because it has just left the heart
Veins contain valves that completely eliminate pressure waves along them
The walls of arteries are thinner and therefore feel the pulse more easily
Arteries carry more red blood cells per unit volume than veins do
grade9-biology.answer: Blood in arteries is at higher pressure because it has just left the heart
acceptableAnswers: Blood in arteries is at higher pressure because it has just left the heart
grade9-biology.hint: Pressure in blood vessels decreases as blood moves further from the heart.
grade9-biology.explanation: Arterial blood is under high pressure from the ventricles; each heartbeat produces a strong pressure wave. By the time blood reaches veins, pressure has dropped too much to feel a distinct pulse.

grade9-biology.question: A doctor measures a patient's pulse at the wrist and finds it is very weak and irregular. What might this suggest?
options: The patient has too many red blood cells, making the pulse imperceptible
Elevated white blood cell levels are dampening the pulse at the wrist
Blood pressure may be low or an artery may be partially blocked
The patient has a very high heart rate that cannot be detected at the wrist
grade9-biology.answer: Blood pressure may be low or an artery may be partially blocked
acceptableAnswers: Blood pressure may be low or an artery may be partially blocked
grade9-biology.hint: A weak pulse suggests reduced pressure or reduced flow in that artery.
grade9-biology.explanation: A weak pulse at the wrist can indicate low blood pressure (e.g. from dehydration or blood loss) or a partial blockage of the radial artery reducing blood flow.

grade9-biology.question: Why is the pulse felt most clearly where an artery passes over a hard underlying bone?
options: The bone acts as a firm surface against which the pulsing artery can be pressed
The skin is thinner over bone, so the artery wall can be seen to move
Arteries run closer to capillaries near bones, amplifying the pressure wave
Bones reflect sound waves from the heartbeat, making the pulse louder
grade9-biology.answer: The bone acts as a firm surface against which the pulsing artery can be pressed
acceptableAnswers: The bone acts as a firm surface against which the pulsing artery can be pressed
grade9-biology.hint: Pressing the artery against something firm makes the pressure wave more detectable.
grade9-biology.explanation: Compressing the artery against the underlying bone concentrates the pressure wave under the fingertips; without this backing, the pulse would be felt as a diffuse throb.

grade9-biology.question: What is atherosclerosis?
options: A build-up of fatty plaques (atheroma) inside the walls of arteries
A blockage in veins caused by a blood clot forming after surgery
An irregular heartbeat caused by faulty electrical signals in heart cells
A weakening of the heart muscle caused by a lack of oxygen supply
grade9-biology.answer: A build-up of fatty plaques (atheroma) inside the walls of arteries
acceptableAnswers: A build-up of fatty plaques (atheroma) inside the walls of arteries
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what material builds up and where it is deposited.
grade9-biology.explanation: Atherosclerosis is the progressive narrowing of arteries due to deposits of fatty material (atheroma) in the artery wall, reducing blood flow and raising blood pressure.

grade9-biology.question: Which of the following is a lifestyle risk factor for cardiovascular disease?
options: Smoking cigarettes on a regular basis
Having a family history of heart disease
grade9-biology.answer: Smoking cigarettes on a regular basis
acceptableAnswers: Smoking cigarettes on a regular basis
grade9-biology.hint: A lifestyle factor is one a person can choose to change.
grade9-biology.explanation: Smoking is a modifiable lifestyle risk factor; age, sex and family history are non-modifiable risk factors that a person cannot change.

grade9-biology.question: What happens during a heart attack?
options: The aorta tears and blood leaks into the space around the heart
A blood clot forms in a vein in the leg and then travels to the brain
A coronary artery is blocked, so part of the heart muscle dies from lack of oxygen
The heart beats too fast and the chambers fill with blood irregularly
grade9-biology.answer: A coronary artery is blocked, so part of the heart muscle dies from lack of oxygen
acceptableAnswers: A coronary artery is blocked, so part of the heart muscle dies from lack of oxygen
grade9-biology.hint: The heart muscle has its own blood supply — what happens if it is cut off?
grade9-biology.explanation: A heart attack (myocardial infarction) occurs when a coronary artery is blocked by a blood clot or atheroma, depriving the heart muscle downstream of oxygen.

grade9-biology.question: What is the key difference between a heart attack and a stroke?
options: A stroke is caused by low cholesterol; a heart attack is caused by high salt
A heart attack blocks blood to the heart muscle; a stroke blocks blood to the brain
A stroke stops the heart beating; a heart attack only slows the heart
A heart attack affects the veins; a stroke affects the arteries only
grade9-biology.answer: A heart attack blocks blood to the heart muscle; a stroke blocks blood to the brain
acceptableAnswers: A heart attack blocks blood to the heart muscle; a stroke blocks blood to the brain
grade9-biology.hint: Think about which organ is deprived of blood in each condition.
grade9-biology.explanation: In a heart attack the blockage is in the coronary arteries supplying the heart; in a stroke the blockage (or burst vessel) is in the cerebral blood vessels supplying the brain.

grade9-biology.question: How does smoking tobacco increase the risk of cardiovascular disease?
options: Nicotine causes red blood cells to clump together inside the veins
Smoking reduces blood cholesterol levels, causing clots to form rapidly
Chemicals in tobacco damage artery walls and raise blood pressure
Carbon monoxide in smoke speeds up metabolism and overloads the heart
grade9-biology.answer: Chemicals in tobacco damage artery walls and raise blood pressure
acceptableAnswers: Chemicals in tobacco damage artery walls and raise blood pressure
grade9-biology.hint: Carbon monoxide and nicotine both have cardiovascular effects.
grade9-biology.explanation: Carbon monoxide in smoke reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood; nicotine raises heart rate and blood pressure; together they damage artery walls and promote atherosclerosis.

grade9-biology.question: How does a diet high in saturated fat increase the risk of cardiovascular disease?
options: It causes blood to carry less oxygen, gradually weakening the heart muscle
It lowers blood pressure so the heart must beat faster to compensate
It reduces the number of white blood cells available to fight infection
It raises blood cholesterol levels, which deposits as plaques in arteries
grade9-biology.answer: It raises blood cholesterol levels, which deposits as plaques in arteries
acceptableAnswers: It raises blood cholesterol levels, which deposits as plaques in arteries
grade9-biology.hint: High cholesterol is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease.
grade9-biology.explanation: Saturated fats raise LDL (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol in the blood; excess LDL is deposited in artery walls, forming atheroma that narrows and hardens them.

grade9-biology.question: A person has chronic high blood pressure (hypertension). How does this specifically increase the risk of a stroke?
options: Persistent high pressure damages artery walls in the brain, raising the risk of a clot or rupture
High pressure reduces the volume of blood reaching the heart muscle each beat
High pressure causes the coronary arteries to collapse from fatigue
High pressure slows the pulse rate, gradually depriving the brain of oxygen
grade9-biology.answer: Persistent high pressure damages artery walls in the brain, raising the risk of a clot or rupture
acceptableAnswers: Persistent high pressure damages artery walls in the brain, raising the risk of a clot or rupture
grade9-biology.hint: What happens to vessel walls that are subjected to abnormally high pressure over many years?
grade9-biology.explanation: Hypertension damages the inner lining of cerebral arteries, making them prone to atherosclerosis, blood clot formation or rupture — all of which can cause a stroke.

grade9-biology.question: How does regular aerobic exercise reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease?
options: It raises the resting pulse rate so the heart pumps less blood per beat
It strengthens the heart, lowers blood pressure and raises HDL cholesterol levels
It increases LDL cholesterol in the blood over the long term
It causes arteries to narrow slightly, which in turn reduces blood pressure
grade9-biology.answer: It strengthens the heart, lowers blood pressure and raises HDL cholesterol levels
acceptableAnswers: It strengthens the heart, lowers blood pressure and raises HDL cholesterol levels
grade9-biology.hint: Exercise has several positive effects on the cardiovascular system.
grade9-biology.explanation: Regular aerobic exercise strengthens the cardiac muscle, lowers resting blood pressure, raises "good" HDL cholesterol and reduces body weight — all of which reduce cardiovascular risk.

grade9-biology.question: Explain how a diet high in salt increases the risk of cardiovascular disease.
options: High salt intake raises blood cholesterol, depositing plaques directly in arteries
High salt intake reduces plasma volume, forcing the heart to work much harder
High salt intake raises blood pressure, putting extra strain on the heart and arteries
High salt intake causes red blood cells to burst, releasing haemoglobin into plasma
grade9-biology.answer: High salt intake raises blood pressure, putting extra strain on the heart and arteries
acceptableAnswers: High salt intake raises blood pressure, putting extra strain on the heart and arteries
grade9-biology.hint: Salt affects fluid balance — how does that link to pressure?
grade9-biology.explanation: Excess salt causes the body to retain water; extra water in the blood increases blood volume and therefore blood pressure, damaging artery walls over time.

grade9-biology.question: A teenager argues that cardiovascular disease only affects elderly people, so there is no point adopting healthy habits now. Evaluate this argument.
options: The argument is correct; fatty plaques only begin to form after the age of fifty
The argument is wrong; atheroma builds up over decades, so early habits reduce long-term risk
The argument is partly right; only exercise matters, not diet or smoking in youth
The argument is correct; cardiovascular disease is entirely determined by genetics
grade9-biology.answer: The argument is wrong; atheroma builds up over decades, so early habits reduce long-term risk
acceptableAnswers: The argument is wrong; atheroma builds up over decades, so early habits reduce long-term risk
grade9-biology.hint: Plaque formation is a slow process that starts in youth.
grade9-biology.explanation: Atherosclerosis begins in childhood and progresses slowly; lifestyle choices in teenage years affect how quickly plaques accumulate, so early healthy habits have a real long-term benefit.

grade9-biology.question: What is the role of cholesterol in the development of cardiovascular disease?
options: Cholesterol attacks the heart valves, causing them to become leaky over time
Excess cholesterol deposits as fatty plaques inside artery walls, narrowing them
Cholesterol dissolves the elastic tissue in capillary walls, causing leaking
Too much cholesterol makes red blood cells clump together inside vessels
grade9-biology.answer: Excess cholesterol deposits as fatty plaques inside artery walls, narrowing them
acceptableAnswers: Excess cholesterol deposits as fatty plaques inside artery walls, narrowing them
grade9-biology.hint: High blood cholesterol is a major risk factor.
grade9-biology.explanation: LDL cholesterol accumulates beneath the endothelium of artery walls, forming plaques (atheroma) that narrow the lumen, restrict blood flow and may trigger clot formation.

grade9-biology.question: Which of the following is a non-modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease?
options: Eating a diet very high in saturated fat and salt
Family history of heart disease passed on through genetics
Smoking cigarettes on a daily basis
Doing no physical exercise throughout the week
grade9-biology.answer: Family history of heart disease passed on through genetics
acceptableAnswers: Family history of heart disease passed on through genetics
grade9-biology.hint: A non-modifiable factor cannot be changed by the individual.
grade9-biology.explanation: Family history (genetic predisposition) and age are risk factors that cannot be changed; smoking, diet and exercise levels are modifiable factors that a person can control.

grade9-biology.question: A government campaigns to reduce salt consumption. What is the mechanism linking lower salt intake to fewer deaths from stroke?
options: Less salt increases the number of platelets, improving clot formation at wounds
Less salt raises HDL cholesterol levels, which sweeps fat from artery walls
Less salt directly reduces blood cholesterol, removing atheroma from artery walls
Less salt lowers blood pressure, reducing the chance of artery rupture in the brain
grade9-biology.answer: Less salt lowers blood pressure, reducing the chance of artery rupture in the brain
acceptableAnswers: Less salt lowers blood pressure, reducing the chance of artery rupture in the brain
grade9-biology.hint: Trace the chain: less salt → less fluid retention → lower blood pressure → what then?
grade9-biology.explanation: Reducing salt intake lowers blood volume and blood pressure; lower pressure means less stress on cerebral artery walls, reducing the risk of rupture or clot formation that causes a stroke.

grade9-biology.question: A graph shows that as daily salt intake increases, deaths from heart disease also increase. What type of relationship does this represent?
options: A positive correlation between salt intake and heart disease death rate
An inverse relationship showing that more salt intake leads to fewer deaths
A causal relationship proving that salt directly kills heart muscle cells
A negative correlation between salt intake and heart disease death rate
grade9-biology.answer: A positive correlation between salt intake and heart disease death rate
acceptableAnswers: A positive correlation between salt intake and heart disease death rate
grade9-biology.hint: A positive correlation means both variables increase together.
grade9-biology.explanation: When two variables rise together, there is a positive correlation; this does not itself prove that one causes the other.

grade9-biology.question: Health data shows that a group eating 2 g of salt per day has a death rate of 10 per 1000 from heart disease, while a group eating 10 g per day has a rate of 60 per 1000. How many more deaths per 1000 occur in the high-salt group?
options: 50 more deaths per 1000 in the high-salt group
6 more deaths per 1000 in the high-salt group
600 more deaths per 1000 in the high-salt group
70 more deaths per 1000 in the high-salt group
grade9-biology.answer: 50 more deaths per 1000 in the high-salt group
acceptableAnswers: 50 more deaths per 1000 in the high-salt group
grade9-biology.hint: Subtract the lower rate from the higher rate.
grade9-biology.explanation: 60 − 10 = 50 more deaths per 1000 in the group eating 10 g of salt compared with the group eating 2 g per day.

grade9-biology.question: A bar chart shows that 42% of heart disease patients smoke, compared with 14% of the general population. What conclusion is best supported?
options: All smokers will eventually develop serious cardiovascular disease
Smoking is the single proven direct cause of every case of heart disease
Non-smokers cannot develop heart disease under any circumstances
Smoking is associated with a higher likelihood of developing heart disease
grade9-biology.answer: Smoking is associated with a higher likelihood of developing heart disease
acceptableAnswers: Smoking is associated with a higher likelihood of developing heart disease
grade9-biology.hint: The data shows an association, but be careful about the strength of the claim.
grade9-biology.explanation: The data shows that smokers are over-represented among heart disease patients, suggesting an association; it does not prove that smoking is the only or inevitable cause.

grade9-biology.question: Health data shows that both obesity rates and cardiovascular disease rates have risen over the same 20-year period. Does this prove that obesity causes cardiovascular disease?
options: Yes — obesity is the only proven direct risk factor for heart disease
No — the data is flawed because obesity and heart disease are completely unrelated
No — a correlation does not prove causation; other factors may explain both trends
Yes — whenever two trends rise together, one must be causing the other
grade9-biology.answer: No — a correlation does not prove causation; other factors may explain both trends
acceptableAnswers: No — a correlation does not prove causation; other factors may explain both trends
grade9-biology.hint: Two things that rise together do not have to be linked by cause and effect.
grade9-biology.explanation: Both variables may be rising due to a third factor (e.g. changes in diet and inactivity); only a controlled experiment can establish a causal link.

grade9-biology.question: A graph shows cardiovascular death rates falling steadily over 20 years in a country that introduced a national anti-smoking campaign in the same period. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: The decline in deaths has nothing to do with the campaign and is due entirely to genetics
The anti-smoking campaign is the sole proven cause of every reduction in deaths
Reduced smoking may have contributed to the fall, though other factors may also be involved
Cardiovascular death rates always decrease over time regardless of any interventions
grade9-biology.answer: Reduced smoking may have contributed to the fall, though other factors may also be involved
acceptableAnswers: Reduced smoking may have contributed to the fall, though other factors may also be involved
grade9-biology.hint: Be cautious about attributing a trend to a single cause from correlation alone.
grade9-biology.explanation: The timing suggests the campaign may have helped, but improved medical treatment, changes in diet and other public health measures could also have contributed to the fall.

grade9-biology.question: Why is a large sample size important when collecting health data about cardiovascular disease?
options: A larger sample means fewer ethical considerations are needed in the study
A larger sample makes the data easier to display in a bar chart format
A larger sample always produces lower death rates because more data is collected
A larger sample produces more reliable results that are less affected by chance
grade9-biology.answer: A larger sample produces more reliable results that are less affected by chance
acceptableAnswers: A larger sample produces more reliable results that are less affected by chance
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what happens to anomalies and chance results in a small group.
grade9-biology.explanation: With a small sample, one or two unusual individuals can distort the data; a large sample contains enough variation for the pattern to be statistically reliable.

grade9-biology.question: Two groups of 5000 adults are followed for 10 years. Group A exercises regularly; Group B does not. Group A has 35% fewer heart attacks. What conclusion can be drawn?
options: Exercise is the only lifestyle factor needed to prevent all heart attacks
The groups must have been randomly selected or the entire data is invalid
Every member of Group B will develop heart disease within 10 years
Regular exercise is associated with a significantly lower risk of heart attack
grade9-biology.answer: Regular exercise is associated with a significantly lower risk of heart attack
acceptableAnswers: Regular exercise is associated with a significantly lower risk of heart attack
grade9-biology.hint: The data shows an association; use careful language about cause.
grade9-biology.explanation: The data shows a strong association between regular exercise and a lower heart attack rate; a 35% difference in a large sample is significant, though other lifestyle differences between the groups should be considered.

grade9-biology.question: A health survey reports that men under 65 are twice as likely as women of the same age to suffer a fatal heart attack. What does this data indicate?
options: Being male is a risk factor for early cardiovascular death
Heart disease is caused mainly by male hormones and nothing else
All men should take preventive medication from birth to avoid this risk
Women are completely immune to heart attacks before the age of 65
grade9-biology.answer: Being male is a risk factor for early cardiovascular death
acceptableAnswers: Being male is a risk factor for early cardiovascular death
grade9-biology.hint: The data shows a difference between groups — interpret it carefully.
grade9-biology.explanation: The data shows sex is a risk factor; being male increases the relative risk of a premature heart attack, though this does not mean women cannot develop heart disease.

grade9-biology.question: Countries with higher average fruit and vegetable intake have lower rates of cardiovascular disease. What is the main limitation of concluding that fruit and vegetables directly prevent heart disease from this data alone?
options: Fruit and vegetables are known to have no measurable effect on cholesterol
The data is collected from different countries, so it cannot be compared at all
People with healthy diets may also exercise more and smoke less, so diet may not be the only factor
The sample sizes in different countries are too small for any comparison
grade9-biology.answer: People with healthy diets may also exercise more and smoke less, so diet may not be the only factor
acceptableAnswers: People with healthy diets may also exercise more and smoke less, so diet may not be the only factor
grade9-biology.hint: Could other lifestyle habits differ between the groups with high and low fruit intake?
grade9-biology.explanation: People who eat more fruit and vegetables tend to differ in many other ways from those who do not (they may exercise more, smoke less); confounding variables make it impossible to attribute the lower heart disease rate to diet alone.

grade9-biology.question: A graph shows a steep downward trend in cardiovascular death rates beginning in the same year as a national cholesterol-lowering programme. What is the strongest conclusion the data supports?
options: The cholesterol-lowering programme is associated with a fall in cardiovascular deaths
The fall in deaths was caused only by better hospital treatment, not prevention
Lowering cholesterol is the proven sole cause of every reduction in heart disease deaths
The graph proves that high cholesterol is the only cause of all cardiovascular disease
grade9-biology.answer: The cholesterol-lowering programme is associated with a fall in cardiovascular deaths
acceptableAnswers: The cholesterol-lowering programme is associated with a fall in cardiovascular deaths
grade9-biology.hint: What is the strongest claim the data can support without overstepping?
grade9-biology.explanation: Correlation with the start of the programme suggests it may have contributed; however, causation requires further evidence, and other improvements in care may also have played a role.

grade9-biology.question: A study finds that people who drink one glass of red wine per day have fewer heart attacks than those who drink no alcohol. A cardiologist says this does not prove wine protects the heart. Why?
options: Non-drinkers in the study must have had unrelated health problems that skewed the results
The cardiologist is wrong because the data clearly proves a direct protective link
The study is completely invalid because alcohol is known to have no cardiovascular effect
Wine drinkers may differ from non-drinkers in other lifestyle factors affecting heart risk
grade9-biology.answer: Wine drinkers may differ from non-drinkers in other lifestyle factors affecting heart risk
acceptableAnswers: Wine drinkers may differ from non-drinkers in other lifestyle factors affecting heart risk
grade9-biology.hint: Think about confounding variables that distinguish the two groups.
grade9-biology.explanation: People who drink moderately may also eat a healthier diet, exercise more or have lower stress; these confounding variables mean the lower heart attack rate cannot be attributed to wine alone.

grade9-biology.question: A health report states that cardiovascular disease risk is higher in people with low levels of physical activity. What does this suggest for public health policy?
options: Public health campaigns about exercise are ineffective because most people ignore them
Physical inactivity is proven beyond doubt to be the sole cause of cardiovascular disease
All inactive people will certainly suffer a heart attack within a fixed number of years
Promoting regular physical activity across the population may help reduce cardiovascular disease rates
grade9-biology.answer: Promoting regular physical activity across the population may help reduce cardiovascular disease rates
acceptableAnswers: Promoting regular physical activity across the population may help reduce cardiovascular disease rates
grade9-biology.hint: Use careful language — the data shows an association, not a certainty.
grade9-biology.explanation: The association between inactivity and cardiovascular risk suggests that population-level promotion of exercise could reduce rates, though the data alone cannot guarantee individual outcomes.

grade9-biology.question: A researcher notes that cardiovascular death rates are higher in lower-income populations. To find out whether diet or stress is the more important factor, which study design would be most appropriate?
options: A controlled study measuring diet and stress separately in income-matched groups
A study measuring only cholesterol levels in high-income and low-income populations
A simple comparison of death rates between different countries with different currencies
A survey asking participants to guess whether they think diet or stress affects them more
grade9-biology.answer: A controlled study measuring diet and stress separately in income-matched groups
acceptableAnswers: A controlled study measuring diet and stress separately in income-matched groups
grade9-biology.hint: Think about how to isolate one variable while keeping others constant.
grade9-biology.explanation: To distinguish the effects of diet from stress, both variables must be measured independently in groups matched for income (to remove that confounding factor); self-reported guesses and single-variable comparisons cannot disentangle the two.

grade9-biology.question: Name the liquid part of blood in which blood cells and platelets are suspended.
grade9-biology.answer: Plasma
grade9-biology.hint: It is pale yellow in colour.
grade9-biology.explanation: Plasma is the aqueous liquid component of blood that transports dissolved substances and suspends the cellular components.

grade9-biology.question: Name the iron-containing protein found in red blood cells that combines with oxygen.
grade9-biology.answer: Haemoglobin
grade9-biology.hint: It gives blood its red colour and binds reversibly to oxygen.
grade9-biology.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells combines with oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin, and releases oxygen at the tissues.

grade9-biology.question: Name the blood vessels that form the site of exchange between blood and body cells.
grade9-biology.answer: Capillaries
grade9-biology.hint: They are the smallest vessels with the thinnest walls.
grade9-biology.explanation: Capillaries have walls only one cell thick, allowing oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide to diffuse between blood and surrounding tissue cells.

grade9-biology.question: A drawing of a red blood cell is 60 mm wide. The actual cell is 0.008 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.
grade9-biology.hint: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Both are in mm — divide directly.
grade9-biology.explanation: 60 ÷ 0.008 = 7500. No unit is written with magnification.

grade9-biology.question: A drawing of a white blood cell is 36 mm wide. The actual cell is 0.012 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.
grade9-biology.hint: Divide the drawing size by the actual size — both are already in mm.

grade9-biology.question: A drawing of a platelet is 20 mm wide. The actual platelet is 0.002 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.
grade9-biology.hint: Divide the drawing size by the actual size — both are already in mm.

grade9-biology.question: A drawing of a red blood cell is 46 mm wide. The actual cell is 0.008 mm wide. What is the magnification?
grade9-biology.hint: Divide the drawing size by the actual size — both are in mm.

grade9-biology.question: A cell is drawn at a magnification of ×2500. The drawing is 50 mm wide. What is the actual width of the cell in mm? (Give your answer as a decimal.)
grade9-biology.hint: Rearrange: actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
grade9-biology.explanation: Actual size = 50 ÷ 2500 = 0.02 mm.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil draws an artery cross-section with a diameter of 54 mm. The actual artery has a diameter of 6 mm. What is the magnification?
grade9-biology.hint: Both sizes are in the same unit — divide directly.

grade9-biology.question: A drawing of a blood vessel is 72 mm in diameter. The actual vessel is 0.009 mm in diameter. Calculate the magnification.
grade9-biology.hint: Divide the drawing size by the actual size — both are in mm.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil counts 18 pulse beats in 15 seconds. Calculate the pulse rate in beats per minute.
grade9-biology.hint: There are four lots of 15 seconds in one minute.
grade9-biology.explanation: 18 × 4 = 72 beats per minute.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil counts 20 pulse beats in 15 seconds. Calculate the pulse rate in beats per minute.
grade9-biology.hint: Multiply by 4 to convert from 15-second count to beats per minute.
grade9-biology.explanation: 20 × 4 = 80 beats per minute.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil counts 35 pulse beats in 30 seconds. Calculate the pulse rate in beats per minute.
grade9-biology.hint: There are two lots of 30 seconds in one minute.
grade9-biology.explanation: 35 × 2 = 70 beats per minute.

grade9-biology.question: Immediately after exercise, a student counts 40 pulse beats in 20 seconds. What is the pulse rate in beats per minute?
grade9-biology.hint: There are three lots of 20 seconds in one minute.
grade9-biology.explanation: 40 × 3 = 120 beats per minute.

grade9-biology.question: What is reproduction?
options: The process by which living things grow larger
The process by which living things produce offspring
The process by which living things remove waste
The process by which living things obtain energy
grade9-biology.answer: The process by which living things produce offspring
acceptableAnswers: The process by which living things produce offspring
grade9-biology.hint: It is about the next generation.
grade9-biology.explanation: Reproduction is the process by which living organisms produce new individuals of their own kind.

grade9-biology.question: Why is reproduction important for a species?
options: Without it the species would die out
It removes waste products from the body
It allows each individual to live longer
