To filter waste products from the developing embryo during pregnancy
To produce eggs each month and release them at ovulation
To provide a site for the fertilised egg to implant and develop into a baby
grade9-biology.answer: To provide a site for the fertilised egg to implant and develop into a baby
acceptableAnswers: To provide a site for the fertilised egg to implant and develop into a baby
grade9-biology.explanation: The uterus is the womb — think about what happens inside it during pregnancy.

grade9-biology.question: A student labels a diagram of the female reproductive system. Which label correctly describes the vagina's role?
options: The birth canal through which the baby passes during delivery, and the passage for menstrual blood
The tube that carries the egg from the ovary to the site of fertilisation
The organ that produces and releases one egg per month under hormonal control
The gland that secretes hormones to maintain pregnancy after implantation
grade9-biology.answer: The birth canal through which the baby passes during delivery, and the passage for menstrual blood
acceptableAnswers: The birth canal through which the baby passes during delivery, and the passage for menstrual blood
grade9-biology.explanation: The vagina is the external opening of the female reproductive tract.

grade9-biology.question: Which of the following sexually transmitted infections (STIs) is caused by a virus?
grade9-biology.answer: HIV/AIDS
grade9-biology.explanation: Some STIs are caused by bacteria and some by viruses — which of the options is viral?

grade9-biology.question: Which type of micro-organism causes gonorrhoea?
grade9-biology.answer: A bacterium (Neisseria gonorrhoeae)
grade9-biology.explanation: Consider which class of micro-organism can be treated by antibiotics.

grade9-biology.question: Which of the following is NOT a route by which HIV can be transmitted from one person to another?
options: Sharing food or drinking from the same cup
Transfer of infected blood during a blood transfusion
Unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected partner
grade9-biology.answer: Sharing food or drinking from the same cup
acceptableAnswers: Sharing food or drinking from the same cup
grade9-biology.explanation: HIV is transmitted through body fluids — think about whether sharing food involves infectious body fluids.

grade9-biology.question: Which method provides the most effective protection against both unintended pregnancy AND sexually transmitted infections?
options: Using a condom correctly during every sexual encounter
Relying on the rhythm method (avoiding sex on fertile days)
Taking the combined contraceptive pill every day
grade9-biology.answer: Using a condom correctly during every sexual encounter
acceptableAnswers: Using a condom correctly during every sexual encounter
grade9-biology.explanation: Think about which method creates a physical barrier to both sperm and pathogens.

grade9-biology.question:
The table shows HIV infection rates in a country over five years.
YearNew cases per 1000
18.2
27.5
36.1
45.3
54.0
A health campaign was launched at the start of Year 2. What is the mean infection rate over all five years, and what trend does the data show?
options: Mean of 5.3 new cases per 1000 per year; a steady upward trend showing the campaign had no effect
Mean of 4.0 new cases per 1000 per year; a downward trend that proves the campaign caused the reduction
Mean of 8.2 new cases per 1000 per year; no clear trend because the figures fluctuate randomly each year
Mean of 6.2 new cases per 1000 per year; a consistent downward trend suggesting the campaign may have contributed to falling rates
grade9-biology.answer: Mean of 6.2 new cases per 1000 per year; a consistent downward trend suggesting the campaign may have contributed to falling rates
acceptableAnswers: Mean of 6.2 new cases per 1000 per year; a consistent downward trend suggesting the campaign may have contributed to falling rates
grade9-biology.explanation: Calculate: (8.2 + 7.5 + 6.1 + 5.3 + 4.0) ÷ 5. Then describe the direction of change carefully.

grade9-biology.question: What is a quadrat used for in a field study of biodiversity?
options: To collect soil samples for analysis of mineral content in a habitat
To measure the speed at which organisms move through a habitat
To count or estimate the number of organisms in a defined sample area
To trap mobile animals for tagging and later population estimates
grade9-biology.answer: To count or estimate the number of organisms in a defined sample area
acceptableAnswers: To count or estimate the number of organisms in a defined sample area
grade9-biology.explanation: A quadrat is a frame placed on the ground — think about what a stationary frame can help you count.

grade9-biology.question: Why is the quadrat method best suited to studying plants and slow-moving animals rather than birds or fish?
options: The quadrat method works only in aquatic habitats, where birds cannot be found
Plants and slow-moving animals have brighter colours that make them easier to see inside the frame
Birds and fish are too rare to be found in any standard-sized quadrat
Plants and slow-moving animals stay within the quadrat long enough to be counted accurately
grade9-biology.answer: Plants and slow-moving animals stay within the quadrat long enough to be counted accurately
acceptableAnswers: Plants and slow-moving animals stay within the quadrat long enough to be counted accurately
grade9-biology.explanation: Think about what happens when you put a frame on the ground and a fast-moving animal is present.

grade9-biology.question: A student places five quadrats of area 0.25 m² in a meadow and counts the daisies in each: 4, 7, 3, 6, 5. What is the estimated mean number of daisies per square metre in the meadow?
grade9-biology.answer: 20 daisies per m²
grade9-biology.explanation: First find the mean per quadrat, then scale up to 1 m².

grade9-biology.question: How does a severe cyclone typically affect the biodiversity of a coastal habitat?
options: It increases biodiversity by mixing organisms from different habitats together
It destroys vegetation and kills animals, reducing species variety and population sizes
It removes invasive species only, allowing native species to recover and thrive
It has no lasting effect because all species quickly return to their original numbers
grade9-biology.answer: It destroys vegetation and kills animals, reducing species variety and population sizes
acceptableAnswers: It destroys vegetation and kills animals, reducing species variety and population sizes
grade9-biology.explanation: Think about the physical effects of extreme wind and flooding on living organisms.

grade9-biology.question: Which of the following best explains why deforestation is considered a major threat to biodiversity?
options: It permanently removes the habitat on which many species depend for food, shelter and reproduction
It increases soil fertility so much that only fast-growing weeds can survive
It introduces new tree species that compete with existing plants and animals
It causes rivers to warm up, which kills only aquatic species but leaves land species unaffected
grade9-biology.answer: It permanently removes the habitat on which many species depend for food, shelter and reproduction
acceptableAnswers: It permanently removes the habitat on which many species depend for food, shelter and reproduction
grade9-biology.explanation: Consider what forest species rely on trees for.

grade9-biology.question: An invasive plant species is introduced to an island and spreads rapidly. What is the most likely immediate threat it poses to native species?
options: It provides additional food sources that allow all native animal populations to increase
It repels invasive animal species, preventing predation of native organisms
It improves soil quality by fixing nitrogen, benefiting all plants equally
It out-competes native plants for light, water and nutrients, reducing their populations
grade9-biology.answer: It out-competes native plants for light, water and nutrients, reducing their populations
acceptableAnswers: It out-competes native plants for light, water and nutrients, reducing their populations
grade9-biology.explanation: Invasive species succeed because they often lack natural predators and grow faster than native species.

grade9-biology.question: Many modern medicines have been developed from chemicals originally found in wild plants. Which benefit of biodiversity does this illustrate?
options: Medical and pharmaceutical value — wild species provide compounds used in drug development
Economic value from ecotourism — visitors pay to see wild species in their natural habitat
Ecological value — species maintain nutrient cycling and clean water in ecosystems
Food security value — wild species can be bred into crops to improve agricultural yields
grade9-biology.answer: Medical and pharmaceutical value — wild species provide compounds used in drug development
acceptableAnswers: Medical and pharmaceutical value — wild species provide compounds used in drug development
grade9-biology.explanation: Think about which type of benefit is specifically related to medicines derived from nature.

grade9-biology.question: Mauritius earns significant revenue from tourists visiting wildlife reserves to observe rare endemic species. Which benefit of biodiversity does this represent?
options: Ecological benefit through nutrient cycling provided by endemic animal species
Agricultural benefit through wild species improving the genetic diversity of local crops
Economic benefit through ecotourism, where the value of wildlife attracts paying visitors
Medical benefit through chemicals extracted from native animals for drug manufacture
grade9-biology.answer: Economic benefit through ecotourism, where the value of wildlife attracts paying visitors
acceptableAnswers: Economic benefit through ecotourism, where the value of wildlife attracts paying visitors
grade9-biology.explanation: Think about which category of biodiversity benefit involves people paying money to see wildlife.

grade9-biology.question: In a food web: grass → grasshopper → lizard → hawk. The hawk population is hunted to near extinction. Predict the most likely effect on the grasshopper population.
options: The grasshopper population decreases, because without hawks the grass disappears and grasshoppers starve
The grasshopper population increases, because hawks fed on grasshoppers and removing them relieves predation pressure
The grasshopper population stays unchanged, because hawks and grasshoppers are not directly linked in this food web
The grasshopper population decreases, because fewer hawks means more lizards survive and eat more grasshoppers
grade9-biology.answer: The grasshopper population decreases, because fewer hawks means more lizards survive and eat more grasshoppers
acceptableAnswers: The grasshopper population decreases, because fewer hawks means more lizards survive and eat more grasshoppers
grade9-biology.explanation: Trace the chain: hawk → lizard → grasshopper. Remove the hawk and work through each link.

grade9-biology.question: A conservation team surveys a forest using quadrats and finds the following number of tree species in five quadrats: 12, 8, 15, 10, 10. What is the mean number of tree species per quadrat, and what does a higher mean value indicate about the forest?
options: Mean = 15 species per quadrat; a higher mean indicates that invasive species are dominating the habitat
Mean = 11 species per quadrat; a higher mean indicates greater species richness, suggesting a healthier and more biodiverse ecosystem
Mean = 10 species per quadrat; a higher mean indicates that the forest is being degraded by human activity
Mean = 55 species per quadrat; a higher mean indicates that fewer quadrats should have been used
grade9-biology.answer: Mean = 11 species per quadrat; a higher mean indicates greater species richness, suggesting a healthier and more biodiverse ecosystem
acceptableAnswers: Mean = 11 species per quadrat; a higher mean indicates greater species richness, suggesting a healthier and more biodiverse ecosystem
grade9-biology.explanation: Calculate: sum all values then divide by the number of quadrats. Then interpret what more species means.

grade9-biology.question: What colour change indicates the presence of starch when iodine solution is added?
options: The iodine turns from blue-black to orange-brown
The iodine turns from orange-brown to red
The iodine turns from orange-brown to colourless
The iodine turns from orange-brown to blue-black
grade9-biology.answer: The iodine turns from orange-brown to blue-black
acceptableAnswers: The iodine turns from orange-brown to blue-black
grade9-biology.explanation: Iodine is orange-brown by default — recall what colour starch turns it.

grade9-biology.question: What is the FIRST step when testing a leaf for starch using the standard iodine test?
options: Rinse the leaf in cold water to remove any surface chlorophyll
Boil the leaf in water to kill it and stop enzyme activity
Boil the leaf in ethanol to remove the green chlorophyll pigment
Dip the leaf in iodine solution to see whether starch is present
grade9-biology.answer: Boil the leaf in water to kill it and stop enzyme activity
acceptableAnswers: Boil the leaf in water to kill it and stop enzyme activity
grade9-biology.explanation: Think about why the leaf must be prepared before being placed in ethanol.

grade9-biology.question: In the iodine starch test, why is the leaf boiled in ethanol (alcohol)?
options: To dissolve the starch out of the leaf before the iodine test is applied
To remove the chlorophyll so the colour change from iodine can be seen clearly
To kill any bacteria on the leaf surface that could affect the result
To harden the leaf tissue so that it does not tear during the iodine step
grade9-biology.answer: To remove the chlorophyll so the colour change from iodine can be seen clearly
acceptableAnswers: To remove the chlorophyll so the colour change from iodine can be seen clearly
grade9-biology.explanation: A green leaf would mask the blue-black colour — what must be removed first?

grade9-biology.question: A variegated leaf (green and white sections) is kept in light, then tested for starch with iodine. What result is expected and what does it show?
options: Blue-black colour only in the green sections; white sections stay orange-brown — showing that chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis
Blue-black colour in all sections, showing that all parts of the leaf can make starch equally
Blue-black colour only in the white sections; green sections stay orange-brown — showing that light is blocked in the white regions
No colour change anywhere, showing that variegated leaves cannot carry out photosynthesis
grade9-biology.answer: Blue-black colour only in the green sections; white sections stay orange-brown — showing that chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis
acceptableAnswers: Blue-black colour only in the green sections; white sections stay orange-brown — showing that chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis
grade9-biology.explanation: White sections lack chlorophyll — trace what this means for their ability to make starch.

grade9-biology.question: A student carries out a starch test on a leaf and lists the steps in this order: (P) add iodine solution, (Q) boil leaf in ethanol, (R) wash leaf in cold water, (S) boil leaf in water. What is the CORRECT sequence?
grade9-biology.answer: S → Q → R → P
grade9-biology.explanation: Think through each step's purpose: which must come before which?

grade9-biology.question: What are the two products of photosynthesis?
grade9-biology.answer: Glucose and oxygen
grade9-biology.explanation: Photosynthesis converts raw materials into products — recall the word equation.

grade9-biology.question: Which two raw materials does a plant take in for photosynthesis?
options: Carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil
Carbon dioxide from the air and glucose from the roots
Nitrogen from the air and water from the leaves
Oxygen from the air and glucose from the soil
grade9-biology.answer: Carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil
acceptableAnswers: Carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil
grade9-biology.explanation: Think about the word equation: what goes INTO the reaction?

grade9-biology.question: In which organelle of a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
grade9-biology.answer: The chloroplast
grade9-biology.explanation: Think about which organelle contains the green pigment chlorophyll.

grade9-biology.question: Which equation correctly summarises photosynthesis?
options: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (using light energy)
Glucose + water → carbon dioxide + oxygen (using light energy)
Carbon dioxide + oxygen → glucose + water (using light energy)
Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy)
grade9-biology.answer: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy)
acceptableAnswers: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy)
grade9-biology.explanation: Recall which substances go in and which come out, and where the energy comes from.

grade9-biology.question: A plant is kept in a sealed transparent box and CO₂ concentration is measured over 24 hours. During daylight the CO₂ level falls; at night it rises. What is the correct explanation?
options: During the day CO₂ is converted to oxygen, which then turns back to CO₂ at night by a reversal reaction
During the day the plant stops respiring so CO₂ falls; at night it begins respiring and CO₂ rises
During the day CO₂ dissolves in the soil and is absorbed by roots; at night the roots release it back
During the day photosynthesis removes more CO₂ than respiration releases; at night only respiration occurs, releasing CO₂
grade9-biology.answer: During the day photosynthesis removes more CO₂ than respiration releases; at night only respiration occurs, releasing CO₂
acceptableAnswers: During the day photosynthesis removes more CO₂ than respiration releases; at night only respiration occurs, releasing CO₂
grade9-biology.explanation: Plants photosynthesise AND respire — consider the balance between the two processes in light versus dark.

grade9-biology.question: How does the broad, flat shape of a leaf help it to carry out photosynthesis efficiently?
options: It allows more carbon dioxide to be stored inside the leaf overnight
It provides a large surface area to absorb the maximum amount of light
It reduces the amount of water lost through the leaf surface during the day
It prevents insects from landing on the leaf and damaging the chloroplasts
grade9-biology.answer: It provides a large surface area to absorb the maximum amount of light
acceptableAnswers: It provides a large surface area to absorb the maximum amount of light
grade9-biology.explanation: A large, flat surface is ideal for capturing something that travels in straight lines from above.

grade9-biology.question: What is the function of the stomata found on the underside of most leaves?
options: To transport water and minerals from the roots to the rest of the leaf
To anchor the leaf to the stem and prevent it from falling off in strong wind
To allow carbon dioxide in and oxygen out, and to let water vapour escape during transpiration
To absorb sunlight and convert it to chemical energy stored in glucose
grade9-biology.answer: To allow carbon dioxide in and oxygen out, and to let water vapour escape during transpiration
acceptableAnswers: To allow carbon dioxide in and oxygen out, and to let water vapour escape during transpiration
grade9-biology.explanation: Stomata are pores — think about what gases need to move in and out of a leaf.

grade9-biology.question: Leaves are very thin, typically less than 1 mm. How does this thinness benefit photosynthesis?
options: It reduces the mass of the leaf, allowing it to orient itself towards the sun more easily
It minimises the distance that carbon dioxide must diffuse to reach the chloroplasts inside cells
It allows the leaf to absorb minerals directly from rainwater that falls on its surface
It prevents excess glucose from being stored in the leaf and blocking the cells
grade9-biology.answer: It minimises the distance that carbon dioxide must diffuse to reach the chloroplasts inside cells
acceptableAnswers: It minimises the distance that carbon dioxide must diffuse to reach the chloroplasts inside cells
grade9-biology.explanation: Diffusion is slow over long distances — a thin leaf means a short journey for gases.

grade9-biology.question: What do the veins (vascular bundles) in a leaf transport, and what structural role do they play?
options: They carry oxygen from photosynthesis to the stem, and they anchor the leaf to the petiole
They carry gases between the stomata and the spongy mesophyll, and they absorb sunlight for energy
They transport water and minerals in (xylem) and sugars out (phloem), and they support the leaf blade
They transport only glucose to the stem for storage, and they contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis
grade9-biology.answer: They transport water and minerals in (xylem) and sugars out (phloem), and they support the leaf blade
acceptableAnswers: They transport water and minerals in (xylem) and sugars out (phloem), and they support the leaf blade
grade9-biology.explanation: Veins contain xylem and phloem — recall what each tissue carries.

grade9-biology.question: Palisade mesophyll cells are found in the upper layer of the leaf, just below the upper epidermis. Why is this position ideal for their function?
options: They are closest to the light source and are packed with chloroplasts to maximise the rate of photosynthesis
They are protected from overheating by the upper epidermis, which reflects excess light away
They are closest to the stomata and absorb carbon dioxide directly before it diffuses to other cells
They are in contact with the veins and absorb water directly from the xylem without diffusion losses
grade9-biology.answer: They are closest to the light source and are packed with chloroplasts to maximise the rate of photosynthesis
acceptableAnswers: They are closest to the light source and are packed with chloroplasts to maximise the rate of photosynthesis
grade9-biology.explanation: Think about where in the leaf light is most intense and what these cells are packed with.

grade9-biology.question: Which mineral ion do plants absorb from the soil to use in the synthesis of proteins?
grade9-biology.answer: Nitrate ions
grade9-biology.explanation: Proteins contain nitrogen — which mineral ion provides it?

grade9-biology.question: Which mineral ion is essential for the production of chlorophyll in plants?
grade9-biology.answer: Magnesium ions
grade9-biology.explanation: Chlorophyll molecules contain a central atom — which mineral provides it?

grade9-biology.question: What roles do phosphate ions play in plant growth?
options: They are components of ATP (for energy transfer) and DNA (for genetic information), and they promote healthy root development
They provide nitrogen for protein synthesis and they strengthen cell walls in the stem
They are the main component of chlorophyll and they promote the growth of new leaves in spring
They regulate water uptake by root hair cells and they produce the sugars used in respiration
grade9-biology.answer: They are components of ATP (for energy transfer) and DNA (for genetic information), and they promote healthy root development
acceptableAnswers: They are components of ATP (for energy transfer) and DNA (for genetic information), and they promote healthy root development
grade9-biology.explanation: Think about which major molecules contain phosphorus in a cell.

grade9-biology.question: A plant grown without magnesium ions shows yellowing (chlorosis) of its older leaves first. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Older leaves are more exposed to sunlight and the magnesium is bleached out of the chlorophyll by UV radiation
Magnesium is mobile in the plant and is moved from older to younger leaves when supplies are low, so older leaves show deficiency first
Older leaves make more chlorophyll than young leaves, so they use up the available magnesium supply faster
The roots absorb magnesium last, so it takes longest to reach the older leaves at the bottom of the plant
grade9-biology.answer: Magnesium is mobile in the plant and is moved from older to younger leaves when supplies are low, so older leaves show deficiency first
acceptableAnswers: Magnesium is mobile in the plant and is moved from older to younger leaves when supplies are low, so older leaves show deficiency first
grade9-biology.explanation: Consider which leaves the plant "sacrifices" first when a mobile nutrient is scarce.

grade9-biology.question: A farmer notices that his plants have small, pale yellow leaves (chlorosis) and very poor root growth. Testing shows adequate nitrate but very low magnesium and phosphate. Which treatment would MOST effectively address both symptoms?
options: Apply a fertiliser containing only nitrogen compounds, as all symptoms result from protein deficiency
Apply more water to improve mineral uptake, since dehydration causes chlorosis and poor roots
Remove the affected leaves so that healthy leaves receive all available minerals from the soil
Apply a fertiliser containing both magnesium and phosphate to correct the two identified deficiencies
grade9-biology.answer: Apply a fertiliser containing both magnesium and phosphate to correct the two identified deficiencies
acceptableAnswers: Apply a fertiliser containing both magnesium and phosphate to correct the two identified deficiencies
grade9-biology.explanation: Match each symptom to its cause: chlorosis → magnesium; poor root growth → phosphate.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question pattern — components of blood.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name the four main components of blood.

options: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
Plasma, haemoglobin, antibodies and clotting proteins
Lymph fluid, red cells, platelets and dissolved hormones
response.answer: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets

parts.hint: One mark for each component.
parts.explanation: The four components are: plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State one function of red blood cells and explain how they are adapted to carry out that function.

options: They carry oxygen using haemoglobin; the biconcave disc shape maximises surface area for oxygen absorption
They defend the body against infection; they engulf and destroy bacteria by phagocytosis
They help blood to clot at wounds; they release chemicals that trigger fibrin formation
They carry dissolved nutrients to cells; their thin membrane allows rapid diffusion of glucose
response.answer: They carry oxygen using haemoglobin; the biconcave disc shape maximises surface area for oxygen absorption

parts.hint: Name the function, then link a structural feature to it.
parts.explanation: Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin; their biconcave disc shape maximises surface area for oxygen absorption.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — blood vessel identification and structure.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A cross-section of a blood vessel shows a thick wall with much elastic tissue and a narrow lumen. Name this type of blood vessel.
parts.hint: Which vessel must withstand high pressure from the heart?
parts.explanation: This describes an artery — thick elastic walls to withstand the high pressure generated by the heart.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A second vessel has a wide lumen and pocket valves along its length. Name this vessel and explain the function of its valves.

options: Vein; the valves prevent backflow and ensure blood moves only towards the heart
Artery; the valves reduce blood pressure to prevent vessel damage
Capillary; the valves control the rate of exchange between blood and tissues
Aorta; the valves prevent blood re-entering the left ventricle after each beat
response.answer: Vein; the valves prevent backflow and ensure blood moves only towards the heart

parts.hint: Which vessel carries blood back to the heart at low pressure?
parts.explanation: This is a vein. The pocket valves prevent blood flowing backwards; they open when blood moves toward the heart and snap shut if blood starts to flow the wrong way.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A third vessel has a wall that is only one cell thick. Name it and explain why its thin wall is an advantage.

options: Capillary; the thin wall minimises diffusion distance so substances move rapidly between blood and cells
Venule; the thin wall allows high blood pressure to be maintained across the capillary bed
Capillary; the thin wall prevents any white blood cells from leaving the bloodstream
Arteriole; the thin wall allows the vessel to stretch when blood pressure increases
response.answer: Capillary; the thin wall minimises diffusion distance so substances move rapidly between blood and cells

parts.hint: Think about the diffusion of substances between blood and body cells.
parts.explanation: This is a capillary. Its single-cell-thick wall minimises the diffusion distance, so oxygen, glucose and other substances pass rapidly between the blood and surrounding tissue cells.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — magnification calculation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A student draws a red blood cell. The width of the drawing is 40 mm. The actual width of the cell is 0.008 mm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
parts.hint: Magnification = drawing size ÷ actual size. Both are already in mm.
parts.explanation: Magnification = 40 ÷ 0.008 = 5000. No unit is written with magnification.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Magnification is written as a pure number with no unit. Which statement correctly explains why?

options: The units cancel when you divide a length by a length in the same unit, giving a pure ratio
Magnification is always measured in micrometres, which are too small to write
Scientists agreed to remove units from magnification to avoid confusion with scale bars
The unit cancels only when the drawing is larger than the actual object
response.answer: The units cancel when you divide a length by a length in the same unit, giving a pure ratio

parts.hint: Think about what happens to the units when you divide mm by mm.
parts.explanation: When both the drawing size and the actual size are in the same unit (e.g. mm ÷ mm), the units cancel, leaving a dimensionless ratio.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which adaptation of a red blood cell gives it the greatest surface area to volume ratio?

options: Its biconcave disc shape, which increases surface area relative to volume
Its lack of a nucleus, which allows more haemoglobin to fit inside
Its very small size compared with other blood cells
Its flexible membrane, which allows it to squeeze through capillaries
response.answer: Its biconcave disc shape, which increases surface area relative to volume

parts.hint: Consider the shape of a mature red blood cell.
parts.explanation: The biconcave disc shape increases the surface area relative to the volume, maximising contact between haemoglobin and the cell surface.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — pulse and heart rate.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State what is meant by the pulse.

options: The rhythmic surge of pressure felt in an artery with each heartbeat
The number of times the heart beats during one minute of rest
The speed at which blood travels through the capillary network
The electrical signal sent by the heart to stimulate muscle contraction
response.answer: The rhythmic surge of pressure felt in an artery with each heartbeat

parts.hint: It is something you can feel in an artery.
parts.explanation: The pulse is the rhythmic surge of pressure felt in an artery each time the heart beats and pumps blood into it.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A student counts 18 pulse beats in 15 seconds. Calculate the pulse rate in beats per minute.
parts.hint: There are four lots of 15 seconds in one minute.
parts.explanation: 18 beats × 4 = 72 beats per minute.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why pulse rate increases during vigorous exercise.

options: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose, so the heart beats faster to deliver more oxygenated blood
The lungs fill with more air, which forces the heart to beat more quickly to use it up
Blood pressure drops during exercise, causing the heart to speed up as a compensation
Body temperature rises during exercise, which directly stretches the heart muscle fibres
response.answer: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose, so the heart beats faster to deliver more oxygenated blood

parts.hint: Think about what muscles need more of during exercise.
parts.explanation: During exercise, muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose; the heart beats faster to pump more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove the extra carbon dioxide produced.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — cardiovascular disease risk and prevention.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State one risk factor for cardiovascular disease that is related to diet.

options: A diet high in saturated fat, which raises blood cholesterol levels
Lack of sleep, which raises blood pressure over time
Exposure to cold weather, which causes arteries to narrow
Working long hours, which reduces the time available for exercise
response.answer: A diet high in saturated fat, which raises blood cholesterol levels

parts.hint: Think about substances in food that affect the arteries.
parts.explanation: A high intake of saturated fat raises blood cholesterol, which contributes to atherosclerosis (fatty deposits in artery walls).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how a build-up of fatty deposits in the coronary arteries can lead to a heart attack.

options: Fatty plaques narrow the coronary arteries; a clot may then block them completely, cutting off oxygen to heart muscle, which dies
Fatty deposits thicken the heart muscle wall so it cannot contract, causing the heart to stop pumping
Cholesterol dissolves into the blood and makes it too thick to flow through the fine capillaries of the heart
Fatty deposits cause the coronary veins to swell, increasing pressure until the heart wall ruptures
response.answer: Fatty plaques narrow the coronary arteries; a clot may then block them completely, cutting off oxygen to heart muscle, which dies

parts.hint: Trace the sequence: fatty deposit → narrowing → blocked blood supply → heart muscle damage.
parts.explanation: Fatty deposits (plaques) narrow the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle. A blood clot may then block the already-narrowed artery completely, cutting off the oxygen supply to heart muscle cells, which begin to die — this is a heart attack (myocardial infarction).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suggest one lifestyle change that could reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. Give a reason for your answer.

options: Stop smoking — nicotine and carbon monoxide damage artery walls and raise blood pressure
Drink more fluids — this thins the blood and prevents clots from forming
Avoid cold weather — low temperatures cause arteries to burst under high pressure
Sleep more hours — extra sleep reduces the number of heartbeats over a lifetime
response.answer: Stop smoking — nicotine and carbon monoxide damage artery walls and raise blood pressure

parts.hint: Consider smoking, diet, exercise or body weight.
parts.explanation: For example, stopping smoking reduces the levels of carbon monoxide and nicotine in the blood, which damage artery walls and raise blood pressure.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — sexual vs asexual reproduction.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State one way in which sexual reproduction differs from asexual reproduction.

options: Sexual reproduction involves two parents and produces offspring with genetic variation; asexual uses only one parent
Sexual reproduction is always faster than asexual reproduction in all organisms
Sexual reproduction never produces more than two offspring at a time; asexual can produce hundreds
Sexual reproduction requires less energy than asexual reproduction in most organisms
response.answer: Sexual reproduction involves two parents and produces offspring with genetic variation; asexual uses only one parent

parts.hint: Think about the number of parents and the genetic variation in offspring.
parts.explanation: Sexual reproduction involves two parents and the fusion of gametes, producing offspring with genetic variation; asexual reproduction involves one parent and produces genetically identical offspring (clones).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Give one advantage of asexual reproduction for an organism living in a stable environment.

options: It allows rapid production of many offspring without finding a mate, useful when the parent is already well adapted
It produces offspring with new combinations of genes, increasing the chance of survival if conditions change
It requires two parents to cooperate, which ensures only the strongest individuals reproduce
It always produces offspring that are larger and stronger than the parent organism
response.answer: It allows rapid production of many offspring without finding a mate, useful when the parent is already well adapted

parts.hint: Consider how quickly and efficiently the organism can reproduce.
parts.explanation: Asexual reproduction produces large numbers of offspring quickly from a single parent without the need to find a mate, which is an advantage in a stable environment where the parent is already well adapted.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why sexual reproduction is an advantage when the environment changes.

options: Variation among offspring means some are likely to be suited to the new conditions and will survive to reproduce
Sexual reproduction always produces more offspring than asexual, so some will survive by chance
Sexual offspring inherit the best features of both parents so they are always better adapted than either parent
Two parents can care for offspring together, which improves survival when conditions become harsh
response.answer: Variation among offspring means some are likely to be suited to the new conditions and will survive to reproduce

parts.hint: Think about variation among offspring and natural selection.
parts.explanation: Sexual reproduction produces offspring with genetic variation; if the environment changes, some individuals will, by chance, have features that suit the new conditions and will survive, while others may not. This variation gives the population a better chance of adapting and surviving.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — male reproductive system.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name the organ in the male reproductive system where sperm are produced.
parts.hint: They are found outside the body in a sac.
parts.explanation: Sperm are produced in the testes (singular: testis), which are located in the scrotum outside the body, keeping them at a temperature slightly below body temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State the function of the sperm duct (vas deferens).

options: To carry sperm from the epididymis towards the urethra during ejaculation
To produce fluids that nourish and protect sperm in the semen
To store sperm until they are mature and ready for release
To produce testosterone, which controls the development of male features
response.answer: To carry sperm from the epididymis towards the urethra during ejaculation

parts.hint: Think about where sperm travel after they are produced.
parts.explanation: The sperm duct (vas deferens) carries sperm from the epididymis to the urethra during ejaculation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the testes are located outside the main body cavity in the scrotum.

options: The scrotum keeps the testes 2–3 °C cooler than body temperature, which is needed for healthy sperm production
The testes are located outside to protect them from infection by bacteria inside the body
Being outside the body allows the testes to receive more oxygen from the surrounding air
The external position allows sperm to be released directly without passing through body organs
response.answer: The scrotum keeps the testes 2–3 °C cooler than body temperature, which is needed for healthy sperm production

parts.hint: Consider the temperature needed for healthy sperm production.
parts.explanation: Sperm production requires a temperature slightly lower than normal body temperature (37 °C). The scrotum keeps the testes at about 34–35 °C, which is the optimal temperature for forming healthy, fertile sperm.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — female reproductive system.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name the organ where an egg cell is produced and released in the female reproductive system.
parts.hint: There are two of them, one on each side.
parts.explanation: The ovary produces and releases egg cells (ova). There are two ovaries, one on each side of the uterus.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State where fertilisation normally takes place in the female reproductive system.
parts.hint: It is the tube that connects the ovary to the uterus.
parts.explanation: Fertilisation — the fusion of a sperm with an egg — normally takes place in the oviduct (fallopian tube).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe the path of an egg cell from release to implantation, naming the structures it passes through.

options: Ovary → oviduct (where fertilisation may occur) → uterus, where the fertilised egg implants in the endometrium
Ovary → cervix → oviduct → uterus, where the egg waits to be fertilised by sperm
Ovary → uterus → oviduct → cervix, with fertilisation occurring inside the uterus
Ovary → vagina → oviduct → uterus, with implantation occurring in the oviduct wall
response.answer: Ovary → oviduct (where fertilisation may occur) → uterus, where the fertilised egg implants in the endometrium

parts.hint: Start at the ovary and end at the uterus wall.
parts.explanation: After ovulation the egg is released from the ovary into the oviduct. Cilia in the oviduct move it towards the uterus. If fertilised by a sperm in the oviduct, the resulting zygote divides as it travels down, arriving at the uterus where it implants in the thickened wall (endometrium).

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — HIV/AIDS transmission and prevention.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State two ways in which HIV can be transmitted from one person to another.

options: Unprotected sexual intercourse, and sharing contaminated needles or syringes
Sharing food or drink, and shaking hands with an infected person
Breathing the same air, and sitting near an infected person who sneezes
Insect bites such as mosquitoes, and contact with infected sweat or tears
response.answer: Unprotected sexual intercourse, and sharing contaminated needles or syringes

parts.hint: Think about bodily fluids and contact routes.
parts.explanation: HIV is transmitted through unprotected sexual intercourse, sharing contaminated needles, blood transfusions with infected blood, and from an infected mother to her baby during childbirth or breastfeeding.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A student claims that HIV can be caught by sharing a meal with an infected person. Is this correct? Explain.

options: No — HIV is not present in saliva in amounts that transmit infection; it requires direct blood-to-blood or sexual contact
Yes — saliva contains HIV in high concentrations, so sharing food always carries a risk of transmission
No — HIV is only transmitted at night when the immune system is weakest, not during mealtimes
Yes — food contaminated by an infected cook can carry the virus into the digestive system
response.answer: No — HIV is not present in saliva in amounts that transmit infection; it requires direct blood-to-blood or sexual contact

parts.hint: Consider how HIV enters the bloodstream.
parts.explanation: This is incorrect. HIV is present in blood, semen and breast milk. It cannot survive outside the body and is not transmitted through saliva, food, or casual contact such as sharing a meal.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suggest two ways to prevent the spread of HIV.

options: Using condoms during sexual intercourse, and using only sterile (never shared) needles
Avoiding contact with infected people in public places, and washing hands after every meal
Taking vitamin supplements to strengthen the immune system, and avoiding eating undercooked food
Wearing gloves when outdoors, and avoiding all insect bites in tropical climates
response.answer: Using condoms during sexual intercourse, and using only sterile (never shared) needles

parts.hint: Think about behaviour changes and medical precautions.
parts.explanation: Using condoms during sexual intercourse; using clean, sterile needles; screening blood donations; HIV-positive mothers avoiding breastfeeding when alternatives are available; antiretroviral treatment that reduces viral load.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — defining and explaining biodiversity.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define the term biodiversity.

options: The variety of all living organisms, including species diversity, genetic variation, and diversity of ecosystems
The total number of individual organisms living in a particular habitat at one time
The number of different species of plants found in a given area of forest or grassland
The study of living organisms and how they interact with their natural environment
response.answer: The variety of all living organisms, including species diversity, genetic variation, and diversity of ecosystems

parts.hint: Include the variety of species and the variety of ecosystems.
parts.explanation: Biodiversity refers to the variety of all living organisms (species diversity), the genetic variation within species, and the variety of different ecosystems and habitats on Earth.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Give one economic reason why high biodiversity is important.

options: It supports ecotourism and provides raw materials such as medicinal plants and food crops
It ensures that individual species become very numerous, making them easier to harvest
It reduces the cost of farming because wild species compete with agricultural pests
It prevents all natural disasters because diverse ecosystems absorb extreme weather events
response.answer: It supports ecotourism and provides raw materials such as medicinal plants and food crops

parts.hint: Think about food, medicines or tourism.
parts.explanation: High biodiversity supports economies through tourism (e.g. ecotourism), and provides raw materials such as food crops, timber and medicines derived from wild species.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why losing a single species from an ecosystem could have wide-ranging effects.

options: Species are connected in food webs; losing one affects what eats it and what it eats, potentially destabilising the ecosystem
Each species occupies exactly one habitat; losing it frees space for invasive species to take over immediately
Every species produces oxygen; removing one species reduces the total oxygen available to other organisms
Losing a species increases biodiversity because the remaining species have more resources to share
response.answer: Species are connected in food webs; losing one affects what eats it and what it eats, potentially destabilising the ecosystem

parts.hint: Think about food webs and the roles different species play.
parts.explanation: Species are linked through food webs; if one is lost, the organisms that feed on it lose a food source and may decline, while the organisms it fed on may increase unchecked. This can destabilise the whole ecosystem.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — quadrat sampling and population estimation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how a student should use a 1 m × 1 m quadrat to estimate the number of daisy plants in a 200 m² field.

options: Place the quadrat at random positions, count daisies inside each time, find the mean count per quadrat, then multiply by 200
Place the quadrat at the edge of the field, count all daisies visible, and multiply by the number of quadrats that fit across the field
Count every daisy along a 10 m transect line and multiply by 20 to estimate the whole field population
Place the quadrat in the centre of the field only, count the daisies once, and record that as the field total
response.answer: Place the quadrat at random positions, count daisies inside each time, find the mean count per quadrat, then multiply by 200

parts.hint: Think about random placement, counting, and then scaling up.
parts.explanation: Place the quadrat at random positions in the field (e.g. using random coordinates). Count the number of daisy plants inside the quadrat each time. Repeat several times and calculate the mean count per quadrat. Multiply the mean by the total field area to estimate the population: mean × 200.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A student places the quadrat five times and finds: 4, 6, 5, 3 and 7 daisy plants. The field area is 200 m² and the quadrat area is 1 m². Calculate the estimated number of daisy plants in the field.
parts.hint: Step 1: find the mean count. Step 2: multiply by field area.
parts.explanation: Mean = (4+6+5+3+7) ÷ 5 = 25 ÷ 5 = 5. Estimated population = 5 × 200 = 1000 plants.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — human threats to biodiversity.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name two human activities that threaten biodiversity.

options: Deforestation and pollution (e.g. of waterways with pesticides or industrial waste)
Ecotourism and nature conservation programmes in national parks
Building wildlife corridors and captive breeding of endangered species
Seasonal migration of large animals and natural forest fires
response.answer: Deforestation and pollution (e.g. of waterways with pesticides or industrial waste)

parts.hint: Think about how land is used and what is released into the environment.
parts.explanation: Deforestation destroys habitats; pollution (air, water, soil) poisons organisms; introduction of invasive alien species outcompetes native species; overhunting drives species to extinction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how deforestation leads to a reduction in biodiversity.

options: Trees provide habitat and food for many species; removing them causes population decline, local extinction and food web collapse
Removing trees increases sunlight, which benefits ground plants and increases total species diversity
Deforestation cools the local climate, which suits cold-adapted species but harms tropical ones only
Fewer trees means less oxygen, which directly suffocates large animals before they can migrate
response.answer: Trees provide habitat and food for many species; removing them causes population decline, local extinction and food web collapse

parts.hint: Think about habitat loss, food sources and the cascade effects through food webs.
parts.explanation: Deforestation removes trees, destroying the habitat of many species that depend on the forest for food, shelter and breeding. This leads directly to population decline and local extinction. Species that fed on forest animals also lose food and decline. Soil erosion after tree removal further degrades the habitat for ground-dwelling species.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — natural threats to biodiversity in Mauritius.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name two natural events that can threaten biodiversity in Mauritius.
parts.hint: Think about extreme weather events that affect the island.
parts.explanation: Cyclones and droughts are the main natural threats to biodiversity in Mauritius; cyclones destroy vegetation and nesting sites, while droughts reduce water availability and can kill plants and animals.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain two ways in which a cyclone can reduce biodiversity in Mauritius.

options: It uproots trees and destroys habitats, and wave action damages coral reefs — both reduce species numbers
It brings heavy rainfall that floods farmland, increasing the numbers of pest species
It drives all animals towards the coast, where they are easier for predators to catch
It cools the ocean temperature, which benefits cold-water species but harms warm-water reef fish
response.answer: It uproots trees and destroys habitats, and wave action damages coral reefs — both reduce species numbers

parts.hint: Think about the physical damage to habitats and how animals and plants are directly affected.
parts.explanation: A cyclone destroys vegetation by uprooting trees and stripping leaves, removing food and shelter for animals; it can also destroy coral reefs and coastal habitats through wave action; nesting birds lose eggs and young; soil erosion after vegetation loss makes re-establishment difficult.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — photosynthesis word equation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.

options: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy and chlorophyll)
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (releasing energy)
Water + minerals → starch + carbon dioxide (using sunlight)
Carbon dioxide + glucose → oxygen + starch (using chlorophyll)
response.answer: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy and chlorophyll)

parts.hint: Reactants on the left, products on the right. Two reactants, two products.
parts.explanation: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. Chlorophyll and light energy are required but are written above/below the arrow, not as reactants.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State in which part of the plant cell photosynthesis takes place.
parts.hint: It contains a green pigment.
parts.explanation: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — leaf adaptations for photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Leaves are broad and flat. Explain how this feature helps photosynthesis.

options: A large flat surface maximises the area available to absorb sunlight
A flat shape reduces water loss by decreasing the area exposed to wind
Being flat allows the leaf to store more glucose for nighttime respiration
A broad shape helps the leaf to absorb more mineral salts from the soil
response.answer: A large flat surface maximises the area available to absorb sunlight

parts.hint: Think about what the leaf is capturing.
parts.explanation: A broad, flat surface provides a large surface area to absorb as much sunlight as possible for photosynthesis.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Leaves contain many stomata on the lower surface. State the function of stomata in photosynthesis.

options: They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse into the leaf for use in photosynthesis
They absorb water from the air to supply the photosynthesis reaction
They release glucose produced by photosynthesis into the surrounding air
They prevent oxygen from escaping so it can be used directly in the leaf
response.answer: They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse into the leaf for use in photosynthesis

parts.hint: Think about which gas the leaf needs to take in.
parts.explanation: Stomata allow carbon dioxide to enter the leaf by diffusion; they also allow oxygen and water vapour to leave. Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The upper layer of a leaf (palisade mesophyll) contains many chloroplasts. Explain why this layer is adapted for maximum photosynthesis.

options: The palisade layer is at the top of the leaf, close to the light, and its cells are densely packed with chloroplasts to absorb maximum light
The palisade cells are at the bottom of the leaf to absorb light reflected from the ground surface
The palisade layer contains large air spaces that allow light to scatter throughout the leaf equally
Palisade cells are thin and transparent so that light passes through them without being absorbed
response.answer: The palisade layer is at the top of the leaf, close to the light, and its cells are densely packed with chloroplasts to absorb maximum light

parts.hint: Think about the position of this layer and the number of chloroplasts.
parts.explanation: The palisade mesophyll is at the top of the leaf, closest to the light source. The tall, column-like cells are packed with chloroplasts and arranged in a row to intercept as much light as possible before it reaches the lower layers.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — limiting factors for photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A graph shows that when light intensity is low, the rate of photosynthesis is low, but when light intensity increases to a certain level, the rate levels off and does not increase further. What does the plateau (flat part) of the graph suggest?

options: Light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature is now limiting the rate
The plant has produced as much glucose as it can store, so photosynthesis stops automatically
The chlorophyll has been bleached by too much light, so the rate cannot rise any further
The stomata close when light is very bright, preventing CO₂ from entering and stopping further increases
response.answer: Light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature is now limiting the rate

parts.hint: If one factor is no longer limiting, something else must be.
parts.explanation: When the graph levels off, light is no longer the limiting factor. Another factor — such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature — has become limiting and is now preventing any further increase in the rate of photosynthesis.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A farmer wants to increase the rate of photosynthesis in a greenhouse. Suggest two conditions they could alter.

options: Increase CO₂ concentration (e.g. by adding a CO₂ burner) and increase light intensity with grow-lights
Decrease temperature to slow respiration, and reduce watering to concentrate the sugars
Increase the amount of soil minerals and decrease the humidity to reduce water loss
Reduce light intensity to prevent chlorophyll bleaching, and add more fertiliser to the soil
response.answer: Increase CO₂ concentration (e.g. by adding a CO₂ burner) and increase light intensity with grow-lights

parts.hint: Think about the three main factors that affect photosynthesis.
parts.explanation: The farmer could increase the concentration of carbon dioxide (e.g. by burning a propane heater), increase the temperature (within the optimum range), or increase the light intensity using artificial lighting.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — testing a leaf for starch.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A student wants to test a leaf for the presence of starch. The first step is to kill the leaf by placing it in boiling water. Why is this step needed?

options: To stop further chemical reactions and kill the cells before the starch test
To remove the waxy cuticle so that iodine solution can enter the leaf directly
To dissolve any starch already present so that new starch can be detected accurately
To break open the stomata so that iodine vapour can diffuse into the leaf cells
response.answer: To stop further chemical reactions and kill the cells before the starch test

parts.hint: Think about what must happen to the leaf before the iodine solution is applied.
parts.explanation: Boiling the leaf kills the cells and stops any further chemical reactions from taking place, ensuring the result reflects what happened during the experiment rather than changes after removal from the plant.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The leaf is then placed in hot ethanol. What does this step remove, and why is it necessary?

options: It removes chlorophyll, decolorising the leaf so the iodine colour change can be seen clearly
It removes the starch so that the leaf can be tested for glucose instead
It hardens the cell walls, making the leaf firm enough to handle without breaking
It kills any bacteria on the leaf surface that might interfere with the iodine result
response.answer: It removes chlorophyll, decolorising the leaf so the iodine colour change can be seen clearly

parts.hint: Think about what would make it hard to see a colour change.
parts.explanation: Hot ethanol removes the green chlorophyll from the leaf. This decolorises the leaf so that the colour change produced by iodine solution (blue-black for starch) can be seen clearly against the pale background.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: After rinsing with water and spreading flat, iodine solution is added to the leaf. What colour change indicates that starch is present?

options: The leaf turns bright red where starch is present
The iodine turns colourless where starch is present
The leaf turns green where starch has been broken down

parts.hint: This is the standard iodine-starch result.
parts.explanation: Iodine solution turns from yellow-brown to blue-black when starch is present. If no starch is present the leaf stays orange-brown.

grade9-biology.source: NCE Science Biology structured question — Elodea oxygen production experiment.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: A student uses an aquatic plant (Elodea) to investigate the effect of light intensity on photosynthesis. Describe how they would vary light intensity without changing any other factor.

options: Move the lamp to different distances from the plant; use a water bath to control temperature and sodium hydrogencarbonate to maintain CO₂
Use bulbs of different colours at the same distance; add ice to cool the water after each colour change
Change the concentration of CO₂ in the water by adding different amounts of acid to the tank
Place the plant at different depths in the water to change the amount of light reaching it
response.answer: Move the lamp to different distances from the plant; use a water bath to control temperature and sodium hydrogencarbonate to maintain CO₂

parts.hint: Think about moving the light source and controlling temperature and CO₂.
parts.explanation: Place the lamp at different measured distances from the plant — the further away, the lower the light intensity. Keep temperature and CO₂ concentration constant by using a water bath (to absorb heat) and sodium hydrogencarbonate solution in the water (to maintain CO₂ level).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The student counts the number of oxygen bubbles produced per minute. Why is this a suitable measure of the rate of photosynthesis?

options: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, so more bubbles per minute indicates a higher rate of photosynthesis
Oxygen bubbles are easy to count, but they actually measure respiration rate rather than photosynthesis
Each bubble contains a fixed amount of glucose, so counting them gives the total glucose produced
Oxygen bubbles measure the rate of water absorption through the roots, which drives photosynthesis
response.answer: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, so more bubbles per minute indicates a higher rate of photosynthesis

parts.hint: Look at the word equation — what is oxygen in photosynthesis?
parts.explanation: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis; the more oxygen produced, the faster photosynthesis is occurring. Counting the bubbles per minute gives a reliable measure of the rate because the bubbles are produced at a rate directly linked to the rate of the reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The student finds that increasing light intensity beyond a certain point does not increase the bubble count any further. Suggest a reason for this result.

options: Another factor such as CO₂ concentration is now limiting the rate, so extra light has no further effect
The plant has used up all its chlorophyll and can no longer absorb any additional light
Too much light destroys the enzyme responsible for photosynthesis, so the rate falls
The plant switches to respiration when light intensity is very high, producing CO₂ instead of O₂
response.answer: Another factor such as CO₂ concentration is now limiting the rate, so extra light has no further effect

parts.hint: Another factor must now be in short supply.
parts.explanation: When light is no longer limiting, another factor — most likely carbon dioxide concentration — is limiting the rate. Even though there is plenty of light, there is not enough CO₂ for photosynthesis to go any faster.

grade9-biology.question: What is a hypothesis?
options: A conclusion drawn after the results are in
A measurement taken during an experiment
A rule that has already been proved true
A prediction that can be tested by an experiment
grade9-biology.answer: A prediction that can be tested by an experiment
acceptableAnswers: A prediction that can be tested by an experiment
grade9-biology.hint: It comes before the experiment, not after it.
grade9-biology.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable prediction, made before the experiment and then tested by it.

grade9-biology.question: Which of these is a testable hypothesis?
options: Plants were here before animals were
Plants are the most beautiful living things
A plant given more light will produce more bubbles
Everyone should look after plants properly
grade9-biology.answer: A plant given more light will produce more bubbles
acceptableAnswers: A plant given more light will produce more bubbles
grade9-biology.hint: A hypothesis must be something an experiment could check.
grade9-biology.explanation: Only the first can be tested by measurement; the others are opinions or claims an experiment cannot settle.

grade9-biology.question: In an experiment, what is the independent variable?
options: The one that is measured as the result
The one the investigator deliberately changes
The one that cannot be measured at all
The one that is deliberately kept the same
grade9-biology.answer: The one the investigator deliberately changes
acceptableAnswers: The one the investigator deliberately changes
grade9-biology.hint: It is the cause being tested.
grade9-biology.explanation: The independent variable is the one deliberately changed to see what effect it has.

grade9-biology.question: What is the dependent variable?
options: The one the investigator deliberately changes
The one that is kept the same throughout
The one that is measured as the result
The one that is written in the title
grade9-biology.answer: The one that is measured as the result
acceptableAnswers: The one that is measured as the result
grade9-biology.hint: It depends on what was changed.
grade9-biology.explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome measured; its value depends on the independent variable.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil changes the light intensity and counts the bubbles from a water plant, keeping the temperature the same. What is the controlled variable?
options: The type of plant used only
grade9-biology.answer: The temperature
grade9-biology.hint: A controlled variable is one deliberately kept the same.
grade9-biology.explanation: Temperature is deliberately held constant so it cannot affect the result - that makes it a controlled variable.

grade9-biology.question: Why must all the other variables be kept the same in a fair test?
options: So the hypothesis is certain to be correct
So that the experiment can be finished much more quickly
So any change in the result is caused by the one variable changed
So the results are always whole numbers
grade9-biology.answer: So any change in the result is caused by the one variable changed
acceptableAnswers: So any change in the result is caused by the one variable changed
grade9-biology.hint: Two changes at once tell you nothing about either.
grade9-biology.explanation: Controlling everything else is what lets the result be attributed to the variable that was changed.

grade9-biology.question: Where should the readings taken during an experiment be written?
options: From memory once the experiment is finished
Only in the conclusion at the end
On loose scraps of paper to be copied later
In a table prepared before the experiment starts
grade9-biology.answer: In a table prepared before the experiment starts
acceptableAnswers: In a table prepared before the experiment starts
grade9-biology.hint: A table drawn in advance means nothing is forgotten.
grade9-biology.explanation: Results go straight into a prepared table, with the quantities and units already headed.

grade9-biology.question: What must the heading of each column in a results table include?
grade9-biology.answer: The quantity and its unit
grade9-biology.hint: A number without a unit means nothing.
grade9-biology.explanation: Each column heading names the quantity and gives its unit, so every value in it can be read correctly.

grade9-biology.question: Which is the best way to show how one measured quantity changes with another?
grade9-biology.answer: A line graph
grade9-biology.hint: Both quantities are numbers that vary.
grade9-biology.explanation: A line graph shows the relationship between two continuous variables and reveals the pattern at a glance.

grade9-biology.question: The table shows results from a water plant. What is the pattern?
options: The number of bubbles stays the same throughout
As the light increases, the number of bubbles decreases
There is no pattern in these results
As the light increases, the number of bubbles increases
grade9-biology.answer: As the light increases, the number of bubbles increases
acceptableAnswers: As the light increases, the number of bubbles increases
grade9-biology.hint: Read down both columns together.
grade9-biology.explanation: Every increase in light is matched by an increase in bubbles, so the two rise together.

grade9-biology.question: Reading the same table, how many bubbles per minute were counted at 40 units of light?
grade9-biology.hint: Find the row for 40 and read across.
grade9-biology.explanation: The row for 40 units gives 25 bubbles per minute.

grade9-biology.question: One reading in a set of results is far away from the pattern of the others. What is it called?
grade9-biology.answer: An anomalous result
grade9-biology.hint: It does not fit the pattern.
grade9-biology.explanation: A result that does not fit the pattern is anomalous, and should be checked or repeated rather than quietly ignored.

grade9-biology.question: Why is an experiment repeated several times?
options: To make the experiment take a whole lesson
To use up the remaining chemicals in the laboratory
To check the results are reliable and find any anomalies
To change the hypothesis while it is running
grade9-biology.answer: To check the results are reliable and find any anomalies
acceptableAnswers: To check the results are reliable and find any anomalies
grade9-biology.hint: One reading could be a fluke.
grade9-biology.explanation: Repeats show whether a result can be trusted and make an odd reading obvious.

grade9-biology.question: What is the difference between a result and a conclusion?
options: A conclusion is written before the experiment starts
A result is what was measured; a conclusion is what it means
A result is an opinion; a conclusion is a measurement
They are two words for exactly the same thing
grade9-biology.answer: A result is what was measured; a conclusion is what it means
acceptableAnswers: A result is what was measured; a conclusion is what it means
grade9-biology.hint: One is data, the other is an interpretation.
grade9-biology.explanation: Results are the measurements themselves; the conclusion is what those measurements show about the hypothesis.

grade9-biology.question: Give the term for the variable that the investigator deliberately changes.
grade9-biology.answer: Independent variable
grade9-biology.hint: It is the cause being tested.
grade9-biology.explanation: The independent variable is the one deliberately changed.

grade9-biology.question: Give the term for the variable that is measured as the result.
grade9-biology.answer: Dependent variable
grade9-biology.hint: Its value depends on what was changed.
grade9-biology.explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome that is measured.

grade9-biology.question: Give the term for a reading that does not fit the pattern of the others.
grade9-biology.answer: Anomalous
grade9-biology.hint: It stands out from the rest.
grade9-biology.explanation: A result that does not fit the pattern is anomalous.

grade9-biology.question: State what must appear in the heading of each column of a results table.
grade9-biology.answer: The quantity and its unit
grade9-biology.hint: A number on its own means nothing.
grade9-biology.explanation: Each heading gives the quantity being recorded and the unit it is measured in.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil predicts that bean seeds kept in the dark will grow taller than seeds kept in the light. Why is this a hypothesis?
options: It is a measurement taken with a ruler each day
It is a conclusion drawn from the results
It is a prediction that an experiment can test
It is an opinion about which plants look best
grade9-biology.answer: It is a prediction that an experiment can test
acceptableAnswers: It is a prediction that an experiment can test
grade9-biology.hint: Ask whether an investigation could settle it.
grade9-biology.explanation: A hypothesis is a prediction stated before the work begins, worded so that measurements can then show whether it holds.

grade9-biology.question: Cress seeds are sown on cotton wool and given 0, 5, 10 or 15 cm³ of water. What is the independent variable?
options: The number of seeds that germinate
The type of cress seed that is sown
The volume of water given to the seeds
The temperature of the room they are in
grade9-biology.answer: The volume of water given to the seeds
acceptableAnswers: The volume of water given to the seeds
grade9-biology.hint: It is the one deliberately changed between the dishes.
grade9-biology.explanation: Water volume is the quantity deliberately varied, so it is the independent variable; the number of seeds that germinate is the result.

grade9-biology.question: In the same cress investigation, what is the dependent variable?
options: The volume of water given each dish
The kind of cotton wool in each dish
The temperature the dishes are kept at
The number of seeds that germinate
grade9-biology.answer: The number of seeds that germinate
acceptableAnswers: The number of seeds that germinate
grade9-biology.hint: It is the outcome counted at the end.
grade9-biology.explanation: The germination count is the outcome measured, and its value depends on the water given, so it is the dependent variable.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil moves a lamp closer to a tube of pond weed and counts the bubbles given off. Which variable must be kept the same?
options: The temperature of the water in the tube
The distance of the lamp from the tube
The brightness of the lamp that is used
The number of bubbles given off each minute
grade9-biology.answer: The temperature of the water in the tube
acceptableAnswers: The temperature of the water in the tube
grade9-biology.hint: Two of these are being changed and one is being measured.
grade9-biology.explanation: The lamp distance is what is changed and the bubble count is the result, so temperature is the variable that must be held constant.

grade9-biology.question: Why does a germination investigation put ten seeds in each dish rather than one?
options: Ten seeds need less water than one seed
One seed may fail for a reason of its own
One seed cannot be measured with a ruler
Ten seeds will always germinate together
grade9-biology.answer: One seed may fail for a reason of its own
acceptableAnswers: One seed may fail for a reason of its own
grade9-biology.hint: Think what a single dead seed would do to the result.
grade9-biology.explanation: A single seed could fail for reasons of its own; using ten means the result reflects the treatment rather than one unlucky seed.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil claims that warmer water makes yeast produce more gas. Which plan tests that claim fairly?
options: Same yeast, different sugars, warm water only
Different amounts of yeast in warm water only
Different yeast and sugar at one temperature
Same yeast and sugar, water at four temperatures
grade9-biology.answer: Same yeast and sugar, water at four temperatures
acceptableAnswers: Same yeast and sugar, water at four temperatures
grade9-biology.hint: Only the thing being tested may change.
grade9-biology.explanation: Temperature is the variable under test, so the yeast, the sugar and the volumes must be identical in every tube.

grade9-biology.question: The results of an investigation do not support the pupil’s hypothesis. What should the pupil do?
options: Change the numbers so the prediction is right
Repeat until the prediction is supported once
Leave out the readings that do not agree
Report the results and say the prediction failed
grade9-biology.answer: Report the results and say the prediction failed
acceptableAnswers: Report the results and say the prediction failed
grade9-biology.hint: Science reports what actually happened.
grade9-biology.explanation: A hypothesis the evidence does not support is reported as such; altering or discarding data to protect a prediction destroys the investigation.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil writes that the pond weed made more bubbles "because it was happier in the light". What is wrong with this?
options: It is the controlled variable of this experiment
It is not a scientific explanation of the result
It is a fair conclusion from the bubble counts
It is the hypothesis the pupil set out to test
grade9-biology.answer: It is not a scientific explanation of the result
acceptableAnswers: It is not a scientific explanation of the result
grade9-biology.hint: Ask what part of the statement could be measured.
grade9-biology.explanation: Being "happier" cannot be measured or tested; the result is explained by more light supplying more energy for photosynthesis.

grade9-biology.question: In a starch test, one destarched leaf is covered with foil and another is left uncovered. Why is the uncovered leaf there?
options: To act as a control for the covered leaf
To make the experiment finish more quickly
To use up the starch left in the plant
To keep the plant warmer than the others
grade9-biology.answer: To act as a control for the covered leaf
acceptableAnswers: To act as a control for the covered leaf
grade9-biology.hint: It is there so the two can be compared.
grade9-biology.explanation: The uncovered leaf is treated identically except that light reaches it, so it shows what the covered leaf would have done had it received light.

grade9-biology.question: A pupil will count germinated seeds every day for a week. Where should each count be written?
options: In a bar chart drawn as each count is made
In a table ruled up before the week starts
From memory at the end of the whole week
On separate scraps of paper each morning
grade9-biology.answer: In a table ruled up before the week starts
acceptableAnswers: In a table ruled up before the week starts
grade9-biology.hint: A table drawn in advance means nothing is forgotten.
