grade9-biology.question: An invasive plant is cleared from a nature reserve by cutting it down. Which is the ethical question here?
options: How many workers are needed here
Which living things we may remove
Which tool cuts the stems fastest
How long the clearing work takes
grade9-biology.answer: Which living things we may remove
acceptableAnswers: Which living things we may remove
grade9-biology.hint: One of these asks what we are entitled to do.
grade9-biology.explanation: Deciding that one species may be destroyed to protect others is a judgement about value; the tools, the workers and the time are practical matters.

grade9-biology.question: Why is testing new medicines on animals debated?
options: It weighs animal suffering against human benefit
It makes the medicines take much longer to develop
It requires laboratories with a great deal of space
It needs more scientists than any other kind of work
grade9-biology.answer: It weighs animal suffering against human benefit
acceptableAnswers: It weighs animal suffering against human benefit
grade9-biology.hint: Two things that both matter are being set against each other.
grade9-biology.explanation: The debate sets real harm to animals against real benefit to patients, and reasonable people weigh those two differently; no measurement settles it.

grade9-biology.question: Which statement about science and ethics is correct?
options: Science and ethics answer the same questions
Ethics can be settled by an experiment alone
Science says what is; ethics says what ought
Ethics says what is; science says what ought
grade9-biology.answer: Science says what is; ethics says what ought
acceptableAnswers: Science says what is; ethics says what ought
grade9-biology.hint: One describes the world; the other judges what to do in it.
grade9-biology.explanation: Science establishes what is the case; ethics asks what we ought to do about it, and an experiment cannot decide the second.

grade9-biology.question: Why should the risks of a new medical technology be explained to the public?
options: The public pays for the research to be done
The scientists then have less to explain
The technology then works more reliably
People affected by it have a right to know
grade9-biology.answer: People affected by it have a right to know
acceptableAnswers: People affected by it have a right to know
grade9-biology.hint: Who bears the risk?
grade9-biology.explanation: Those who carry the risk are entitled to know what it is, and a decision made without that information is not a free choice at all.

grade9-biology.question: A company conceals a harmful side effect of its medicine. Which principle has it broken?
options: Speed in bringing a product to sale
Secrecy about a new discovery made
grade9-biology.answer: Honesty about the evidence collected
grade9-biology.hint: What did the company do with what it knew?
grade9-biology.explanation: Reporting evidence honestly, including results that harm the case, is the basic duty of science; concealing a side effect puts patients in danger.

grade9-biology.question: Who should decide how a new scientific discovery is used?
options: The scientists working on it alone
The company that paid for the work
Nobody, because it cannot be used
grade9-biology.answer: Society, informed by the scientists
grade9-biology.hint: The knowledge and its use are two different things.
grade9-biology.explanation: Scientists explain what a discovery can and cannot do; deciding how it is used affects everyone, so that decision belongs to society as a whole.

grade9-biology.question: Give the year in which the first human-to-human heart transplant was performed.
grade9-biology.hint: It was two years before the first Moon landing.
grade9-biology.explanation: Christiaan Barnard performed the first human-to-human heart transplant in December 1967.

grade9-biology.question: Give the term for a person whose organ is given for transplant into another person.
grade9-biology.answer: Donor
grade9-biology.hint: The organ is given, not taken.
grade9-biology.explanation: The donor supplies the organ and the recipient receives it; matching the two reduces the chance of rejection.

grade9-biology.question: Give the word for a source that favours one conclusion because it has something to gain.
grade9-biology.answer: Biased
grade9-biology.hint: It leans one way.
grade9-biology.explanation: A biased source leans towards a conclusion it benefits from, so its evidence must be checked against an independent source.

grade9-biology.question: State what should be looked for behind any scientific claim before it is believed.
grade9-biology.answer: Evidence
grade9-biology.hint: It is not how confidently the claim is stated.
grade9-biology.explanation: A claim stands on the evidence collected for it and on whether independent scientists have checked that evidence.

grade9-biology.question: Give the word describing a question about what ought to be done rather than about what is true.
grade9-biology.answer: Ethical
grade9-biology.hint: It is about right and wrong.
grade9-biology.explanation: An ethical question asks what we ought to do, and no measurement or experiment can settle it on its own.

grade9-biology.question: State what must be obtained from a person before they may take part in a medical trial.
grade9-biology.answer: Consent
grade9-biology.hint: They must understand the risks and agree freely.
grade9-biology.explanation: Informed consent means the volunteer has been told the risks and has agreed without pressure to take part.

grade9-biology.question: Name the four main components of blood.
grade9-biology.hint: One mark for each component.
grade9-biology.explanation: The four components are: plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
options: Plasma, haemoglobin, antibodies and clotting proteins
Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
Lymph fluid, red cells, platelets and dissolved hormones
grade9-biology.answer: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets
acceptableAnswers: Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets

grade9-biology.question: State one function of red blood cells and explain how they are adapted to carry out that function.
grade9-biology.hint: Name the function, then link a structural feature to it.
grade9-biology.explanation: Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin; their biconcave disc shape maximises surface area for oxygen absorption.
options: They help blood to clot at wounds; they release chemicals that trigger fibrin formation
They defend the body against infection; they engulf and destroy bacteria by phagocytosis
They carry dissolved nutrients to cells; their thin membrane allows rapid diffusion of glucose
They carry oxygen using haemoglobin; the biconcave disc shape maximises surface area for oxygen absorption
grade9-biology.answer: They carry oxygen using haemoglobin; the biconcave disc shape maximises surface area for oxygen absorption
acceptableAnswers: They carry oxygen using haemoglobin; the biconcave disc shape maximises surface area for oxygen absorption

grade9-biology.question: A cross-section of a blood vessel shows a thick wall with much elastic tissue and a narrow lumen. Name this type of blood vessel.
grade9-biology.hint: Which vessel must withstand high pressure from the heart?
grade9-biology.explanation: This describes an artery — thick elastic walls to withstand the high pressure generated by the heart.
grade9-biology.answer: Artery

grade9-biology.question: A second vessel has a wide lumen and pocket valves along its length. Name this vessel and explain the function of its valves.
grade9-biology.hint: Which vessel carries blood back to the heart at low pressure?
grade9-biology.explanation: This is a vein. The pocket valves prevent blood flowing backwards; they open when blood moves toward the heart and snap shut if blood starts to flow the wrong way.
options: Capillary; the valves control the rate of exchange between blood and tissues
Aorta; the valves prevent blood re-entering the left ventricle after each beat
Vein; the valves prevent backflow and ensure blood moves only towards the heart
Artery; the valves reduce blood pressure to prevent vessel damage
grade9-biology.answer: Vein; the valves prevent backflow and ensure blood moves only towards the heart
acceptableAnswers: Vein; the valves prevent backflow and ensure blood moves only towards the heart

grade9-biology.question: A third vessel has a wall that is only one cell thick. Name it and explain why its thin wall is an advantage.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about the diffusion of substances between blood and body cells.
grade9-biology.explanation: This is a capillary. Its single-cell-thick wall minimises the diffusion distance, so oxygen, glucose and other substances pass rapidly between the blood and surrounding tissue cells.
options: Arteriole; the thin wall allows the vessel to stretch when blood pressure increases
Capillary; the thin wall minimises diffusion distance so substances move rapidly between blood and cells
Venule; the thin wall allows high blood pressure to be maintained across the capillary bed
Capillary; the thin wall prevents any white blood cells from leaving the bloodstream
grade9-biology.answer: Capillary; the thin wall minimises diffusion distance so substances move rapidly between blood and cells
acceptableAnswers: Capillary; the thin wall minimises diffusion distance so substances move rapidly between blood and cells

grade9-biology.question: A student draws a red blood cell. The width of the drawing is 40 mm. The actual width of the cell is 0.008 mm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
grade9-biology.hint: Magnification = drawing size ÷ actual size. Both are already in mm.
grade9-biology.explanation: Magnification = 40 ÷ 0.008 = 5000. No unit is written with magnification.

grade9-biology.question: Magnification is written as a pure number with no unit. Which statement correctly explains why?
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what happens to the units when you divide mm by mm.
grade9-biology.explanation: When both the drawing size and the actual size are in the same unit (e.g. mm ÷ mm), the units cancel, leaving a dimensionless ratio.
options: The unit cancels only when the drawing is larger than the actual object
Scientists agreed to remove units from magnification to avoid confusion with scale bars
Magnification is always measured in micrometres, which are too small to write
The units cancel when you divide a length by a length in the same unit, giving a pure ratio
grade9-biology.answer: The units cancel when you divide a length by a length in the same unit, giving a pure ratio
acceptableAnswers: The units cancel when you divide a length by a length in the same unit, giving a pure ratio

grade9-biology.question: Which adaptation of a red blood cell gives it the greatest surface area to volume ratio?
grade9-biology.hint: Consider the shape of a mature red blood cell.
grade9-biology.explanation: The biconcave disc shape increases the surface area relative to the volume, maximising contact between haemoglobin and the cell surface.
options: Its flexible membrane, which allows it to squeeze through capillaries
Its biconcave disc shape, which increases surface area relative to volume
Its lack of a nucleus, which allows more haemoglobin to fit inside
Its very small size compared with other blood cells
grade9-biology.answer: Its biconcave disc shape, which increases surface area relative to volume
acceptableAnswers: Its biconcave disc shape, which increases surface area relative to volume

grade9-biology.question: State what is meant by the pulse.
grade9-biology.hint: It is something you can feel in an artery.
grade9-biology.explanation: The pulse is the rhythmic surge of pressure felt in an artery each time the heart beats and pumps blood into it.
options: The number of times the heart beats during one minute of rest
The speed at which blood travels through the capillary network
The rhythmic surge of pressure felt in an artery with each heartbeat
The electrical signal sent by the heart to stimulate muscle contraction
grade9-biology.answer: The rhythmic surge of pressure felt in an artery with each heartbeat
acceptableAnswers: The rhythmic surge of pressure felt in an artery with each heartbeat

grade9-biology.question: A student counts 18 pulse beats in 15 seconds. Calculate the pulse rate in beats per minute.
grade9-biology.hint: There are four lots of 15 seconds in one minute.
grade9-biology.explanation: 18 beats × 4 = 72 beats per minute.

grade9-biology.question: Explain why pulse rate increases during vigorous exercise.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what muscles need more of during exercise.
grade9-biology.explanation: During exercise, muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose; the heart beats faster to pump more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove the extra carbon dioxide produced.
options: Blood pressure drops during exercise, causing the heart to speed up as a compensation
Body temperature rises during exercise, which directly stretches the heart muscle fibres
The lungs fill with more air, which forces the heart to beat more quickly to use it up
Muscles need more oxygen and glucose, so the heart beats faster to deliver more oxygenated blood
grade9-biology.answer: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose, so the heart beats faster to deliver more oxygenated blood
acceptableAnswers: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose, so the heart beats faster to deliver more oxygenated blood

grade9-biology.question: State one risk factor for cardiovascular disease that is related to diet.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about substances in food that affect the arteries.
grade9-biology.explanation: A high intake of saturated fat raises blood cholesterol, which contributes to atherosclerosis (fatty deposits in artery walls).
options: Working long hours, which reduces the time available for exercise
Lack of sleep, which raises blood pressure over time
A diet high in saturated fat, which raises blood cholesterol levels
Exposure to cold weather, which causes arteries to narrow
grade9-biology.answer: A diet high in saturated fat, which raises blood cholesterol levels
acceptableAnswers: A diet high in saturated fat, which raises blood cholesterol levels

grade9-biology.question: Explain how a build-up of fatty deposits in the coronary arteries can lead to a heart attack.
grade9-biology.hint: Trace the sequence: fatty deposit → narrowing → blocked blood supply → heart muscle damage.
grade9-biology.explanation: Fatty deposits (plaques) narrow the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle. A blood clot may then block the already-narrowed artery completely, cutting off the oxygen supply to heart muscle cells, which begin to die — this is a heart attack (myocardial infarction).
options: Cholesterol dissolves into the blood and makes it too thick to flow through the fine capillaries of the heart
Fatty deposits cause the coronary veins to swell, increasing pressure until the heart wall ruptures
Fatty deposits thicken the heart muscle wall so it cannot contract, causing the heart to stop pumping
Fatty plaques narrow the coronary arteries; a clot may then block them completely, cutting off oxygen to heart muscle, which dies
grade9-biology.answer: Fatty plaques narrow the coronary arteries; a clot may then block them completely, cutting off oxygen to heart muscle, which dies
acceptableAnswers: Fatty plaques narrow the coronary arteries; a clot may then block them completely, cutting off oxygen to heart muscle, which dies

grade9-biology.question: Suggest one lifestyle change that could reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. Give a reason for your answer.
grade9-biology.hint: Consider smoking, diet, exercise or body weight.
grade9-biology.explanation: For example, stopping smoking reduces the levels of carbon monoxide and nicotine in the blood, which damage artery walls and raise blood pressure.
options: Sleep more hours — extra sleep reduces the number of heartbeats over a lifetime
Stop smoking — nicotine and carbon monoxide damage artery walls and raise blood pressure
Drink more fluids — this thins the blood and prevents clots from forming
Avoid cold weather — low temperatures cause arteries to burst under high pressure
grade9-biology.answer: Stop smoking — nicotine and carbon monoxide damage artery walls and raise blood pressure
acceptableAnswers: Stop smoking — nicotine and carbon monoxide damage artery walls and raise blood pressure

grade9-biology.question: State one way in which sexual reproduction differs from asexual reproduction.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about the number of parents and the genetic variation in offspring.
grade9-biology.explanation: Sexual reproduction involves two parents and the fusion of gametes, producing offspring with genetic variation; asexual reproduction involves one parent and produces genetically identical offspring (clones).
options: Sexual reproduction never produces more than two offspring at a time; asexual can produce hundreds
Sexual reproduction requires less energy than asexual reproduction in most organisms
Sexual reproduction involves two parents and produces offspring with genetic variation; asexual uses only one parent
Sexual reproduction is always faster than asexual reproduction in all organisms
grade9-biology.answer: Sexual reproduction involves two parents and produces offspring with genetic variation; asexual uses only one parent
acceptableAnswers: Sexual reproduction involves two parents and produces offspring with genetic variation; asexual uses only one parent

grade9-biology.question: Give one advantage of asexual reproduction for an organism living in a stable environment.
grade9-biology.hint: Consider how quickly and efficiently the organism can reproduce.
grade9-biology.explanation: Asexual reproduction produces large numbers of offspring quickly from a single parent without the need to find a mate, which is an advantage in a stable environment where the parent is already well adapted.
options: It allows rapid production of many offspring without finding a mate, useful when the parent is already well adapted
It produces offspring with new combinations of genes, increasing the chance of survival if conditions change
It requires two parents to cooperate, which ensures only the strongest individuals reproduce
It always produces offspring that are larger and stronger than the parent organism
grade9-biology.answer: It allows rapid production of many offspring without finding a mate, useful when the parent is already well adapted
acceptableAnswers: It allows rapid production of many offspring without finding a mate, useful when the parent is already well adapted

grade9-biology.question: Explain why sexual reproduction is an advantage when the environment changes.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about variation among offspring and natural selection.
grade9-biology.explanation: Sexual reproduction produces offspring with genetic variation; if the environment changes, some individuals will, by chance, have features that suit the new conditions and will survive, while others may not. This variation gives the population a better chance of adapting and surviving.
options: Sexual reproduction always produces more offspring than asexual, so some will survive by chance
Two parents can care for offspring together, which improves survival when conditions become harsh
Sexual offspring inherit the best features of both parents so they are always better adapted than either parent
Variation among offspring means some are likely to be suited to the new conditions and will survive to reproduce
grade9-biology.answer: Variation among offspring means some are likely to be suited to the new conditions and will survive to reproduce
acceptableAnswers: Variation among offspring means some are likely to be suited to the new conditions and will survive to reproduce

grade9-biology.question: Name the organ in the male reproductive system where sperm are produced.
grade9-biology.hint: They are found outside the body in a sac.
grade9-biology.explanation: Sperm are produced in the testes (singular: testis), which are located in the scrotum outside the body, keeping them at a temperature slightly below body temperature.
grade9-biology.answer: The testes

grade9-biology.question: State the function of the sperm duct (vas deferens).
grade9-biology.hint: Think about where sperm travel after they are produced.
grade9-biology.explanation: The sperm duct (vas deferens) carries sperm from the epididymis to the urethra during ejaculation.
options: To produce testosterone, which controls the development of male features
To store sperm until they are mature and ready for release
To produce fluids that nourish and protect sperm in the semen
To carry sperm from the epididymis towards the urethra during ejaculation
grade9-biology.answer: To carry sperm from the epididymis towards the urethra during ejaculation
acceptableAnswers: To carry sperm from the epididymis towards the urethra during ejaculation

grade9-biology.question: Explain why the testes are located outside the main body cavity in the scrotum.
grade9-biology.hint: Consider the temperature needed for healthy sperm production.
grade9-biology.explanation: Sperm production requires a temperature slightly lower than normal body temperature (37 °C). The scrotum keeps the testes at about 34–35 °C, which is the optimal temperature for forming healthy, fertile sperm.
options: The testes are located outside to protect them from infection by bacteria inside the body
The scrotum keeps the testes 2–3 °C cooler than body temperature, which is needed for healthy sperm production
Being outside the body allows the testes to receive more oxygen from the surrounding air
The external position allows sperm to be released directly without passing through body organs
grade9-biology.answer: The scrotum keeps the testes 2–3 °C cooler than body temperature, which is needed for healthy sperm production
acceptableAnswers: The scrotum keeps the testes 2–3 °C cooler than body temperature, which is needed for healthy sperm production

grade9-biology.question: Name the organ where an egg cell is produced and released in the female reproductive system.
grade9-biology.hint: There are two of them, one on each side.
grade9-biology.explanation: The ovary produces and releases egg cells (ova). There are two ovaries, one on each side of the uterus.
grade9-biology.answer: The ovary

grade9-biology.question: State where fertilisation normally takes place in the female reproductive system.
grade9-biology.hint: It is the tube that connects the ovary to the uterus.
grade9-biology.explanation: Fertilisation — the fusion of a sperm with an egg — normally takes place in the oviduct (fallopian tube).
grade9-biology.answer: In the oviduct (fallopian tube)

grade9-biology.question: Describe the path of an egg cell from release to implantation, naming the structures it passes through.
grade9-biology.hint: Start at the ovary and end at the uterus wall.
grade9-biology.explanation: After ovulation the egg is released from the ovary into the oviduct. Cilia in the oviduct move it towards the uterus. If fertilised by a sperm in the oviduct, the resulting zygote divides as it travels down, arriving at the uterus where it implants in the thickened wall (endometrium).
options: Ovary → cervix → oviduct → uterus, where the egg waits to be fertilised by sperm
Ovary → oviduct (where fertilisation may occur) → uterus, where the fertilised egg implants in the endometrium
Ovary → vagina → oviduct → uterus, with implantation occurring in the oviduct wall
Ovary → uterus → oviduct → cervix, with fertilisation occurring inside the uterus
grade9-biology.answer: Ovary → oviduct (where fertilisation may occur) → uterus, where the fertilised egg implants in the endometrium
acceptableAnswers: Ovary → oviduct (where fertilisation may occur) → uterus, where the fertilised egg implants in the endometrium

grade9-biology.question: State two ways in which HIV can be transmitted from one person to another.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about bodily fluids and contact routes.
grade9-biology.explanation: HIV is transmitted through unprotected sexual intercourse, sharing contaminated needles, blood transfusions with infected blood, and from an infected mother to her baby during childbirth or breastfeeding.
options: Unprotected sexual intercourse, and sharing contaminated needles or syringes
Breathing the same air, and sitting near an infected person who sneezes
Sharing food or drink, and shaking hands with an infected person
Insect bites such as mosquitoes, and contact with infected sweat or tears
grade9-biology.answer: Unprotected sexual intercourse, and sharing contaminated needles or syringes
acceptableAnswers: Unprotected sexual intercourse, and sharing contaminated needles or syringes

grade9-biology.question: A student claims that HIV can be caught by sharing a meal with an infected person. Is this correct? Explain.
grade9-biology.hint: Consider how HIV enters the bloodstream.
grade9-biology.explanation: This is incorrect. HIV is present in blood, semen and breast milk. It cannot survive outside the body and is not transmitted through saliva, food, or casual contact such as sharing a meal.
options: Yes — food contaminated by an infected cook can carry the virus into the digestive system
No — HIV is not present in saliva in amounts that transmit infection; it requires direct blood-to-blood or sexual contact
Yes — saliva contains HIV in high concentrations, so sharing food always carries a risk of transmission
No — HIV is only transmitted at night when the immune system is weakest, not during mealtimes
grade9-biology.answer: No — HIV is not present in saliva in amounts that transmit infection; it requires direct blood-to-blood or sexual contact
acceptableAnswers: No — HIV is not present in saliva in amounts that transmit infection; it requires direct blood-to-blood or sexual contact

grade9-biology.question: Suggest two ways to prevent the spread of HIV.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about behaviour changes and medical precautions.
grade9-biology.explanation: Using condoms during sexual intercourse; using clean, sterile needles; screening blood donations; HIV-positive mothers avoiding breastfeeding when alternatives are available; antiretroviral treatment that reduces viral load.
options: Using condoms during sexual intercourse, and using only sterile (never shared) needles
Taking vitamin supplements to strengthen the immune system, and avoiding eating undercooked food
Avoiding contact with infected people in public places, and washing hands after every meal
Wearing gloves when outdoors, and avoiding all insect bites in tropical climates
grade9-biology.answer: Using condoms during sexual intercourse, and using only sterile (never shared) needles
acceptableAnswers: Using condoms during sexual intercourse, and using only sterile (never shared) needles

grade9-biology.question: Define the term biodiversity.
grade9-biology.hint: Include the variety of species and the variety of ecosystems.
grade9-biology.explanation: Biodiversity refers to the variety of all living organisms (species diversity), the genetic variation within species, and the variety of different ecosystems and habitats on Earth.
options: The number of different species of plants found in a given area of forest or grassland
The variety of all living organisms, including species diversity, genetic variation, and diversity of ecosystems
The study of living organisms and how they interact with their natural environment
The total number of individual organisms living in a particular habitat at one time
grade9-biology.answer: The variety of all living organisms, including species diversity, genetic variation, and diversity of ecosystems
acceptableAnswers: The variety of all living organisms, including species diversity, genetic variation, and diversity of ecosystems

grade9-biology.question: Give one economic reason why high biodiversity is important.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about food, medicines or tourism.
grade9-biology.explanation: High biodiversity supports economies through tourism (e.g. ecotourism), and provides raw materials such as food crops, timber and medicines derived from wild species.
options: It reduces the cost of farming because wild species compete with agricultural pests
It supports ecotourism and provides raw materials such as medicinal plants and food crops
It ensures that individual species become very numerous, making them easier to harvest
It prevents all natural disasters because diverse ecosystems absorb extreme weather events
grade9-biology.answer: It supports ecotourism and provides raw materials such as medicinal plants and food crops
acceptableAnswers: It supports ecotourism and provides raw materials such as medicinal plants and food crops

grade9-biology.question: Explain why losing a single species from an ecosystem could have wide-ranging effects.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about food webs and the roles different species play.
grade9-biology.explanation: Species are linked through food webs; if one is lost, the organisms that feed on it lose a food source and may decline, while the organisms it fed on may increase unchecked. This can destabilise the whole ecosystem.
options: Each species occupies exactly one habitat; losing it frees space for invasive species to take over immediately
Species are connected in food webs; losing one affects what eats it and what it eats, potentially destabilising the ecosystem
Every species produces oxygen; removing one species reduces the total oxygen available to other organisms
Losing a species increases biodiversity because the remaining species have more resources to share
grade9-biology.answer: Species are connected in food webs; losing one affects what eats it and what it eats, potentially destabilising the ecosystem
acceptableAnswers: Species are connected in food webs; losing one affects what eats it and what it eats, potentially destabilising the ecosystem

grade9-biology.question: Describe how a student should use a 1 m × 1 m quadrat to estimate the number of daisy plants in a 200 m² field.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about random placement, counting, and then scaling up.
grade9-biology.explanation: Place the quadrat at random positions in the field (e.g. using random coordinates). Count the number of daisy plants inside the quadrat each time. Repeat several times and calculate the mean count per quadrat. Multiply the mean by the total field area to estimate the population: mean × 200.
options: Place the quadrat at the edge of the field, count all daisies visible, and multiply by the number of quadrats that fit across the field
Count every daisy along a 10 m transect line and multiply by 20 to estimate the whole field population
Place the quadrat in the centre of the field only, count the daisies once, and record that as the field total
Place the quadrat at random positions, count daisies inside each time, find the mean count per quadrat, then multiply by 200
grade9-biology.answer: Place the quadrat at random positions, count daisies inside each time, find the mean count per quadrat, then multiply by 200
acceptableAnswers: Place the quadrat at random positions, count daisies inside each time, find the mean count per quadrat, then multiply by 200

grade9-biology.question: A student places the quadrat five times and finds: 4, 6, 5, 3 and 7 daisy plants. The field area is 200 m² and the quadrat area is 1 m². Calculate the estimated number of daisy plants in the field.
grade9-biology.hint: Step 1: find the mean count. Step 2: multiply by field area.
grade9-biology.explanation: Mean = (4+6+5+3+7) ÷ 5 = 25 ÷ 5 = 5. Estimated population = 5 × 200 = 1000 plants.

grade9-biology.question: Name two human activities that threaten biodiversity.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about how land is used and what is released into the environment.
grade9-biology.explanation: Deforestation destroys habitats; pollution (air, water, soil) poisons organisms; introduction of invasive alien species outcompetes native species; overhunting drives species to extinction.
options: Seasonal migration of large animals and natural forest fires
Ecotourism and nature conservation programmes in national parks
Deforestation and pollution (e.g. of waterways with pesticides or industrial waste)
Building wildlife corridors and captive breeding of endangered species
grade9-biology.answer: Deforestation and pollution (e.g. of waterways with pesticides or industrial waste)
acceptableAnswers: Deforestation and pollution (e.g. of waterways with pesticides or industrial waste)

grade9-biology.question: Explain how deforestation leads to a reduction in biodiversity.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about habitat loss, food sources and the cascade effects through food webs.
grade9-biology.explanation: Deforestation removes trees, destroying the habitat of many species that depend on the forest for food, shelter and breeding. This leads directly to population decline and local extinction. Species that fed on forest animals also lose food and decline. Soil erosion after tree removal further degrades the habitat for ground-dwelling species.
options: Fewer trees means less oxygen, which directly suffocates large animals before they can migrate
Removing trees increases sunlight, which benefits ground plants and increases total species diversity
Deforestation cools the local climate, which suits cold-adapted species but harms tropical ones only
Trees provide habitat and food for many species; removing them causes population decline, local extinction and food web collapse
grade9-biology.answer: Trees provide habitat and food for many species; removing them causes population decline, local extinction and food web collapse
acceptableAnswers: Trees provide habitat and food for many species; removing them causes population decline, local extinction and food web collapse

grade9-biology.question: Name two natural events that can threaten biodiversity in Mauritius.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about extreme weather events that affect the island.
grade9-biology.explanation: Cyclones and droughts are the main natural threats to biodiversity in Mauritius; cyclones destroy vegetation and nesting sites, while droughts reduce water availability and can kill plants and animals.
grade9-biology.answer: Cyclones and droughts

grade9-biology.question: Explain two ways in which a cyclone can reduce biodiversity in Mauritius.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about the physical damage to habitats and how animals and plants are directly affected.
grade9-biology.explanation: A cyclone destroys vegetation by uprooting trees and stripping leaves, removing food and shelter for animals; it can also destroy coral reefs and coastal habitats through wave action; nesting birds lose eggs and young; soil erosion after vegetation loss makes re-establishment difficult.
options: It cools the ocean temperature, which benefits cold-water species but harms warm-water reef fish
It drives all animals towards the coast, where they are easier for predators to catch
It brings heavy rainfall that floods farmland, increasing the numbers of pest species
It uproots trees and destroys habitats, and wave action damages coral reefs — both reduce species numbers
grade9-biology.answer: It uproots trees and destroys habitats, and wave action damages coral reefs — both reduce species numbers
acceptableAnswers: It uproots trees and destroys habitats, and wave action damages coral reefs — both reduce species numbers

grade9-biology.question: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
grade9-biology.hint: Reactants on the left, products on the right. Two reactants, two products.
grade9-biology.explanation: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. Chlorophyll and light energy are required but are written above/below the arrow, not as reactants.
options: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy and chlorophyll)
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (releasing energy)
Water + minerals → starch + carbon dioxide (using sunlight)
Carbon dioxide + glucose → oxygen + starch (using chlorophyll)
grade9-biology.answer: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy and chlorophyll)
acceptableAnswers: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy and chlorophyll)

grade9-biology.question: State in which part of the plant cell photosynthesis takes place.
grade9-biology.hint: It contains a green pigment.
grade9-biology.explanation: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy.
grade9-biology.answer: In the chloroplasts

grade9-biology.question: Leaves are broad and flat. Explain how this feature helps photosynthesis.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what the leaf is capturing.
grade9-biology.explanation: A broad, flat surface provides a large surface area to absorb as much sunlight as possible for photosynthesis.
options: A large flat surface maximises the area available to absorb sunlight
Being flat allows the leaf to store more glucose for nighttime respiration
A broad shape helps the leaf to absorb more mineral salts from the soil
A flat shape reduces water loss by decreasing the area exposed to wind
grade9-biology.answer: A large flat surface maximises the area available to absorb sunlight
acceptableAnswers: A large flat surface maximises the area available to absorb sunlight

grade9-biology.question: Leaves contain many stomata on the lower surface. State the function of stomata in photosynthesis.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about which gas the leaf needs to take in.
grade9-biology.explanation: Stomata allow carbon dioxide to enter the leaf by diffusion; they also allow oxygen and water vapour to leave. Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis.
options: They absorb water from the air to supply the photosynthesis reaction
They prevent oxygen from escaping so it can be used directly in the leaf
They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse into the leaf for use in photosynthesis
They release glucose produced by photosynthesis into the surrounding air
grade9-biology.answer: They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse into the leaf for use in photosynthesis
acceptableAnswers: They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse into the leaf for use in photosynthesis

grade9-biology.question: The upper layer of a leaf (palisade mesophyll) contains many chloroplasts. Explain why this layer is adapted for maximum photosynthesis.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about the position of this layer and the number of chloroplasts.
grade9-biology.explanation: The palisade mesophyll is at the top of the leaf, closest to the light source. The tall, column-like cells are packed with chloroplasts and arranged in a row to intercept as much light as possible before it reaches the lower layers.
options: The palisade layer is at the top of the leaf, close to the light, and its cells are densely packed with chloroplasts to absorb maximum light
The palisade layer contains large air spaces that allow light to scatter throughout the leaf equally
The palisade cells are at the bottom of the leaf to absorb light reflected from the ground surface
Palisade cells are thin and transparent so that light passes through them without being absorbed
grade9-biology.answer: The palisade layer is at the top of the leaf, close to the light, and its cells are densely packed with chloroplasts to absorb maximum light
acceptableAnswers: The palisade layer is at the top of the leaf, close to the light, and its cells are densely packed with chloroplasts to absorb maximum light

grade9-biology.question: A graph shows that when light intensity is low, the rate of photosynthesis is low, but when light intensity increases to a certain level, the rate levels off and does not increase further. What does the plateau (flat part) of the graph suggest?
grade9-biology.hint: If one factor is no longer limiting, something else must be.
grade9-biology.explanation: When the graph levels off, light is no longer the limiting factor. Another factor — such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature — has become limiting and is now preventing any further increase in the rate of photosynthesis.
options: The chlorophyll has been bleached by too much light, so the rate cannot rise any further
Light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature is now limiting the rate
The stomata close when light is very bright, preventing CO₂ from entering and stopping further increases
The plant has produced as much glucose as it can store, so photosynthesis stops automatically
grade9-biology.answer: Light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature is now limiting the rate
acceptableAnswers: Light is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as CO₂ concentration or temperature is now limiting the rate

grade9-biology.question: A farmer wants to increase the rate of photosynthesis in a greenhouse. Suggest two conditions they could alter.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about the three main factors that affect photosynthesis.
grade9-biology.explanation: The farmer could increase the concentration of carbon dioxide (e.g. by burning a propane heater), increase the temperature (within the optimum range), or increase the light intensity using artificial lighting.
options: Decrease temperature to slow respiration, and reduce watering to concentrate the sugars
Increase CO₂ concentration (e.g. by adding a CO₂ burner) and increase light intensity with grow-lights
Increase the amount of soil minerals and decrease the humidity to reduce water loss
Reduce light intensity to prevent chlorophyll bleaching, and add more fertiliser to the soil
grade9-biology.answer: Increase CO₂ concentration (e.g. by adding a CO₂ burner) and increase light intensity with grow-lights
acceptableAnswers: Increase CO₂ concentration (e.g. by adding a CO₂ burner) and increase light intensity with grow-lights

grade9-biology.question: A student wants to test a leaf for the presence of starch. The first step is to kill the leaf by placing it in boiling water. Why is this step needed?
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what must happen to the leaf before the iodine solution is applied.
grade9-biology.explanation: Boiling the leaf kills the cells and stops any further chemical reactions from taking place, ensuring the result reflects what happened during the experiment rather than changes after removal from the plant.
options: To break open the stomata so that iodine vapour can diffuse into the leaf cells
To stop further chemical reactions and kill the cells before the starch test
To remove the waxy cuticle so that iodine solution can enter the leaf directly
To dissolve any starch already present so that new starch can be detected accurately
grade9-biology.answer: To stop further chemical reactions and kill the cells before the starch test
acceptableAnswers: To stop further chemical reactions and kill the cells before the starch test

grade9-biology.question: The leaf is then placed in hot ethanol. What does this step remove, and why is it necessary?
grade9-biology.hint: Think about what would make it hard to see a colour change.
grade9-biology.explanation: Hot ethanol removes the green chlorophyll from the leaf. This decolorises the leaf so that the colour change produced by iodine solution (blue-black for starch) can be seen clearly against the pale background.
options: It hardens the cell walls, making the leaf firm enough to handle without breaking
It removes the starch so that the leaf can be tested for glucose instead
It removes chlorophyll, decolorising the leaf so the iodine colour change can be seen clearly
It kills any bacteria on the leaf surface that might interfere with the iodine result
grade9-biology.answer: It removes chlorophyll, decolorising the leaf so the iodine colour change can be seen clearly
acceptableAnswers: It removes chlorophyll, decolorising the leaf so the iodine colour change can be seen clearly

grade9-biology.question: After rinsing with water and spreading flat, iodine solution is added to the leaf. What colour change indicates that starch is present?
grade9-biology.hint: This is the standard iodine-starch result.
grade9-biology.explanation: Iodine solution turns from yellow-brown to blue-black when starch is present. If no starch is present the leaf stays orange-brown.
options: The iodine turns colourless where starch is present
The leaf turns bright red where starch is present
The leaf turns green where starch has been broken down
grade9-biology.answer: Yellow-brown iodine turns blue-black

grade9-biology.question: A student uses an aquatic plant (Elodea) to investigate the effect of light intensity on photosynthesis. Describe how they would vary light intensity without changing any other factor.
grade9-biology.hint: Think about moving the light source and controlling temperature and CO₂.
grade9-biology.explanation: Place the lamp at different measured distances from the plant — the further away, the lower the light intensity. Keep temperature and CO₂ concentration constant by using a water bath (to absorb heat) and sodium hydrogencarbonate solution in the water (to maintain CO₂ level).
options: Use bulbs of different colours at the same distance; add ice to cool the water after each colour change
Place the plant at different depths in the water to change the amount of light reaching it
Move the lamp to different distances from the plant; use a water bath to control temperature and sodium hydrogencarbonate to maintain CO₂
Change the concentration of CO₂ in the water by adding different amounts of acid to the tank
grade9-biology.answer: Move the lamp to different distances from the plant; use a water bath to control temperature and sodium hydrogencarbonate to maintain CO₂
acceptableAnswers: Move the lamp to different distances from the plant; use a water bath to control temperature and sodium hydrogencarbonate to maintain CO₂

grade9-biology.question: The student counts the number of oxygen bubbles produced per minute. Why is this a suitable measure of the rate of photosynthesis?
grade9-biology.hint: Look at the word equation — what is oxygen in photosynthesis?
grade9-biology.explanation: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis; the more oxygen produced, the faster photosynthesis is occurring. Counting the bubbles per minute gives a reliable measure of the rate because the bubbles are produced at a rate directly linked to the rate of the reaction.
options: Oxygen bubbles are easy to count, but they actually measure respiration rate rather than photosynthesis
Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, so more bubbles per minute indicates a higher rate of photosynthesis
Oxygen bubbles measure the rate of water absorption through the roots, which drives photosynthesis
Each bubble contains a fixed amount of glucose, so counting them gives the total glucose produced
grade9-biology.answer: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, so more bubbles per minute indicates a higher rate of photosynthesis
acceptableAnswers: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, so more bubbles per minute indicates a higher rate of photosynthesis

grade9-biology.question: The student finds that increasing light intensity beyond a certain point does not increase the bubble count any further. Suggest a reason for this result.
grade9-biology.hint: Another factor must now be in short supply.
grade9-biology.explanation: When light is no longer limiting, another factor — most likely carbon dioxide concentration — is limiting the rate. Even though there is plenty of light, there is not enough CO₂ for photosynthesis to go any faster.
options: The plant has used up all its chlorophyll and can no longer absorb any additional light
Too much light destroys the enzyme responsible for photosynthesis, so the rate falls
The plant switches to respiration when light intensity is very high, producing CO₂ instead of O₂
Another factor such as CO₂ concentration is now limiting the rate, so extra light has no further effect
grade9-biology.answer: Another factor such as CO₂ concentration is now limiting the rate, so extra light has no further effect
acceptableAnswers: Another factor such as CO₂ concentration is now limiting the rate, so extra light has no further effect

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these is a cause of water pollution?
options: Sunlight reaching the surface of a river
Rainwater falling onto a clean river
Untreated sewage released into a river
grade9-chemistry.answer: Untreated sewage released into a river
acceptableAnswers: Untreated sewage released into a river
grade9-chemistry.hint: Pollution means something harmful being added.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Untreated sewage adds harmful material to the water, which is water pollution.

grade9-chemistry.question: Fertiliser washed off a field into a river is a pollutant because it:
options: Removes all the salt from the water
Turns the water permanently into acid
Makes the water flow much more quickly downstream
Adds nutrients that upset the balance of life in the water
grade9-chemistry.answer: Adds nutrients that upset the balance of life in the water
acceptableAnswers: Adds nutrients that upset the balance of life in the water
grade9-chemistry.hint: Fertiliser feeds plants - including the ones in the river.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Fertiliser adds nitrates and phosphates, which feed algae and set off the chain of events called eutrophication.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these would best reduce water pollution from a factory?
options: Treating the waste water before it is released
Using a wider pipe to release the waste
Releasing the waste at night instead of by day
grade9-chemistry.answer: Treating the waste water before it is released
acceptableAnswers: Treating the waste water before it is released
grade9-chemistry.hint: Only one of these changes what is in the water.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Treatment removes the harmful material; moving it or diluting it leaves the pollutant in the river.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is an oil spill at sea so damaging to sea birds?
options: Oil removes all of the light from the surface of the sea
Oil coats their feathers so they can no longer keep warm or float
Oil makes the sea water too salty for them to drink
Oil makes the sea water freeze around them
grade9-chemistry.answer: Oil coats their feathers so they can no longer keep warm or float
acceptableAnswers: Oil coats their feathers so they can no longer keep warm or float
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what the feathers normally do.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Feathers trap air for warmth and buoyancy; oil destroys that, so the birds become cold and cannot float.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is eutrophication?
options: Excess nutrients cause algae to grow rapidly in water
A river dries up completely during a drought
Water becomes acidic because of acid rain
Salt builds up in a river until fish cannot live
grade9-chemistry.answer: Excess nutrients cause algae to grow rapidly in water
acceptableAnswers: Excess nutrients cause algae to grow rapidly in water
grade9-chemistry.hint: It starts with fertiliser reaching the water.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Eutrophication begins when extra nutrients make algae grow rapidly, forming a bloom on the surface.

grade9-chemistry.question: Put the stages of eutrophication in the right order.
options: Algae bloom, nutrients enter, oxygen rises, fish die, algae decay
Oxygen falls, nutrients enter, fish die, algae bloom, algae decay
Fish die, oxygen falls, algae bloom, nutrients enter, algae decay
Nutrients enter, algae bloom, algae die and decay, oxygen falls, fish die
grade9-chemistry.answer: Nutrients enter, algae bloom, algae die and decay, oxygen falls, fish die
acceptableAnswers: Nutrients enter, algae bloom, algae die and decay, oxygen falls, fish die
grade9-chemistry.hint: Follow the chain from the fertiliser to the fish.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Nutrients feed an algal bloom; when the algae die, decay bacteria use up the oxygen, and the fish suffocate.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why do fish die during eutrophication even though nothing poisonous was added?
options: The algae remove all of the salt dissolved in the water
The water becomes far too cold for the fish to survive
The algae feed on the fish directly as they grow
Bacteria decaying the dead algae use up the dissolved oxygen
grade9-chemistry.answer: Bacteria decaying the dead algae use up the dissolved oxygen
acceptableAnswers: Bacteria decaying the dead algae use up the dissolved oxygen
grade9-chemistry.hint: The fish are short of something they need, not poisoned.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Decay bacteria respire and consume the dissolved oxygen, so the fish suffocate.

grade9-chemistry.question: The table shows the oxygen in a river below a farm. Where is the water most polluted?
options: At 1 km, where the oxygen is 6 units
At 4 km, where the oxygen has recovered
At 2 km, where the oxygen is lowest
At 0 km, where the oxygen is highest
grade9-chemistry.answer: At 2 km, where the oxygen is lowest
acceptableAnswers: At 2 km, where the oxygen is lowest
grade9-chemistry.hint: Low dissolved oxygen is the sign of pollution here.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Oxygen falls to 3 units at 2 km, the lowest value in the table, so that is where the pollution is worst.

grade9-chemistry.question: Reading the same table, what does the value at 4 km show?
options: The river is equally polluted all the way along
The river is recovering as it flows further downstream
The pollution becomes worse the further it flows
The farm is releasing more waste at 4 km
grade9-chemistry.answer: The river is recovering as it flows further downstream
acceptableAnswers: The river is recovering as it flows further downstream
grade9-chemistry.hint: Compare 4 km with 2 km.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Oxygen rises from 3 units at 2 km to 8 units at 4 km, so the river is recovering downstream.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which gas is produced when a fuel burns in too little air?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Carbon monoxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: Incomplete burning gives a gas with one oxygen atom.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Burning in a limited supply of air is incomplete combustion, which produces poisonous carbon monoxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is carbon monoxide so dangerous?
options: It burns the skin as soon as it is touched
It has a very strong smell that quickly causes headaches
It stops the blood from carrying oxygen, and it has no smell
It makes the air far too cold to breathe
grade9-chemistry.answer: It stops the blood from carrying oxygen, and it has no smell
acceptableAnswers: It stops the blood from carrying oxygen, and it has no smell
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what it does in the blood, and why it is not noticed.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen, and being colourless and odourless it gives no warning.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which pollutant is released mainly by burning coal that contains sulfur?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sulfur dioxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: The sulfur in the fuel combines with oxygen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sulfur in the coal burns to sulfur dioxide, one of the two main causes of acid rain.

grade9-chemistry.question: Read the table. A power station burning coal releases which gas?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sulfur dioxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: Find the row for the coal power station.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The table gives sulfur dioxide as the main gas released by a coal power station.

grade9-chemistry.question: Read the table. Which source is given for CFCs?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Old refrigerators
grade9-chemistry.hint: Find CFCs in the right-hand column and read across.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The table gives old refrigerators as the source of CFCs.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why were CFCs banned in most countries?
options: They make the rain far more acidic than it used to be
They turn directly into carbon monoxide once in the air
They damage the ozone layer that shields us from ultraviolet light
They cause the level of the sea to rise very quickly
grade9-chemistry.answer: They damage the ozone layer that shields us from ultraviolet light
acceptableAnswers: They damage the ozone layer that shields us from ultraviolet light
grade9-chemistry.hint: Their damage is high in the atmosphere.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: CFCs break down ozone in the upper atmosphere, thinning the layer that absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these is a greenhouse gas?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Carbon dioxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: It is released whenever a carbon fuel burns.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Carbon dioxide absorbs heat radiated from the Earth, so it is a greenhouse gas. Nitrogen and oxygen are not.

grade9-chemistry.question: How does a greenhouse gas warm the Earth?
options: It pushes the Earth slowly closer to the Sun over time
It produces heat of its own high inside the atmosphere
It absorbs heat radiated from the Earth instead of letting it escape
It stops the sunlight from reaching the surface of the Earth
grade9-chemistry.answer: It absorbs heat radiated from the Earth instead of letting it escape
acceptableAnswers: It absorbs heat radiated from the Earth instead of letting it escape
grade9-chemistry.hint: The energy arrives as light and tries to leave as heat.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sunlight passes in and warms the surface; greenhouse gases absorb the heat radiated back out, keeping it in the atmosphere.

grade9-chemistry.question: Read the table. Which greenhouse gas comes from cattle and rice fields?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Methane
grade9-chemistry.hint: Find the row for cattle and rice fields.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The table gives methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, for cattle and rice fields.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which human activity has added most carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Burning fossil fuels
grade9-chemistry.hint: Which of these releases carbon that was locked away?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon that had been stored underground for millions of years.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which two gases are the main causes of acid rain?
options: Oxygen and nitrogen from the air
Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
acceptableAnswers: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: Both are released when fuels burn.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rain water to form sulfuric and nitric acids.

grade9-chemistry.question: How does acid rain form?
options: The Sun heats rain water until it turns to acid
Sea water evaporates and carries acid into the clouds
Pollutant gases dissolve in water droplets in the clouds
Rain water becomes acidic as it soaks into the soil
grade9-chemistry.answer: Pollutant gases dissolve in water droplets in the clouds
acceptableAnswers: Pollutant gases dissolve in water droplets in the clouds
grade9-chemistry.hint: The acid is made in the air, before the rain falls.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in cloud droplets, forming acids that fall as rain.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these is a harmful effect of acid rain?
options: Lakes become far too warm for fish to survive
Lakes become too acidic for fish to survive
Rivers dry up completely in summer
The soil becomes too salty for any crop
grade9-chemistry.answer: Lakes become too acidic for fish to survive
acceptableAnswers: Lakes become too acidic for fish to survive
grade9-chemistry.hint: The clue is in the word acid.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Acid rain lowers the pH of lakes and rivers until fish and other water life can no longer survive.

grade9-chemistry.question: Acid rain damages limestone statues and buildings. Why?
options: The acid freezes inside the stone and cracks it
The acid changes the colour of the stone only
The acid reacts with the limestone and wears it away
The acid makes the stone much heavier than before
grade9-chemistry.answer: The acid reacts with the limestone and wears it away
acceptableAnswers: The acid reacts with the limestone and wears it away
grade9-chemistry.hint: Limestone is a carbonate, and acids react with carbonates.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Limestone is calcium carbonate; acid reacts with it, dissolving the surface and eroding the detail.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which measure would most directly reduce acid rain?
options: Building the chimneys of power stations taller
Burning the same fuel more quickly
Adding lime to the chimneys of every house
Removing sulfur from fuels before they are burned
grade9-chemistry.answer: Removing sulfur from fuels before they are burned
acceptableAnswers: Removing sulfur from fuels before they are burned
grade9-chemistry.hint: Deal with the cause, not with where it lands.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Taking the sulfur out before burning stops the sulfur dioxide being made at all; a taller chimney only moves it.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is meant by global warming?
options: A rise in temperature in one country only
The hot weather that comes every summer
A rise in the average temperature of the Earth
The warming of water in a kettle
grade9-chemistry.answer: A rise in the average temperature of the Earth
acceptableAnswers: A rise in the average temperature of the Earth
grade9-chemistry.hint: Global means worldwide, and it is an average.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Global warming is the rise in the average temperature of the whole Earth over many years.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these is a consequence of global warming?
options: The atmosphere loses all its oxygen
Sea levels rise as ice melts and water expands
Days become longer than nights everywhere
The Earth moves further from the Sun
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sea levels rise as ice melts and water expands
acceptableAnswers: Sea levels rise as ice melts and water expands
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about ice, and about what warm water does.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Warming melts land ice and makes sea water expand, so sea levels rise - a serious risk for an island like Mauritius.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is a rising sea level a particular concern for Mauritius?
options: The island would drift further from Africa
The lagoon water would become fresh instead of salty
Much of the population and infrastructure is near the coast
The island would become permanently colder
grade9-chemistry.answer: Much of the population and infrastructure is near the coast
acceptableAnswers: Much of the population and infrastructure is near the coast
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about where people live on a small island.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A small island has most of its people, roads, hotels and farmland close to the shore, so coastal flooding and erosion matter greatly.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which action would do most to slow global warming?
options: Using private cars instead of buses and public transport
Cutting down more forest to make additional farmland
Generating electricity from renewable sources instead of coal
Fitting air conditioners into a great many more buildings
grade9-chemistry.answer: Generating electricity from renewable sources instead of coal
acceptableAnswers: Generating electricity from renewable sources instead of coal
grade9-chemistry.hint: The cause is carbon dioxide from burning fuels.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Replacing fossil fuels with renewables cuts carbon dioxide emissions at their largest source.

grade9-chemistry.question: Give the term for the rapid growth of algae caused by excess nutrients entering water.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Eutrophication
grade9-chemistry.hint: It begins with fertiliser reaching a river.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Eutrophication is the enrichment of water by nutrients, causing algae to grow rapidly.

grade9-chemistry.question: Name the poisonous gas formed when a fuel burns in too little air.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Carbon monoxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: It has no smell and no colour.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: Name the gas released by burning coal that is a main cause of acid rain.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sulfur dioxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: It comes from the sulfur in the fuel.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain water to form an acid.

grade9-chemistry.question: Name the greenhouse gas released whenever a carbon fuel is burned.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Carbon dioxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: Two words.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Burning a carbon fuel releases carbon dioxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: State one effect of global warming on the sea.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sea levels rise
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about ice melting and water expanding.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Melting land ice and the expansion of warming water both raise sea levels.

grade9-chemistry.question: State one way of reducing water pollution from a factory.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Treat the waste water before releasing it
acceptableAnswers: Treat the waste water before releasing it
grade9-chemistry.hint: Change what is in the water, not where it goes.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Treating waste water removes the harmful material before it reaches the river.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of the following is a non-biodegradable water pollutant?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Plastic waste
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about which material does not break down naturally.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Plastic is non-biodegradable — micro-organisms cannot decompose it — so it persists in rivers and oceans for centuries.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which human activity is the greatest cause of nitrate pollution in rivers?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Using fertilisers on farmland
grade9-chemistry.hint: Nitrates come from a material added to soil.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Fertilisers containing nitrates and phosphates are washed by rain from fields into rivers, enriching the water and causing pollution.

grade9-chemistry.question: A factory releases hot water into a river. Why does this reduce the oxygen dissolved in the river?
options: The heat drives all the fish to the surface where they breathe it
Warm water is denser and sinks, trapping the oxygen at the bottom
Hot water reacts with oxygen to form water vapour
Warm water holds less dissolved gas than cold water
grade9-chemistry.answer: Warm water holds less dissolved gas than cold water
acceptableAnswers: Warm water holds less dissolved gas than cold water
grade9-chemistry.hint: Solubility of gases changes with temperature.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The solubility of oxygen in water decreases as temperature rises, so thermal pollution lowers the dissolved oxygen level and harms aquatic life.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these best describes a point source of water pollution?
options: Rain washing fertiliser from fields into a stream
Soil erosion along the banks of a river
A pipe releasing factory waste directly into a river
Acid rain falling onto the surface of a lake
grade9-chemistry.answer: A pipe releasing factory waste directly into a river
acceptableAnswers: A pipe releasing factory waste directly into a river
grade9-chemistry.hint: A point source is one identifiable discharge location.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A factory discharge pipe is a single, identifiable point; other examples (fertiliser runoff, acid rain) are diffuse or non-point sources.

grade9-chemistry.question: Heavy metals such as lead and mercury are water pollutants. What makes them especially dangerous?
options: They dissolve in water and make it turn bright colours
They make water taste salty, so fish cannot survive
They evaporate from the river and become air pollutants
They accumulate in living tissues and become more concentrated up the food chain
grade9-chemistry.answer: They accumulate in living tissues and become more concentrated up the food chain
acceptableAnswers: They accumulate in living tissues and become more concentrated up the food chain
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what happens when small fish are eaten by larger fish.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Heavy metals are not excreted; they build up in body tissues (bioaccumulation) and become progressively more concentrated at each level of the food chain (biomagnification).

grade9-chemistry.question: Detergents in river water cause foam to form on the surface. What effect does a thick layer of foam have on the river ecosystem?
options: It blocks sunlight, reducing photosynthesis by aquatic plants
It makes the water taste bitter, deterring birds from drinking
It heats the water, encouraging fish to breed more rapidly
It increases the dissolved oxygen level in the water
grade9-chemistry.answer: It blocks sunlight, reducing photosynthesis by aquatic plants
acceptableAnswers: It blocks sunlight, reducing photosynthesis by aquatic plants
grade9-chemistry.hint: What do aquatic plants need to produce oxygen?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A foam layer blocks sunlight, preventing photosynthesis by submerged plants and algae, which then produce less oxygen, harming other aquatic life.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these is the best method of treating sewage before releasing it into a river?
options: Diluting it with ten times as much clean river water
Filtering it through a layer of sand to remove the colour
Heating it to kill any fish swimming in it
Biological treatment using micro-organisms to break down waste
grade9-chemistry.answer: Biological treatment using micro-organisms to break down waste
acceptableAnswers: Biological treatment using micro-organisms to break down waste
grade9-chemistry.hint: Only one method actually removes the harmful material.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Biological sewage treatment uses bacteria to decompose organic waste, removing it rather than merely diluting or masking it.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student tests water at three points along a river: above a factory, 200 m below it, and 1 km below it. The pH values are 7.2, 4.8, and 6.9. What does this suggest?
options: The factory is releasing an acidic effluent that the river gradually neutralises
The river is producing acid naturally as it flows downstream
The pH meter was faulty at the 200 m measurement point
The factory is removing pollutants from the water at 1 km
grade9-chemistry.answer: The factory is releasing an acidic effluent that the river gradually neutralises
acceptableAnswers: The factory is releasing an acidic effluent that the river gradually neutralises
grade9-chemistry.hint: Compare the pH values: what changes and what does the trend show?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The pH drops sharply near the factory discharge and recovers downstream, showing the river is self-purifying as the acidic effluent is diluted and neutralised.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these best describes the effect of oil on a marine ecosystem?
options: It coats the surface, reducing gas exchange and harming wildlife
It dissolves in seawater and has no lasting effect
It makes seawater denser, helping ships float more easily
It causes the seawater to evaporate more quickly than normal
grade9-chemistry.answer: It coats the surface, reducing gas exchange and harming wildlife
acceptableAnswers: It coats the surface, reducing gas exchange and harming wildlife
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what oil does when it floats on water.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: An oil slick on the sea surface reduces oxygen transfer from air to water, smothers marine organisms, and coats seabirds' feathers, destroying their insulation and buoyancy.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why are pesticides considered persistent water pollutants?
options: They are produced continuously by aquatic plants
They evaporate from the water surface within a few hours
They resist biodegradation and remain in the environment for years
They are always present in rain water in large amounts
grade9-chemistry.answer: They resist biodegradation and remain in the environment for years
acceptableAnswers: They resist biodegradation and remain in the environment for years
grade9-chemistry.hint: Persistent means lasting a very long time.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Many pesticides are not easily broken down by micro-organisms; they persist in water and sediment and accumulate in the food chain.

grade9-chemistry.question: What does the term BOD (Biological Oxygen Demand) measure?
options: The amount of oxygen used by micro-organisms decomposing organic matter in water
The rate at which fish absorb oxygen from water through their gills
The volume of oxygen released by aquatic plants during photosynthesis
The total dissolved oxygen content of unpolluted river water
grade9-chemistry.answer: The amount of oxygen used by micro-organisms decomposing organic matter in water
acceptableAnswers: The amount of oxygen used by micro-organisms decomposing organic matter in water
grade9-chemistry.hint: High BOD means micro-organisms are very active — why would that be?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A high BOD indicates a large amount of organic pollutant, because decomposer bacteria consume more oxygen as they break down the waste.

grade9-chemistry.question: A river's BOD is measured upstream and downstream of a sewage outlet. Upstream BOD = 2 mg/L; downstream BOD = 12 mg/L. What can you conclude?
options: The upstream sample was taken from a different river
The river water is unusually clean downstream of the outlet
Micro-organisms are producing oxygen faster downstream
The sewage outlet is adding significant organic pollution to the river
grade9-chemistry.answer: The sewage outlet is adding significant organic pollution to the river
acceptableAnswers: The sewage outlet is adding significant organic pollution to the river
grade9-chemistry.hint: BOD rises when more organic matter is being decomposed.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The six-fold increase in BOD downstream of the sewage outlet shows that organic matter from the sewage is fuelling bacterial decomposition, greatly increasing oxygen demand.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these actions would most effectively reduce water pollution from a large farm?
options: Creating buffer strips of vegetation between fields and waterways
Spreading fertiliser only at night when the weather is cooler
Planting more crops to absorb the rain water before it runs off
Building deeper drainage ditches to carry water away faster
grade9-chemistry.answer: Creating buffer strips of vegetation between fields and waterways
acceptableAnswers: Creating buffer strips of vegetation between fields and waterways
grade9-chemistry.hint: What can slow or filter water before it reaches a river?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Vegetated buffer strips intercept surface runoff, absorbing and filtering out excess nitrates and pesticides before they reach the waterway.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which nutrient ions entering a lake most directly trigger eutrophication?
options: Sulfate and calcium ions from limestone quarrying
Carbonate and bicarbonate ions from acid rain
Chloride and sodium ions from road salt
Nitrate and phosphate ions from fertilisers
grade9-chemistry.answer: Nitrate and phosphate ions from fertilisers
acceptableAnswers: Nitrate and phosphate ions from fertilisers
grade9-chemistry.hint: These ions are nutrients for plant growth.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Nitrates and phosphates act as plant nutrients; their excess causes an explosive growth of algae that begins the eutrophication process.

grade9-chemistry.question: During eutrophication, why does the population of decomposer bacteria increase rapidly?
options: Warm water temperatures encourage them to photosynthesise
Dead algae provide them with a large supply of organic matter
The algal bloom shades them from harmful ultraviolet light
Reduced competition from fish allows them to breed freely
grade9-chemistry.answer: Dead algae provide them with a large supply of organic matter
acceptableAnswers: Dead algae provide them with a large supply of organic matter
grade9-chemistry.hint: Decomposers break down dead organic material.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: When the algal bloom collapses and the algae die, the mass of dead organic matter is an ideal food source for decomposer bacteria, whose population explodes.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does an algal bloom initially block light from reaching submerged plants?
options: The algae produce carbon dioxide that absorbs visible light
The algal bloom heats the water so rapidly that it evaporates
The dense mat of algae on the surface intercepts the sunlight
The algae release dark pigments that cloud the water
grade9-chemistry.answer: The dense mat of algae on the surface intercepts the sunlight
acceptableAnswers: The dense mat of algae on the surface intercepts the sunlight
grade9-chemistry.hint: The algae are floating at the surface.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A dense algal bloom on the water surface shades the water below, so submerged aquatic plants receive insufficient light for photosynthesis and die.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the correct order of events in eutrophication?
options: Algal bloom → nutrient enrichment → fish die → oxygen depletion → decomposition
Nutrient enrichment → algal bloom → algal die-off → decomposition → oxygen depletion → death of fish
Oxygen depletion → algal bloom → decomposition → nutrient enrichment → fish die
Fish die → oxygen depletion → algal bloom → nutrient enrichment → decomposition
grade9-chemistry.answer: Nutrient enrichment → algal bloom → algal die-off → decomposition → oxygen depletion → death of fish
acceptableAnswers: Nutrient enrichment → algal bloom → algal die-off → decomposition → oxygen depletion → death of fish
grade9-chemistry.hint: Follow the chain from the fertiliser to the final effect.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Nutrients stimulate algal growth; when the bloom dies, bacteria decompose it using up oxygen, leaving too little for fish to survive.

grade9-chemistry.question: A pond has the following dissolved oxygen readings: 9 mg/L in January, 11 mg/L in April, 2 mg/L in July, 8 mg/L in October. What most likely caused the July reading?
options: Heavy July rainfall diluted the pond water and washed in oxygen
An algal bloom died in summer, and bacterial decomposition removed dissolved oxygen
Fish were released into the pond in July and consumed all the oxygen
Cold winter water holds more oxygen than warm summer water
grade9-chemistry.answer: An algal bloom died in summer, and bacterial decomposition removed dissolved oxygen
acceptableAnswers: An algal bloom died in summer, and bacterial decomposition removed dissolved oxygen
grade9-chemistry.hint: Link the season to algal growth, then consider what happens when algae die.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Warm summer conditions favour an algal bloom; when the algae die their decomposition consumes dissolved oxygen, causing the crash to 2 mg/L.

grade9-chemistry.question: Deoxygenation during eutrophication is said to be a secondary effect. Why?
options: Only a secondary pollutant such as carbon monoxide can remove dissolved oxygen
Oxygen is only removed when the temperature rises above a threshold value
The deoxygenation happens a long time after the nutrients enter, so it is secondary in time only
