grade9-chemistry.answer: To produce a concentrated solution that becomes highly supersaturated on cooling, maximising crystal yield
acceptableAnswers: To produce a concentrated solution that becomes highly supersaturated on cooling, maximising crystal yield
grade9-chemistry.hint: Less solvent means more of the product is forced out of solution when cooled.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: With a minimum volume of hot solvent the solution is concentrated; on cooling it quickly becomes supersaturated with respect to the product, maximising the mass of pure crystals recovered.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which technique — evaporation or cooling — gives larger, purer crystals, and why?
options: Boiling gives the purest crystals because impurities are decomposed by the heat
Filtration is what determines crystal size — evaporation and cooling have no effect
Rapid evaporation gives larger crystals because the solute is concentrated quickly
Slow cooling gives larger, purer crystals because ions have time to join the crystal lattice selectively
grade9-chemistry.answer: Slow cooling gives larger, purer crystals because ions have time to join the crystal lattice selectively
acceptableAnswers: Slow cooling gives larger, purer crystals because ions have time to join the crystal lattice selectively
grade9-chemistry.hint: Large crystals grow slowly.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Slow cooling allows ions (or molecules) to migrate to the correct positions in the growing crystal lattice; rapid crystallisation traps impurities and produces small, impure crystals.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the name given to the liquid that remains after the crystals are filtered off?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Mother liquor
grade9-chemistry.hint: It is the "mother" from which the crystals grew.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The solution left after crystallisation and filtration is called the mother liquor; it is a saturated solution at the lower temperature and still contains dissolved solute.

grade9-chemistry.question: Copper sulfate crystals are blue (CuSO₄·5H₂O) but anhydrous copper sulfate is white. What does this tell you about the crystals?
options: The crystals are naturally coloured by a dye present in the copper ore
The blue colour shows the crystals are still wet with surface moisture
The crystals contain water of crystallisation chemically bonded in the crystal structure
The crystals are blue because copper ions absorb all light except blue
grade9-chemistry.answer: The crystals contain water of crystallisation chemically bonded in the crystal structure
acceptableAnswers: The crystals contain water of crystallisation chemically bonded in the crystal structure
grade9-chemistry.hint: Anhydrous means without water.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Water of crystallisation (5 molecules per formula unit in CuSO₄·5H₂O) is chemically incorporated into the crystal lattice; when this water is driven off by strong heating the structure changes and the compound becomes white anhydrous CuSO₄.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why would evaporation to dryness NOT be recommended for crystallising sodium chloride?
options: Sodium chloride is insoluble and will not form a solution in the first place
Rapid evaporation produces tiny impure crystals and can cause the salt to spit out of the dish
Sodium chloride crystals are too large to fit in an evaporating dish
Heating sodium chloride to dryness causes it to decompose into sodium and chlorine
grade9-chemistry.answer: Rapid evaporation produces tiny impure crystals and can cause the salt to spit out of the dish
acceptableAnswers: Rapid evaporation produces tiny impure crystals and can cause the salt to spit out of the dish
grade9-chemistry.hint: Evaporation to dryness is too fast and too hot for good crystal formation.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Evaporating to complete dryness produces a fine, impure crust; it also risks the solution spitting as it approaches dryness. The recommended approach is to evaporate until a saturated solution remains, then allow it to cool and crystallise slowly.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the purpose of seeding a supersaturated solution with a tiny crystal of the solute?
options: The seed crystal dissolves and lowers the concentration to allow crystallisation
The seed crystal provides a surface on which larger crystals can grow
The seed crystal raises the temperature of the solution to produce better crystals
The seed crystal acts as a filter to remove impurities from the solution
grade9-chemistry.answer: The seed crystal provides a surface on which larger crystals can grow
acceptableAnswers: The seed crystal provides a surface on which larger crystals can grow
grade9-chemistry.hint: Crystallisation needs a starting point.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A supersaturated solution will not crystallise spontaneously without a nucleus; a seed crystal provides the ordered surface on which solute particles can deposit and grow, initiating crystallisation.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student evaporates a salt solution and measures the mass of crystals: 8.4 g. She then redissolves them in water and recrystallises once more, obtaining 7.9 g. What is the most likely reason for the lower mass on the second occasion?
options: Recrystallisation converts some salt into an insoluble compound
The crystals decomposed during redissolving, releasing a gas
The second crop of crystals was larger, so their mass was less despite the same number of ions
Some solute was lost in the mother liquor left behind after filtration
grade9-chemistry.answer: Some solute was lost in the mother liquor left behind after filtration
acceptableAnswers: Some solute was lost in the mother liquor left behind after filtration
grade9-chemistry.hint: Where does the missing solute go?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: After cooling, some solute remains dissolved in the mother liquor at the new saturation point; this is not recovered by filtration, so each recrystallisation reduces the yield slightly while improving purity.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is sublimation?
options: The dissolving of a solid directly into a gas phase
The change of state from gas to solid by cooling
The change of state from liquid to gas by heating
The change of state directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state
grade9-chemistry.answer: The change of state directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state
acceptableAnswers: The change of state directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state
grade9-chemistry.hint: It misses out the liquid state entirely.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sublimation is a direct phase transition from solid to gas (and the reverse, deposition, is gas directly to solid); the substance never becomes liquid.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these substances is well known for undergoing sublimation at room temperature?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Iodine
grade9-chemistry.hint: It is a purple-coloured solid that produces a purple vapour.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Iodine is a classic example of a subliming substance: at room temperature it slowly produces a visible purple vapour, and on gentle warming it rapidly sublimes without melting.

grade9-chemistry.question: How is sublimation used to separate a mixture of iodine and sand?
options: The mixture is dissolved in water; iodine floats to the top and sand sinks
The mixture is gently heated; iodine sublimes to vapour and re-solidifies on a cold surface above, leaving sand behind
A magnet is passed through the mixture; iodine is attracted and sand is not
The mixture is filtered; iodine passes through the filter paper and sand is retained
grade9-chemistry.answer: The mixture is gently heated; iodine sublimes to vapour and re-solidifies on a cold surface above, leaving sand behind
acceptableAnswers: The mixture is gently heated; iodine sublimes to vapour and re-solidifies on a cold surface above, leaving sand behind
grade9-chemistry.hint: Iodine sublimes; sand does not change state.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Gentle heating converts iodine directly to vapour (sublimation); the vapour rises and deposits as pure iodine crystals on the cool surface of an inverted cold water-filled flask placed above. Sand stays at the bottom.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is dry ice, and why is sublimation useful in its application?
options: Frozen water with all hydrogen removed; it sublimes at 0 °C leaving the room dry
Frozen ammonia; its sublimation absorbs heat and is used in refrigerators
Solid carbon dioxide; it sublimes at −78 °C, producing cooling without any liquid mess
Solidified nitrogen; it sublimes at room temperature leaving no residue
grade9-chemistry.answer: Solid carbon dioxide; it sublimes at −78 °C, producing cooling without any liquid mess
acceptableAnswers: Solid carbon dioxide; it sublimes at −78 °C, producing cooling without any liquid mess
grade9-chemistry.hint: CO₂ skips the liquid phase at atmospheric pressure.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Solid CO₂ (dry ice) sublimes directly to CO₂ gas at −78.5 °C under atmospheric pressure; this makes it ideal for cooling food in transport because it leaves no liquid residue.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which property of a substance determines whether it can be separated from a non-subliming solid by sublimation?
options: A much higher melting point than the other component
A different colour that makes it easy to see when it has moved
A much higher density so that gravity separates the two solids
The ability to convert directly from solid to gas at a temperature where the other component does not vaporise
grade9-chemistry.answer: The ability to convert directly from solid to gas at a temperature where the other component does not vaporise
acceptableAnswers: The ability to convert directly from solid to gas at a temperature where the other component does not vaporise
grade9-chemistry.hint: Only one of them changes to gas when heated.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: For sublimation to achieve separation, only one component must sublime; the non-subliming component stays as a solid, and the sublimed component is deposited as a pure solid elsewhere.

grade9-chemistry.question: Ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl) sublimes on gentle heating, dissociating into ammonia and hydrogen chloride gas, which recombine on cooling. Is this pure sublimation?
options: Yes — both gases are colourless and recombine, so the overall process is physical
No — pure sublimation involves no chemical change; this involves dissociation and recombination (a chemical process)
No — sublimation can only occur in vacuum; at atmospheric pressure this must be decomposition
Yes — the solid disappears and reappears without melting, which is the definition of sublimation
grade9-chemistry.answer: No — pure sublimation involves no chemical change; this involves dissociation and recombination (a chemical process)
acceptableAnswers: No — pure sublimation involves no chemical change; this involves dissociation and recombination (a chemical process)
grade9-chemistry.hint: Sublimation is a physical change; splitting into two different gases is a chemical change.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: True sublimation is a physical phase change with no change in chemical composition; NH₄Cl undergoes thermal decomposition (NH₄Cl → NH₃ + HCl) on heating — a chemical reaction — even though the product appears in the same form on cooling.

grade9-chemistry.question: What happens to the vapour from a subliming substance when it meets a cold surface?
options: It deposits back as a solid (deposition)
It reacts with the surface to form a new compound
It stays as a gas and does not change
grade9-chemistry.answer: It deposits back as a solid (deposition)
acceptableAnswers: It deposits back as a solid (deposition)
grade9-chemistry.hint: The reverse of sublimation is called deposition.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: When the vapour of a subliming substance cools on contact with a cold surface, it deposits directly as a solid without first becoming liquid — this is called deposition (or reverse sublimation).

grade9-chemistry.question: A technician wants to separate naphthalene (sublimes around 80 °C) from a mixture with potassium chloride (does not sublime, m.p. 770 °C). She heats the mixture to 70 °C. What does she observe?
options: KCl dissolves in the naphthalene as it melts, and the mixture runs to the bottom
No change — naphthalene only sublimes above 100 °C
Both substances sublime and deposit separately on different parts of the cold surface
White naphthalene vapour rises and deposits as white crystals on a cold surface; KCl remains as a solid
grade9-chemistry.answer: White naphthalene vapour rises and deposits as white crystals on a cold surface; KCl remains as a solid
acceptableAnswers: White naphthalene vapour rises and deposits as white crystals on a cold surface; KCl remains as a solid
grade9-chemistry.hint: Naphthalene begins to sublime below its melting point.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Even below the melting point (80 °C) naphthalene sublimes slowly; at 70 °C sufficient vapour forms to be collected on a cold surface. KCl, with melting point 770 °C and negligible vapour pressure at 70 °C, remains solid.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is sublimation used in the pharmaceutical industry to purify drugs?
options: It dissolves the drug in a gas and allows impurities to precipitate
It is faster than filtration and requires no solvent
It separates the desired compound from non-subliming impurities with minimal heat damage to the product
It forces the drug to react with impurities, making them insoluble and easier to remove
grade9-chemistry.answer: It separates the desired compound from non-subliming impurities with minimal heat damage to the product
acceptableAnswers: It separates the desired compound from non-subliming impurities with minimal heat damage to the product
grade9-chemistry.hint: Sublimation avoids dissolving in solvent and extreme temperatures.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sublimation purifies heat-sensitive compounds without using solvent; the product sublimes away from non-volatile impurities and is collected as a pure solid, avoiding oxidation or hydrolysis that might occur in solution.

grade9-chemistry.question: Moth balls (paradichlorobenzene) are placed in a wardrobe. Over time they disappear. What is the correct explanation?
options: They sublime slowly at room temperature, releasing vapour that deters moths
They evaporate by first melting and then vaporising as a liquid
They dissolve in the moisture in the air inside the wardrobe
They are eaten by the moths themselves as part of the pest-control mechanism
grade9-chemistry.answer: They sublime slowly at room temperature, releasing vapour that deters moths
acceptableAnswers: They sublime slowly at room temperature, releasing vapour that deters moths
grade9-chemistry.hint: The solid disappears without leaving any liquid puddle.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Paradichlorobenzene has a measurable vapour pressure at room temperature and sublimes slowly; the vapour has a strong smell that repels moths.

grade9-chemistry.question: Freeze-drying (lyophilisation) removes water from food by freezing it then reducing the pressure so the ice sublimes. Why is this preferable to ordinary drying at high temperature?
options: Sublimation at low temperature preserves the nutritional content and flavour that heat would destroy
Sublimation removes the water molecules more completely than evaporation at any temperature
Freeze-drying uses less energy than any other drying method
The reduced pressure causes all the moisture to leave the food instantly
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sublimation at low temperature preserves the nutritional content and flavour that heat would destroy
acceptableAnswers: Sublimation at low temperature preserves the nutritional content and flavour that heat would destroy
grade9-chemistry.hint: Low temperature processing is gentler on the product.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Freeze-drying occurs at low temperature (below 0 °C), avoiding the heat-induced degradation of vitamins, proteins and aromatic compounds that ordinary thermal drying causes, while still removing essentially all of the water.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these evidence items confirms that a substance has sublimed rather than evaporated?
options: The vapour condenses on a cold surface to form the same substance
The process is endothermic and requires an input of heat
No liquid is present at any stage — the solid converts directly to vapour
The mass of vapour produced equals the mass of solid that disappeared
grade9-chemistry.answer: No liquid is present at any stage — the solid converts directly to vapour
acceptableAnswers: No liquid is present at any stage — the solid converts directly to vapour
grade9-chemistry.hint: The key distinction is the absence of a liquid phase.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Evaporation involves a liquid phase (solid→liquid→gas); sublimation jumps directly from solid to gas with no liquid stage. Observing no melting or puddle at any point distinguishes sublimation from evaporation.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which statement about the pressure dependence of sublimation is correct?
options: Increasing the pressure lowers the sublimation temperature
Reducing the pressure lowers the sublimation temperature, making sublimation easier
Only at exactly 1 atmosphere pressure can a substance sublime
Pressure has no effect on sublimation because sublimation is a surface effect
grade9-chemistry.answer: Reducing the pressure lowers the sublimation temperature, making sublimation easier
acceptableAnswers: Reducing the pressure lowers the sublimation temperature, making sublimation easier
grade9-chemistry.hint: Phase diagrams show that lower pressure shifts the solid-gas boundary to lower temperatures.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: At reduced pressure the vapour pressure needed to sublime is easier to achieve at lower temperatures; freeze-drying exploits this by subliming ice at temperatures well below 0 °C under vacuum.

grade9-chemistry.question: In a distillation apparatus, what is the piece of glassware labelled A, which is the main glass vessel where the mixture is heated?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Distillation flask (round-bottomed flask)
grade9-chemistry.hint: It is the vessel that sits on the heat source.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The distillation flask (usually round-bottomed) is the vessel in which the mixture is placed and heated; it has a side arm through which vapour escapes to the condenser.

grade9-chemistry.question: In a crystallisation set-up, an evaporating dish is placed on a wire gauze over a Bunsen burner. What is the purpose of the wire gauze?
options: To provide a cold surface on which crystals begin to form
To prevent the liquid from evaporating too quickly
To spread the heat evenly and support the evaporating dish above the flame
To filter any solid particles rising from the Bunsen burner
grade9-chemistry.answer: To spread the heat evenly and support the evaporating dish above the flame
acceptableAnswers: To spread the heat evenly and support the evaporating dish above the flame
grade9-chemistry.hint: The gauze supports the glassware and distributes heat.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The wire gauze (usually with a ceramic centre) acts as a support for the evaporating dish and spreads the heat from the Bunsen burner evenly, preventing hot spots that could crack the dish.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student sets up sublimation apparatus using a round-bottomed flask, an inverted funnel, and a cold wet cloth. What is the function of the cold wet cloth?
options: To prevent the flask from overheating by conducting heat away from the bottom
To filter the vapour and remove impurities before deposition
To dissolve the sublimed vapour so it drips back as a liquid into the flask
To cool the inner surface of the funnel so that the sublimed vapour deposits as solid crystals
grade9-chemistry.answer: To cool the inner surface of the funnel so that the sublimed vapour deposits as solid crystals
acceptableAnswers: To cool the inner surface of the funnel so that the sublimed vapour deposits as solid crystals
grade9-chemistry.hint: The vapour needs a cool surface to deposit on.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The cold cloth lowers the temperature of the funnel surface; when sublimed vapour contacts this cool surface it undergoes deposition, forming a layer of pure solid crystals on the inside of the funnel.

grade9-chemistry.question: In a fractional distillation apparatus, the fractionating column is packed with glass beads. What role do they play?
options: They act as a catalyst that lowers the boiling point of the mixture
They slow the vapour to allow impurities to settle by gravity
They provide a large surface area for repeated condensation and re-evaporation, improving separation of components with similar boiling points
They absorb the less volatile component so only the more volatile one passes through
grade9-chemistry.answer: They provide a large surface area for repeated condensation and re-evaporation, improving separation of components with similar boiling points
acceptableAnswers: They provide a large surface area for repeated condensation and re-evaporation, improving separation of components with similar boiling points
grade9-chemistry.hint: Each bead surface is a mini-condensation and re-evaporation step.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: As vapour rises, it condenses on the cool glass beads and re-evaporates, enriching the vapour in the more volatile component with each cycle; this is equivalent to multiple simple distillations and allows close-boiling liquids to be separated.

grade9-chemistry.question: In a crystallisation experiment, the thermometer is placed in the solution in the evaporating dish. What does it monitor?
options: The cooling rate after the dish is removed from the heat
The purity of the salt, which is indicated by the boiling point
The temperature of the solution to ensure it does not boil and to judge when to stop evaporating
The rate at which crystals are forming in the solution
grade9-chemistry.answer: The temperature of the solution to ensure it does not boil and to judge when to stop evaporating
acceptableAnswers: The temperature of the solution to ensure it does not boil and to judge when to stop evaporating
grade9-chemistry.hint: You heat the solution to reduce its volume, but not to boiling.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The thermometer monitors temperature; the student stops heating before boiling point to avoid splattering and checks for crystallisation (a crystalline crust on the stirring rod) at the saturation point.

grade9-chemistry.question: In a standard filtration apparatus, what is the function of the conical flask placed beneath the funnel?
options: To measure the volume of liquid filtered per minute
To catch the residue that is retained on the filter paper
To heat the liquid so it flows through the filter faster
To collect the filtrate (the liquid that passes through the filter paper)
grade9-chemistry.answer: To collect the filtrate (the liquid that passes through the filter paper)
acceptableAnswers: To collect the filtrate (the liquid that passes through the filter paper)
grade9-chemistry.hint: The filtrate drips through and must be collected.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The conical (Erlenmeyer) flask receives the filtrate — the clear liquid that has passed through the filter paper — while the residue (the solid) remains on the filter paper in the funnel.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is a Buchner funnel and flask used instead of gravity filtration in crystallisation experiments involving large quantities?
options: Gravity filtration is not possible in a laboratory without a Buchner flask
The Buchner funnel heats the liquid to make impurities more soluble
Reduced pressure below the filter paper speeds up filtration and gives drier crystals
The Buchner funnel uses a finer pore size that removes all dissolved salts
grade9-chemistry.answer: Reduced pressure below the filter paper speeds up filtration and gives drier crystals
acceptableAnswers: Reduced pressure below the filter paper speeds up filtration and gives drier crystals
grade9-chemistry.hint: The water pump or vacuum pump reduces the pressure beneath the filter.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A water pump (or vacuum pump) connected to the Buchner flask reduces the pressure below the filter paper, increasing the pressure difference across it and speeding up filtration; the crystals are also drawn drier.

grade9-chemistry.question: In a distillation apparatus, the thermometer bulb is placed at the junction of the flask and the condenser arm. Why is it not placed in the liquid?
options: The thermometer measures the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser, which equals the boiling point of the distillate being collected
The thermometer cannot reach the liquid through the still-head design
Placing it in the liquid would dissolve the thermometer in the solvent
The liquid boils at a higher temperature than the vapour, so liquid placement would give a false reading
grade9-chemistry.answer: The thermometer measures the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser, which equals the boiling point of the distillate being collected
acceptableAnswers: The thermometer measures the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser, which equals the boiling point of the distillate being collected
grade9-chemistry.hint: You want the boiling point of what is distilling over, not the temperature of the whole liquid.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Vapour above a boiling mixture has the composition and boiling point of the most volatile component currently distilling; placing the bulb in vapour at the still-head gives the true boiling point of the distillate being collected.

grade9-chemistry.question: After collecting crystals by filtration, the student washes them with a small volume of ice-cold distilled water. Why ice-cold and not warm water?
options: Warm water would react with the crystals and change their chemical composition
Cold water evaporates more slowly, giving the crystals time to dry
Ice-cold water removes impurities more effectively because they are more soluble when cold
Cold water dissolves less of the product, so less is lost during washing
grade9-chemistry.answer: Cold water dissolves less of the product, so less is lost during washing
acceptableAnswers: Cold water dissolves less of the product, so less is lost during washing
grade9-chemistry.hint: Washing removes impurities from the surface — but not too much of the product.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ice-cold water is used to minimise the amount of product that re-dissolves during washing; impurities on the crystal surface are removed, but the low temperature keeps the solubility of the desired product very low.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student notices that her distillate is cloudy rather than clear. What is the most likely cause and how should she check?
options: The thermometer has leaked mercury into the condensate
The receiving flask was not dry and the distillate reacted with water in it
The condenser is too cold, converting the vapour to a solid inside the tube
Some liquid droplets were carried over from the boiling flask; she should check whether the cloudiness clears when cooled — a second immiscible liquid would not clear
grade9-chemistry.answer: Some liquid droplets were carried over from the boiling flask; she should check whether the cloudiness clears when cooled — a second immiscible liquid would not clear
acceptableAnswers: Some liquid droplets were carried over from the boiling flask; she should check whether the cloudiness clears when cooled — a second immiscible liquid would not clear
grade9-chemistry.hint: Cloudiness in a distillate usually means something was carried over.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Bumping or overfilling can cause fine droplets of the original solution to be carried over; if the cloudiness is from dissolved gas it will clear on cooling; if from droplets of a second immiscible liquid it will stay — she should also check she did not overfill the flask.

grade9-chemistry.question: In the apparatus for sublimation, what shape of surface is placed above the heating substance to collect the purified solid?
options: An inverted cold cone or watch glass above the sample
A piece of filter paper placed inside the sample to absorb the vapour
A flat-bottomed flask placed directly on top of the substance
A curved mirror to reflect the heat downwards
grade9-chemistry.answer: An inverted cold cone or watch glass above the sample
acceptableAnswers: An inverted cold cone or watch glass above the sample
grade9-chemistry.hint: The vapour rises and needs a cool surface above it to deposit on.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: An inverted funnel, cold watch glass or cold-water-filled evaporating dish placed above the substance provides the cool surface on which the sublimed vapour deposits as a pure solid.

grade9-chemistry.question: In a crystallisation experiment, a student pours her hot saturated solution through a hot funnel with a fluted filter paper. Why must the funnel be hot?
options: To increase the pressure and drive the solution through the filter more quickly
To prevent premature crystallisation of the solution inside the funnel before filtration is complete
To dissolve the filter paper and allow a finer filtration
To speed up evaporation inside the funnel so crystals form faster
grade9-chemistry.answer: To prevent premature crystallisation of the solution inside the funnel before filtration is complete
acceptableAnswers: To prevent premature crystallisation of the solution inside the funnel before filtration is complete
grade9-chemistry.hint: If the funnel cools, crystallisation starts in the wrong place.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A hot funnel keeps the solution above its crystallisation temperature during filtration; if the funnel were cold, crystals would form inside it and block the filter, reducing yield and making filtration very slow.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student uses a water condenser but connects the water inlet at the top rather than the bottom. What is the practical consequence?
options: The condenser works identically — the direction of water flow has no effect
Water enters at higher pressure, improving cooling more than the standard connection
The condenser fills with water from the top, leaving an air gap at the bottom, reducing cooling efficiency
Water boils inside the condenser because it is heated by the vapour flowing in the same direction
grade9-chemistry.answer: The condenser fills with water from the top, leaving an air gap at the bottom, reducing cooling efficiency
acceptableAnswers: The condenser fills with water from the top, leaving an air gap at the bottom, reducing cooling efficiency
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about where air would be trapped if water enters at the top.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Water entering at the top creates a downward flow; air trapped at the bottom cannot escape and creates an insulating air pocket, reducing the surface area in contact with cooling water and lowering efficiency — this is why countercurrent flow (bottom inlet) is standard.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which separation technique would you use to obtain pure water from sea water?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Distillation
grade9-chemistry.hint: The water must be separated from dissolved salt.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Distillation vaporises the water and condenses it as pure distillate, leaving behind the dissolved salts in the flask.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which technique separates an insoluble solid from a liquid?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Filtration
grade9-chemistry.hint: The solid is trapped by the filter and the liquid passes through.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Filtration uses a porous barrier (filter paper) to retain the solid while the liquid (filtrate) passes through; it works because the solid does not dissolve.

grade9-chemistry.question: A mixture contains iodine and common salt (sodium chloride). Iodine sublimes; NaCl does not. Which technique separates them most efficiently?
options: Crystallisation — both dissolve in water and crystallise at different temperatures
Distillation — iodine has a lower boiling point and distils over first
Filtration — iodine particles are larger than NaCl and are retained by the filter
Sublimation — the iodine vapourises and is collected as a pure solid, leaving NaCl behind
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sublimation — the iodine vapourises and is collected as a pure solid, leaving NaCl behind
acceptableAnswers: Sublimation — the iodine vapourises and is collected as a pure solid, leaving NaCl behind
grade9-chemistry.hint: Only one substance sublimes.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Gently heating the mixture causes iodine to sublime; the vapour deposits as pure iodine crystals on a cold surface above, while NaCl (which does not sublime) remains as a solid.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student wants to obtain pure copper sulfate crystals from a solution that also contains a small amount of an insoluble brown solid. What should she do first?
options: Sublime the mixture to drive off the insoluble solid
Distil the solution to separate copper sulfate from water, then re-dissolve
Allow the solution to evaporate completely at room temperature
Filter the solution to remove the insoluble solid, then crystallise the filtrate
grade9-chemistry.answer: Filter the solution to remove the insoluble solid, then crystallise the filtrate
acceptableAnswers: Filter the solution to remove the insoluble solid, then crystallise the filtrate
grade9-chemistry.hint: Remove the insoluble impurity before crystallising.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Filtration first removes the insoluble brown solid; the clear blue filtrate is then evaporated and cooled to crystallise the copper sulfate.

grade9-chemistry.question: Two liquids, ethanol and water, are completely miscible and have boiling points of 78 °C and 100 °C. Which technique separates them?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Fractional distillation
grade9-chemistry.hint: They are both liquids and mix completely; boiling points are different but close.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Miscible liquids with different boiling points are separated by distillation; because the boiling points are relatively close (22 °C apart), fractional distillation gives a better separation than simple distillation.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which separation principle does chromatography rely on, and how does this differ from distillation?
options: Different magnetic properties; distillation relies on different melting points
Differential adsorption/partition between a mobile phase and a stationary phase; distillation relies on different boiling points
Selective sublimation of one component; distillation relies on evaporation of a solvent
Different densities of components; distillation relies on different solubilities
grade9-chemistry.answer: Differential adsorption/partition between a mobile phase and a stationary phase; distillation relies on different boiling points
acceptableAnswers: Differential adsorption/partition between a mobile phase and a stationary phase; distillation relies on different boiling points
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about how each technique actually moves components apart.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Chromatography separates because each component is attracted to the stationary phase to a different degree (differential partition), causing them to move at different speeds in the mobile phase; distillation separates because of different vapour pressures (boiling points).

grade9-chemistry.question: A mixture of naphthalene (sublimes at 80 °C) and benzoic acid (sublimes at higher temperatures) needs to be separated. Which technique and conditions would work?
options: Sublimation at about 80 °C so only naphthalene sublimes, leaving benzoic acid behind
Crystallisation from hot water, since both have very different solubilities
Filtration using a membrane with pore size between the two molecular sizes
Distillation at 80 °C to vaporise naphthalene and collect it as liquid in the condenser
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sublimation at about 80 °C so only naphthalene sublimes, leaving benzoic acid behind
acceptableAnswers: Sublimation at about 80 °C so only naphthalene sublimes, leaving benzoic acid behind
grade9-chemistry.hint: One sublimes much more readily than the other at this temperature.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Heating to ~80 °C causes naphthalene to sublime while benzoic acid (which requires a much higher temperature) remains solid; the naphthalene vapour deposits on a cold surface above as pure crystals.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is distillation a better method than evaporation for purifying river water?
options: Distillation is faster than evaporation because the condenser accelerates the vaporisation
Distillation collects the pure water vapour; evaporation to dryness would leave all dissolved impurities including any heavy metals in the water
Distillation works at room temperature; evaporation requires heating
Evaporation removes the water but distillation removes the pollutants, so they achieve opposite things
grade9-chemistry.answer: Distillation collects the pure water vapour; evaporation to dryness would leave all dissolved impurities including any heavy metals in the water
acceptableAnswers: Distillation collects the pure water vapour; evaporation to dryness would leave all dissolved impurities including any heavy metals in the water
grade9-chemistry.hint: What do you collect in each technique?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: In distillation you collect the condensed water vapour as pure distillate; in evaporation the liquid is driven off and you collect the solid residue (all the impurities), so the water is lost, not purified.

grade9-chemistry.question: A mixture of three dyes in a single solution has components that are: water-insoluble, water-soluble with high Rf value, and water-soluble with low Rf value. Which technique separates all three in one operation?
options: Distillation — each dye boils at a different temperature and is collected separately
Crystallisation — each dye crystallises at a different temperature from the solution
Filtration — the insoluble dye is retained; the two soluble dyes pass through together
Paper chromatography — the insoluble dye stays at the baseline, the others travel different distances
grade9-chemistry.answer: Paper chromatography — the insoluble dye stays at the baseline, the others travel different distances
acceptableAnswers: Paper chromatography — the insoluble dye stays at the baseline, the others travel different distances
grade9-chemistry.hint: Different Rf values and different solubilities all appear in one chromatogram.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Paper chromatography separates the three dyes simultaneously: the insoluble one stays at the origin, the two soluble ones are carried different distances by the solvent according to their partition between the mobile and stationary phases.

grade9-chemistry.question: Salt and sand are mixed together. How would you recover the salt?
options: Dissolve both in acid, then neutralise to precipitate the sand
Use a magnet to separate them, then filter
Heat the mixture strongly until the sand melts and the salt floats to the top
Add water to dissolve the salt; filter to remove sand; evaporate the filtrate to recover salt crystals
grade9-chemistry.answer: Add water to dissolve the salt; filter to remove sand; evaporate the filtrate to recover salt crystals
acceptableAnswers: Add water to dissolve the salt; filter to remove sand; evaporate the filtrate to recover salt crystals
grade9-chemistry.hint: Which solid dissolves and which does not?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Salt dissolves in water; sand does not. Filtering separates the insoluble sand; evaporating the filtrate (or allowing it to crystallise by cooling) recovers the solid salt.

grade9-chemistry.question: Ink contains a mixture of dyes dissolved in water. Which pair of techniques would give pure water AND identify the individual dyes?
options: Distillation (to collect pure water) and chromatography (to identify the dyes)
Evaporation (to collect pure water) and distillation (to identify the dyes)
Filtration (to remove the dyes) and crystallisation (to get the water as ice)
Crystallisation (to get water) and sublimation (to identify dyes)
grade9-chemistry.answer: Distillation (to collect pure water) and chromatography (to identify the dyes)
acceptableAnswers: Distillation (to collect pure water) and chromatography (to identify the dyes)
grade9-chemistry.hint: One technique gives pure water; the other analyses the components.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Distillation of ink gives pure water as the distillate; chromatography of the original ink separates and identifies the individual dye components by their Rf values.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why would crystallisation NOT be a good method to separate two salts that have very similar solubility curves?
options: Two salts in the same solution would react and form a third compound that cannot be crystallised
Crystallisation cannot separate ionic compounds because they all dissolve equally in water
If both salts have nearly the same solubility at all temperatures, cooling will not preferentially crystallise one without the other
The filter paper would dissolve in the solution containing two different salts
grade9-chemistry.answer: If both salts have nearly the same solubility at all temperatures, cooling will not preferentially crystallise one without the other
acceptableAnswers: If both salts have nearly the same solubility at all temperatures, cooling will not preferentially crystallise one without the other
grade9-chemistry.hint: Crystallisation exploits differences in solubility with temperature.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: For fractional crystallisation to work, one salt must become significantly less soluble than the other as the solution is cooled; if their solubility curves are nearly identical, both crystallise together and cannot be separated.

grade9-chemistry.question: A mixture of solid sulfur and solid potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) needs to be separated. Sulfur is insoluble in water; KMnO₄ is soluble. Which sequence of techniques would work?
options: Dissolve in water (KMnO₄ dissolves, sulfur does not); filter (sulfur stays on paper); crystallise the filtrate to recover KMnO₄
Heat the mixture; sulfur sublimes and KMnO₄ remains; collect the sulfur vapour
Distil the mixture; the sulfur boils first and is collected; KMnO₄ stays in the flask
Use a magnet; KMnO₄ is magnetic and sulfur is not
grade9-chemistry.answer: Dissolve in water (KMnO₄ dissolves, sulfur does not); filter (sulfur stays on paper); crystallise the filtrate to recover KMnO₄
acceptableAnswers: Dissolve in water (KMnO₄ dissolves, sulfur does not); filter (sulfur stays on paper); crystallise the filtrate to recover KMnO₄
grade9-chemistry.hint: Use the difference in water solubility.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Water dissolves KMnO₄ but not sulfur; filtration separates insoluble sulfur (on paper) from the purple filtrate; evaporation and cooling of the filtrate crystallises KMnO₄ — a three-step combination using two techniques.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student compares two ways of getting salt from brine (salt solution): (i) distillation, (ii) solar evaporation in shallow pans. Which gives purer salt and which gives more salt from the same amount of brine?
options: Distillation gives both purer and more salt than solar evaporation in all circumstances
Distillation gives a purer water product (not salt); solar evaporation gives more concentrated salt at lower energy cost but less pure than distillation would allow
Both give identical purity; solar evaporation gives more salt
Distillation gives more salt because it concentrates the brine; solar evaporation gives purer salt because sunlight kills bacteria
grade9-chemistry.answer: Distillation gives a purer water product (not salt); solar evaporation gives more concentrated salt at lower energy cost but less pure than distillation would allow
acceptableAnswers: Distillation gives a purer water product (not salt); solar evaporation gives more concentrated salt at lower energy cost but less pure than distillation would allow
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what each method actually collects.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Distillation collects the pure water vapour — not the salt; the salt is the residue. Solar evaporation collects the salt by evaporating the water using free solar energy; it gives impure salt but at very low cost. Recrystallisation of the solar-evaporation salt would improve its purity.

grade9-chemistry.question: What happens to the atoms during a chemical reaction?
options: New atoms are created from nothing
Some of them are destroyed completely
They are rearranged into new substances
They stay joined exactly as they were
grade9-chemistry.answer: They are rearranged into new substances
acceptableAnswers: They are rearranged into new substances
grade9-chemistry.hint: Nothing is created and nothing is lost.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A chemical reaction rearranges the same atoms into different combinations; none is created or destroyed.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why must the total mass be the same before and after a reaction in a sealed container?
options: The container adds mass as the reaction proceeds
Gases have no mass, so nothing is lost
The same atoms are present, only joined differently
Some atoms are destroyed and replaced by others
grade9-chemistry.answer: The same atoms are present, only joined differently
acceptableAnswers: The same atoms are present, only joined differently
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count the atoms before and after.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Because the atoms are only rearranged, the same atoms - and so the same mass - are present at the end.

grade9-chemistry.question: A candle burns and seems to lose mass. Has mass been destroyed?
options: Yes, but only the mass of the wick is lost
Yes, mass is destroyed whenever something burns
No, gases escape into the air and carry the mass away
No, the mass is stored inside the flame
grade9-chemistry.answer: No, gases escape into the air and carry the mass away
acceptableAnswers: No, gases escape into the air and carry the mass away
grade9-chemistry.hint: Where do the products of burning go?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Carbon dioxide and water vapour escape into the air; weigh them too and the total mass is unchanged.

grade9-chemistry.question: In a chemical equation, the substances on the left are the:
grade9-chemistry.answer: Reactants
grade9-chemistry.hint: They are the ones present at the start.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The starting substances on the left are the reactants; the substances formed on the right are the products.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the formula of water?
grade9-chemistry.answer: H<sub>2</sub>O
grade9-chemistry.hint: Two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, so its formula is H<sub>2</sub>O.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the formula of carbon dioxide?
grade9-chemistry.answer: CO<sub>2</sub>
grade9-chemistry.hint: The prefix "di" tells you how many oxygen atoms.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Carbon dioxide has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms: CO<sub>2</sub>.

grade9-chemistry.question: How many atoms in total are there in one molecule of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
grade9-chemistry.hint: Add up 2 hydrogen, 1 sulfur and 4 oxygen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2 + 1 + 4 = 7 atoms in total.

grade9-chemistry.question: How many oxygen atoms are there in one formula unit of Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>?
grade9-chemistry.hint: The bracket subscript multiplies everything inside it.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The 2 outside the bracket applies to both the O and the H, so there are 2 oxygen atoms.

grade9-chemistry.question: How many atoms in total are there in one formula unit of Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>?
grade9-chemistry.hint: One calcium, plus twice everything inside the bracket.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 1 calcium + 2 oxygen + 2 hydrogen = 5 atoms.

grade9-chemistry.question: In the formula 2H<sub>2</sub>O, how many hydrogen atoms are represented?
grade9-chemistry.hint: The big number in front multiplies the whole formula.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Each molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms and there are 2 molecules, so 2 × 2 = 4.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which formula represents an element rather than a compound?
grade9-chemistry.answer: O<sub>2</sub>
grade9-chemistry.hint: An element contains only one kind of atom.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: O<sub>2</sub> contains only oxygen atoms, so it is an element; the others contain two different elements each.

grade9-chemistry.question: In a word equation, what separates the reactants from the products?
grade9-chemistry.answer: An arrow
grade9-chemistry.hint: It shows the direction of the change.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: An arrow separates reactants from products and shows which way the reaction goes.

grade9-chemistry.question: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Which word equation is correct?
grade9-chemistry.answer: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: The starting substances go on the left of the arrow.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Magnesium and oxygen are the reactants and magnesium oxide is the product.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which word equation describes zinc reacting with hydrochloric acid?
options: zinc chloride + hydrogen → zinc + hydrochloric acid
zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + oxygen
zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen
zinc + hydrogen → zinc chloride + hydrochloric acid
grade9-chemistry.answer: zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen
acceptableAnswers: zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: A metal and an acid give a salt and hydrogen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Metal + acid gives a salt plus hydrogen: zinc chloride and hydrogen here.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which chemical equation matches "carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide"?
grade9-chemistry.answer: C + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub>
grade9-chemistry.hint: Oxygen gas exists as O<sub>2</sub>.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Carbon is C, oxygen gas is O<sub>2</sub> and carbon dioxide is CO<sub>2</sub>, and the equation already balances.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
options: The products always weigh more than the reactants did
Every equation must contain the same number of substances on each side
It makes the equation look tidier and easier to read
Atoms are not created or destroyed, so each kind must balance
grade9-chemistry.answer: Atoms are not created or destroyed, so each kind must balance
acceptableAnswers: Atoms are not created or destroyed, so each kind must balance
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what a reaction does to atoms.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A reaction only rearranges atoms, so every kind of atom must appear the same number of times on each side.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which equation is correctly balanced?
grade9-chemistry.answer: 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count hydrogen and oxygen on each side.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 4 hydrogen and 2 oxygen appear on both sides, so this one balances.

grade9-chemistry.question: What number is missing? ___Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count the magnesium atoms on the right.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2MgO contains 2 magnesium atoms, so 2 magnesium atoms are needed on the left.

grade9-chemistry.question: What number is missing? N<sub>2</sub> + ___H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count the hydrogen atoms on the right.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2NH<sub>3</sub> contains 6 hydrogen atoms, and each H<sub>2</sub> gives 2, so 3 are needed.

grade9-chemistry.question: What number is missing? 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 2H<sub>2</sub> + ___O<sub>2</sub>
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count the oxygen atoms on the left.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2H<sub>2</sub>O contains 2 oxygen atoms, which is exactly one O<sub>2</sub> molecule.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which is the balanced equation for calcium reacting with oxygen?
grade9-chemistry.answer: 2Ca + O<sub>2</sub> → 2CaO
grade9-chemistry.hint: Oxygen gas comes as O<sub>2</sub>, so two CaO are needed.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: One O<sub>2</sub> supplies two oxygen atoms, making two CaO, so two Ca are needed on the left.

grade9-chemistry.question: In balancing an equation, which of these may you change?
options: The identity of any product you choose
The small subscript numbers inside a formula
The arrow, into an equals sign
The big numbers in front of the formulae
grade9-chemistry.answer: The big numbers in front of the formulae
acceptableAnswers: The big numbers in front of the formulae
grade9-chemistry.hint: Changing a subscript changes what the substance is.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Only the coefficients may be changed; altering a subscript turns the substance into a different one.

grade9-chemistry.question: How many atoms in total are there in one molecule of CH<sub>4</sub>?
grade9-chemistry.hint: One carbon and four hydrogen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 1 + 4 = 5 atoms.

grade9-chemistry.question: How many oxygen atoms are there in one formula unit of CaCO<sub>3</sub>?
grade9-chemistry.hint: Read the subscript after the O.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The subscript 3 gives 3 oxygen atoms.

grade9-chemistry.question: How many hydrogen atoms are represented by 3H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
grade9-chemistry.hint: Multiply the 2 hydrogen in the formula by the 3 in front.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 3 × 2 = 6 hydrogen atoms.

grade9-chemistry.question: How many atoms in total are there in one formula unit of Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>?
grade9-chemistry.hint: One magnesium, then twice everything inside the bracket.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 1 Mg + 2 N + 6 O = 9 atoms.

grade9-chemistry.question: What number balances this equation? ___H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count the hydrogen atoms on the right.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2H<sub>2</sub>O has 4 hydrogen atoms, and each H<sub>2</sub> supplies 2, so 2 are needed.

grade9-chemistry.question: What number balances this equation? 2Na + Cl<sub>2</sub> → ___NaCl
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count the sodium atoms on the left.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2 sodium atoms and 2 chlorine atoms give 2NaCl.

grade9-chemistry.question: What number balances this equation? CH<sub>4</sub> + ___O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count the oxygen atoms on the right: 2 in CO<sub>2</sub> and 2 in 2H<sub>2</sub>O.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The right-hand side has 4 oxygen atoms, and each O<sub>2</sub> supplies 2, so 2 are needed.

grade9-chemistry.question: Give the name for the starting substances in a chemical reaction.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Reactants
grade9-chemistry.hint: They are written on the left of the arrow.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The substances present at the start are the reactants.

grade9-chemistry.question: Give the name for the new substances formed in a chemical reaction.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Products
grade9-chemistry.hint: They are written on the right of the arrow.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The substances formed are the products.

grade9-chemistry.question: Complete the word equation: magnesium + oxygen → ______
grade9-chemistry.answer: Magnesium oxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: A metal burning in oxygen gives its oxide.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: Complete the word equation: zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + ______
grade9-chemistry.answer: Hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: A metal and an acid always give a salt and one gas.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Metal + acid gives a salt plus hydrogen.

grade9-chemistry.question: Give the chemical formula of water.
grade9-chemistry.answer: H2O
grade9-chemistry.hint: Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Water is H<sub>2</sub>O.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which statement best describes what happens to atoms during a chemical reaction?
options: Atoms are created from energy when two substances react
Atoms are destroyed and replaced by energy during the reaction
Atoms change their identity to become different elements during the reaction
Atoms are rearranged to form new substances but are neither created nor destroyed
grade9-chemistry.answer: Atoms are rearranged to form new substances but are neither created nor destroyed
acceptableAnswers: Atoms are rearranged to form new substances but are neither created nor destroyed
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about conservation of mass.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The law of conservation of mass states that atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction — they are rearranged into different combinations to form the products.

grade9-chemistry.question: In the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, which statement about mass is correct?
options: The mass decreases because some atoms are lost as heat
The mass increases because the reaction releases energy
The products weigh more because oxygen is heavier than hydrogen
The total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants
grade9-chemistry.answer: The total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants
acceptableAnswers: The total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants
grade9-chemistry.hint: Atoms are just rearranged, not destroyed.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Conservation of mass: 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms appear in the reactants and the same 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms appear in the 2 H₂O molecules on the product side.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student burns 12 g of carbon completely in oxygen and collects the gas produced. What mass of carbon dioxide is formed? (Relative atomic masses: C = 12, O = 16)
grade9-chemistry.hint: C + O₂ → CO₂. One mole of C gives one mole of CO₂.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: C + O₂ → CO₂. 12 g of C is 1 mole; 1 mole of CO₂ = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g. By conservation of mass, 12 g C + 32 g O₂ → 44 g CO₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does a piece of iron that rusts appear to gain mass?
options: Water from the air replaces the iron atoms and adds extra mass
Rusting releases energy that is converted to mass
The rust is more tightly packed than iron so the density increases the apparent mass
It combines with oxygen from the air, and the oxygen adds to the mass of the iron
grade9-chemistry.answer: It combines with oxygen from the air, and the oxygen adds to the mass of the iron
acceptableAnswers: It combines with oxygen from the air, and the oxygen adds to the mass of the iron
grade9-chemistry.hint: Rusting is a chemical reaction — where does the extra element come from?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Rusting: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 2H₂O → iron oxide (rust). The oxygen and water from the air become part of the product, adding their mass to the iron, consistent with conservation of mass.

grade9-chemistry.question: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. A student starts with 24 g of Mg and burns it completely. How much oxygen is used? (Mg = 24, O = 16)
grade9-chemistry.hint: 2 moles Mg react with 1 mole O₂.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 24 g of Mg = 1 mole Mg (but the equation shows 2 mol Mg per 1 mol O₂, so 1 mol Mg reacts with 0.5 mol O₂ = 0.5 × 32 = 16 g of O₂).

grade9-chemistry.question: In a closed container, 4 g of hydrogen and 32 g of oxygen react to form water. What is the total mass inside the container after the reaction?
grade9-chemistry.hint: No atoms enter or leave a closed container.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Conservation of mass in a closed system: total mass before = 4 + 32 = 36 g; total mass after = 36 g (all converted to water). No mass is lost.

grade9-chemistry.question: When wood burns in air it seems to lose mass. What is the correct explanation?
options: Atoms in the wood are destroyed by the energy of combustion
Mass is lost as heat energy radiates from the fire
Gaseous products (CO₂ and H₂O vapour) escape into the air; the mass of solid ash left is less than wood plus oxygen consumed
The carbon in the wood is converted to energy, reducing the mass
grade9-chemistry.answer: Gaseous products (CO₂ and H₂O vapour) escape into the air; the mass of solid ash left is less than wood plus oxygen consumed
acceptableAnswers: Gaseous products (CO₂ and H₂O vapour) escape into the air; the mass of solid ash left is less than wood plus oxygen consumed
grade9-chemistry.hint: The system is open — gases escape.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: In an open system, CO₂ and water vapour escape; weighed correctly (closed system), the total mass of products equals wood mass plus oxygen consumed. The apparent loss is because the gaseous products are not collected.

grade9-chemistry.question: How many atoms are present in total in one molecule of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆?
grade9-chemistry.hint: Add up all the subscript numbers.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 6 carbon + 12 hydrogen + 6 oxygen = 24 atoms in one molecule of glucose.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the chemical formula of water?
grade9-chemistry.answer: H₂O
grade9-chemistry.hint: Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Water contains 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom per molecule: H₂O.

grade9-chemistry.question: Calcium has valency 2 and chlorine has valency 1. What is the formula of calcium chloride?
grade9-chemistry.answer: CaCl₂
grade9-chemistry.hint: Cross the valencies to get the subscripts.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ca²⁺ requires two Cl⁻ ions to balance the charges: CaCl₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: Aluminium has valency 3 and oxygen has valency 2. What is the formula of aluminium oxide?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Al₂O₃
grade9-chemistry.hint: Cross-multiply the valencies and simplify if needed.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Al has valency 3 and O has valency 2: crossing gives Al₂O₃ (2 × 3 = 3 × 2 = 6 positive and negative charges balanced).

grade9-chemistry.question: Which formula correctly represents iron(III) sulfate? (Fe³⁺, SO₄²⁻)
grade9-chemistry.answer: Fe₂(SO₄)₃
grade9-chemistry.hint: Total positive charge must equal total negative charge.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2 × Fe³⁺ = +6; 3 × SO₄²⁻ = −6. Balanced: Fe₂(SO₄)₃.

grade9-chemistry.question: What does the small number 2 represent in the formula H₂SO₄?
options: Two hydrogen atoms in one molecule of sulfuric acid
grade9-chemistry.answer: Two hydrogen atoms in one molecule of sulfuric acid
acceptableAnswers: Two hydrogen atoms in one molecule of sulfuric acid
grade9-chemistry.hint: A subscript after a symbol refers to that element only.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: In H₂SO₄, the subscript 2 after H means there are 2 hydrogen atoms in each molecule; S appears once (1 atom) and O appears 4 times.

grade9-chemistry.question: How many atoms in total are in the formula unit Ca₃(PO₄)₂?
grade9-chemistry.hint: Multiply the subscript outside the bracket by each element inside.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ca₃ = 3 Ca atoms; (PO₄)₂ = 2P + 8O = 10 atoms; total = 3 + 2 + 8 = 13 atoms.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the chemical formula of sodium carbonate?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Na₂CO₃
grade9-chemistry.hint: Na⁺ has valency 1; CO₃²⁻ has valency 2.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Na⁺ (valency 1) and CO₃²⁻ (valency 2): two Na⁺ are needed to balance one CO₃²⁻, giving Na₂CO₃.

grade9-chemistry.question: A compound has the empirical formula CH₂. Its relative molecular mass is 56. What is its molecular formula? (C = 12, H = 1)
grade9-chemistry.answer: C₄H₈
grade9-chemistry.hint: Find the mass of the empirical unit, then divide the Mr by it.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Mass of CH₂ = 12 + 2 = 14. 56 ÷ 14 = 4, so molecular formula = (CH₂)₄ = C₄H₈.

grade9-chemistry.question: The formula MgSO₄ represents magnesium sulfate. How many elements does this compound contain?
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count the number of different chemical symbols.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: MgSO₄ contains Mg (magnesium), S (sulfur) and O (oxygen) — 3 different elements.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these is the correct word equation for the burning of methane?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
grade9-chemistry.hint: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon in excess oxygen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Complete combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O; the word equation names the reactants and products.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the word equation for the neutralisation of sodium hydroxide by hydrochloric acid?
options: Hydrochloric acid + water → sodium hydroxide + chlorine
Sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water
acceptableAnswers: Sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water
grade9-chemistry.hint: Acid + alkali → salt + water.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The general rule for neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O.

grade9-chemistry.question: Write the word equation for the reaction between zinc and sulfuric acid.
options: Zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc chloride + sulfur
Zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc oxide + water
Zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen
Zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc hydroxide + sulfur dioxide
grade9-chemistry.answer: Zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen
acceptableAnswers: Zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen gas.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. The salt is zinc sulfate (metal + sulfate from H₂SO₄) and hydrogen gas is released.

grade9-chemistry.question: What are the products when calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid?
options: Calcium chloride, carbon dioxide, and water
grade9-chemistry.answer: Calcium chloride, carbon dioxide, and water
acceptableAnswers: Calcium chloride, carbon dioxide, and water
grade9-chemistry.hint: Metal carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The carbonate ion reacts with acid to give CO₂ as well as the salt and water.

grade9-chemistry.question: The thermal decomposition of copper carbonate gives two products. What are they?
options: Copper and oxygen and carbon dioxide
grade9-chemistry.answer: Copper oxide and carbon dioxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: Decomposition of a metal carbonate on heating.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. Metal carbonates decompose on heating to give the metal oxide and carbon dioxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: Iron reacts with steam to form iron oxide (Fe₃O₄) and hydrogen. Write the word equation.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Iron + steam → iron(II,III) oxide + hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: Iron reacts with steam but not cold water.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂. The product iron(II,III) oxide (magnetite) is the specific oxide formed with steam.

grade9-chemistry.question: What does the symbol "(g)" mean in a chemical equation?
options: The substance is in the gaseous state
The substance is dissolved in water (aqueous)
grade9-chemistry.answer: The substance is in the gaseous state
acceptableAnswers: The substance is in the gaseous state
grade9-chemistry.hint: State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: State symbols indicate the physical state: (s) = solid, (l) = liquid, (g) = gas, (aq) = dissolved in water (aqueous solution).

grade9-chemistry.question: Which word equation describes the reaction used to make ammonia industrially?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Nitrogen + hydrogen → ammonia
grade9-chemistry.hint: The Haber process uses atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen from natural gas.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. The Haber process combines nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from natural gas over an iron catalyst under high pressure and temperature.

grade9-chemistry.question: Sodium reacts vigorously with water. What are the products?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sodium hydroxide and hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: Alkali metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen gas.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Sodium reacts with water to give sodium hydroxide (an alkali) and hydrogen gas, which often ignites due to the heat produced.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these equations is correctly balanced?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count Mg, H and Cl atoms on both sides.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Left: 1 Mg, 2 H, 2 Cl. Right: 1 Mg, 2 Cl (in MgCl₂), 2 H (in H₂). Balanced.

grade9-chemistry.question: Balance the equation: _Fe + _O₂ → _Fe₂O₃. What coefficient goes in front of Fe?
grade9-chemistry.hint: Start with Fe₂O₃ and balance Fe, then O.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. Four Fe atoms on each side (2 × 2 = 4); six O atoms on each side (3 × 2 = 6). Coefficient in front of Fe is 4.

grade9-chemistry.question: Balance: _H₂ + _O₂ → _H₂O. What is the coefficient in front of H₂O?
grade9-chemistry.hint: Start by balancing oxygen: you need an even number of O atoms on the right.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Two water molecules contain 4 H and 2 O, matching 2 H₂ and 1 O₂ on the left.

grade9-chemistry.question: Balance: _Ca + _H₂O → _Ca(OH)₂ + _H₂. What is the coefficient in front of H₂O?
grade9-chemistry.hint: How many OH groups are needed for Ca(OH)₂?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Ca(OH)₂ needs 2 OH, so 2 H₂O are required; this releases 1 H₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: What does a large number placed in FRONT of a formula in a balanced equation represent?
options: The number of atoms in one molecule of the substance
The number of formula units (molecules or moles) of that substance
The number of electrons transferred in the reaction
grade9-chemistry.answer: The number of formula units (molecules or moles) of that substance
acceptableAnswers: The number of formula units (molecules or moles) of that substance
grade9-chemistry.hint: In 3H₂O, the 3 is in front, not a subscript.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A large number (coefficient) in front of a formula multiplies the entire formula unit; it is the number of molecules (or moles) of that substance involved in the reaction, not a change to the formula itself.

grade9-chemistry.question: Balance: _C₃H₈ + _O₂ → _CO₂ + _H₂O. What is the coefficient in front of O₂?
grade9-chemistry.hint: Balance C and H first, then count the O atoms needed.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. 3 C → 3CO₂; 8 H → 4H₂O; O needed = 6 + 4 = 10 O atoms = 5 O₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which balanced equation correctly represents the combustion of ethanol, C₂H₅OH?
grade9-chemistry.answer: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
grade9-chemistry.hint: Count C, H and O on both sides.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Left: 2 C, 6 H, 1 O (in ethanol) + 6 O (in 3O₂) = 7 O total. Right: 2 CO₂ (4 O) + 3 H₂O (3 O) = 7 O, 2 C, 6 H. Balanced.

grade9-chemistry.question: Balance: _Al + _HCl → _AlCl₃ + _H₂. What is the smallest whole-number coefficient for Al?
grade9-chemistry.hint: Al needs 3 Cl, but H₂ has 2 H — find the LCM.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂. LCM of 2 and 3 for H and Cl: 6 HCl provides 6 Cl (for 2 AlCl₃) and 6 H (for 3 H₂); 2 Al balances 2 Al on the right.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student writes: 2H₂ + 2O₂ → 2H₂O. Why is this equation incorrect even though atoms appear balanced?
options: Hydrogen and oxygen cannot react at room temperature so the equation is physically wrong
The coefficients are not in the simplest whole-number ratio; the correct equation is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
The arrow should point both ways because the reaction is reversible
The product should be H₂O₂ not H₂O because two oxygen atoms react
grade9-chemistry.answer: The coefficients are not in the simplest whole-number ratio; the correct equation is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
acceptableAnswers: The coefficients are not in the simplest whole-number ratio; the correct equation is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
grade9-chemistry.hint: A balanced equation should use the simplest whole-number ratios.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2H₂ + 2O₂ → 2H₂O has all coefficients divisible by 2; dividing through gives 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, the conventional balanced equation. An equation with non-simplest ratios is technically not wrong for atom count but is not the standard form.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is formed when a metal burns in oxygen?
grade9-chemistry.answer: A metal oxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: The metal joins with the oxygen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A metal burning in oxygen forms the metal oxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: Magnesium burns in air with a bright white flame. What is the white solid left behind?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Magnesium oxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: Only magnesium and oxygen were present.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Magnesium reacts with the oxygen of the air to form white magnesium oxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does gold jewellery keep its shine for centuries while an iron nail rusts?
options: Gold is polished more often than an iron nail
Gold is heavier than iron, so air cannot reach it
Gold is much harder than iron, so it cannot be scratched
Gold is far less reactive than iron, so it does not react with air
grade9-chemistry.answer: Gold is far less reactive than iron, so it does not react with air
acceptableAnswers: Gold is far less reactive than iron, so it does not react with air
grade9-chemistry.hint: Look at where each metal sits in the reactivity series.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Gold is at the bottom of the reactivity series and does not react with oxygen or water; iron does, and rusts.

grade9-chemistry.question: What two products are formed when a metal reacts with a dilute acid?
grade9-chemistry.answer: A salt and hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: One of them is a gas that pops with a lighted splint.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Metal + acid gives a salt plus hydrogen gas.

grade9-chemistry.question: How is the gas given off when zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid identified?
options: It gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint
It turns damp litmus paper bright red
grade9-chemistry.answer: It gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint
acceptableAnswers: It gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint
grade9-chemistry.hint: The gas is hydrogen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Hydrogen gives the squeaky pop test; the milky limewater test is for carbon dioxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which salt is formed when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Magnesium chloride
grade9-chemistry.hint: The acid decides the second half of the salt name.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides, so the salt is magnesium chloride.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which salt is formed when zinc reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Zinc sulfate
grade9-chemistry.hint: The acid decides the second half of the salt name.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sulfuric acid gives sulfates, so the salt is zinc sulfate.

grade9-chemistry.question: Copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid. What does this show?
options: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
Copper reacts only with water instead
Copper is above hydrogen in the reactivity series
grade9-chemistry.answer: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
acceptableAnswers: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
grade9-chemistry.hint: A metal must be more reactive than hydrogen to push it out of an acid.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Only metals above hydrogen displace it from an acid; copper is below it, so nothing happens.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is formed when a very reactive metal reacts with cold water?
options: A metal chloride and hydrogen gas
grade9-chemistry.answer: A metal hydroxide and hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: The gas given off is the same one as with an acid.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A reactive metal with cold water gives the metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

grade9-chemistry.question: Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water but vigorously with steam. What does this show?
options: Hotter conditions make the reaction much faster
Steam is a different substance from water
Magnesium is less reactive than gold
Magnesium does not react with water at all
grade9-chemistry.answer: Hotter conditions make the reaction much faster
acceptableAnswers: Hotter conditions make the reaction much faster
grade9-chemistry.hint: Steam is simply water that is far hotter.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Steam is much hotter than cold water, so the same reaction goes far faster.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which metal would you expect to react most vigorously with cold water?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Potassium
grade9-chemistry.hint: Use the reactivity series: the highest reacts most.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Potassium sits at the top of the reactivity series, so it reacts most vigorously.

grade9-chemistry.question: Using the series shown, which metal is the most reactive?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Potassium
grade9-chemistry.hint: Read the top of the list.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Potassium is at the top of the list, which is the most reactive end.

grade9-chemistry.question: Using the series shown, which metal is the least reactive?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Gold
grade9-chemistry.hint: Read the bottom of the list.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Gold is at the bottom of the list, which is the least reactive end.

grade9-chemistry.question: Using the series shown, which of these pairs is in the correct order, more reactive first?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Magnesium, then copper
grade9-chemistry.hint: The one higher in the list is the more reactive.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Magnesium is above copper in the series, so magnesium is the more reactive of the two.

grade9-chemistry.question: Using the series shown, which metals would react with dilute acid to give hydrogen?
options: Only gold, because it is unreactive
Only the two at the very bottom
Those above copper and gold in the list
Every metal in the list, equally
grade9-chemistry.answer: Those above copper and gold in the list
acceptableAnswers: Those above copper and gold in the list
grade9-chemistry.hint: The unreactive metals at the bottom do not attack an acid.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The metals higher in the series displace hydrogen from an acid; copper and gold, at the bottom, do not.

grade9-chemistry.question: The table shows how four metals behave. Which is the most reactive?
grade9-chemistry.answer: X
grade9-chemistry.hint: Look for the metal that reacts fastest with both.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: X reacts very fast with acid and fast with cold water, so it is the most reactive of the four.

grade9-chemistry.question: From the same table, which metal is the least reactive?
grade9-chemistry.answer: W
grade9-chemistry.hint: Look for the metal that does nothing at all.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: W does not react with the acid or with cold water, so it is the least reactive.

grade9-chemistry.question: From the same table, what is the correct order, most reactive first?
grade9-chemistry.answer: X, Z, Y, W
