grade9-chemistry.hint: Rank them by how strongly each reacts with the acid.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: X is very fast, Z fast, Y slow and W not at all, so the order is X, Z, Y, W.

grade9-chemistry.question: A more reactive metal is placed in a solution of a less reactive metal salt. What happens?
options: The more reactive metal displaces the less reactive one
The less reactive metal displaces the more reactive one
grade9-chemistry.answer: The more reactive metal displaces the less reactive one
acceptableAnswers: The more reactive metal displaces the less reactive one
grade9-chemistry.hint: The stronger competitor takes the place in the compound.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: In a displacement reaction the more reactive metal takes the place of the less reactive one in its compound.

grade9-chemistry.question: An iron nail is placed in copper sulfate solution. What is observed?
options: Bubbles of hydrogen are given off rapidly
Nothing at all happens to the nail or the solution
The nail dissolves completely and nothing is deposited
A brown coating forms on the nail and the blue colour fades
grade9-chemistry.answer: A brown coating forms on the nail and the blue colour fades
acceptableAnswers: A brown coating forms on the nail and the blue colour fades
grade9-chemistry.hint: Iron is above copper in the reactivity series.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Iron displaces copper, so copper is deposited on the nail as a brown coating and the blue copper sulfate fades.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does no reaction occur when a copper strip is placed in magnesium sulfate solution?
options: Copper is less reactive than magnesium, so it cannot displace it
Magnesium sulfate does not dissolve in water
Copper reacts only with acids, never with salts
Copper is more reactive than the magnesium, so it dissolves instead
grade9-chemistry.answer: Copper is less reactive than magnesium, so it cannot displace it
acceptableAnswers: Copper is less reactive than magnesium, so it cannot displace it
grade9-chemistry.hint: Displacement only works one way round.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A metal can only displace one below it in the series; copper is below magnesium, so nothing happens.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which word equation describes magnesium reacting with dilute sulfuric acid?
options: magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium oxide + water
magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen
magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + oxygen
magnesium sulfate + hydrogen → magnesium + sulfuric acid
grade9-chemistry.answer: magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen
acceptableAnswers: magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: Metal + acid gives a salt and one gas.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sulfuric acid gives a sulfate, and the gas released is hydrogen.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which is the balanced equation for magnesium burning in oxygen?
grade9-chemistry.answer: 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO
grade9-chemistry.hint: One O<sub>2</sub> supplies two oxygen atoms.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Two magnesium atoms are needed to use both oxygen atoms of the O<sub>2</sub> molecule.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which word equation describes iron displacing copper from copper sulfate?
options: iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper
iron + copper → iron sulfate + copper sulfate
iron + copper sulfate → iron oxide + copper
copper + iron sulfate → copper sulfate + iron
grade9-chemistry.answer: iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper
acceptableAnswers: iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper
grade9-chemistry.hint: The more reactive metal ends up in the compound.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Iron, being more reactive, takes the sulfate and copper is set free as the metal.

grade9-chemistry.question: Name the gas given off when a metal reacts with a dilute acid.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: It pops with a lighted splint.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Metal + acid always releases hydrogen.

grade9-chemistry.question: State the test that identifies hydrogen gas.
grade9-chemistry.answer: It pops with a lighted splint
acceptableAnswers: It pops with a lighted splint
a squeaky pop with a lighted splint
grade9-chemistry.hint: It involves a lighted splint.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop when a lighted splint is held at the mouth of the tube.

grade9-chemistry.question: Give the name of the compound formed when a metal burns in oxygen.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Metal oxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: The metal joins with the oxygen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A metal burning in oxygen gives the metal oxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: Give the name for the list of metals arranged in order of how vigorously they react.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Reactivity series
grade9-chemistry.hint: Two words.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The reactivity series ranks the metals from most to least reactive.

grade9-chemistry.question: Give the term for a reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive one in its compound.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Displacement
grade9-chemistry.hint: The less reactive metal is pushed out.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: This is a displacement reaction.

grade9-chemistry.question: Name the gas released when a reactive metal reacts with cold water.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: The same gas as with an acid.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A reactive metal with water gives the hydroxide and hydrogen.

grade9-chemistry.question: What type of compound is formed when a metal reacts with oxygen?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Metal oxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: Oxygen is added to the metal.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: When a metal burns in oxygen the metal combines with oxygen to form a metal oxide: metal + oxygen → metal oxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which observation is seen when magnesium burns in air?
options: A blue flame and a clear liquid residue
A dazzling white flame and a white powdery ash (magnesium oxide)
A colourless flame and a grey powder
A green flame and a brown solid residue
grade9-chemistry.answer: A dazzling white flame and a white powdery ash (magnesium oxide)
acceptableAnswers: A dazzling white flame and a white powdery ash (magnesium oxide)
grade9-chemistry.hint: Magnesium is a reactive metal that burns very brightly.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Magnesium burns with an intense white flame (used in flares and fireworks) and the white powder is magnesium oxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: Copper reacts slowly with oxygen at high temperature to form a black coating. What is this coating?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Copper(II) oxide (CuO)
grade9-chemistry.hint: Copper forms a black product with oxygen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO. Copper forms black copper(II) oxide on prolonged heating in air.

grade9-chemistry.question: Iron does not burn in air under normal conditions. Under what conditions does iron react with oxygen?
options: When iron wool is heated strongly in pure oxygen it burns with bright glowing sparks
When iron is submerged in liquid oxygen it reacts instantly
Iron always burns in air if the surface is polished
Iron reacts with oxygen only at extremely low temperatures
grade9-chemistry.answer: When iron wool is heated strongly in pure oxygen it burns with bright glowing sparks
acceptableAnswers: When iron wool is heated strongly in pure oxygen it burns with bright glowing sparks
grade9-chemistry.hint: Fine iron particles have a much larger surface area.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Iron wool, with its large surface area, burns vigorously in pure oxygen: 3Fe + 2O₂ → Fe₃O₄, producing bright orange sparks.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does the reaction of sodium with oxygen have to be done carefully in a laboratory?
options: The reaction is endothermic and causes the surrounding apparatus to freeze
Sodium is stored in oil because it reacts rapidly and violently with both air and moisture
Sodium must be heated to 1000 °C before it will react with oxygen
Sodium produces a toxic purple gas when it burns in oxygen
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sodium is stored in oil because it reacts rapidly and violently with both air and moisture
acceptableAnswers: Sodium is stored in oil because it reacts rapidly and violently with both air and moisture
grade9-chemistry.hint: Sodium is one of the most reactive metals.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sodium reacts rapidly with O₂ and with water in the air; it is stored under oil to prevent contact. When it burns in oxygen it produces sodium peroxide (Na₂O₂) as well as Na₂O.

grade9-chemistry.question: Gold does not react with oxygen even at very high temperatures. What does this tell us about gold?
options: Gold is too light to hold the oxygen that reacts with it
Gold is very unreactive, which is why it does not tarnish and is used for jewellery
Gold reacts with nitrogen instead of oxygen when heated
Gold already contains oxygen in its ore, so no further reaction occurs
grade9-chemistry.answer: Gold is very unreactive, which is why it does not tarnish and is used for jewellery
acceptableAnswers: Gold is very unreactive, which is why it does not tarnish and is used for jewellery
grade9-chemistry.hint: Reactivity with oxygen is a measure of how reactive a metal is.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Gold's extreme lack of reactivity means it does not oxidise; this makes it unreactive with air, acids and water — hence its use in jewellery, electronics and dentistry.

grade9-chemistry.question: The product of reacting potassium with oxygen is mainly potassium superoxide (KO₂). What does this suggest about potassium?
options: Potassium is unique in that its oxide is a liquid at room temperature
Potassium reacts with the nitrogen in air rather than the oxygen
Potassium is less reactive than sodium because sodium only forms Na₂O
Potassium is so reactive it can oxidise beyond the normal K₂O to form higher oxides
grade9-chemistry.answer: Potassium is so reactive it can oxidise beyond the normal K₂O to form higher oxides
acceptableAnswers: Potassium is so reactive it can oxidise beyond the normal K₂O to form higher oxides
grade9-chemistry.hint: More reactive metals can form more highly oxidised products.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Potassium's high reactivity means it has enough energy to form KO₂ (superoxide) in air, not just the simple oxide K₂O; sodium gives Na₂O₂ (peroxide), and lithium gives the normal oxide Li₂O.

grade9-chemistry.question: When aluminium is exposed to air, a thin oxide layer forms rapidly. Why does aluminium then appear not to corrode further?
options: Aluminium reacts with nitrogen in the air to form a protective nitride coating instead
The Al₂O₃ layer dissolves in rain water and exposes fresh metal which then re-oxidises every day
Aluminium has no further reactivity after the first atom layer has reacted
The thin, adherent Al₂O₃ layer acts as a barrier, preventing further oxygen from reaching the metal underneath
grade9-chemistry.answer: The thin, adherent Al₂O₃ layer acts as a barrier, preventing further oxygen from reaching the metal underneath
acceptableAnswers: The thin, adherent Al₂O₃ layer acts as a barrier, preventing further oxygen from reaching the metal underneath
grade9-chemistry.hint: Some oxides protect; some (like rust on iron) do not.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Al₂O₃ is a hard, insoluble oxide that sticks firmly to the aluminium surface; unlike rust (which is porous and flaky), this layer seals the surface and prevents further oxidation.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these metals forms a red oxide (Fe₂O₃) that we commonly call rust?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Iron
grade9-chemistry.hint: This is the most common form of metal corrosion in everyday life.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Iron rusts in the presence of both water and oxygen: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 2H₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·H₂O; the red-brown product is hydrated iron(III) oxide.

grade9-chemistry.question: When zinc is heated in air it forms zinc oxide. A student notes the white powder turns yellow when hot and white again when cold. This is an example of:
options: A chemical reaction that is reversed on cooling — ZnO decomposes back to Zn and O₂
A thermochromic colour change — ZnO changes colour reversibly with temperature
The zinc melting and resolidifying in a different crystalline form
Contamination of the zinc oxide by the Bunsen burner gas
grade9-chemistry.answer: A thermochromic colour change — ZnO changes colour reversibly with temperature
acceptableAnswers: A thermochromic colour change — ZnO changes colour reversibly with temperature
grade9-chemistry.hint: The composition does not change, only the colour.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: ZnO is white at room temperature but turns yellow on heating because thermal excitation changes the optical properties of the crystal; on cooling it reverts to white — a physical (thermochromic) change, not a chemical decomposition.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is the combustion of magnesium used in photography and distress flares?
options: It produces an extremely bright white light because the reaction is highly exothermic and emits visible radiation
It burns slowly and steadily, giving a controlled source of heat
It produces a coloured flame (green) that can be seen at great distances
It is the only metal that burns in air without producing any smoke
grade9-chemistry.answer: It produces an extremely bright white light because the reaction is highly exothermic and emits visible radiation
acceptableAnswers: It produces an extremely bright white light because the reaction is highly exothermic and emits visible radiation
grade9-chemistry.hint: The brightness comes from the energy released.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO releases a large amount of energy as light and heat; the temperature is high enough to produce brilliant white emission in the visible spectrum.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which product is formed when lead burns in oxygen?
options: Lead dioxide (PbO₂), a dark brown solid
grade9-chemistry.answer: Lead(II) oxide (PbO), a yellow solid
grade9-chemistry.hint: Lead is below iron in the reactivity series and forms a simple oxide.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2Pb + O₂ → 2PbO. Lead(II) oxide is a yellow solid (also known as litharge, historically used in pigments).

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the general rule for the vigour of the reaction of a metal with oxygen?
options: The more reactive the metal, the more vigorous its reaction with oxygen
All metals react with oxygen at the same rate
Only metals below iron in the reactivity series react with oxygen
The less reactive the metal, the more vigorous its reaction with oxygen
grade9-chemistry.answer: The more reactive the metal, the more vigorous its reaction with oxygen
acceptableAnswers: The more reactive the metal, the more vigorous its reaction with oxygen
grade9-chemistry.hint: Reactivity with oxygen is a direct measure of how reactive the metal is.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Reactivity with oxygen is one of the key criteria used to rank metals in the reactivity series; sodium burns violently, iron rusts slowly, and gold does not react at all.

grade9-chemistry.question: Tin is used to coat steel cans (food tins). If the tin coating is scratched, which metal corrodes first?
options: Neither corrodes because tin's oxide layer protects the whole surface
The iron (steel) corrodes rapidly because tin is below iron in the reactivity series, offering no cathodic protection
Both corrode at the same rate once the tin is scratched
The tin corrodes first because it is on the outside and exposed to more oxygen
grade9-chemistry.answer: The iron (steel) corrodes rapidly because tin is below iron in the reactivity series, offering no cathodic protection
acceptableAnswers: The iron (steel) corrodes rapidly because tin is below iron in the reactivity series, offering no cathodic protection
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about which metal is more reactive when they are connected.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Tin is less reactive than iron; when the coating is scratched, the more reactive iron acts as the anode in an electrochemical cell with the less reactive tin and corrodes preferentially — opposite to galvanising with zinc.

grade9-chemistry.question: What gas is produced when a metal reacts with a dilute acid?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: Test for it with a lighted splint.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Metal + dilute acid → salt + hydrogen. The hydrogen test: hold a lighted splint to the mouth of the tube — a "squeaky pop" confirms H₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which salt is produced when iron reacts with hydrochloric acid?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Iron(II) chloride
grade9-chemistry.hint: Metal + HCl → metal chloride + H₂.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂. With dilute HCl, iron forms iron(II) chloride because the Fe²⁺ ion is the stable product; concentrated acid can give Fe³⁺.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does gold not react with dilute sulfuric acid?
options: Gold reacts with water in the acid instead of the acid itself
Gold dissolves too slowly in all liquids to react measurably
Gold is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and cannot displace hydrogen from acids
Gold reacts only with concentrated acids, not dilute ones
grade9-chemistry.answer: Gold is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and cannot displace hydrogen from acids
acceptableAnswers: Gold is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and cannot displace hydrogen from acids
grade9-chemistry.hint: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Only metals more reactive than hydrogen can displace H⁺ from acids; gold (and platinum, copper, silver) are all below hydrogen in the series and do not react with dilute acids.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which observation shows that zinc reacts more vigorously with dilute sulfuric acid than iron?
options: Zinc produces bubbles of hydrogen more rapidly than iron under the same conditions
Iron produces more bubbles than zinc but the total yield of hydrogen is the same
Zinc forms a bright blue solution whereas iron forms a pale green one
Zinc dissolves at the same rate as iron but produces a different gas
grade9-chemistry.answer: Zinc produces bubbles of hydrogen more rapidly than iron under the same conditions
acceptableAnswers: Zinc produces bubbles of hydrogen more rapidly than iron under the same conditions
grade9-chemistry.hint: Rate of reaction is shown by rate of gas production.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series; it reacts more vigorously, so the rate of hydrogen production (bubbling) is faster.

grade9-chemistry.question: What would you observe if you added calcium to dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Nothing — calcium does not react with acids
The calcium sinks to the bottom and slowly dissolves with no visible gas
Very vigorous effervescence (hydrogen produced rapidly); the calcium disappears; the solution warms up
A green gas is produced and the calcium melts
grade9-chemistry.answer: Very vigorous effervescence (hydrogen produced rapidly); the calcium disappears; the solution warms up
acceptableAnswers: Very vigorous effervescence (hydrogen produced rapidly); the calcium disappears; the solution warms up
grade9-chemistry.hint: Calcium is a reactive metal high in the reactivity series.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ca + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂. Calcium is highly reactive, so the reaction is vigorous; the heat produced is measurable and the hydrogen produced rapidly.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student adds the same mass of three metals to equal volumes of the same concentration of hydrochloric acid: Mg, Fe, Cu. Rank them by rate of hydrogen production, fastest first.
options: All three produce the same amount at the same rate
grade9-chemistry.answer: Mg > Fe > Cu (copper produces none)
grade9-chemistry.hint: Use the reactivity series to predict order.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Mg is above Fe which is above H₂ in the reactivity series; Cu is below H₂. So Mg reacts fastest, Fe more slowly, and Cu not at all.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which salt is formed when zinc reacts with sulfuric acid?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Zinc sulfate
grade9-chemistry.hint: The salt takes the metal and the anion of the acid.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. The salt is zinc sulfate, formed from zinc ions and sulfate ions from the acid.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student adds excess zinc to dilute sulfuric acid. What does "excess zinc" ensure?
options: All the acid is consumed, so maximum hydrogen yield is obtained
The hydrogen produced is twice as pure as with the stoichiometric amount
The reaction continues indefinitely until all the zinc dissolves
The concentration of the zinc sulfate solution is doubled
grade9-chemistry.answer: All the acid is consumed, so maximum hydrogen yield is obtained
acceptableAnswers: All the acid is consumed, so maximum hydrogen yield is obtained
grade9-chemistry.hint: Excess of one reactant ensures the other (the limiting reactant) is completely used up.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Using excess zinc ensures the acid (the limiting reagent) is fully consumed; this maximises H₂ yield. Some zinc remains unreacted at the end.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does iron react faster with concentrated hydrochloric acid than with dilute acid?
options: The iron dissolves better in concentrated acid because the oxide layer is thicker
Higher concentration means more H⁺ ions per unit volume, increasing the collision frequency
Concentrated acid changes the type of salt formed, which is more soluble
Concentrated acid is hotter, providing more activation energy
grade9-chemistry.answer: Higher concentration means more H⁺ ions per unit volume, increasing the collision frequency
acceptableAnswers: Higher concentration means more H⁺ ions per unit volume, increasing the collision frequency
grade9-chemistry.hint: Rate depends on the concentration of the reacting species.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Reaction rate increases with concentration because there are more H⁺ ions in the same volume, leading to more frequent collisions between H⁺ and the metal surface.

grade9-chemistry.question: The graph of volume of hydrogen against time for Mg + HCl shows a steep initial gradient that levels off. What does the levelling off indicate?
options: The hydrogen has reacted with oxygen in the air above the reaction
The magnesium has run out and there is excess acid remaining
The temperature has dropped and the reaction has slowed permanently
The acid has been completely consumed and the reaction has stopped
grade9-chemistry.answer: The acid has been completely consumed and the reaction has stopped
acceptableAnswers: The acid has been completely consumed and the reaction has stopped
grade9-chemistry.hint: The reaction stops when one of the reactants is used up.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The gradient (rate) falls as acid is consumed; once all the acid has reacted the curve is flat — total H₂ evolved equals the theoretical maximum for the amount of acid used (assuming Mg is in excess).

grade9-chemistry.question: Lead reacts only very slowly with dilute sulfuric acid even though it is above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Why?
options: The lead surface has no oxide layer to dissolve before the metal can react
Sulfuric acid is too concentrated for lead to dissolve in it
Lead sulfate (PbSO₄) is insoluble and coats the lead surface, blocking further reaction
Lead is actually below hydrogen in the reactivity series and cannot displace H⁺
grade9-chemistry.answer: Lead sulfate (PbSO₄) is insoluble and coats the lead surface, blocking further reaction
acceptableAnswers: Lead sulfate (PbSO₄) is insoluble and coats the lead surface, blocking further reaction
grade9-chemistry.hint: The product of the reaction is the key here.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: PbSO₄ is almost insoluble; it coats the lead surface immediately, preventing further contact between the acid and the metal — a classic example of a passivating insoluble product.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which test confirms that the gas produced in a metal–acid reaction is hydrogen?
options: The gas turns damp red litmus paper blue
A lighted splint held near the gas causes a squeaky pop as it ignites
The gas turns lime water milky
The gas relights a glowing splint
grade9-chemistry.answer: A lighted splint held near the gas causes a squeaky pop as it ignites
acceptableAnswers: A lighted splint held near the gas causes a squeaky pop as it ignites
grade9-chemistry.hint: Hydrogen is flammable — it burns with a small explosion.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Hydrogen ignites with a distinctive squeaky pop when a lighted splint is applied; CO₂ turns lime water milky; O₂ relights a glowing splint; NH₃ turns litmus blue.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does copper dissolve in concentrated nitric acid but not in dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Dilute HCl dissolves copper oxide but not the copper metal itself
Concentrated nitric acid is an oxidising acid; it oxidises copper even though Cu is below H in the reactivity series
Copper is above hydrogen in the reactivity series and displaces it only from hot concentrated acid
Copper reacts with the concentrated nitrogen in the acid, not the hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.answer: Concentrated nitric acid is an oxidising acid; it oxidises copper even though Cu is below H in the reactivity series
acceptableAnswers: Concentrated nitric acid is an oxidising acid; it oxidises copper even though Cu is below H in the reactivity series
grade9-chemistry.hint: Some acids react by oxidising rather than by releasing H₂.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Cu is below H₂ in the reactivity series and does not displace H⁺ from non-oxidising acids; but HNO₃ (concentrated) uses NO₃⁻ as the oxidising agent, dissolving Cu to form Cu(NO₃)₂ and releasing brown NO₂ gas.

grade9-chemistry.question: Magnesium reacts with dilute nitric acid to form magnesium nitrate and hydrogen. Which statement about this reaction is true?
options: No hydrogen is produced because nitric acid always produces nitrogen dioxide
Dilute nitric acid is too weak to react with magnesium
Mg + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂ — the reaction follows the same pattern as with other dilute acids
Magnesium dissolves in nitric acid to give magnesium oxide and water
grade9-chemistry.answer: Mg + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂ — the reaction follows the same pattern as with other dilute acids
acceptableAnswers: Mg + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂ — the reaction follows the same pattern as with other dilute acids
grade9-chemistry.hint: Dilute nitric acid behaves as a typical acid with very reactive metals.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Very reactive metals (Mg, Zn) do release H₂ with dilute HNO₃; with less reactive metals or with concentrated HNO₃, nitrogen oxides are formed instead. Mg reacts vigorously with dilute HNO₃ to give H₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these metals reacts vigorously with cold water?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Potassium
grade9-chemistry.hint: Only the most reactive metals react with cold water.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Potassium reacts explosively with cold water: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂. Sodium and calcium also react with cold water, but iron, copper and zinc do not.

grade9-chemistry.question: Sodium is added to water. The solution formed turns universal indicator purple. What does this show about the solution?
options: It is strongly acidic — the sodium released acid as it reacted
It is slightly acidic — sodium dissolves to form a weak acid
It is strongly alkaline — sodium hydroxide (NaOH) has dissolved in the water
It is neutral — the purple is due to dissolved sodium metal
grade9-chemistry.answer: It is strongly alkaline — sodium hydroxide (NaOH) has dissolved in the water
acceptableAnswers: It is strongly alkaline — sodium hydroxide (NaOH) has dissolved in the water
grade9-chemistry.hint: The product of sodium + water is a metal hydroxide.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. NaOH is a strong alkali; purple on universal indicator indicates high pH (strongly alkaline).

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does zinc react with steam but not with liquid cold water?
options: Steam provides enough energy to overcome the activation energy for the reaction with zinc
Zinc is less reactive than hydrogen so it cannot react with any water
Zinc reacts only with the oxygen dissolved in liquid water, not with the H₂O molecules
Liquid water freezes around the zinc and stops the reaction
grade9-chemistry.answer: Steam provides enough energy to overcome the activation energy for the reaction with zinc
acceptableAnswers: Steam provides enough energy to overcome the activation energy for the reaction with zinc
grade9-chemistry.hint: Temperature (energy) determines whether a reaction proceeds at a useful rate.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Zinc is in the middle of the reactivity series; it requires the higher temperature of steam to provide sufficient activation energy for the reaction: Zn + H₂O(steam) → ZnO + H₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: What products are formed when calcium reacts with water?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Calcium hydroxide and hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.hint: Reactive metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Calcium reacts steadily with cold water to form slightly soluble calcium hydroxide (limewater) and hydrogen gas.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which observation distinguishes the reaction of potassium with water from that of sodium with water?
options: Potassium produces oxygen instead of hydrogen while sodium produces hydrogen
Potassium sinks to the bottom of the water while sodium floats
Sodium dissolves completely in cold water while potassium leaves an insoluble residue
Potassium ignites the hydrogen produced, giving a lilac-coloured flame, while sodium's flame is orange
grade9-chemistry.answer: Potassium ignites the hydrogen produced, giving a lilac-coloured flame, while sodium's flame is orange
acceptableAnswers: Potassium ignites the hydrogen produced, giving a lilac-coloured flame, while sodium's flame is orange
grade9-chemistry.hint: The greater reactivity of K provides more energy.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: K is more reactive than Na; the extra heat from the K reaction ignites the H₂ immediately, producing a lilac flame (characteristic of K); with Na, the hydrogen is released but does not usually ignite at room temperature.

grade9-chemistry.question: When iron reacts with steam, the product is Fe₃O₄. What is the common name of this compound?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Iron(II,III) oxide (magnetite)
grade9-chemistry.hint: Steam reacts with iron at red heat to give a mixed oxide.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 3Fe + 4H₂O(steam) → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂. Fe₃O₄ is a mixed oxide of Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, commonly called magnetite; haematite (Fe₂O₃) is the oxide in rust.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student passes steam over heated iron and collects the gas. She tests the gas with a lighted splint and gets a squeaky pop. What does this confirm, and why is the reaction reversible?
options: Hydrogen is produced; the reaction is irreversible because Fe₃O₄ is a very stable compound
Steam itself ignites in the test; the reaction is not reversible
Oxygen is produced; the iron is acting as a catalyst splitting water
Hydrogen is produced; the reaction is reversible because the products (Fe₃O₄ and H₂) can react with each other at the same temperature
grade9-chemistry.answer: Hydrogen is produced; the reaction is reversible because the products (Fe₃O₄ and H₂) can react with each other at the same temperature
acceptableAnswers: Hydrogen is produced; the reaction is reversible because the products (Fe₃O₄ and H₂) can react with each other at the same temperature
grade9-chemistry.hint: The squeaky pop means H₂; think about equilibrium in a closed tube.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The squeaky pop confirms H₂; the reaction 3Fe + 4H₂O ⇌ Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂ is reversible — this industrial fact is used in the steam-iron process for hydrogen production, where steam is continually removed to drive the equilibrium right.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these metals does NOT react with steam even at very high temperatures?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Copper
grade9-chemistry.hint: Use the reactivity series — only metals above copper react with steam.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series; it cannot displace H₂ from steam or water. Zinc, iron and aluminium are all above hydrogen and can react with steam.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is the reaction of very reactive metals like sodium with water described as "dangerous" in a laboratory context?
options: The hydrogen produced can be ignited by the heat of the exothermic reaction, and the alkali produced can cause severe chemical burns
The reaction releases a toxic gas (nitrogen dioxide) that must be captured in a fume cupboard
The sodium liquefies and spatters, but this is only a burn hazard if the temperature exceeds 200 °C
The metal dissolves too quickly, making the solution acidic and corrosive to laboratory bench surfaces
grade9-chemistry.answer: The hydrogen produced can be ignited by the heat of the exothermic reaction, and the alkali produced can cause severe chemical burns
acceptableAnswers: The hydrogen produced can be ignited by the heat of the exothermic reaction, and the alkali produced can cause severe chemical burns
grade9-chemistry.hint: Two hazards: the flammable gas and the corrosive product.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂. The reaction is highly exothermic; H₂ can ignite; molten Na can spatter; and NaOH is corrosive (pH > 13). Potassium is even more dangerous as the H₂ always ignites.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student compares the reactions of small pieces of Li, Na and K with water in a class demonstration. What trend does she observe?
options: Li reacts most violently because it is the smallest and has the most concentrated charge
All three react identically because they are all alkali metals
K reacts most gently because it is heavier and denser than the others
Li reacts gently, Na more vigorously, K most vigorously — reactivity increases down Group 1
grade9-chemistry.answer: Li reacts gently, Na more vigorously, K most vigorously — reactivity increases down Group 1
acceptableAnswers: Li reacts gently, Na more vigorously, K most vigorously — reactivity increases down Group 1
grade9-chemistry.hint: Reactivity increases going down Group 1 of the periodic table.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Going down Group 1, the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more easily lost, making each successive metal more reactive with water and all other reagents.

grade9-chemistry.question: Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but rapidly with steam. What does this show about activation energy?
options: Magnesium reacts with the oxygen in steam, not with the water molecules
The reaction of Mg with water has a high activation energy that steam (higher temperature) provides, while cold water does not
Steam is purer water than cold water and purity affects the reaction rate
Steam contains more water molecules per unit volume, giving more collisions
grade9-chemistry.answer: The reaction of Mg with water has a high activation energy that steam (higher temperature) provides, while cold water does not
acceptableAnswers: The reaction of Mg with water has a high activation energy that steam (higher temperature) provides, while cold water does not
grade9-chemistry.hint: High temperature means more particles have energy above the activation energy.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: At the higher temperature of steam, a much larger proportion of H₂O molecules have kinetic energy exceeding the activation energy for reacting with Mg; at room temperature, too few molecules overcome the barrier for the reaction to be observable.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which product of the reaction between potassium and water makes the resulting solution alkaline?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Potassium hydroxide (KOH)
grade9-chemistry.hint: Hydroxides of Group 1 metals are strong bases.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂. KOH is a strong alkali that fully dissociates in water, giving a high concentration of OH⁻ ions and a high pH.

grade9-chemistry.question: Aluminium is above zinc in the reactivity series, yet powdered aluminium reacts less vigorously than zinc with steam at first. Why?
options: Aluminium is actually below zinc in the reactivity series for steam reactions
Aluminium reacts with the nitrogen in steam rather than the oxygen in water
Aluminium has a much higher melting point than zinc so the steam cannot heat it enough
A thin layer of aluminium oxide on the surface prevents immediate reaction; once breached the reaction is fast
grade9-chemistry.answer: A thin layer of aluminium oxide on the surface prevents immediate reaction; once breached the reaction is fast
acceptableAnswers: A thin layer of aluminium oxide on the surface prevents immediate reaction; once breached the reaction is fast
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about the oxide layer on aluminium.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The protective Al₂O₃ coating on aluminium surface slows initial reaction; once the surface is activated (e.g., in strongly acidic or alkaline conditions), aluminium reacts vigorously consistent with its position above zinc in the reactivity series.

grade9-chemistry.question: In which situation would you use the reaction of a metal with steam to produce hydrogen industrially?
options: The Haber process: reacting steam with nitrogen at 450 °C to give hydrogen and ammonia together
Electrolysis of water: passing steam through an electric arc to split it
Thermal decomposition: heating steam to above 2500 °C until it decomposes into H₂ and O₂
The steam-iron process: passing steam over iron at ~750 °C, then using hydrogen to make ammonia
grade9-chemistry.answer: The steam-iron process: passing steam over iron at ~750 °C, then using hydrogen to make ammonia
acceptableAnswers: The steam-iron process: passing steam over iron at ~750 °C, then using hydrogen to make ammonia
grade9-chemistry.hint: This was a historical industrial process for making hydrogen.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The steam-iron (Messerschmitt) process: 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂ at ~750 °C. The Fe₃O₄ is reduced back with more steam or with coal gas. It was used before steam reforming became dominant.

grade9-chemistry.question: In the standard reactivity series, which metal is the MOST reactive?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Potassium (K)
grade9-chemistry.hint: The most reactive metal is at the top of the series.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The reactivity series (most to least reactive) starts: K > Na > Li > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Sn > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au > Pt.

grade9-chemistry.question: Where does hydrogen appear in the reactivity series?
options: Between lead and copper (below most common metals)
grade9-chemistry.answer: Between lead and copper (below most common metals)
acceptableAnswers: Between lead and copper (below most common metals)
grade9-chemistry.hint: Its position explains which metals can displace hydrogen from acids.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Hydrogen is placed in the reactivity series between lead and copper; metals above hydrogen can displace it from acids, metals below (Cu, Ag, Au) cannot.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student adds four metals — Cu, Zn, Ag, Mg — to separate test tubes of dilute sulfuric acid. Which two produce bubbles?
options: Zn and Mg (both above H in the reactivity series)
Cu and Ag (as the most common metals)
All four react with dilute sulfuric acid
Only Mg reacts; Zn does not react with sulfuric acid
grade9-chemistry.answer: Zn and Mg (both above H in the reactivity series)
acceptableAnswers: Zn and Mg (both above H in the reactivity series)
grade9-chemistry.hint: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series displace H₂ from acids.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Mg and Zn are above H in the reactivity series; Cu and Ag are below it. Only Mg and Zn displace H⁺ from H₂SO₄ to give H₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which observation is used to place metals in the reactivity series using displacement reactions?
options: Whether a metal floats on water
Whether a metal displaces another metal from a solution of its salt
Whether a metal reacts with oxygen more quickly than it dissolves in acid
Whether a metal has a high or low melting point
grade9-chemistry.answer: Whether a metal displaces another metal from a solution of its salt
acceptableAnswers: Whether a metal displaces another metal from a solution of its salt
grade9-chemistry.hint: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its compound.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: If metal A displaces metal B from a solution of B's salt (A + BSO₄ → ASO₄ + B), then A is more reactive than B; this displacement experiment is a key method for ranking metals.

grade9-chemistry.question: A piece of copper is placed in silver nitrate solution. A silvery deposit forms on the copper and the solution turns blue. What does this show?
options: Copper and silver react to form a copper-silver alloy
Copper is more reactive than silver and displaces it from the solution
Silver is more reactive and has displaced copper from the solid
The blue colour is silver dissolving, making the solution blue
grade9-chemistry.answer: Copper is more reactive than silver and displaces it from the solution
acceptableAnswers: Copper is more reactive than silver and displaces it from the solution
grade9-chemistry.hint: The more reactive metal displaces the less reactive one.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. Copper displaces silver (Ag) forming a silvery deposit; Cu²⁺ ions enter solution, turning it blue. This confirms Cu > Ag in reactivity.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student performs four displacement reactions and records whether a reaction occurs (✓) or not (✗): Fe in CuSO₄ (✓), Cu in FeSO₄ (✗), Zn in FeSO₄ (✓), Fe in ZnSO₄ (✗). What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Zn > Fe > Cu
grade9-chemistry.hint: Which metal can displace which?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Fe displaces Cu (Fe > Cu); Cu cannot displace Fe (Cu < Fe); Zn displaces Fe (Zn > Fe); Fe cannot displace Zn (Fe < Zn). Therefore Zn > Fe > Cu.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is sodium stored under oil rather than in water?
options: Water would rust the sodium; oil prevents oxidation of the metal surface
Oil makes sodium more reactive, which is useful for starting the reaction when needed
Sodium dissolves in water very slowly and the oil prevents this
Sodium is so reactive it reacts vigorously and dangerously with water, but oil does not react with it
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sodium is so reactive it reacts vigorously and dangerously with water, but oil does not react with it
acceptableAnswers: Sodium is so reactive it reacts vigorously and dangerously with water, but oil does not react with it
grade9-chemistry.hint: Storage method reflects how reactive the metal is with common substances.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Na + H₂O: the reaction is highly exothermic and can start fires; oil is non-reactive and provides an inert barrier. Reactivity series position (very high for Na) determines storage requirements.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of the following statements about the reactivity series is correct?
options: Metals lower in the series are easier to extract from their ores by heating alone
Metals lower in the series are more reactive in all chemical reactions
Metals higher in the series are more readily oxidised (lose electrons more easily)
Both A and B are correct
grade9-chemistry.answer: Both A and B are correct
acceptableAnswers: Both A and B are correct
grade9-chemistry.hint: The reactivity series tells us about two things simultaneously.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Both statements are true: (A) higher metals lose electrons more readily (more reactive); (B) lower metals (Cu, Hg) can be extracted just by heating their oxides because the bond to oxygen is weak — e.g. 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is platinum used in jewellery?
options: It is the hardest of all metals, making it the most durable
It is the most reactive metal and therefore the purest and brightest
It reacts with oxygen to form a thin protective layer that gives it a shine
It is very unreactive and resists tarnishing, acids and corrosion
grade9-chemistry.answer: It is very unreactive and resists tarnishing, acids and corrosion
acceptableAnswers: It is very unreactive and resists tarnishing, acids and corrosion
grade9-chemistry.hint: Its position at the bottom of the reactivity series explains its use.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Platinum is at the bottom of the reactivity series (along with gold) — it does not react with oxygen, water or dilute acids, making it ideal for jewellery and catalytic converters.

grade9-chemistry.question: Iron can be extracted from iron ore (Fe₂O₃) by heating with carbon monoxide. Why can potassium not be extracted the same way?
options: Potassium melts at too low a temperature for the reaction with CO to work
Potassium ore does not contain any oxygen and carbon monoxide has no effect on it
Potassium is more reactive than carbon and carbon cannot displace it from its compounds
Carbon monoxide is toxic and would contaminate the potassium
grade9-chemistry.answer: Potassium is more reactive than carbon and carbon cannot displace it from its compounds
acceptableAnswers: Potassium is more reactive than carbon and carbon cannot displace it from its compounds
grade9-chemistry.hint: Carbon/CO can only displace metals that are less reactive than carbon.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: In the reactivity series, carbon sits between aluminium and zinc; it can reduce metals below it (Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu) but cannot reduce metals above it (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al). Potassium must be extracted by electrolysis.

grade9-chemistry.question: The reactivity series is sometimes called the electrochemical series. Why?
options: It was determined entirely by electrical experiments in which metals were used as electrodes
Reactivity determines how well a metal conducts electricity
Each position in the series corresponds to the electrical resistance of the metal
It reflects how easily each metal loses electrons (is oxidised), which also determines standard electrode potential
grade9-chemistry.answer: It reflects how easily each metal loses electrons (is oxidised), which also determines standard electrode potential
acceptableAnswers: It reflects how easily each metal loses electrons (is oxidised), which also determines standard electrode potential
grade9-chemistry.hint: Reactivity = tendency to lose electrons = electrochemical potential.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The more reactive a metal, the more readily it loses electrons (is oxidised); this is measured as a more negative standard electrode potential. The two series (reactivity and electrochemical) order metals in the same sequence.

grade9-chemistry.question: Zinc is used to galvanise steel (iron). Why does zinc protect iron even when the zinc coating is scratched?
options: Zinc is more reactive than iron; when both are exposed, Zn corrodes preferentially, protecting Fe
Zinc and iron react together to form an alloy that is more resistant to corrosion than either alone
Zinc is less reactive than iron; it acts as a physical barrier only and so scratching destroys the protection
Zinc forms a thick oxide layer that seals the scratch and prevents air reaching the iron
grade9-chemistry.answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron; when both are exposed, Zn corrodes preferentially, protecting Fe
acceptableAnswers: Zinc is more reactive than iron; when both are exposed, Zn corrodes preferentially, protecting Fe
grade9-chemistry.hint: The more reactive metal sacrifices itself.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Zn > Fe in the reactivity series; where both are exposed, Zn is oxidised (sacrificed) in preference to Fe. This sacrificial protection continues even through a scratch — unlike tin coating, which accelerates iron corrosion once scratched.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these is the correct order of metals from LEAST reactive to MOST reactive?
options: Na < K < Zn < Fe < Au < Cu
K < Na < Zn < Fe < Cu < Au
Au < Cu < Fe < Zn < Na < K
Fe < Zn < Cu < Na < K < Au
grade9-chemistry.answer: Au < Cu < Fe < Zn < Na < K
acceptableAnswers: Au < Cu < Fe < Zn < Na < K
grade9-chemistry.hint: Learn the series from the bottom up: Au, Ag, Hg, Cu, Pb, Sn, Fe, Zn, Al, Mg, Ca, Na, K.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The standard reactivity series (least to most reactive): Au, Ag, Hg, Cu, Pb, Sn, Fe, Zn, Al, Mg, Ca, Na, K. So Au < Cu < Fe < Zn < Na < K.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student performs a thermite reaction: aluminium powder reacts with iron(III) oxide to give aluminium oxide and iron. What does this show?
options: Both metals are equally reactive; the reaction is driven by the heat applied
Aluminium is more reactive than iron and can displace it from its oxide
The reaction works only because Fe₂O₃ is soluble and aluminium is not
Iron is more reactive than aluminium and displaces aluminium from its oxide
grade9-chemistry.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than iron and can displace it from its oxide
acceptableAnswers: Aluminium is more reactive than iron and can displace it from its oxide
grade9-chemistry.hint: The more reactive metal displaces the less reactive metal even from its oxide.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe. Al is above Fe in the reactivity series; it displaces Fe from Fe₂O₃ in a highly exothermic reaction (thermite) used for welding railway tracks.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which metal is extracted by electrolysis because it is too reactive to be reduced by carbon or carbon monoxide?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Aluminium
grade9-chemistry.hint: Al is above carbon in the reactivity series.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series; carbon cannot reduce Al₂O₃. Al is extracted industrially by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide (the Hall-Héroult process).

grade9-chemistry.question: Will copper react with iron(II) sulfate solution? Explain why.
options: Yes — copper always reacts with sulfate solutions regardless of reactivity
No — copper only reacts with nitrate solutions
No — copper is less reactive than iron and cannot displace it from solution
Yes — copper is more reactive than iron and displaces it
grade9-chemistry.answer: No — copper is less reactive than iron and cannot displace it from solution
acceptableAnswers: No — copper is less reactive than iron and cannot displace it from solution
grade9-chemistry.hint: A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Cu < Fe in the reactivity series; a metal can only displace a less reactive metal from solution. Cu cannot displace Fe²⁺, so no reaction occurs.

grade9-chemistry.question: Will zinc react with copper(II) sulfate solution?
options: Yes — zinc is more reactive than copper and displaces it from solution
Yes — but only if the solution is heated
No — zinc cannot react with sulfate solutions
No — copper is more reactive than zinc
grade9-chemistry.answer: Yes — zinc is more reactive than copper and displaces it from solution
acceptableAnswers: Yes — zinc is more reactive than copper and displaces it from solution
grade9-chemistry.hint: Zn is above Cu in the reactivity series.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Zinc displaces copper, depositing a reddish-brown layer of copper on the zinc surface and the blue colour of the copper solution fades.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these reactions will NOT occur?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Fe + MgSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Mg
grade9-chemistry.hint: Can Fe displace Mg? Use the reactivity series.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Mg > Fe in the reactivity series; iron cannot displace magnesium from its salt solution. The other three reactions are all possible because a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student places an iron nail in copper sulfate solution. After 20 minutes, what does she observe?
options: A reddish-brown deposit forms on the nail and the blue solution becomes paler
The nail dissolves completely and the solution turns green
No change — iron and copper sulfate do not react
The solution turns orange and the nail remains shiny
grade9-chemistry.answer: A reddish-brown deposit forms on the nail and the blue solution becomes paler
acceptableAnswers: A reddish-brown deposit forms on the nail and the blue solution becomes paler
grade9-chemistry.hint: Fe displaces Cu: the displaced copper deposits on the nail.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. Copper (reddish-brown) deposits on the iron nail; the blue Cu²⁺ solution becomes paler as Cu²⁺ is removed and replaced by pale green Fe²⁺.

grade9-chemistry.question: Metal X reacts with dilute acid but not with cold water; metal Y reacts with neither acid nor cold water; metal Z reacts with cold water and with dilute acid. Rank X, Y, Z in order of reactivity (most reactive first).
grade9-chemistry.answer: Z > X > Y
grade9-chemistry.hint: Use the observations to place each in the reactivity series.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Z reacts with cold water → above Ca level (or at least above Fe level that reacts with steam/acid). X reacts with acid but not cold water → between Mg and Cu (e.g. Zn, Fe level). Y does not react with acid → below H in the series (e.g. Cu, Ag). Order: Z > X > Y.

grade9-chemistry.question: Predict the product when lead is added to silver nitrate solution. (Pb > Ag in reactivity series)
options: No reaction occurs because lead and silver are adjacent in the reactivity series
Silver displaces lead: Ag + Pb(NO₃)₂ → AgNO₃ + Pb
Lead reacts with the nitrate ion only, forming lead nitrate and releasing nitrogen gas
Lead displaces silver: Pb + 2AgNO₃ → Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag (silver crystals form)
grade9-chemistry.answer: Lead displaces silver: Pb + 2AgNO₃ → Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag (silver crystals form)
acceptableAnswers: Lead displaces silver: Pb + 2AgNO₃ → Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag (silver crystals form)
grade9-chemistry.hint: The more reactive metal (Pb) displaces the less reactive (Ag).
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Pb > Ag in the reactivity series; Pb displaces Ag from AgNO₃ solution, forming silvery Ag crystals and dissolving to give colourless Pb(NO₃)₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: A strip of magnesium is placed in a solution containing both copper sulfate and zinc sulfate at the same concentration. Which metal, if any, deposits on the magnesium first?
options: Only Zn deposits because Mg is only just more reactive than Zn
Both Cu and Zn deposit, but Cu deposits faster because the greater the difference in reactivity, the faster the displacement
Neither deposits because Mg dissolves before any displacement can occur
Only Cu deposits because Mg displaces only the least reactive metal present
grade9-chemistry.answer: Both Cu and Zn deposit, but Cu deposits faster because the greater the difference in reactivity, the faster the displacement
acceptableAnswers: Both Cu and Zn deposit, but Cu deposits faster because the greater the difference in reactivity, the faster the displacement
grade9-chemistry.hint: Mg displaces both Zn and Cu; the one with greater reactivity difference displaces faster.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Mg > Zn > Cu in reactivity. Mg displaces both; the Cu²⁺ displacement is more exothermic (greater ΔEᵣ) and proceeds faster. A mixed deposit of Zn and Cu would form, with Cu depositing more rapidly.

grade9-chemistry.question: Will iron(III) oxide be reduced by carbon monoxide at high temperature? Why?
options: Yes — CO reduces all metal oxides regardless of their position in the reactivity series
No — iron is more reactive than carbon, so CO cannot reduce iron oxide
Yes — CO (like C) can act as a reducing agent for metals below aluminium in the reactivity series
No — only carbon (not CO) can reduce metal oxides
grade9-chemistry.answer: Yes — CO (like C) can act as a reducing agent for metals below aluminium in the reactivity series
acceptableAnswers: Yes — CO (like C) can act as a reducing agent for metals below aluminium in the reactivity series
grade9-chemistry.hint: This is how iron is extracted in a blast furnace.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Fe is below C in the reactivity series, so C (and CO, which is produced from C in the furnace) can reduce iron oxide — the basis of the blast furnace process.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student mixes silver powder with copper sulfate solution. She observes no reaction. Then she mixes copper powder with silver nitrate solution and observes a deposit. What can she conclude?
options: Silver is more reactive than copper: Ag > Cu
Copper is more reactive than silver: Cu > Ag in the reactivity series
Silver and copper have equal reactivity
The observations are contradictory and do not allow a conclusion
grade9-chemistry.answer: Copper is more reactive than silver: Cu > Ag in the reactivity series
acceptableAnswers: Copper is more reactive than silver: Cu > Ag in the reactivity series
grade9-chemistry.hint: Which metal displaces which?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ag cannot displace Cu from CuSO₄ → Ag < Cu. Cu displaces Ag from AgNO₃ → Cu > Ag. Both observations are consistent: Cu > Ag.

grade9-chemistry.question: Predict whether calcium will react with cold water, steam only, dilute acid only, or none of these.
options: Calcium reacts only with dilute acid and not with water
Calcium does not react with water, steam or dilute acid
Calcium reacts vigorously with cold water and also with dilute acid
Calcium reacts with steam only and not with cold water
grade9-chemistry.answer: Calcium reacts vigorously with cold water and also with dilute acid
acceptableAnswers: Calcium reacts vigorously with cold water and also with dilute acid
grade9-chemistry.hint: Calcium is a reactive metal above magnesium in the reactivity series.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ca is high in the reactivity series (K > Na > Ca > Mg). Metals above Mg react with cold water; Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. It also reacts with dilute acids.

grade9-chemistry.question: Tin is used inside food cans (tinplate). If exposed to an electrolyte (e.g. fruit juice), does the tin-iron couple corrode the iron or the tin first?
options: Iron corrodes first because tin is below iron in the reactivity series and acts as the cathode
Both corrode at the same rate because they are in electrical contact
Neither corrodes because the tin seals the iron completely
Tin corrodes first because it is on the outside and exposed to more electrolyte
grade9-chemistry.answer: Iron corrodes first because tin is below iron in the reactivity series and acts as the cathode
acceptableAnswers: Iron corrodes first because tin is below iron in the reactivity series and acts as the cathode
grade9-chemistry.hint: In a galvanic cell, the less reactive metal is the cathode (protected) and the more reactive is the anode (corroded).
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sn < Fe is wrong — actually Sn is just below Fe in the reactivity series (Fe > Sn). When the tin coating is scratched, iron is the more reactive metal and acts as anode, corroding preferentially. This is why tinned cans should not be used once opened and scraped.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these statements correctly uses the reactivity series to predict behaviour?
options: A metal high in the reactivity series is the most useful because it reacts with everything
A metal high in the reactivity series will react more vigorously with oxygen, water and acids
A metal in the middle of the series will not react with anything
A metal low in the reactivity series is harder to extract from its ore
grade9-chemistry.answer: A metal high in the reactivity series will react more vigorously with oxygen, water and acids
acceptableAnswers: A metal high in the reactivity series will react more vigorously with oxygen, water and acids
grade9-chemistry.hint: Reactivity series = vigour of reactions.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A high position in the reactivity series means the metal is more easily oxidised, reacting more vigorously with all common reagents; metals low in the series are less reactive but actually more useful in their elemental form (e.g. Au for jewellery).

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does calcium react with cold water but magnesium reacts only with steam?
options: Calcium is more reactive than magnesium; it has a lower activation energy for the reaction with water and reacts at room temperature
Both metals react equally with cold water; the difference is in their product solubility
Calcium reacts with the oxygen dissolved in cold water; magnesium reacts only with pure H₂O in steam
Magnesium reacts with cold water at the same rate as calcium but produces a different gas
grade9-chemistry.answer: Calcium is more reactive than magnesium; it has a lower activation energy for the reaction with water and reacts at room temperature
acceptableAnswers: Calcium is more reactive than magnesium; it has a lower activation energy for the reaction with water and reacts at room temperature
grade9-chemistry.hint: Position in reactivity series: Ca > Mg.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ca > Mg in reactivity; the reaction Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂ proceeds at room temperature because the lower activation energy is met by the thermal energy at 25 °C. Mg requires the higher temperature of steam to supply sufficient activation energy.

grade9-chemistry.question: An unknown metal M reacts slowly with dilute acid but not with cold water. Which position does it most likely occupy in the reactivity series?
options: At exactly the position of hydrogen because it does not react with water
Between hydrogen and calcium — it reacts with acid but not water, placing it in the middle (e.g. Zn, Fe, Sn level)
Above potassium — it is so reactive it skips water reactions
Below copper — it cannot react with dilute acid
grade9-chemistry.answer: Between hydrogen and calcium — it reacts with acid but not water, placing it in the middle (e.g. Zn, Fe, Sn level)
acceptableAnswers: Between hydrogen and calcium — it reacts with acid but not water, placing it in the middle (e.g. Zn, Fe, Sn level)
grade9-chemistry.hint: Divide the series by what each metal can and cannot react with.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Metals that react with acid but not cold water are in the middle band: below Ca (which reacts with cold water) but above H (below which metals do not react with dilute acid). Examples: Mg (steam only), Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb.

grade9-chemistry.question: Write the balanced equation for magnesium burning in oxygen.
grade9-chemistry.answer: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
grade9-chemistry.hint: Oxygen exists as diatomic O₂; balance Mg on both sides.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: One mole of O₂ provides 2 O atoms; 2 Mg atoms react to give 2 MgO: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which equation correctly represents the reaction of sodium with water?
grade9-chemistry.answer: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
grade9-chemistry.hint: Balance Na, O and H carefully.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Left: 2 Na, 4 H, 2 O. Right: 2 Na, 2 O, 2 H (in 2NaOH) + 2 H (in H₂) = 4 H total, 2 O. Balanced.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which is the correct balanced equation for the displacement of copper by iron from copper sulfate solution?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu
grade9-chemistry.hint: Fe forms Fe²⁺, so one Fe replaces one Cu²⁺.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Fe²⁺ (from Fe) replaces Cu²⁺ (from CuSO₄): one Fe replaces one Cu, giving FeSO₄. Atoms: 1 Fe, 1 Cu, 1 S, 4 O both sides. Balanced.

grade9-chemistry.question: Balance the equation for zinc reacting with hydrochloric acid: Zn + _HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
grade9-chemistry.answer: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
grade9-chemistry.hint: ZnCl₂ needs 2 Cl atoms from 2 HCl; those 2 H become H₂.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. 2 HCl provide 2 Cl (for ZnCl₂) and 2 H (for H₂). Balanced: 1 Zn, 2 H, 2 Cl each side.

grade9-chemistry.question: Write the balanced equation for aluminium reacting with dilute sulfuric acid.
grade9-chemistry.answer: 2Al + 3H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3H₂
grade9-chemistry.hint: Al³⁺ reacts with SO₄²⁻; find the formula of aluminium sulfate first.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ give Al₂(SO₄)₃. 2 Al react with 3 H₂SO₄: left 4 H, right 3H₂ = 6H. Wait — 2Al + 3H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3H₂: left 6H, right 6H. Left: 2Al, 3S, 12O; right: 2Al, 3S, 12O. Balanced.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the balanced equation for calcium reacting with water?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂
grade9-chemistry.hint: Ca forms Ca²⁺, so Ca(OH)₂ needs 2 OH groups from 2 H₂O.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Left: 1 Ca, 4 H, 2 O. Right: 1 Ca, 2 OH (2 O, 2 H) + H₂ (2 H) = 4 H, 2 O. Balanced.

grade9-chemistry.question: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of iron with steam.
grade9-chemistry.answer: 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂
grade9-chemistry.hint: The product with steam is Fe₃O₄, not Fe₂O₃.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Left: 3 Fe, 8 H, 4 O. Right: 3 Fe (in Fe₃O₄), 4 O (in Fe₃O₄), 8 H (in 4H₂). Balanced.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which equation correctly shows copper reacting with oxygen?
grade9-chemistry.answer: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO
grade9-chemistry.hint: Copper(II) oxide formula is CuO; oxygen is diatomic.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO. Two Cu atoms react with one O₂ to give two CuO units. Balanced: 2 Cu, 2 O each side.

grade9-chemistry.question: The thermite reaction: Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + Fe. Balance this equation.
grade9-chemistry.answer: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe
grade9-chemistry.hint: Balance Al first (Al₂O₃ needs 2 Al), then check Fe and O.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Left: 2 Al, 2 Fe, 3 O. Right: 2 Al (in Al₂O₃), 3 O (in Al₂O₃), 2 Fe. Balanced.

grade9-chemistry.question: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of potassium with water.
grade9-chemistry.answer: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂
grade9-chemistry.hint: This has the same pattern as the sodium–water equation.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Left: 2 K, 4 H, 2 O. Right: 2 K, 2 O, 2 H (in 2KOH) + 2 H (in H₂) = 4 H total. Balanced.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which equation represents the reaction of iron(III) oxide with carbon monoxide in a blast furnace?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
grade9-chemistry.hint: Balance O atoms: Fe₂O₃ has 3 O; each CO needs one extra O to become CO₂.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Fe₂O₃ has 3 O; 3 CO molecules each gain one O to form 3 CO₂; 2 Fe are released. Left: 2 Fe, 3 O + 3 C + 3 O = 6 O. Right: 3 CO₂ = 6 O, 3 C; 2 Fe. Balanced.

grade9-chemistry.question: Write the balanced ionic equation for the displacement of copper by zinc from copper sulfate solution.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu
grade9-chemistry.hint: Spectator ions (SO₄²⁻) are not included in the ionic equation.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The ionic equation shows only the species that change: Zn loses 2 electrons (is oxidised) to form Zn²⁺; Cu²⁺ gains 2 electrons (is reduced) to form Cu. SO₄²⁻ is a spectator ion.

grade9-chemistry.question: Lead oxide (PbO) is reduced by hydrogen gas. What is the balanced equation?
grade9-chemistry.answer: PbO + H₂ → Pb + H₂O
grade9-chemistry.hint: H₂ removes the oxygen from PbO; this is a reduction.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Left: 1 Pb, 1 O, 2 H. Right: 1 Pb, 1 H₂O (1 O, 2 H). Balanced. H₂ reduces PbO by combining with its oxygen to form water.

grade9-chemistry.question: Write the balanced equation for magnesium reacting with steam.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂
grade9-chemistry.hint: With steam, Mg forms the oxide, not the hydroxide.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂. Left: 1 Mg, 2 H, 1 O. Right: 1 Mg, 1 O (MgO), 2 H (H₂). Balanced. With liquid water, Mg(OH)₂ may also form.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is a neutralisation reaction?
options: An acid reacting with a metal to form hydrogen
A liquid boiling and turning into a gas
An acid reacting with a base to form a salt and water
A solid dissolving completely in water
grade9-chemistry.answer: An acid reacting with a base to form a salt and water
acceptableAnswers: An acid reacting with a base to form a salt and water
grade9-chemistry.hint: Two products are always formed, and one of them is water.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Acid + base gives a salt and water: that is neutralisation.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the pH of a neutral solution?
grade9-chemistry.hint: It sits exactly in the middle of the scale.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A neutral solution has a pH of 7; below that is acidic and above it is alkaline.

grade9-chemistry.question: An acid of pH 2 is slowly neutralised by adding an alkali. What happens to the pH?
grade9-chemistry.answer: It rises towards 7
grade9-chemistry.hint: Neutralising means moving towards neutral.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Adding alkali to an acid raises the pH towards 7, the neutral point.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which two products are always formed when an acid neutralises an alkali?
grade9-chemistry.answer: A salt and water
grade9-chemistry.hint: One of them is the commonest liquid on Earth.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Acid + alkali always gives a salt and water.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which colour does universal indicator show in a strongly acidic solution?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Red
grade9-chemistry.hint: Green is neutral; the acid end is the warm colour.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Universal indicator is red in strong acid, green at neutral and purple in strong alkali.

grade9-chemistry.question: Hydrochloric acid neutralises sodium hydroxide. Which salt is formed?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sodium chloride
grade9-chemistry.hint: The metal comes from the base, the rest from the acid.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sodium comes from the sodium hydroxide and chloride from the hydrochloric acid, giving sodium chloride.

grade9-chemistry.question: Sulfuric acid neutralises potassium hydroxide. Which salt is formed?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Potassium sulfate
grade9-chemistry.hint: Sulfuric acid always gives a sulfate.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Potassium from the base and sulfate from the sulfuric acid gives potassium sulfate.

grade9-chemistry.question: A salt that dissolves in water is described as:
grade9-chemistry.answer: Soluble
grade9-chemistry.hint: The word comes from "dissolve".
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A soluble salt dissolves in water; an insoluble one does not.

grade9-chemistry.question: All sodium and potassium salts are soluble. Which of these dissolves in water?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sodium chloride
grade9-chemistry.hint: Use the rule given in the question.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The rule states that all sodium salts are soluble, so sodium chloride dissolves.

grade9-chemistry.question: All nitrates are soluble, but most carbonates are insoluble. Which of these does NOT dissolve in water?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Calcium carbonate
grade9-chemistry.hint: Apply both halves of the rule given.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Every nitrate listed is soluble; calcium carbonate is a carbonate and is insoluble.

grade9-chemistry.question: An insoluble salt is made by mixing two solutions. How is the salt separated from the mixture?
options: By sublimation, because the salt turns straight into a gas
By crystallisation, because the salt is already dissolved
By filtration, because the salt is a solid that does not dissolve
By distillation, because the salt boils off before the water
grade9-chemistry.answer: By filtration, because the salt is a solid that does not dissolve
acceptableAnswers: By filtration, because the salt is a solid that does not dissolve
grade9-chemistry.hint: An insoluble solid in a liquid is a filtration job.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The insoluble salt forms as a solid precipitate, so it is filtered off, washed and dried.

grade9-chemistry.question: A soluble salt has been made by neutralising an acid with a base. How is the solid salt obtained from the solution?
options: By crystallisation, evaporating the water away
By cooling the solution until it freezes
By adding more acid to the solution
By filtration, using a filter paper
grade9-chemistry.answer: By crystallisation, evaporating the water away
acceptableAnswers: By crystallisation, evaporating the water away
grade9-chemistry.hint: The salt is dissolved, so a paper will not catch it.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A dissolved salt passes through filter paper, so the water is evaporated and the salt crystallises out.

grade9-chemistry.question: Indigestion tablets contain a base. How do they work?
options: They stop the stomach producing any fluid
They coat the food so it cannot be digested
They add more acid to the stomach
They neutralise excess acid in the stomach
grade9-chemistry.answer: They neutralise excess acid in the stomach
acceptableAnswers: They neutralise excess acid in the stomach
grade9-chemistry.hint: The problem is too much acid.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The base in the tablet neutralises the excess hydrochloric acid that causes the pain.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is a weak base, rather than a strong alkali, used in an indigestion tablet?
options: A strong alkali would damage the lining of the stomach
A weak base works far more slowly than is needed
A weak base tastes much better than a strong alkali
A strong alkali would not react with the stomach acid at all
grade9-chemistry.answer: A strong alkali would damage the lining of the stomach
acceptableAnswers: A strong alkali would damage the lining of the stomach
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what a strong alkali would do to tissue.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Strong alkalis are corrosive and would injure the stomach; a mild base neutralises the acid safely.

grade9-chemistry.question: A bee sting is acidic. Which treatment would relieve it by neutralisation?
options: A mild base such as baking soda
Lemon juice, which is an acid
grade9-chemistry.answer: A mild base such as baking soda
acceptableAnswers: A mild base such as baking soda
grade9-chemistry.hint: Neutralise an acid with a base.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Baking soda is a mild base, so it neutralises the acidic sting.

grade9-chemistry.question: A wasp sting is alkaline. Which treatment would relieve it by neutralisation?
options: Baking soda, which is a base
grade9-chemistry.answer: Vinegar, which is an acid
grade9-chemistry.hint: This time the sting is alkaline, so the opposite is needed.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: An alkaline sting is neutralised by a weak acid such as vinegar.

grade9-chemistry.question: A farmer finds that a field is too acidic for a crop. What is added to the soil?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Lime, which is a base
grade9-chemistry.hint: Neutralise acid with a base.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Lime is a base, so it neutralises the acid in the soil and raises its pH.

grade9-chemistry.question: Powdered limestone is sometimes added to a lake damaged by acid rain. Why?
options: It removes all the oxygen dissolved in the water
It makes the water more acidic for the fish
It makes the lake deeper and colder
It neutralises the acid so that fish can live there again
grade9-chemistry.answer: It neutralises the acid so that fish can live there again
acceptableAnswers: It neutralises the acid so that fish can live there again
grade9-chemistry.hint: Limestone is a carbonate, and carbonates react with acids.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Limestone neutralises the acid, raising the pH back towards a level that water life can survive.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which everyday problem is NOT solved by a neutralisation reaction?
options: Putting baking soda on a bee sting
Filtering mud out of river water
Treating acid indigestion with a tablet
grade9-chemistry.answer: Filtering mud out of river water
acceptableAnswers: Filtering mud out of river water
grade9-chemistry.hint: Three of these involve an acid and a base.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Removing mud is a physical separation by filtration; the other three are neutralisation.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which salt is used to flavour and preserve food?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Sodium chloride
grade9-chemistry.hint: It is the salt found on every table.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sodium chloride is common table salt, used for flavouring and for preserving food.

grade9-chemistry.question: Calcium carbonate is the main compound in limestone. What is it widely used for?
options: Filling the batteries in a torch
Making cement and neutralising acid soil
grade9-chemistry.answer: Making cement and neutralising acid soil
acceptableAnswers: Making cement and neutralising acid soil
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about building, and about farming.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Limestone is used to make cement and, as lime, to neutralise acid soils.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which salt is used in agriculture as a fertiliser because plants need its nitrogen?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Ammonium nitrate
grade9-chemistry.hint: Look for the salt whose name contains nitrogen twice over.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ammonium nitrate supplies nitrogen, which plants need for growth, so it is used as a fertiliser.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why must a fertiliser salt be soluble in water?
options: So it can be filtered back out of the soil later
So it can be stored more easily in a shed
So it neutralises the acid in the air
So the plant roots can take it up in solution
grade9-chemistry.answer: So the plant roots can take it up in solution
acceptableAnswers: So the plant roots can take it up in solution
grade9-chemistry.hint: How does a root take anything in?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Roots absorb dissolved substances, so a fertiliser has to dissolve before the plant can use it.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which statement about a salt is correct?
options: It is formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal
It is always sodium chloride and never any other compound
It is always completely insoluble in water, whatever it is
It is formed only when two different metals react together
grade9-chemistry.answer: It is formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal
acceptableAnswers: It is formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal
grade9-chemistry.hint: Salt is a general chemical word, not just the one on the table.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A salt is the compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal, so there are very many salts.

grade9-chemistry.question: Give the pH of a neutral solution.
grade9-chemistry.hint: The middle of the pH scale.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A neutral solution has a pH of 7.

grade9-chemistry.question: Complete the general equation: acid + base → salt + ______
grade9-chemistry.answer: Water
grade9-chemistry.hint: It is the commonest liquid on Earth.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Acid + base gives a salt and water.

grade9-chemistry.question: Give the term for the reaction between an acid and a base that gives a salt and water.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Neutralisation
grade9-chemistry.hint: The product is neither acidic nor alkaline.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Acid + base is a neutralisation reaction.

grade9-chemistry.question: Name the substance a farmer adds to soil that is too acidic.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Lime
