As a building material in plaster and casts
As a laxative to relieve constipation
As a fertiliser to improve crop growth
grade9-chemistry.answer: As a laxative to relieve constipation
acceptableAnswers: As a laxative to relieve constipation
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) is used medically as a laxative. It is also dissolved in bath water to soothe muscle pain.

grade9-chemistry.question: Calcium sulfate (CaSO₄) is used to make plaster of Paris. What is plaster of Paris mainly used for?
options: Setting broken bones and making moulds and casts
grade9-chemistry.answer: Setting broken bones and making moulds and casts
acceptableAnswers: Setting broken bones and making moulds and casts
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O) sets hard when mixed with water. It is used in medical casts for fractures and in making moulds and sculptures.

grade9-chemistry.question: A student prepares copper(II) sulfate by reacting copper(II) oxide with a dilute acid. Which acid should be used?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Dilute sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄)
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The anion in the salt tells you which acid to use. Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) comes from sulfuric acid: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O.

grade9-chemistry.question: A metal oxide is neutralised with a dilute acid to produce a chloride salt. Which acid was used?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Hydrochloric acid (HCl)
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The anion of the salt determines the acid: chloride salts come from hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulfate salts from sulfuric acid, and nitrate salts from nitric acid.

grade9-chemistry.question: Sodium hydroxide solution is added gradually to hydrochloric acid containing a pH indicator. What happens to the pH as the NaOH is added?
options: The pH falls from above 7 to below 7 as the NaOH is consumed
The pH stays at 7 throughout because a salt forms
The pH starts below 7 and rises towards 7, then continues above 7 as excess NaOH is added
The pH starts above 7 and falls steadily to 7 at neutralisation
grade9-chemistry.answer: The pH starts below 7 and rises towards 7, then continues above 7 as excess NaOH is added
acceptableAnswers: The pH starts below 7 and rises towards 7, then continues above 7 as excess NaOH is added
grade9-chemistry.explanation: HCl is acidic (pH < 7). NaOH neutralises it: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. At the exact neutralisation point pH = 7; further NaOH makes the solution alkaline (pH > 7).

grade9-chemistry.question: A student needs to prepare a sample of barium sulfate (BaSO₄), which is insoluble. The rule states: insoluble salts are made by mixing two soluble solutions that each contain one of the required ions. Which two solutions should be mixed?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Barium chloride (BaCl₂) and sodium sulfate (Na₂SO₄)
grade9-chemistry.explanation: BaCl₂ supplies Ba²⁺ and Na₂SO₄ supplies SO₄²⁻. When mixed: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄↓. Both starting solutions must be soluble — BaO and BaCO₃ are not soluble salts.

grade9-chemistry.question: Potassium nitrate (KNO₃) is used as a fertiliser. Why is it particularly valuable for plant growth?
options: It is the only salt soluble enough to be absorbed by plant roots
It supplies both potassium and nitrogen, which are essential nutrients for plants
It makes the soil more acidic, which benefits most crops
It provides calcium and phosphorus for strong root development
grade9-chemistry.answer: It supplies both potassium and nitrogen, which are essential nutrients for plants
acceptableAnswers: It supplies both potassium and nitrogen, which are essential nutrients for plants
grade9-chemistry.explanation: KNO₃ is a dual-nutrient fertiliser. Potassium (K⁺) aids enzyme function and disease resistance; nitrogen (as NO₃⁻) is needed for protein and chlorophyll synthesis.

grade9-chemistry.question: When a strong acid reacts with a strong alkali, the reaction can be summarised by a net ionic equation. Which of the following is that net ionic equation?
grade9-chemistry.answer: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The full equation includes spectator ions (Na⁺ and Cl⁻). Cancelling them leaves only the reacting ions: H⁺ from the acid combines with OH⁻ from the alkali to form water.

grade9-chemistry.question: The hydroxide group has the formula OH. It carries one negative charge (OH⁻). What is the valency of the hydroxide group?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Valency equals the number of charges. OH⁻ carries one negative charge, so its valency is 1. Example: Ca(OH)₂ needs two OH groups to balance Ca²⁺.

grade9-chemistry.question: The carbonate group has the formula CO₃. It carries two negative charges (CO₃²⁻). What is the valency of the carbonate group?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: CO₃²⁻ carries two negative charges, so its valency is 2. Example: CaCO₃ — one CO₃²⁻ (valency 2) balances one Ca²⁺ (valency 2) in a 1:1 ratio.

grade9-chemistry.question: Calcium has valency 2. The hydroxide group (OH) has valency 1. What is the correct formula of calcium hydroxide?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Ca(OH)₂
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Valency 2 (Ca²⁺) and valency 1 (OH⁻) cross over: two OH groups are needed to balance one Ca²⁺, giving Ca(OH)₂.

grade9-chemistry.question: Magnesium has valency 2. The carbonate group (CO₃) has valency 2. What is the correct formula of magnesium carbonate?
grade9-chemistry.answer: MgCO₃
grade9-chemistry.explanation: When both groups have the same valency (both 2), they combine in a 1:1 ratio. One Mg²⁺ balances one CO₃²⁻: MgCO₃.

grade9-chemistry.question: Some elements exist as diatomic molecules (pairs of atoms bonded together) under normal conditions. Which of the following exists as a diatomic molecule?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Chlorine (Cl₂)
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The diatomic elements are H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂. Sulfur forms S₈ rings, carbon forms giant covalent lattices, and zinc is a metal with individual atoms in a lattice.

grade9-chemistry.question: Oxygen (O₂), hydrogen (H₂) and nitrogen (N₂) all exist as diatomic molecules. Which of the following does NOT exist as a diatomic molecule under normal conditions?
grade9-chemistry.answer: Carbon
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Carbon forms giant covalent structures (diamond and graphite) — not diatomic molecules. O₂, H₂ and N₂ are all diatomic.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of the following is an example of a CHEMICAL change?
options: Iron rusting in moist air to form iron oxide
A glass rod being cut into shorter pieces
grade9-chemistry.answer: Iron rusting in moist air to form iron oxide
acceptableAnswers: Iron rusting in moist air to form iron oxide
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Rusting is a chemical change — a new substance (iron oxide) forms through an irreversible chemical reaction. Melting, dissolving and cutting are physical changes; no new substance is formed.

grade9-chemistry.question: The ammonium group has the formula NH₄. It carries one positive charge (NH₄⁺). What is the valency of the ammonium group?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: NH₄⁺ carries one positive charge, so its valency is 1. Example: (NH₄)₂SO₄ needs two NH₄⁺ ions to balance one SO₄²⁻ (valency 2).

grade9-chemistry.question: The sulfate group has the formula SO₄. It carries two negative charges (SO₄²⁻). What is the valency of the sulfate group?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: SO₄²⁻ carries two negative charges, so its valency is 2. Example: Na₂SO₄ — two Na⁺ ions (valency 1 each) balance one SO₄²⁻.

grade9-chemistry.question: The ammonium group (NH₄) has valency 1 and the sulfate group (SO₄) has valency 2. What is the correct formula of ammonium sulfate?
grade9-chemistry.answer: (NH₄)₂SO₄
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Valency 1 (NH₄⁺) and valency 2 (SO₄²⁻) cross over: two NH₄⁺ are needed to balance one SO₄²⁻, giving (NH₄)₂SO₄.

grade9-chemistry.intro: A student monitored dissolved oxygen (DO) levels at four points along a river below a farm that uses nitrate fertiliser.

stimulus.html: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 130" width="320" role="img" aria-label="a table of dissolved oxygen data at four river sampling points"><text x="160" y="14" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#0f172a">Dissolved Oxygen Along the River</text><rect x="10" y="20" width="300" height="105" fill="none" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="130" y1="20" x2="130" y2="125" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="10" y1="41" x2="310" y2="41" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="16" y="35" font-size="9" fill="#0f172a">Sampling point</text><text x="136" y="35" font-size="9" fill="#0f172a">DO (mg/L)</text><line x1="10" y1="62" x2="310" y2="62" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="10" y1="83" x2="310" y2="83" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="10" y1="104" x2="310" y2="104" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="1"/><text x="16" y="56" font-size="9" fill="#334155">A (500 m above farm)</text><text x="136" y="56" font-size="9" fill="#334155">9.2</text><text x="16" y="77" font-size="9" fill="#334155">B (200 m below farm)</text><text x="136" y="77" font-size="9" fill="#334155">4.1</text><text x="16" y="98" font-size="9" fill="#334155">C (800 m below farm)</text><text x="136" y="98" font-size="9" fill="#334155">1.8</text><text x="16" y="119" font-size="9" fill="#334155">D (2 km below farm)</text><text x="136" y="119" font-size="9" fill="#334155">7.5</text></svg>
stimulus.altText: a table showing dissolved oxygen at four river points above and below a farm

grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C1 structured data-interpretation pattern.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the dissolved oxygen reading at point A.
parts.hint: Read the value from the table for point A.
parts.explanation: Point A, 500 m above the farm, shows 9.2 mg/L — the baseline before any farm runoff.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Between which two points is the dissolved oxygen the lowest? Suggest why.
parts.hint: Find the minimum value, then explain what causes oxygen to fall near the farm.
parts.explanation: Point C (1.8 mg/L) is the lowest. After the fertiliser enters the river, algae bloom; the algae die and are decomposed by bacteria whose aerobic respiration removes oxygen, reaching the lowest level at C before the river recovers at D.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The dissolved oxygen at D (2 km from the farm) has risen to 7.5 mg/L. Explain this observation.
parts.hint: The river has had more distance to recover — what processes restore oxygen?
parts.explanation: Further downstream the organic matter is fully decomposed, bacterial activity falls, and the river re-oxygenates by diffusion of atmospheric oxygen and photosynthesis by recovering aquatic plants. This is called the oxygen sag recovery.
parts.rubric: 1 mark each, to a maximum of 2: the organic matter has been fully decomposed so bacterial respiration falls; oxygen re-enters the water by diffusion from the atmosphere; aquatic plants recovering downstream add oxygen by photosynthesis; this is the recovery limb of the oxygen sag curve.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Name the process by which excess fertiliser in a river causes fish to die. Describe the chain of events.
parts.hint: Nutrient enrichment → algae → decomposition → deoxygenation.
parts.explanation: Eutrophication. Nitrates/phosphates from the fertiliser stimulate rapid algal growth (algal bloom). The bloom shades submerged plants, which die; then the algae die and decomposer bacteria use up dissolved oxygen by aerobic respiration, leaving too little O₂ for fish to survive (deoxygenation).
parts.rubric: 1 mark for naming eutrophication. Then 1 mark each, to a maximum of 2 more, for the chain: nitrates and phosphates enrich the water and stimulate an algal bloom; the bloom shades submerged plants, which die; decomposer bacteria break down the dead algae and plants and their aerobic respiration removes dissolved oxygen; the fish die of deoxygenation.

grade9-chemistry.intro: The diagram below shows the apparatus used to separate a salt solution by distillation. Parts are labelled A–D.

stimulus.html: <svg viewBox="0 0 340 200" width="340" role="img" aria-label="a labelled distillation apparatus diagram"><ellipse cx="80" cy="140" rx="55" ry="40" fill="none" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="135" y1="115" x2="230" y2="85" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="215" y="65" width="80" height="30" rx="4" fill="none" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="295" y1="80" x2="320" y2="100" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse cx="325" cy="108" rx="12" ry="8" fill="none" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="5" y="155" width="150" height="10" rx="3" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#b45309" stroke-width="1"/><text x="60" y="125" font-size="10" fill="#0f172a" font-weight="bold">A</text><text x="120" y="75" font-size="10" fill="#0f172a" font-weight="bold">B</text><text x="248" y="60" font-size="10" fill="#0f172a" font-weight="bold">C</text><text x="312" y="60" font-size="10" fill="#0f172a" font-weight="bold">D</text><text x="60" y="178" font-size="9" fill="#78350f">Heat source</text></svg>
stimulus.altText: a distillation apparatus with parts A (flask), B (side arm/still-head), C (condenser), D (receiving flask) labelled

grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C2 apparatus question pattern.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify part C in the diagram.
parts.hint: The long slanted tube where vapour is cooled.
parts.explanation: Part C is the condenser (Liebig condenser). Cold water flows through its outer jacket to cool and condense the vapour back into a liquid.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State the purpose of part A in this experiment.
parts.hint: Where is the mixture placed?
parts.explanation: Part A is the distillation flask (round-bottomed flask) where the salt solution is placed and heated. The mixture boils in this vessel.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the thermometer should be positioned at the junction of the side arm (B) rather than immersed in the boiling liquid.
parts.hint: What does the thermometer measure, and why is vapour temperature the important quantity?
parts.explanation: The thermometer measures the boiling point of the vapour entering the condenser, which equals the boiling point of the substance being collected as distillate. If placed in the liquid, it would record the temperature of the whole mixture (which is higher), not just the component that is distilling over.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: The thermometer measures the boiling point of the vapour entering the condenser, which equals the boiling point of the substance being collected as distillate; If placed in the liquid, it would record the temperature of the whole mixture (which is higher), not just the component that is distilling over.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: After distillation, the student tests the distillate and finds it conducts electricity poorly. What does this confirm?
parts.hint: Pure water vs. salt solution: which conducts?
parts.explanation: Pure water is a very poor conductor of electricity because it contains very few ions; the salt solution conducts because dissolved Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions carry charge. Poor conductivity in the distillate confirms that the salt was separated and the distillate is (essentially) pure water.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Pure water is a very poor conductor of electricity because it contains very few ions; the salt solution conducts because dissolved Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions carry charge; Poor conductivity in the distillate confirms that the salt was separated and the distillate is (essentially) pure water.

grade9-chemistry.intro: A student investigates the reactions of three metals — magnesium, iron and copper — with dilute hydrochloric acid.
grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C3/C4 equation-writing structured question pattern.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.hint: Metal + HCl → metal chloride + hydrogen gas.
parts.explanation: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ ions; two HCl provide two Cl and two H, forming one H₂.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write a balanced equation for the reaction of iron with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.hint: Iron forms Fe²⁺ with dilute acid.
parts.explanation: Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂. Iron(II) chloride is formed because Fe loses 2 electrons to become Fe²⁺.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.hint: Use the reactivity series.
parts.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series. A metal can only displace hydrogen from an acid if it is more reactive than hydrogen. Since Cu < H in reactivity, it cannot displace H⁺ ions from HCl.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series; A metal can only displace hydrogen from an acid if it is more reactive than hydrogen; Since Cu < H in reactivity, it cannot displace H⁺ ions from HCl.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The student measures the time taken to collect 20 cm³ of hydrogen from excess magnesium in 50 cm³ of 1 mol/dm³ HCl: 45 seconds. She then repeats with 0.5 mol/dm³ HCl. Predict whether the new time will be greater or smaller than 45 s. Explain.
parts.hint: How does halving the acid concentration affect the rate of reaction?
parts.explanation: The time will be greater (longer). Halving the concentration reduces the number of H⁺ ions per unit volume, decreasing the frequency of successful collisions between H⁺ and Mg surface atoms, so the rate of H₂ production is lower and it takes longer to collect 20 cm³.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: The time will be greater (longer); Halving the concentration reduces the number of H⁺ ions per unit volume, decreasing the frequency of successful collisions between H⁺ and Mg surface atoms, so the rate of H₂ production is lower and it takes longer to collect 20 cm³.

stimulus.altText: a results table for displacement reactions between zinc, iron, copper and solutions of copper sulfate, iron sulfate, zinc sulfate

grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C4 reactivity series structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the order of reactivity of these three metals, from most reactive to least reactive, using the data in the table.
parts.hint: The most reactive metal displaces the most other metals from their solutions.
parts.explanation: Zn displaces both Cu and Fe (2 reactions). Fe displaces only Cu (1 reaction). Cu displaces none (0). Order: Zn > Fe > Cu.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write a balanced ionic equation for the reaction of zinc with copper sulfate solution.
parts.hint: Spectator ions do not appear in the ionic equation.
parts.explanation: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). The SO₄²⁻ ion is a spectator ion and is omitted.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict what would be observed if silver wire were placed into zinc sulfate solution. Explain your reasoning.
parts.hint: Where does Ag sit relative to Zn in the reactivity series?
parts.explanation: No visible reaction. Silver is less reactive than zinc (Ag < Zn); a less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive metal from its salt solution. The wire remains unchanged and the solution stays colourless.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: No visible reaction; Silver is less reactive than zinc (Ag < Zn); a less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive metal from its salt solution; The wire remains unchanged and the solution stays colourless.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Iron is used to galvanise steel (coat it). How does this protect the steel from rusting, even when the coating is scratched?
parts.hint: Wait — is it iron or zinc used for galvanising? Which is more reactive?
parts.explanation: Galvanising uses ZINC, not iron. Zinc is more reactive than iron; when both metals are exposed at a scratch, zinc is preferentially oxidised (sacrificial protection), protecting the iron from corrosion. The zinc acts as a sacrificial anode.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Galvanising uses ZINC, not iron; Zinc is more reactive than iron; when both metals are exposed at a scratch, zinc is preferentially oxidised (sacrificial protection), protecting the iron from corrosion; The zinc acts as a sacrificial anode.

grade9-chemistry.intro: Acid rain is formed when sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen dissolve in atmospheric water droplets.
grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C1 acid rain structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name the two main gaseous pollutants that cause acid rain and state one source of each.
parts.hint: SO₂ and NOₓ — where does each come from?
parts.explanation: SO₂: burning of sulfur-containing coal in power stations. NOₓ (nitrogen monoxide/dioxide): high-temperature combustion in car engines, where atmospheric N₂ and O₂ react.
parts.rubric: 4 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 4: SO₂: burning of sulfur-containing coal in power stations; NOₓ (nitrogen monoxide/dioxide): high-temperature combustion in car engines, where atmospheric N₂ and O₂ react.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write the equation for the formation of sulfuric acid from sulfur dioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.hint: SO₂ + water + oxygen → an acid.
parts.explanation: 2SO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 2H₂SO₄. (Or acceptably: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃, then H₂SO₃ + ½O₂ → H₂SO₄.)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Give two harmful effects of acid rain on the environment.
parts.hint: Think about effects on lakes, forests and buildings.
parts.explanation: Any two from: (1) lowers pH of lakes and rivers, killing fish and aquatic life; (2) damages forests by leaching essential minerals from the soil and destroying leaf cuticles; (3) erodes limestone and marble buildings and statues; (4) acidifies soil, reducing crop yields.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Any two from: (1) lowers pH of lakes and rivers, killing fish and aquatic life; (2) damages forests by leaching essential minerals from the soil and destroying leaf cuticles; (3) erodes limestone and marble buildings and statues; (4) acidifies soil, reducing crop yields.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest one industrial and one agricultural measure that would reduce acid rain.
parts.hint: Reduce emissions OR neutralise the acid.
parts.explanation: Industrial: fit flue-gas desulfurisation (scrubbers) to power stations to remove SO₂ before it is emitted. Agricultural: apply lime (CaCO₃ or Ca(OH)₂) to acidified farmland and lakes to neutralise the acid.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Industrial: fit flue-gas desulfurisation (scrubbers) to power stations to remove SO₂ before it is emitted; Agricultural: apply lime (CaCO₃ or Ca(OH)₂) to acidified farmland and lakes to neutralise the acid.

grade9-chemistry.intro: A student wishes to prepare pure copper sulfate crystals starting from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.
grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C5 salt preparation structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of copper oxide with sulfuric acid.
parts.hint: Base + acid → salt + water.
parts.explanation: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why excess copper oxide is added to the acid rather than the exact stoichiometric amount.
parts.hint: What happens if excess acid remains in the product?
parts.explanation: Excess solid CuO ensures all the acid is neutralised; any remaining acid would contaminate the final crystals. The excess CuO (undissolved solid) can then be removed by filtration, leaving a pure CuSO₄ solution.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Excess solid CuO ensures all the acid is neutralised; any remaining acid would contaminate the final crystals; The excess CuO (undissolved solid) can then be removed by filtration, leaving a pure CuSO₄ solution.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe how the student would obtain dry copper sulfate crystals from the pure CuSO₄ solution.
parts.hint: Evaporate, then cool, then dry.
parts.explanation: Gently heat the solution in an evaporating dish until a saturated solution is produced (test by dipping a cooled glass rod — crystals form on it). Remove from heat and allow to cool slowly — crystals form. Filter off the crystals. Pat dry between sheets of filter paper or leave in a warm oven at low temperature (not too hot, or crystals lose water of crystallisation and turn white).
parts.rubric: 3 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 3: Gently heat the solution in an evaporating dish until a saturated solution is produced (test by dipping a cooled glass rod — crystals form on it); Remove from heat and allow to cool slowly — crystals form; Filter off the crystals; Pat dry between sheets of filter paper or leave in a warm oven at low temperature (not too hot, or crystals lose water of crystallisation and turn white).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The student notices her crystals are blue. A friend says anhydrous copper sulfate is white. Explain the difference.
parts.hint: What is different about the two forms?
parts.explanation: The blue crystals are CuSO₄·5H₂O (copper sulfate pentahydrate); they contain five water molecules of crystallisation chemically incorporated into the crystal lattice, which gives the blue colour. Anhydrous CuSO₄ (CuSO₄ with no water) is white because the absence of water changes the coordination environment of the Cu²⁺ ion.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: The blue crystals are CuSO₄·5H₂O (copper sulfate pentahydrate); they contain five water molecules of crystallisation chemically incorporated into the crystal lattice, which gives the blue colour; Anhydrous CuSO₄ (CuSO₄ with no water) is white because the absence of water changes the coordination environment of the Cu²⁺ ion.

grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C1 global warming structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Which gas in the table has the highest global warming potential per molecule?
parts.hint: Read the GWP column.
parts.explanation: SF₆ has the highest GWP (23,500 times that of CO₂ over 100 years).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Methane has a shorter atmospheric lifetime than CO₂ but a much higher GWP. Explain the significance of this for climate policy.
parts.hint: Short lifetime = fast results; high GWP = large impact while present.
parts.explanation: Methane is 28× more potent than CO₂ while present. Its short lifetime (12 years) means that if methane emissions are cut sharply, atmospheric concentrations drop relatively quickly, giving faster climate benefit than CO₂ reduction (which takes centuries to clear). This makes methane a high-priority short-term target for slowing near-term warming.
parts.rubric: 3 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 3: Methane is 28× more potent than CO₂ while present; Its short lifetime (12 years) means that if methane emissions are cut sharply, atmospheric concentrations drop relatively quickly, giving faster climate benefit than CO₂ reduction (which takes centuries to clear); This makes methane a high-priority short-term target for slowing near-term warming.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State one human activity that produces nitrous oxide (N₂O) and explain why this makes it an environmental concern.
parts.hint: N₂O is produced in agriculture.
parts.explanation: N₂O is produced by nitrification and denitrification of nitrogen fertilisers in soil. It is a concern because it has a GWP of 265 and an atmospheric lifetime of 114 years, so even small amounts make a large long-term contribution to warming; it also destroys stratospheric ozone.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: N₂O is produced by nitrification and denitrification of nitrogen fertilisers in soil; It is a concern because it has a GWP of 265 and an atmospheric lifetime of 114 years, so even small amounts make a large long-term contribution to warming; it also destroys stratospheric ozone.

grade9-chemistry.intro: A student has the following four mixtures to separate. She must choose the best technique for each.
grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C2 separation choice structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Mixture 1: Iodine crystals mixed with sodium chloride powder. Name the separation technique and explain the principle.
parts.hint: Only one substance changes state when gently heated.
parts.explanation: Sublimation. Iodine sublimes (converts directly from solid to vapour) when gently heated; sodium chloride does not sublime. The iodine vapour is collected as pure crystals on a cold surface, leaving NaCl behind.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Sublimation; Iodine sublimes (converts directly from solid to vapour) when gently heated; sodium chloride does not sublime; The iodine vapour is collected as pure crystals on a cold surface, leaving NaCl behind.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Mixture 2: Salt dissolved in water. Name the technique to recover PURE WATER (not the salt).
parts.hint: You need to collect the water, not the salt.
parts.explanation: Distillation. The water is evaporated from the solution and condensed as pure distillate; the salt remains in the flask.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Mixture 3: Copper sulfate dissolved in water. Name the technique to obtain copper sulfate crystals.
parts.hint: You want the solid, not the liquid.
parts.explanation: Crystallisation (evaporation to saturation followed by cooling). The solution is evaporated to a saturated solution and then cooled slowly; CuSO₄·5H₂O crystals form and are collected by filtration.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Mixture 4: Ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) and water (b.p. 100 °C) — both liquids, fully miscible. Name the most effective technique.
parts.hint: They are both liquids with different but fairly close boiling points.
parts.explanation: Fractional distillation. Because the boiling points are different but relatively close (22 °C apart), a fractionating column is needed to achieve good separation — the more volatile ethanol is enriched at the top of the column and collected first.

grade9-chemistry.intro: Use the reactivity series (K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Sn > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au) to answer the following questions.
grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C4 prediction and explanation structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt:
Predict whether the following reaction will occur and explain why:
Cu(s) + ZnSO₄(aq) → ?
parts.hint: Compare positions of Cu and Zn in the reactivity series.
parts.explanation: No reaction. Cu is less reactive than Zn (Cu < Zn), so it cannot displace Zn from zinc sulfate solution. Only a more reactive metal can displace a less reactive one.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: No reaction; Cu is less reactive than Zn (Cu < Zn), so it cannot displace Zn from zinc sulfate solution; Only a more reactive metal can displace a less reactive one.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Predict the products and write a balanced equation for: Mg(s) + 2AgNO₃(aq) → ?
parts.hint: Mg > Ag in reactivity; Mg²⁺ will form.
parts.explanation: Mg + 2AgNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. Magnesium displaces silver: Mg gives 2 electrons to 2 Ag⁺ ions, forming Mg²⁺ and 2 Ag atoms. Silvery solid (Ag) deposits on the magnesium; the solution becomes colourless as Ag⁺ is removed.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student places a tin strip into lead nitrate solution. She observes a grey deposit on the tin. Which metal is the grey deposit and what does this tell us about the relative reactivity of tin and lead?
parts.hint: The deposited metal is the one displaced from solution.
parts.explanation: The grey deposit is lead (Pb). Tin has displaced lead from lead nitrate solution, which means Sn > Pb in reactivity. The tin is more reactive and loses electrons to Pb²⁺ ions: Sn + Pb(NO₃)₂ → Sn(NO₃)₂ + Pb.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: The grey deposit is lead (Pb); Tin has displaced lead from lead nitrate solution, which means Sn > Pb in reactivity; The tin is more reactive and loses electrons to Pb²⁺ ions: Sn + Pb(NO₃)₂ → Sn(NO₃)₂ + Pb.

grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C1 water pollution structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the pollutant most likely released from source X (the factory).
parts.hint: Factories can release heavy metals, toxic chemicals or hot water.
parts.explanation: Likely pollutants from a factory include heavy metals (e.g. lead, mercury), toxic organic chemicals (e.g. pesticides, solvents) or thermal pollution (hot water reducing dissolved oxygen). Any one of these with a brief explanation is acceptable.
parts.rubric: 1 mark. Award the mark for: Likely pollutants from a factory include heavy metals (e.g; lead, mercury), toxic organic chemicals (e.g; pesticides, solvents) or thermal pollution (hot water reducing dissolved oxygen); Any one of these with a brief explanation is acceptable.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the runoff from source Y (the farm) can lead to fish dying in the river even though the fertiliser itself is not directly toxic to fish.
parts.hint: Nutrient enrichment → algae → decomposition → oxygen depletion.
parts.explanation: Farm runoff carries nitrate/phosphate fertilisers into the river. These nutrients trigger an algal bloom. The algae die; decomposer bacteria break down the algal biomass by aerobic respiration, consuming dissolved oxygen. The dissolved oxygen falls so low that fish suffocate (deoxygenation). This chain of events is eutrophication.
parts.rubric: 3 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 3: Farm runoff carries nitrate/phosphate fertilisers into the river; These nutrients trigger an algal bloom; The algae die; decomposer bacteria break down the algal biomass by aerobic respiration, consuming dissolved oxygen; The dissolved oxygen falls so low that fish suffocate (deoxygenation); This chain of events is eutrophication.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State one biological indicator organism that would be found in abundance near source Z (sewage) and one that would be absent. Explain.
parts.hint: Pollution-tolerant organisms thrive in low-oxygen, organic-rich water.
parts.explanation: Present: sludge worms (rat-tailed maggots / Tubifex worms) — they tolerate very low dissolved oxygen. Absent: stonefly larvae / mayfly larvae — these require well-oxygenated, clean water and cannot survive in sewage-polluted conditions.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Present: sludge worms (rat-tailed maggots / Tubifex worms) — they tolerate very low dissolved oxygen; Absent: stonefly larvae / mayfly larvae — these require well-oxygenated, clean water and cannot survive in sewage-polluted conditions.

grade9-chemistry.intro: A student investigates the combustion of different fuels.
grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C3 balancing and equation-writing structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of butane, C₄H₁₀.
parts.hint: Balance C, then H, then O. Oxygen is always the last to balance.
parts.explanation: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O. C: 8 on each side; H: 20 on each side; O: 26 on each side (from 13O₂). Note: multiplying through by 2 avoids fractions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The student burns methane (CH₄) in a limited air supply. Name the two carbon-containing products that form and explain why both can be present.
parts.hint: What happens when there is not enough oxygen for complete combustion?
parts.explanation: Carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). In limited air, some CH₄ undergoes complete combustion (→ CO₂) but where oxygen is depleted, incomplete combustion occurs (→ CO, and sometimes C as soot). Both products can coexist because different regions of the flame have different oxygen concentrations.
parts.rubric: 3 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 3: Carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide (CO₂); In limited air, some CH₄ undergoes complete combustion (→ CO₂) but where oxygen is depleted, incomplete combustion occurs (→ CO, and sometimes C as soot); Both products can coexist because different regions of the flame have different oxygen concentrations.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous, and how is it detected in a home?
parts.hint: Colour? Smell? What does it do in the blood?
parts.explanation: CO is colourless and odourless, giving no sensory warning; it binds to haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen, preventing oxygen transport and causing death by asphyxiation. It is detected using an electronic carbon monoxide alarm that sounds when CO reaches a dangerous concentration.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: CO is colourless and odourless, giving no sensory warning; it binds to haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen, preventing oxygen transport and causing death by asphyxiation; It is detected using an electronic carbon monoxide alarm that sounds when CO reaches a dangerous concentration.

grade9-chemistry.intro: A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of unknown concentration with 0.10 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. The mean titre is 22.4 cm³.
grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C5 titration structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the balanced equation for the reaction between HCl and NaOH.
parts.explanation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of HCl used in the titration.
parts.hint: n = c × V (remember to convert cm³ to dm³).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using your answer to part (b), calculate the concentration of the NaOH solution. Show your working.
parts.hint: Moles of NaOH = moles of HCl (1:1 ratio). Then c = n/V.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The student uses phenolphthalein indicator. State the colour change at the end point when acid is added to alkali.
parts.explanation: Pink to colourless (at the point of neutralisation, when the last drop of acid decolorises the solution permanently).

grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C2 practical skills structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Whose method of adding CuO is better — Student A or B? Explain.
parts.hint: What happens if excess acid remains in the product?
parts.explanation: Student B. Adding excess CuO ensures all the H₂SO₄ is neutralised; excess solid CuO can be removed by filtration, leaving only the pure CuSO₄ solution. Student A's exact amount risks leaving unreacted acid, which would contaminate the final crystals.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Student B; Adding excess CuO ensures all the H₂SO₄ is neutralised; excess solid CuO can be removed by filtration, leaving only the pure CuSO₄ solution; Student A's exact amount risks leaving unreacted acid, which would contaminate the final crystals.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Whose method of drying is better — Student A or B? Explain.
parts.hint: Blue copper sulfate crystals contain water of crystallisation.
parts.explanation: Student B. Strong heating in an oven (Student A) drives off the water of crystallisation, converting the blue CuSO₄·5H₂O to white anhydrous CuSO₄, destroying the crystals. Gentle patting between filter papers preserves the water of crystallisation and the crystalline form.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Student B; Strong heating in an oven (Student A) drives off the water of crystallisation, converting the blue CuSO₄·5H₂O to white anhydrous CuSO₄, destroying the crystals; Gentle patting between filter papers preserves the water of crystallisation and the crystalline form.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Student A obtained 4.2 g of crystals; Student B obtained 3.9 g. Does the lower yield of Student B necessarily mean her method is worse? Explain.
parts.hint: Think about purity vs. yield.
parts.explanation: No. Student B's lower yield may be because some product remained dissolved in the mother liquor or was lost during washing — but her crystals are purer. Student A's higher yield may be contaminated with residual acid or anhydrous CuSO₄ from overheating. Yield and purity are two different criteria.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: No; Student B's lower yield may be because some product remained dissolved in the mother liquor or was lost during washing — but her crystals are purer; Student A's higher yield may be contaminated with residual acid or anhydrous CuSO₄ from overheating; Yield and purity are two different criteria.

grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C4 metals with water/steam structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of calcium with cold water.
parts.explanation: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the table to deduce the order of reactivity of the five metals (most reactive first).
parts.hint: Compare the vigour and conditions needed.
parts.explanation: Sodium > Calcium > Magnesium > Iron > Copper. Sodium reacts with cold water most vigorously; copper does not react with water or steam at all.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of iron with steam.
parts.explanation: 3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂. (Note: the product is iron(II,III) oxide, Fe₃O₄, not Fe₂O₃.)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why the reaction of sodium with steam is described as "dangerous" in the table.
parts.hint: Two hazards: the gas and the product.
parts.explanation: Steam provides more energy than cold water, making the already vigorous sodium-water reaction extremely exothermic; the hydrogen gas produced ignites immediately from the heat of the reaction, causing an explosion. The sodium hydroxide produced is also strongly corrosive.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Steam provides more energy than cold water, making the already vigorous sodium-water reaction extremely exothermic; the hydrogen gas produced ignites immediately from the heat of the reaction, causing an explosion; The sodium hydroxide produced is also strongly corrosive.

grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C1 global warming mechanism structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the mechanism of the enhanced greenhouse effect, starting with sunlight arriving at the Earth.
parts.hint: Sunlight in → Earth warms → infrared out → greenhouse gases absorb → re-radiate back.
parts.explanation: (1) Short-wave solar radiation passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the Earth's surface, warming it. (2) The warmed surface emits long-wave infrared (heat) radiation. (3) Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) absorb this outgoing infrared instead of letting it escape to space. (4) The gases re-radiate the energy in all directions, including back to the surface, warming it further. The enhanced effect is due to increased concentrations of greenhouse gases from human activities.
parts.rubric: 4 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 4: (1) Short-wave solar radiation passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the Earth's surface, warming it; (2) The warmed surface emits long-wave infrared (heat) radiation; (3) Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) absorb this outgoing infrared instead of letting it escape to space; (4) The gases re-radiate the energy in all directions, including back to the surface, warming it further; The enhanced effect is due to increased concentrations of greenhouse gases from human activities.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Give two consequences of global warming on natural ecosystems.
parts.hint: Ice, sea level, species ranges, weather patterns.
parts.explanation: Any two from: (1) melting of polar ice caps and glaciers, reducing habitat for species such as polar bears; (2) rising sea levels threatening coastal and island ecosystems; (3) coral bleaching due to ocean warming and acidification; (4) poleward and uphill shifts in species ranges, disrupting ecosystems; (5) increased frequency and severity of droughts and floods affecting biodiversity.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Any two from: (1) melting of polar ice caps and glaciers, reducing habitat for species such as polar bears; (2) rising sea levels threatening coastal and island ecosystems; (3) coral bleaching due to ocean warming and acidification; (4) poleward and uphill shifts in species ranges, disrupting ecosystems; (5) increased frequency and severity of droughts and floods affecting biodiversity.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State two actions that individuals or governments could take to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
parts.hint: Reduce, switch fuel, capture, plant.
parts.explanation: Any two from: (1) switch electricity generation to renewable sources (solar, wind, hydroelectric); (2) improve insulation and energy efficiency of buildings; (3) use electric or hydrogen-powered vehicles instead of petrol/diesel; (4) reduce deforestation and plant new forests; (5) adopt carbon capture and storage (CCS) at power stations; (6) reduce methane from agriculture by changing livestock diet or rice cultivation practices.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Any two from: (1) switch electricity generation to renewable sources (solar, wind, hydroelectric); (2) improve insulation and energy efficiency of buildings; (3) use electric or hydrogen-powered vehicles instead of petrol/diesel; (4) reduce deforestation and plant new forests; (5) adopt carbon capture and storage (CCS) at power stations; (6) reduce methane from agriculture by changing livestock diet or rice cultivation practices.

grade9-chemistry.intro: Match each named salt to its use and explain the chemistry behind each application.
grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C5 uses of salts structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is spread on icy roads in winter. Explain the chemical reason it melts ice.
parts.hint: Dissolving a solute changes the freezing point of the solvent.
parts.explanation: NaCl dissolves in any surface water, dissociating into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. The dissolved ions lower the freezing point of the solution below 0 °C (freezing-point depression), so the mixture does not freeze at normal winter temperatures and ice is melted.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: NaCl dissolves in any surface water, dissociating into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; The dissolved ions lower the freezing point of the solution below 0 °C (freezing-point depression), so the mixture does not freeze at normal winter temperatures and ice is melted.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Barium sulfate (BaSO₄) is used as a barium meal for X-ray imaging of the gut. Explain why its insolubility is essential to its safe use.
parts.hint: Ba²⁺ ions are toxic — what happens if the salt dissolves?
parts.explanation: Ba²⁺ ions are highly poisonous. BaSO₄ is almost completely insoluble (Ksp ≈ 10⁻¹⁰), so essentially no Ba²⁺ enters the bloodstream from the gut. Its insolubility makes it safe to swallow; it also blocks X-rays effectively, providing contrast for imaging.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Ba²⁺ ions are highly poisonous; BaSO₄ is almost completely insoluble (Ksp ≈ 10⁻¹⁰), so essentially no Ba²⁺ enters the bloodstream from the gut; Its insolubility makes it safe to swallow; it also blocks X-rays effectively, providing contrast for imaging.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Potassium nitrate (KNO₃) is used as a fertiliser. State which two nutrients it provides and explain why these are important for plant growth.
parts.explanation: Potassium (K) — needed for flower and fruit development, and to regulate water in cells. Nitrogen (N) — needed for synthesis of amino acids and proteins, promoting leaf and stem growth. Both are macronutrients essential for healthy plant development.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: Potassium (K) — needed for flower and fruit development, and to regulate water in cells; Nitrogen (N) — needed for synthesis of amino acids and proteins, promoting leaf and stem growth; Both are macronutrients essential for healthy plant development.

grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C3 language of chemistry structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Work out the formula of magnesium nitrate given that Mg has valency 2 and NO₃ has valency 1.
parts.hint: Cross the valencies: Mg²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻ ions.
parts.explanation: Mg²⁺ and NO₃⁻ (valency 1): two nitrate ions balance one Mg²⁺ ion. Formula: Mg(NO₃)₂.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: How many atoms are in one formula unit of Mg(NO₃)₂?
parts.hint: Expand the bracket first.
parts.explanation: 1 Mg + 2 N + 6 O = 9 atoms.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the difference between the formulae 2H₂O and H₂O₂.
parts.hint: One has a large number in front; one has a subscript.
parts.explanation: 2H₂O means two molecules of water, each containing 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom (total: 4 H, 2 O). H₂O₂ is one molecule of hydrogen peroxide, containing 2 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms (total: 2 H, 2 O) — a completely different substance.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: 2H₂O means two molecules of water, each containing 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom (total: 4 H, 2 O); H₂O₂ is one molecule of hydrogen peroxide, containing 2 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms (total: 2 H, 2 O) — a completely different substance.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Write a word equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.

response.answer: calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide

parts.hint: What two products are formed when CaCO₃ is heated strongly?
parts.explanation: Calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide. (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂)

grade9-chemistry.source: NCE Chemistry C1 air pollutants structured question.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why carbon monoxide (CO) is so dangerous to humans.
parts.hint: What does it do in the blood? Why is it not noticed?
parts.explanation: CO is colourless and odourless, giving no sensory warning. It binds to haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen. This causes oxygen starvation of tissues and, at high concentrations, death.
parts.rubric: 2 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 2: CO is colourless and odourless, giving no sensory warning; It binds to haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen; This causes oxygen starvation of tissues and, at high concentrations, death.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Name the acid produced when sulfur dioxide reacts with water in the atmosphere.
parts.explanation: Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄). (Also accept sulfurous acid H₂SO₃ as an intermediate.)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the mechanism by which CFCs destroy the ozone layer.
parts.hint: UV breaks the CFC, releasing chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone.
parts.explanation: UV radiation in the upper atmosphere breaks a C–Cl bond in the CFC molecule, releasing a chlorine radical (Cl•). The chlorine radical reacts with ozone: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂. Then ClO• reacts with O to regenerate Cl•: ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂. The Cl• is regenerated and can destroy thousands more ozone molecules — acting as a catalyst. Overall: O₃ + O → 2O₂ (each Cl• repeating many times).
parts.rubric: 3 marks. Award one mark per point, to a maximum of 3: UV radiation in the upper atmosphere breaks a C–Cl bond in the CFC molecule, releasing a chlorine radical (Cl•); The chlorine radical reacts with ozone: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; Then ClO• reacts with O to regenerate Cl•: ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂; The Cl• is regenerated and can destroy thousands more ozone molecules — acting as a catalyst; Overall: O₃ + O → 2O₂ (each Cl• repeating many times).

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest one method used industrially to reduce SO₂ emissions from coal-fired power stations.
parts.hint: The technique involves spraying an alkaline substance into the flue gases.
parts.explanation: Flue-gas desulfurisation (FGD / wet scrubbing): spraying calcium hydroxide solution (or limestone slurry) into the exhaust gases to react with SO₂ — SO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaSO₃ + H₂O — removing up to 95% of SO₂ before it reaches the atmosphere.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why are safety goggles worn in a school laboratory?
options: To make it easier to see very small objects
To protect the eyes from splashes and flying pieces
To stop dust settling on the bench
To keep the face warm near a flame
grade9-chemistry.answer: To protect the eyes from splashes and flying pieces
acceptableAnswers: To protect the eyes from splashes and flying pieces
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what could reach the eyes.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Goggles protect the eyes from chemical splashes and from anything that shatters or spits.

grade9-chemistry.question: What should be done first if a chemical is spilled on the skin?
options: Rub it in until it disappears
Wait to see whether it starts to hurt at all
Cover it with a cloth and carry on
Wash it off with plenty of water and tell the teacher
grade9-chemistry.answer: Wash it off with plenty of water and tell the teacher
acceptableAnswers: Wash it off with plenty of water and tell the teacher
grade9-chemistry.hint: Dilute and remove it at once.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Washing with plenty of water dilutes and removes the chemical; the teacher must always be told.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is long hair tied back in a laboratory?
options: So the pupil can see the bench more easily
So the hair does not become dusty
So it cannot catch fire or fall into the apparatus
So the pupil looks tidy for the lesson
grade9-chemistry.answer: So it cannot catch fire or fall into the apparatus
acceptableAnswers: So it cannot catch fire or fall into the apparatus
grade9-chemistry.hint: There are flames on the bench.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Loose hair can reach a flame or trail into chemicals, so it is tied back.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is a test tube heated with its mouth pointed away from everyone?
options: It keeps the flame from being blown out
The contents can spit out suddenly when heated
It makes the contents heat up more quickly
It stops the glass from becoming too hot to hold
grade9-chemistry.answer: The contents can spit out suddenly when heated
acceptableAnswers: The contents can spit out suddenly when heated
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what a boiling liquid can do.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Heated liquids can bump and spit, so the open end must point away from every person.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which section of a report says what was found out?
grade9-chemistry.answer: The conclusion
grade9-chemistry.hint: It comes at the end.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The conclusion states what the results show, and whether they support the hypothesis.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is the method written in enough detail for someone else to follow?
options: So another person can repeat the experiment and check it
So the conclusion does not need to be written
So the report is as long as possible
So the apparatus does not have to be listed
grade9-chemistry.answer: So another person can repeat the experiment and check it
acceptableAnswers: So another person can repeat the experiment and check it
grade9-chemistry.hint: Science is checked by being repeated.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A method that can be followed exactly lets others repeat the work and confirm or challenge the findings.

grade9-chemistry.question: A pupil concludes "the plant made more bubbles because it liked the light". Why is this a poor conclusion?
options: It states a feeling rather than what the data shows
It uses the word bubbles instead of oxygen
It mentions the plant, which is not allowed
It is too short to be a conclusion
grade9-chemistry.answer: It states a feeling rather than what the data shows
acceptableAnswers: It states a feeling rather than what the data shows
grade9-chemistry.hint: A conclusion must come from the measurements.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A conclusion must be supported by the data; "liked" attributes a feeling that nothing was measured about.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which source of information about a science topic is most likely to be reliable?
options: A university or government science website
A comment posted under a video
A message forwarded on a phone
grade9-chemistry.answer: A university or government science website
acceptableAnswers: A university or government science website
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about who is responsible for the content.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Information from a scientific institution is checked and attributable; the others are anonymous or are selling something.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why should the same fact be checked in more than one source?
options: It makes the report look much longer
Every source always says exactly the same thing
One source may be wrong, out of date or biased
It is the only way to find a source at all
grade9-chemistry.answer: One source may be wrong, out of date or biased
acceptableAnswers: One source may be wrong, out of date or biased
grade9-chemistry.hint: Agreement between independent sources is what builds confidence.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Cross-checking guards against a single source being mistaken, outdated or one-sided.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why must the sources used in a science report be listed?
options: So the report reaches the required number of pages
So the conclusion does not have to be written
So no one else can use the same sources
So a reader can check where the information came from
grade9-chemistry.answer: So a reader can check where the information came from
acceptableAnswers: So a reader can check where the information came from
grade9-chemistry.hint: It is the same reason a method is written out.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Listing sources lets a reader verify the claims and credits the work of others.

grade9-chemistry.question: State one safety precaution to take when heating a liquid in a test tube.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Point the mouth away from everyone
acceptableAnswers: Point the mouth away from everyone
do not point it at anyone
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about spitting, and about eyes.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Pointing the tube away, wearing goggles and using a holder are all correct precautions.

grade9-chemistry.question: Name the section of a report that states what the results show.
grade9-chemistry.answer: Conclusion
grade9-chemistry.hint: It comes at the end.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The conclusion states what the results mean.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is concentrated acid always added to water, and never water to acid?
options: The water would become far too cold for the acid to mix
The acid would lose its strength and stop reacting at all
A great deal of heat is released and the mixture can spit
The acid would turn into a gas that cannot be collected
grade9-chemistry.answer: A great deal of heat is released and the mixture can spit
acceptableAnswers: A great deal of heat is released and the mixture can spit
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about the heat produced when the two meet.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Diluting acid releases heat. Adding acid slowly to a large volume of water spreads that heat through the water; pouring water onto acid heats a small volume, which can boil and throw acid out of the beaker.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which protective equipment should be worn when handling a corrosive acid?
options: Safety goggles and a laboratory coat
A sun hat and a pair of oven gloves
A woollen scarf and canvas sandals
A paper apron and cotton mittens
grade9-chemistry.answer: Safety goggles and a laboratory coat
acceptableAnswers: Safety goggles and a laboratory coat
grade9-chemistry.hint: Protect the eyes before anything else.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Goggles keep splashes out of the eyes and a laboratory coat protects skin and clothing from a corrosive liquid.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why are anti-bumping granules added before a liquid is boiled?
options: They raise the boiling point so the liquid heats up faster
They colour the liquid so that the level can be seen easily
They let bubbles form steadily so the liquid does not spit
They soak up the liquid so that less of it has to be used
grade9-chemistry.answer: They let bubbles form steadily so the liquid does not spit
acceptableAnswers: They let bubbles form steadily so the liquid does not spit
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about how a liquid boils when they are left out.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Without them a liquid superheats and boils in sudden bursts, called bumping. The granules give small bubbles somewhere to start, so boiling is smooth and nothing is thrown out of the flask.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is a flammable liquid such as ethanol heated in a water bath rather than over a flame?
options: Its vapour could catch fire if it met the naked flame
A flame would not make the liquid hot enough to boil
A water bath makes the liquid boil at a much lower point
The flame would change the liquid into a different one
grade9-chemistry.answer: Its vapour could catch fire if it met the naked flame
acceptableAnswers: Its vapour could catch fire if it met the naked flame
grade9-chemistry.hint: Ethanol vapour and a flame are a dangerous pair.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Ethanol vapour is flammable. A water bath heats the liquid to below 100 °C with no naked flame anywhere near the vapour.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is a gas such as sulfur dioxide prepared in a fume cupboard?
options: The gas is toxic and must be drawn safely away
The cupboard keeps the apparatus at one steady heat
The gas is very light and would float upwards
The gas is expensive and none of it may be wasted
grade9-chemistry.answer: The gas is toxic and must be drawn safely away
acceptableAnswers: The gas is toxic and must be drawn safely away
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what breathing it in would do.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Sulfur dioxide is toxic and irritates the lungs. A fume cupboard draws the gas away from everyone in the room.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the correct way to smell a gas in a test tube?
options: Pour it into an open beaker and lean over the top
Warm the tube first and then sniff it very quickly
Waft a little of it towards the nose with the hand
Hold the tube under the nose and breathe in deeply
grade9-chemistry.answer: Waft a little of it towards the nose with the hand
acceptableAnswers: Waft a little of it towards the nose with the hand
grade9-chemistry.hint: Never take a full breath of an unknown gas.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Wafting brings a very small, diluted amount to the nose. Breathing a gas in directly can damage the lungs.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why must a chemical in the laboratory never be tasted?
options: Tasting would cool the chemical down far too quickly
Most chemicals have no taste that could be noticed
The taste changes once the bottle has been opened
Many chemicals are poisonous even in small amounts
grade9-chemistry.answer: Many chemicals are poisonous even in small amounts
acceptableAnswers: Many chemicals are poisonous even in small amounts
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about what a trace of it could do.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Even a trace of a laboratory chemical can be poisonous or corrosive, and a label tells you nothing about how a substance tastes.

grade9-chemistry.question: A crucible has just been heated strongly. How should it be moved?
options: By pouring cold water over it and lifting it out
With a paper towel wrapped around it for grip
With bare hands, because it cools very quickly
With tongs, onto a heat-proof mat to cool down
grade9-chemistry.answer: With tongs, onto a heat-proof mat to cool down
acceptableAnswers: With tongs, onto a heat-proof mat to cool down
grade9-chemistry.hint: Hot porcelain looks exactly like cold porcelain.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A hot crucible gives no sign that it is hot. Tongs and a heat-proof mat keep hands and bench safe, and cold water would crack it.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is a Bunsen burner left with a yellow flame when it is not being used?
options: A yellow flame cannot set fire to anything at all
A yellow flame uses far less gas than a blue one
A yellow flame is easy to see and warns people
A yellow flame keeps the barrel from becoming hot
grade9-chemistry.answer: A yellow flame is easy to see and warns people
acceptableAnswers: A yellow flame is easy to see and warns people
grade9-chemistry.hint: Which flame can you see across a bench?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The safety flame is luminous and visible. A blue flame is almost invisible in a bright room, so somebody can reach through it without knowing.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is the label on a bottle read before the chemical is used?
options: It gives the date on which the bottle was last washed
It gives the name, the hazards and how to handle it
It gives the price and the shop where it was bought
It gives the number of pupils allowed to use it
grade9-chemistry.answer: It gives the name, the hazards and how to handle it
acceptableAnswers: It gives the name, the hazards and how to handle it
grade9-chemistry.hint: A label carries more than a name.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A label names the substance, shows its hazard symbols and states the precautions, so it must be read before the stopper is removed.

grade9-chemistry.question: A pupil has some leftover dilute acid at the end of a practical. What should be done with it?
options: Return it to the stock bottle it was taken from
Follow the instructions given for disposing of waste
Pour it straight down the sink with no water at all
Leave it in the beaker on the bench for the next class
grade9-chemistry.answer: Follow the instructions given for disposing of waste
acceptableAnswers: Follow the instructions given for disposing of waste
grade9-chemistry.hint: Two of these would contaminate something.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Waste is disposed of as the teacher instructs, usually diluted with plenty of running water. Returning it contaminates the stock bottle, and leaving it out is a hazard for whoever comes next.

grade9-chemistry.question: A beaker of hot solution cracks and the liquid spreads across the bench. What is the first thing to do?
options: Wipe it up quickly with a handful of paper towel
Tell the teacher at once and keep everyone back
Pick the broken glass out with your fingers first
Carry on and clear it up at the end of the lesson
grade9-chemistry.answer: Tell the teacher at once and keep everyone back
acceptableAnswers: Tell the teacher at once and keep everyone back
grade9-chemistry.hint: Hot liquid and broken glass are both on that bench.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The teacher decides how a spill of hot liquid and broken glass is cleared. Keeping people away prevents a burn or a cut before the clean-up begins.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which section of a report states what the investigation set out to find?
grade9-chemistry.answer: The aim
grade9-chemistry.hint: It is written before the work begins.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The aim states the purpose of the investigation. The method says how it was done and the results say what happened.

grade9-chemistry.question: In which section of a report is the list of chemicals and equipment given?
grade9-chemistry.answer: The apparatus and materials
grade9-chemistry.hint: It is what you collect together before you start.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The apparatus and materials section lists everything used, so that the work can be set up again exactly as it was.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which of these is an observation rather than a conclusion?
options: Magnesium reacts faster than zinc does in acid
Bubbles were seen and the ribbon disappeared
Magnesium is above copper in the reactivity series
The gas given off must have been hydrogen
grade9-chemistry.answer: Bubbles were seen and the ribbon disappeared
acceptableAnswers: Bubbles were seen and the ribbon disappeared
grade9-chemistry.hint: Which one is only what your eyes saw?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: An observation records what happened. The other three interpret what happened, which makes them conclusions drawn from an observation.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does a method say “25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid” rather than “some acid”?
options: So the conclusion can be written before the results
So the acid does not have to be measured out at all
So another person can repeat it exactly as it was done
So the report reaches the length the teacher asked for
grade9-chemistry.answer: So another person can repeat it exactly as it was done
acceptableAnswers: So another person can repeat it exactly as it was done
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about somebody else trying to follow it.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Exact quantities make the work repeatable. “Some acid” gives a different result each time and cannot be checked by anybody else.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is a labelled diagram of the apparatus drawn in a report?
options: It shows what the results are expected to look like
It makes the report look neater than it really was
It shows how the parts were arranged more clearly
It takes the place of listing any of the apparatus
grade9-chemistry.answer: It shows how the parts were arranged more clearly
acceptableAnswers: It shows how the parts were arranged more clearly
grade9-chemistry.hint: Some arrangements are hard to describe in words.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A labelled diagram shows the set-up at a glance, such as where the delivery tube runs and where the thermometer sits, which prose describes clumsily.

grade9-chemistry.question: A pupil gets one result far from all the others. What should the report do with it?
options: Change it to the value that was expected
Record it and say that it does not fit
Leave it out and repeat until it agrees
Rub it out so the pattern looks tidier
grade9-chemistry.answer: Record it and say that it does not fit
acceptableAnswers: Record it and say that it does not fit
grade9-chemistry.hint: Honest reporting comes before a tidy graph.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: An anomalous result is recorded and identified. Deleting or altering it hides evidence that something went wrong, which is the opposite of science.

grade9-chemistry.question: A results table records a temperature as 26.5 with nothing written after it. What is missing?
grade9-chemistry.answer: The unit
grade9-chemistry.hint: A number on its own does not say how much.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Every measurement needs its unit, so this should read 26.5 °C. Without a unit the number could mean anything at all.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which tense is used to write up a method that has already been carried out?
options: The future tense, saying what will happen
A list of the names of everyone in the group
The past tense, saying what was done
The present tense, saying what is planned
grade9-chemistry.answer: The past tense, saying what was done
acceptableAnswers: The past tense, saying what was done
grade9-chemistry.hint: The work has already been done.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A write-up reports work already carried out, so it is written in the past tense: “the acid was added”, not “add the acid”.

grade9-chemistry.question: A conclusion says “copper is the least useful metal”. Why is that not acceptable?
options: A conclusion may not mention a metal by name
Copper was not named anywhere in the aim
Nothing in the results measured usefulness
The word least may not be used in a report
grade9-chemistry.answer: Nothing in the results measured usefulness
acceptableAnswers: Nothing in the results measured usefulness
grade9-chemistry.hint: A conclusion may only say what was measured.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The experiment measured reactivity, not usefulness. A conclusion must stay inside what the results actually show.

grade9-chemistry.question: A pupil wants to show the class how three antacids compared. Which is the clearest way?
options: A photograph of the three bottles side by side
A bar chart of the volume neutralised by each
A list of the apparatus that was used for each
A long paragraph describing each one in turn
grade9-chemistry.answer: A bar chart of the volume neutralised by each
acceptableAnswers: A bar chart of the volume neutralised by each
grade9-chemistry.hint: Three separate items are being compared.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A bar chart compares separate items at a glance. Prose and a photograph do not show how big the difference between them was.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why are the individual titre readings given as well as the mean?
options: They give the volume of acid in the burette
They show how closely the repeats agreed
They are needed because a mean cannot be used
They make the results table look much fuller
grade9-chemistry.answer: They show how closely the repeats agreed
acceptableAnswers: They show how closely the repeats agreed
grade9-chemistry.hint: A mean on its own hides something important.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The spread of the raw readings shows how reliable the mean is. Three titres within 0.10 cm³ mean far more than three that differ by 2 cm³.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why does a report state the safety precautions that were taken?
options: So the report can be marked more quickly
So anyone repeating it knows the risks
So the apparatus list can be left out
So the results do not need repeating
grade9-chemistry.answer: So anyone repeating it knows the risks
acceptableAnswers: So anyone repeating it knows the risks
grade9-chemistry.hint: Somebody else may set this up next week.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The precautions are part of the method. Whoever repeats the work must know what the hazards are before they begin.

grade9-chemistry.question: A conclusion says the reaction sped up, but the results table shows it slowed down. What should happen?
options: Both are left in and the reader chooses one
The results are changed to match the conclusion
The results table is removed from the report
The conclusion is rewritten to match the results
grade9-chemistry.answer: The conclusion is rewritten to match the results
acceptableAnswers: The conclusion is rewritten to match the results
grade9-chemistry.hint: Which of the two is the evidence?
grade9-chemistry.explanation: The results are the evidence. A conclusion that contradicts them is simply wrong and has to be rewritten.

grade9-chemistry.question: Where is the most reliable information about the hazards of a chemical found?
options: A comment left underneath a video clip
The safety data sheet from the supplier
A message forwarded by a friend online
grade9-chemistry.answer: The safety data sheet from the supplier
acceptableAnswers: The safety data sheet from the supplier
grade9-chemistry.hint: Ask who is responsible for the information.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A supplier must publish a safety data sheet giving the hazards, the handling and the first aid. The other three are anonymous or are selling something.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is the date of a web page checked before its information is used?
options: A page written last week is always correct
Older pages take much longer to load fully
Advice about a chemical can change over time
The date shows who paid for the page to exist
grade9-chemistry.answer: Advice about a chemical can change over time
acceptableAnswers: Advice about a chemical can change over time
grade9-chemistry.hint: Safety advice is not fixed for ever.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Hazard classifications and recommended practice are revised. An out-of-date page may give advice that has since been withdrawn.

grade9-chemistry.question: How is a spreadsheet most useful after a titration has been carried out?
options: It calculates the mean titre and draws a graph
It decides which indicator should have been used
It measures the volume delivered by the burette
It tells you when the end point has been reached
grade9-chemistry.answer: It calculates the mean titre and draws a graph
acceptableAnswers: It calculates the mean titre and draws a graph
grade9-chemistry.hint: It works with numbers you have already taken.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A spreadsheet processes recorded data into means, differences and charts. It cannot make a measurement for you.

grade9-chemistry.question: What is the advantage of using a data logger with a pH probe?
options: It records readings automatically at set times
It makes the neutralisation happen more quickly
It changes the pH of the solution as it is added
It removes the need to plan the experiment at all
grade9-chemistry.answer: It records readings automatically at set times
acceptableAnswers: It records readings automatically at set times
grade9-chemistry.hint: Think about how often a reading is needed near the end point.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: A logger takes readings at fixed intervals with nobody watching, so the rapid change near the end point is not missed.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why must the author of any text copied into a report be named?
options: A named author makes any claim true at once
Using their words as your own is dishonest
Named text does not have to be understood
The report has to reach a set number of words
grade9-chemistry.answer: Using their words as your own is dishonest
acceptableAnswers: Using their words as your own is dishonest
grade9-chemistry.hint: The writing belongs to somebody.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Presenting somebody else’s words as your own is plagiarism. Naming the source credits the author and lets a reader check the claim.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why is a fertiliser advertisement a poor source of evidence about water pollution?
options: The claims in it are never printed in any language
Advertisements are always written far too briefly
The seller gains if the product looks harmless
Advertisements can only be read by farmers
grade9-chemistry.answer: The seller gains if the product looks harmless
acceptableAnswers: The seller gains if the product looks harmless
grade9-chemistry.hint: Ask who benefits from the message.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: An advertiser has an interest in the answer, so its claims are not independent. Evidence should come from a source with nothing to sell.

grade9-chemistry.question: Which search would give the most useful results about acid rain in Mauritius?
options: something interesting about rain and weather
the best website about science in the world
chemistry homework answers for tonight please
grade9-chemistry.answer: “acid rain” Mauritius effects on buildings
grade9-chemistry.hint: Precise words return precise results.
grade9-chemistry.explanation: Naming the topic, the place and what you want narrows the search. Vague words return millions of unrelated pages.

grade9-chemistry.question: Why might a simulation be used instead of carrying out a reaction?
options: A simulation always gives the exact real value
A simulation needs no thought about variables
The real reaction can never be repeated twice
The real reaction may be far too dangerous
grade9-chemistry.answer: The real reaction may be far too dangerous
acceptableAnswers: The real reaction may be far too dangerous
