grade9-english.explanation: Will have returned (future perfect) places the handover as finished before next weekend. "Will return" does not specify that it is done before the deadline.

grade9-english.question: Before the committee meets on Monday, the treasurer _____ the accounts.
grade9-english.hint: "Before the committee meets" places the audit prior to a future event.
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect will have audited makes the audit clearly complete before Monday's meeting. "Will audit" does not convey that sequence.

grade9-english.question: A student writes: "By the time the nurse arrives, the patient will recover." What error has been made?
options: The past perfect should be used instead.
The tense is wrong — use "will have recovered".
"Will be recovering" is the only correct option.
grade9-english.answer: The tense is wrong — use "will have recovered".
acceptableAnswers: The tense is wrong — use "will have recovered".
grade9-english.hint: The recovery is complete before the nurse arrives — which tense shows that?
grade9-english.explanation: Two future events, one before the other, need the future perfect: will have recovered. "Will recover" suggests they happen at the same time.

grade9-english.question: By midnight tonight, the rescue team _____ the last of the survivors.
grade9-english.hint: "By midnight tonight" is the deadline for completion.
grade9-english.explanation: Will have found shows the action complete at or before midnight — the future perfect tense.

grade9-english.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses the future perfect in the passive.
options: The bridge had been built by 2028.
The bridge will be built by 2028.
The bridge will have been built by 2028.
The bridge has been built by 2028.
grade9-english.answer: The bridge will have been built by 2028.
acceptableAnswers: The bridge will have been built by 2028.
grade9-english.hint: Passive future perfect = will have been + past participle.
grade9-english.explanation: Will have been built combines passive and future perfect: construction is done by someone and is complete before 2028.

grade9-english.question: By the time this song ends, I _____ it fifty times.
grade9-english.hint: The fiftieth hearing is complete at the moment the song ends.
grade9-english.explanation: Will have heard counts an action completed by a future point. The future perfect stacks up repeated actions against a deadline.

grade9-english.question: "She will have left the office long before you get there." The verb phrase "will have left" is in the _____ tense.
grade9-english.hint: will have + past participle = which tense?
grade9-english.explanation: Will have left is the future perfect: it places her departure before your future arrival. Present perfect uses "has/have" and past perfect uses "had".

grade9-english.question: Complete the sentence: "By the time the review is published, the author _____ the second draft."
grade9-english.hint: The finishing happens before the publication — both are future.
grade9-english.explanation: Future perfect (will have finished) shows a sequence of two future events: finishing comes before publishing.

grade9-english.question: Which time expression most commonly signals the future perfect tense?
grade9-english.hint: Think about which phrase sets a future deadline for completion.
grade9-english.explanation: "By the time" signals a future deadline — exactly what the future perfect describes: an action completed before that point.

grade9-english.question: "By nine o'clock, the sun will have risen." What does this sentence tell us?
options: A completed action before a future point
An action completed in the past
An action happening exactly at nine o'clock
grade9-english.answer: A completed action before a future point
acceptableAnswers: A completed action before a future point
grade9-english.hint: Will have + past participle — what kind of action does this describe?
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect shows the sunrise as complete before nine o'clock. It links a future deadline to a finished action.

grade9-english.question: Before the year is out, the government _____ five new hospitals.
grade9-english.hint: "Before the year is out" is a future deadline — the openings are done before then.
grade9-english.explanation: Future perfect (will have opened) marks all five openings as finished before the end of the year.

grade9-english.question: "Is the report ready?" "Not quite — the editor _____ it long before noon."
grade9-english.hint: "Long before noon" shows finishing is complete before the deadline.
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect will have finished emphasises that the work is done well before noon. "Will finish" does not clearly place the action before noon.

grade9-english.question: The journalist predicts that by the next election, the new party _____ enough support to win.
grade9-english.hint: The support is built up before the election — which tense shows that?
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect will have gained describes the support as complete and ready by the future election date.

grade9-english.question: Transform "She leaves the office" into the future perfect with "by 5 p.m."
options: She has left the office by 5 p.m.
She will have left the office by 5 p.m.
She had left the office by 5 p.m.
She will leave the office by 5 p.m.
grade9-english.answer: She will have left the office by 5 p.m.
acceptableAnswers: She will have left the office by 5 p.m.
grade9-english.hint: Future perfect = will have + past participle.
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect of "leave" is will have left. "By 5 p.m." anchors the completed departure to a future time.

grade9-english.question: By the end of this century, many species of wildlife _____ extinct.
grade9-english.hint: "By the end of this century" is a future deadline — the process is complete before then.
grade9-english.explanation: Will have become is the future perfect, placing the extinction as done before the century ends.

grade9-english.question: "They _____ the experiment three times before the end of the lesson," the teacher announced.
grade9-english.hint: "Before the end of the lesson" is the future point; the repetitions are complete by then.
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect will have repeated shows all three repetitions finished before the lesson ends — a completed sequence within a future timeline.

grade9-english.question: By the time the school reunion takes place, Priya _____ in London for five years.
grade9-english.hint: "For five years" emphasises duration up to a future point.
grade9-english.explanation: Will have been living (future perfect continuous) stresses five continuous years of residence up to the reunion. "Will have lived" focuses on completion rather than the ongoing experience.

grade9-english.question: By this time tomorrow, we _____ for twelve hours.
grade9-english.hint: A twelve-hour stretch leading up to a future point — which tense captures that?
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect continuous will have been driving highlights the twelve-hour stretch of driving continuing right up to "this time tomorrow".

grade9-english.question: What does "will have been + -ing" emphasise compared to "will have + past participle"?
options: The duration or ongoing nature of an action
That an action happened only once
The starting point of an action
grade9-english.answer: The duration or ongoing nature of an action
acceptableAnswers: The duration or ongoing nature of an action
grade9-english.hint: Compare "I will have read the book" with "I will have been reading the book for hours".
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect continuous draws attention to how long an action continues up to a future point; the simple future perfect focuses on the fact of completion.

grade9-english.question: By the time the election results are announced, journalists _____ the story for twenty-four hours.
grade9-english.hint: "For twenty-four hours" signals a sustained period of activity up to a future point.
grade9-english.explanation: When a time phrase stresses how long an action continues to a future moment, the future perfect continuous is preferred over the simple future perfect.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence uses the future perfect continuous correctly?
options: By next month, she has been studying French for two years.
By next month, she will study French for two years.
By next month, she will have been studying French for two years.
By next month, she had studied French for two years.
grade9-english.answer: By next month, she will have been studying French for two years.
acceptableAnswers: By next month, she will have been studying French for two years.
grade9-english.hint: "For two years, by next month" — duration up to a future point.
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect continuous places a two-year stretch of study ending at a specified future point. It is formed with will have been + -ing.

grade9-english.question: By the time he retires, he _____ medicine for forty years.
grade9-english.hint: Is the sentence emphasising the total duration of an ongoing career?
grade9-english.explanation: Retirement closes a forty-year stretch of practice. Will have been practising marks the duration; "will have practised" stresses completion and counts the years less vividly.

grade9-english.question: Form the future perfect continuous of "teach": "By June, Mrs Ramful _____ at this school for thirty years."
grade9-english.hint: will have been + -ing form of the verb.
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect continuous of "teach" is will have been teaching. It highlights the continuous thirty-year career ending at the future point of June.

grade9-english.question: A marathon runner says: "By the finish line, I _____ for four hours." Choose the correct form.
grade9-english.hint: "For four hours" stresses continuous effort leading to the finish line.
grade9-english.explanation: The runner emphasises how long the effort continues — four hours of sustained running — so the future perfect continuous is the better choice.

grade9-english.question: Why might a speaker choose "will have been waiting" over "will have waited"?
options: To indicate the wait never happened
To show the wait is already over
To stress how long the wait lasts
To suggest only one moment of waiting
grade9-english.answer: To stress how long the wait lasts
acceptableAnswers: To stress how long the wait lasts
grade9-english.hint: The continuous form draws attention to the process; the simple form to the result.
grade9-english.explanation: Will have been waiting foregrounds the stretched-out experience of waiting. "Will have waited" simply records that waiting happened before a future point.

grade9-english.question: Identify the future perfect continuous verb phrase: "By July, the research team will have been collecting data for five years."
grade9-english.hint: The whole verb phrase, not just part of it, is the answer.
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect continuous is the full verb phrase will have been collecting. "For five years" is the time expression showing duration, not part of the tense.

grade9-english.question: By the time they land, the passengers _____ in economy class for nine hours.
grade9-english.hint: Nine hours of continuous discomfort leading to a future landing — which tense fits?
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect continuous will have been sitting highlights the nine-hour stretch that ends when the plane lands.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence best expresses a tiresome duration leading to a future point?
options: By midnight, I will have marked papers.
By midnight, I will mark papers.
By midnight, I will have been marking papers for six hours.
grade9-english.answer: By midnight, I will have been marking papers for six hours.
acceptableAnswers: By midnight, I will have been marking papers for six hours.
grade9-english.hint: Which option makes the reader feel the length of the effort?
grade9-english.explanation: Will have been marking with "for six hours" communicates the exhausting stretch of effort. The simple future perfect only records that marking happened.

grade9-english.question: Transform "She has been studying" into the future perfect continuous (by next year, for three years).
options: She will have been studying for three years by next year.
She had been studying for three years by next year.
She will study for three years by next year.
She has been studying for three years by next year.
grade9-english.answer: She will have been studying for three years by next year.
acceptableAnswers: She will have been studying for three years by next year.
grade9-english.hint: Move the action forward to "next year" and stress the three-year duration.
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect continuous will have been studying carries the ongoing action to a future point while keeping the emphasis on the three-year duration.

grade9-english.question: By the time we finish this project, the team _____ together for two years.
grade9-english.hint: "For two years, by the time we finish" — duration up to a future point.
grade9-english.explanation: Future perfect continuous will have been working captures the two-year stretch of collaboration ending at project completion.

grade9-english.question: When I meet her at the airport next Sunday, she _____ non-stop for twenty hours.
grade9-english.hint: "Non-stop" and "twenty hours" together emphasise a continuous stretch of effort.
grade9-english.explanation: "Non-stop" and "twenty hours" point to the future perfect continuous will have been travelling, which stresses the continuous effort rather than just its completion.

grade9-english.question: Choose the sentence that uses the future perfect continuous to highlight a lifelong, continuous effort.
options: By her sixtieth birthday, she had been painting.
By her sixtieth birthday, she has painted.
By her sixtieth birthday, she will have been painting for forty years.
By her sixtieth birthday, she will paint.
grade9-english.answer: By her sixtieth birthday, she will have been painting for forty years.
acceptableAnswers: By her sixtieth birthday, she will have been painting for forty years.
grade9-english.hint: Which sentence captures forty years of unbroken dedication?
grade9-english.explanation: Will have been painting stresses forty years of continuous creative work. The simple forms in the other options lose the sense of ongoing dedication.

grade9-english.question: "They will have been rehearsing for three months by opening night." What does this tell us?
options: They rehearse continuously in the lead-up to opening night.
They will begin rehearsing on opening night.
They rehearsed once, three months ago.
grade9-english.answer: They rehearse continuously in the lead-up to opening night.
acceptableAnswers: They rehearse continuously in the lead-up to opening night.
grade9-english.hint: The future perfect continuous stresses an ongoing process up to a future point.
grade9-english.explanation: The sentence pictures continuous rehearsal across three months, arriving at opening night — that is what the future perfect continuous communicates.

grade9-english.question: By the time the charity race ends, the organisers _____ for twelve months.
grade9-english.hint: Twelve months of continuous planning leads to the future race day.
grade9-english.explanation: The future perfect continuous will have been planning pictures twelve months of ongoing preparation finishing at the race.

grade9-english.question: Which form is grammatically correct? "By the age of eighteen, he _____ music for twelve years."
grade9-english.hint: Future perfect continuous = will + have + been + -ing form.
grade9-english.explanation: The correct structure is will have been + the -ing form: learning. "Will been" omits "have"; "will have learn" uses the base form instead of the -ing.

grade9-english.question: "By nine tomorrow morning, the bakers will have been making bread for five hours." What does the future perfect continuous add here?
options: It shows the baking is a continuous process ending at nine tomorrow.
It shows the baking happened only once.
It shows the baking has not started yet.
It shows the baking finished yesterday.
grade9-english.answer: It shows the baking is a continuous process ending at nine tomorrow.
acceptableAnswers: It shows the baking is a continuous process ending at nine tomorrow.
grade9-english.hint: Five hours of sustained work — the continuous form shows the process, not just the result.
grade9-english.explanation: Will have been making pictures a five-hour stretch of continuous work. It stresses the activity itself rather than just the loaves produced — the main function of the future perfect continuous.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence keeps its tenses consistent?
options: The scientist measures the temperature and recorded the result.
The scientist measured the temperature and recorded the result.
The scientist will measure the temperature and recorded the result.
The scientist measured the temperature and records the result.
grade9-english.answer: The scientist measured the temperature and recorded the result.
acceptableAnswers: The scientist measured the temperature and recorded the result.
grade9-english.hint: Both actions happen at the same time in the past.
grade9-english.explanation: Both verbs — measured and recorded — are in the simple past, so the tenses are consistent. Mixing past and present creates an unnatural jump in time.

grade9-english.question: Spot the tense inconsistency: "The wind had picked up speed and the sky turns dark."
grade9-english.hint: "Had picked up" sets the scene in the past — what tense should the second verb match?
grade9-english.explanation: "Had picked up" is past perfect; the parallel action must be in the past too: turned. "Turns" pulls the sentence into the present without reason.

grade9-english.question: A student writes a past-tense story and then writes: "Suddenly the door opens and a man walks in." What should this sentence read?
options: No change — both tenses are acceptable here.
Suddenly the door opened and a man walked in.
Suddenly the door opens and a man will walk in.
Suddenly the door had opened and a man walks in.
grade9-english.answer: Suddenly the door opened and a man walked in.
acceptableAnswers: Suddenly the door opened and a man walked in.
grade9-english.hint: The story is in the past tense — every narrative event must match.
grade9-english.explanation: Once a past-tense narrative is established, new events stay in the simple past: opened and walked. Slipping into the present breaks the tense frame.

grade9-english.question: Which paragraph is written in a consistent tense throughout?
options: The fisherman woke early. He packs his nets and rowed out to sea.
The fisherman woke early. He will pack his nets and rowed out to sea.
The fisherman woke early. He packed his nets and rowed out to sea.
The fisherman wakes early. He packed his nets and rowed out to sea.
grade9-english.answer: The fisherman woke early. He packed his nets and rowed out to sea.
acceptableAnswers: The fisherman woke early. He packed his nets and rowed out to sea.
grade9-english.hint: Every verb in the passage should be in the same tense.
grade9-english.explanation: Woke, packed and rowed are all simple past, making the sequence consistent. The other options each mix a different tense into the past-tense frame.

grade9-english.question: In a formal essay about climate change, a student alternates between "is" and "was" for the same ongoing situation. What rule have they broken?
options: Subject-verb agreement — "is" and "was" cannot share a paragraph.
No rule — "is" and "was" are always interchangeable.
Tense consistency — a stable situation should stay in one tense.
grade9-english.answer: Tense consistency — a stable situation should stay in one tense.
acceptableAnswers: Tense consistency — a stable situation should stay in one tense.
grade9-english.hint: If climate change is still ongoing, which tense should be used throughout?
grade9-english.explanation: An ongoing situation needs a consistent tense. Switching between "is" and "was" implies the situation has ended and returned. Tense consistency means one tense for one stable situation.

grade9-english.question: Choose the version that corrects the tense inconsistency: "He studied hard, so he passes the exam."
options: He had studied hard, so he passes the exam.
He studied hard, so he is passing the exam.
He studied hard, so he passed the exam.
He studies hard, so he passes the exam.
grade9-english.answer: He studied hard, so he passed the exam.
acceptableAnswers: He studied hard, so he passed the exam.
grade9-english.hint: "Studied" is simple past — the result should match.
grade9-english.explanation: "Studied" sets the past tense; passed maintains it. A past cause cannot logically lead to a present-tense result in a narrative sequence.

grade9-english.question: Identify the sentence that has a tense shift error.
options: She was reading when the lights go out.
She was reading when the lights went out.
She read and then she went to bed.
She had finished before he arrived.
grade9-english.answer: She was reading when the lights go out.
acceptableAnswers: She was reading when the lights go out.
grade9-english.hint: "Was reading" is past continuous — the interrupting event should be past too.
grade9-english.explanation: "Was reading" establishes a past background; the interruption must be past: went out. "Go out" switches to the present tense without reason.

grade9-english.question: A history essay reads: "Napoleon invaded Russia in 1812. The campaign was disastrous and many soldiers die." Correct the error.
grade9-english.hint: The essay uses simple past throughout — the last verb must match.
grade9-english.explanation: Historical narrative uses the simple past. "Die" switches to the present; died restores consistency.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence avoids a tense inconsistency?
options: The coach had blown the whistle and the players stop immediately.
The coach blew the whistle and the players stop immediately.
The coach blows the whistle and the players stopped immediately.
The coach blew the whistle and the players stopped immediately.
grade9-english.answer: The coach blew the whistle and the players stopped immediately.
acceptableAnswers: The coach blew the whistle and the players stopped immediately.
grade9-english.hint: Both actions happen at the same moment in the past.
grade9-english.explanation: Blew and stopped are both simple past, placing both actions in the same moment without ambiguity.

grade9-english.question: Why is tense consistency important in written English?
options: It makes sentences shorter and easier to punctuate.
It is only important in formal letters, not in stories.
It tells the reader clearly when events happen relative to each other.
It limits the writer to one verb per sentence.
grade9-english.answer: It tells the reader clearly when events happen relative to each other.
acceptableAnswers: It tells the reader clearly when events happen relative to each other.
grade9-english.hint: Think about what a reader does with tense information.
grade9-english.explanation: Tense signals time. Keeping the tense consistent means the reader always knows when events occur — past, present or future — without confusion from unexpected switches.

grade9-english.question: A student switches from simple past to present tense in the middle of a narrative. What is the likely effect on the reader?
options: A stronger ending to the story
Confusion about when events are happening
A clearer sense of the events' sequence
grade9-english.answer: Confusion about when events are happening
acceptableAnswers: Confusion about when events are happening
grade9-english.hint: Tense tells the reader where to place events in time.
grade9-english.explanation: An unexplained tense shift disrupts the reader's sense of the timeline, causing confusion. Deliberate shifts are possible but must be handled with clear intent.

grade9-english.question: Correct the tense inconsistency: "By the time we reached the station, the train leaves."
options: By the time we reached the station, the train leaves.
By the time we reach the station, the train had left.
By the time we reached the station, the train had left.
By the time we reached the station, the train will leave.
grade9-english.answer: By the time we reached the station, the train had left.
acceptableAnswers: By the time we reached the station, the train had left.
grade9-english.hint: "By the time we reached" sets a past moment — what comes before that in the past?
grade9-english.explanation: When one past action precedes another, the earlier one uses the past perfect: had left. "Leaves" is present tense and breaks the past frame entirely.

grade9-english.question: Which rule should guide the tense of verbs in a science report describing an experiment completed last week?
options: Use the future tense for results.
Use the simple past for methods and results.
grade9-english.answer: Use the simple past for methods and results.
acceptableAnswers: Use the simple past for methods and results.
grade9-english.hint: The experiment is already over — which tense fits completed actions?
grade9-english.explanation: Completed experiments are reported in the simple past: "we heated the solution", "the temperature rose". Conclusions may shift to the present ("This shows…"), but the narrative of what was done stays past.

grade9-english.question: Find the tense error: "Last Tuesday, she visits her grandmother and cooked dinner."
grade9-english.hint: "Last Tuesday" signals the past — both verbs must follow.
grade9-english.explanation: "Cooked" is correctly past, but "visits" drifts to the present. Changing it to visited makes both verbs consistent with "Last Tuesday".

grade9-english.question: The narrator is writing in the present tense. Which version is tense-consistent?
options: She opens the letter and reads it slowly.
She opened the letter and reads it slowly.
She opens the letter and will read it slowly.
She opens the letter and read it slowly.
grade9-english.answer: She opens the letter and reads it slowly.
acceptableAnswers: She opens the letter and reads it slowly.
grade9-english.hint: If the narrative frame is present tense, every verb should be present.
grade9-english.explanation: When the narrative uses the present tense, all verbs must be present too: opens and reads. Mixing in past or future breaks the frame.

grade9-english.question: A student is told their essay has a "tense shift" problem. What does this mean?
options: The essay moves between tenses without a clear reason.
The essay has too many verbs.
The essay uses the future tense when the past would be better.
The essay is written entirely in the wrong tense.
grade9-english.answer: The essay moves between tenses without a clear reason.
acceptableAnswers: The essay moves between tenses without a clear reason.
grade9-english.hint: "Shift" means a movement or change.
grade9-english.explanation: A tense shift is an unexplained movement from one tense to another in the middle of a text. It confuses the reader and signals a lack of control over the writing.

grade9-english.question: Pick the sentence that corrects the tense error: "After the rain stopped, the children run outside and play."
options: After the rain stops, the children ran outside and played.
After the rain stopped, the children run outside and played.
After the rain stops, the children run outside and play.
After the rain stopped, the children ran outside and played.
grade9-english.answer: After the rain stopped, the children ran outside and played.
acceptableAnswers: After the rain stopped, the children ran outside and played.
grade9-english.hint: "Stopped" is simple past — all the following verbs should match.
grade9-english.explanation: "Ran" and "played" are both simple past, consistent with "stopped". "Run" and "play" are present and create a tense break with the past-tense beginning.

grade9-english.question: Identify the correct version of a news report about an event that happened yesterday.
options: The parade begins at noon. Thousands of people lined the streets and cheered.
The parade began at noon. Thousands of people line the streets and cheered.
The parade began at noon. Thousands of people lined the streets and cheered.
The parade began at noon. Thousands of people lined the streets and will cheer.
grade9-english.answer: The parade began at noon. Thousands of people lined the streets and cheered.
acceptableAnswers: The parade began at noon. Thousands of people lined the streets and cheered.
grade9-english.hint: A past event uses the simple past throughout.
grade9-english.explanation: All three verbs — began, lined, cheered — are simple past, making the report consistent. Any present or future verb breaks the "yesterday" time frame.

grade9-english.question: A writer begins in the simple past and shifts to the present for dramatic effect. Which example does this deliberately and correctly?
options: He reached the summit. Suddenly, everything will change.
He reached the summit. Suddenly, everything changed.
He reached the summit. Suddenly, everything changes — the cloud lifts and the valley appears below.
He reached the summit. Suddenly, everything had changed.
grade9-english.answer: He reached the summit. Suddenly, everything changes — the cloud lifts and the valley appears below.
acceptableAnswers: He reached the summit. Suddenly, everything changes — the cloud lifts and the valley appears below.
grade9-english.hint: The historical present uses the present tense for vividness at a key moment — it is deliberate, not an error.
grade9-english.explanation: Writers sometimes shift to the present at a dramatic moment — this is the historical present. The pattern "Suddenly…" signals intent. The plain past in the last option is consistent but less vivid; the others are ungrammatical.

grade9-english.question: Which best describes "maintaining tense consistency across a whole text"?
options: Alternating between past and present to keep the reader interested.
Choosing one time frame and keeping all verbs in that frame unless there is a clear reason to shift.
Using the present tense in every sentence regardless of the subject.
Avoiding all forms of the verb "to be" throughout the text.
grade9-english.answer: Choosing one time frame and keeping all verbs in that frame unless there is a clear reason to shift.
acceptableAnswers: Choosing one time frame and keeping all verbs in that frame unless there is a clear reason to shift.
grade9-english.hint: Consistency allows exceptions — but those exceptions need to be deliberate.
grade9-english.explanation: Tense consistency means anchoring the text in one time frame and only departing from it when there is a clear purpose. Random shifts without reason undermine the writing.

grade9-english.question: A poem begins: "We marched through the dust, our boots worn to nothing." What narrative voice is used?
grade9-english.hint: Look at the pronoun "we".
grade9-english.explanation: "We" is a first person plural pronoun, so this is a first person plural narrative. The narrator is part of the group being described.

grade9-english.question: A story begins: "Priya stared at the letter. She had waited three months for this moment." What narrative voice is used?
grade9-english.hint: "Priya" and "She" are the clues.
grade9-english.explanation: The narrator refers to the character by name and uses "She", making this a third person narrative. The narrator is outside the story.

grade9-english.question: A novel uses: "You open your eyes. You are in a field you do not recognise." What is the effect of this voice?
options: It pulls the reader directly into the action
It tells the story from a character's childhood
It creates distance between reader and story
It shows the narrator is all-knowing
grade9-english.answer: It pulls the reader directly into the action
acceptableAnswers: It pulls the reader directly into the action
grade9-english.hint: "You" addresses the reader as though they are the character.
grade9-english.explanation: The second person ("you") places the reader inside the character's experience, making the action feel immediate and personal.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence is evidence that a narrator is unreliable?
options: "I remember it perfectly, though everyone else says I was not there"
grade9-english.answer: "I remember it perfectly, though everyone else says I was not there"
acceptableAnswers: "I remember it perfectly, though everyone else says I was not there"
grade9-english.hint: Look for a contradiction between what the narrator claims and what others say.
grade9-english.explanation: An unreliable narrator gives an account that the reader has reason to doubt. The contradiction — remembering something they could not have witnessed — is the evidence.

grade9-english.question: A story is told in the first person. What is one limitation of this voice?
options: The reader only knows what the narrator knows
The story cannot have a plot
The narrator cannot use descriptive language
The story cannot have more than one character
grade9-english.answer: The reader only knows what the narrator knows
acceptableAnswers: The reader only knows what the narrator knows
grade9-english.hint: What happens to events the narrator is not present for?
grade9-english.explanation: A first person narrator can only report what they see, hear, and feel. Events outside their experience must be described as rumour or hearsay — if at all.

grade9-english.question: Read: "From where I stood at the window, I watched the whole street fill with smoke." What does this tell us about the narrator?
options: The narrator is an eyewitness to the events
The narrator heard about the events later
grade9-english.answer: The narrator is an eyewitness to the events
acceptableAnswers: The narrator is an eyewitness to the events
grade9-english.hint: "From where I stood" and "I watched" are the key phrases.
grade9-english.explanation: "I watched" places the narrator physically at the scene, so they are an eyewitness. First person narrators who are present give direct accounts.

grade9-english.question: A novelist writes: "What Jonas could not know was that, at that very moment, his sister was boarding a ship three hundred miles away." What does this reveal about the narrator?
options: The narrator knows more than any character
The narrator can only guess at events
grade9-english.answer: The narrator knows more than any character
acceptableAnswers: The narrator knows more than any character
grade9-english.hint: No character could know events happening at the same moment three hundred miles away.
grade9-english.explanation: An omniscient narrator has access to events and thoughts that no single character could witness. This technique lets the author build irony and suspense.

grade9-english.question: In a poem, the speaker says: "My mother's hands, rough with work, tucked me in each night." Who is the speaker most likely?
grade9-english.hint: "My mother" and "me" are the clues.
grade9-english.explanation: "My mother" and "tucked me in" show the speaker is the child — the poem is a memory spoken from the child's perspective.

grade9-english.question: A character narrates: "I told the truth — or what I believed to be the truth." What does this admission suggest?
options: The narrator may have been mistaken
grade9-english.answer: The narrator may have been mistaken
acceptableAnswers: The narrator may have been mistaken
grade9-english.hint: The phrase "what I believed to be" qualifies the first claim.
grade9-english.explanation: The narrator qualifies their account with "what I believed", opening the possibility that their version is wrong. This is a mark of a potentially unreliable narrator who may be mistaken rather than dishonest.

grade9-english.question: A story uses "he", "she", and "they" throughout, with no "I". What narrative voice is this?
grade9-english.hint: Third person uses pronouns for characters, never for the narrator.
grade9-english.explanation: Consistent use of "he", "she", and "they" without "I" or "you" identifies a third person narrator, who stands outside the story.

grade9-english.question: A poem shifts from "I" to "we" midway. What effect does this create?
options: It shows the poem changing language
It shows the narrator losing their memory
It shows the narrator joining a community or group
It shows that two poets wrote the poem
grade9-english.answer: It shows the narrator joining a community or group
acceptableAnswers: It shows the narrator joining a community or group
grade9-english.hint: Moving from "I" to "we" expands who the speaker represents.
grade9-english.explanation: Shifting from I to we signals that the narrator is no longer speaking solely for themselves — they are now part of, or speaking for, a wider group.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence provides evidence that the narrator is telling the story from memory?
options: "Looking back now, I understand what she meant"
grade9-english.answer: "Looking back now, I understand what she meant"
acceptableAnswers: "Looking back now, I understand what she meant"
grade9-english.hint: "Looking back now" signals retrospective narration.
grade9-english.explanation: "Looking back now" places the narrator in the present, reflecting on a past event. This is retrospective narration — the story is recounted from memory.

grade9-english.question: A novel is told in third person but the reader only ever hears one character's thoughts. What technique is this?
grade9-english.hint: "Limited" means only one character's inner world is accessible.
grade9-english.explanation: In limited third person, the narrator uses "he" or "she" but only accesses one character's thoughts. The reader is closely aligned with that character without the narrator using "I".

grade9-english.question: What is the effect of a first person narrator on the reader's sympathy?
options: It tends to make the reader sympathise with the narrator
It removes the narrator from the story entirely
It tends to make the reader dislike the narrator
It makes every character equally important
grade9-english.answer: It tends to make the reader sympathise with the narrator
acceptableAnswers: It tends to make the reader sympathise with the narrator
grade9-english.hint: Think about how it feels to be told a story directly by someone.
grade9-english.explanation: A first person narrator speaks directly to the reader, which creates intimacy. Readers often sympathise with or trust the narrator because they hear only that voice.

grade9-english.question: Read: "She smiled at him, though inside her heart was breaking." Which narrative technique does this use?
options: Access to inner thoughts (third person limited)
grade9-english.answer: Access to inner thoughts (third person limited)
acceptableAnswers: Access to inner thoughts (third person limited)
grade9-english.hint: The narrator tells us what she feels inside, not just what she shows.
grade9-english.explanation: The narrator knows something the other character cannot — what is happening "inside her heart". This access to private feeling is the mark of a third person limited narrator.

grade9-english.question: A poem says "I" throughout. Can we always assume the "I" is the poet?
options: No — the "I" always means the reader
Yes — poems cannot use fictional characters
No — the "I" is a speaker the poet has created
grade9-english.answer: No — the "I" is a speaker the poet has created
acceptableAnswers: No — the "I" is a speaker the poet has created
grade9-english.hint: Think about poems written from the point of view of a tree, a soldier, or a child.
grade9-english.explanation: The speaker of a poem is the voice the poet creates, which may be entirely fictional. Assuming the "I" is the poet is a common error — it must be proved, not assumed.

grade9-english.question: An author chooses third person omniscient. What is the main advantage over first person?
options: The story can only focus on one character
The narrator can show events and thoughts of multiple characters
The narrator sounds more personal and trustworthy
The reader cannot question the narrator's version
grade9-english.answer: The narrator can show events and thoughts of multiple characters
acceptableAnswers: The narrator can show events and thoughts of multiple characters
grade9-english.hint: "Omniscient" means all-knowing.
grade9-english.explanation: An omniscient narrator can move freely between characters and scenes, revealing any thought or event. This flexibility is its main advantage over the limited view of a first person narrator.

grade9-english.question: A poem's four lines end: tree / stone / free / alone. What is the rhyme scheme?
grade9-english.hint: Give each new sound a new letter and repeat the letter when the sound returns.
grade9-english.explanation: "Tree" and "free" share a sound (A), "stone" and "alone" share a sound (B), alternating: ABAB.

grade9-english.question: A poem's four lines end: rain / pain / sea / free. What is the rhyme scheme?
grade9-english.hint: "Rain" and "pain" rhyme; "sea" and "free" rhyme — in what order?
grade9-english.explanation: "Rain"/"pain" are the first pair (AA) and "sea"/"free" the second (BB): AABB, also known as rhyming couplets.

grade9-english.question: Which word best completes the rhyme? "The stars burn bright above the sea, / A lantern lit for you and .......... ."
grade9-english.hint: The second line must rhyme with "sea".
grade9-english.explanation: "Sea" and "me" share the /iː/ vowel sound, completing the rhyming couplet. "Night", "dreams", and "shore" do not rhyme with "sea".

grade9-english.question: A poem's four lines end: sky / ground / high / sound. What is the rhyme scheme?
grade9-english.hint: Match each line's ending sound to the others: sky/high rhyme, ground/sound rhyme.
grade9-english.explanation: "Sky" (A) / "ground" (B) / "high" (A) / "sound" (B) = ABAB. Lines 1 and 3 rhyme; lines 2 and 4 rhyme.

grade9-english.question: Which pair of words is a rhyming pair?
grade9-english.hint: In English, spelling and sound often disagree — focus on how the words are pronounced.
grade9-english.explanation: "Through" is pronounced /θruː/ and "blue" is /bluː/ — both end in the same /uː/ sound, making them a rhyming pair. "Rough" is /rʌf/, which does not match.

grade9-english.question: A poem has four stanzas, each with the scheme ABAB. What does this regular rhyme scheme suggest about the poem's tone?
grade9-english.hint: A pattern that repeats exactly suggests a steady hand.
grade9-english.explanation: A consistent, regular rhyme scheme gives a poem a sense of order and control. A poem about chaos would more likely use irregular or no rhyme.

grade9-english.question: What is a couplet?
options: Two words that sound the same
Two stanzas with the same rhyme scheme
A poem of exactly two lines
grade9-english.hint: The word comes from the French for "couple" — a pair.
grade9-english.explanation: A couplet is a pair of consecutive lines that rhyme. A Shakespearean sonnet famously ends with a couplet that summarises or turns the argument.

grade9-english.question: A poem has lines ending: love / hate / dove / fate / war. What is the rhyme scheme of the first four lines?
grade9-english.hint: "Love" and "dove" rhyme; "hate" and "fate" rhyme.
grade9-english.explanation: "Love" (A) / "hate" (B) / "dove" (A) / "fate" (B) = ABAB. The fifth line, "war", introduces a new sound and breaks the pattern.

grade9-english.question: Which word best completes the rhyme? "I stood upon the mountain tall, / And watched the golden leaves .......... ."
grade9-english.hint: "Tall" must rhyme with the last word.
grade9-english.explanation: "Tall" and "fall" share the /ɔːl/ sound. The other options do not rhyme with "tall".

grade9-english.question: Why might a poet choose not to use rhyme?
options: Because rhyme only works in short poems
To create a more natural, conversational tone
Because rhyme is too difficult to write
Because all modern poems avoid rhyme
grade9-english.answer: To create a more natural, conversational tone
acceptableAnswers: To create a more natural, conversational tone
grade9-english.hint: Think about how everyday speech sounds compared to a song.
grade9-english.explanation: Free verse (poetry without rhyme or regular metre) sounds closer to spoken language, which can make a poem feel more natural and honest. Rhyme is a tool, not a requirement.

grade9-english.question: In the scheme ABBA, which lines rhyme with each other?
grade9-english.hint: Match the letters: A appears in positions 1 and 4; B in positions 2 and 3.
grade9-english.explanation: In ABBA, the outer lines (1, 4) rhyme and the inner lines (2, 3) rhyme — an enclosed or "envelope" rhyme scheme.

grade9-english.question: Which pair of words is not a rhyming pair?
grade9-english.hint: Say each pair aloud and listen carefully.
grade9-english.explanation: "Love" is /lʌv/ and "move" is /muːv/ — different vowel sounds, so they do not rhyme. The other pairs all share vowel and consonant sounds.

grade9-english.question: What is an internal rhyme?
options: A rhyme that occurs within a single line
A rhyme between the last words of two lines
A rhyme between the first words of two lines
A rhyme that is almost but not exactly the same
grade9-english.answer: A rhyme that occurs within a single line
acceptableAnswers: A rhyme that occurs within a single line
grade9-english.hint: Think about rhyme that does not wait for the end of the line.
grade9-english.explanation: An internal rhyme places rhyming words within the same line: "The beat of the heat in the street". This differs from end rhyme, which occurs at the line endings.

grade9-english.question: Which word best completes the rhyme? "Beyond the reef where dolphins play, / The fishermen have gone .......... ."
grade9-english.hint: "Play" must rhyme with the last word.
grade9-english.explanation: "Play" and "away" both end in the /eɪ/ sound. "Out", "before", and "far" do not rhyme with "play".

grade9-english.question: What is a near rhyme (also called a half rhyme or slant rhyme)?
options: Words that share some but not all sounds
Words that have the same number of syllables
Words that begin with the same sound
grade9-english.answer: Words that share some but not all sounds
acceptableAnswers: Words that share some but not all sounds
grade9-english.hint: The match is partial, not perfect.
grade9-english.explanation: A near rhyme creates an imperfect match — "stone" / "one", "love" / "move". Poets use it to create a slight tension or unease, or when a perfect rhyme would feel forced.

grade9-english.question: A poem has four lines ending: bright / dark / light / spark. What is the rhyme scheme?
grade9-english.hint: "Bright" and "light" rhyme; "dark" and "spark" rhyme.
grade9-english.explanation: "Bright" (A) / "dark" (B) / "light" (A) / "spark" (B) = ABAB.

grade9-english.question: A poem's final couplet reads: "And so we stand where fathers stood, / And find the world is mostly good." What is the effect of ending with a couplet?
options: It introduces a new and unexpected idea
It gives the poem a sense of conclusion and resolution
It makes the poem feel unfinished
It changes the poem's subject entirely
grade9-english.answer: It gives the poem a sense of conclusion and resolution
acceptableAnswers: It gives the poem a sense of conclusion and resolution
grade9-english.hint: A rhyming pair at the end "closes" the poem.
grade9-english.explanation: A closing couplet creates a sense of completion — the rhyme locks the ideas together and signals that the poem is finished and its argument settled.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence contains a simile?
options: The bells sang in the morning air
Her voice was like silver bells
Silver bells rang across the valley
grade9-english.answer: Her voice was like silver bells
acceptableAnswers: Her voice was like silver bells
grade9-english.hint: A simile uses "like" or "as" to make a comparison.
grade9-english.explanation: "Like silver bells" is a simile: it compares the voice to bells using "like". Without "like" or "as", the same comparison would be a metaphor.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence contains a metaphor?
options: Life is a journey with no map
Life is like a journey with no map
Life can sometimes feel like a journey
Life and journeys have much in common
grade9-english.answer: Life is a journey with no map
acceptableAnswers: Life is a journey with no map
grade9-english.hint: A metaphor states the comparison directly, without "like" or "as".
grade9-english.explanation: "Life is a journey" is a metaphor — it says life IS the thing, not that it is LIKE the thing. Metaphors make comparisons more striking than similes.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device: "The sun smiled down on the sleeping village."
grade9-english.hint: Which action is being given to a non-human thing?
grade9-english.explanation: "Smiled" is a human action given to the sun, which is personification. A simile would need "like" or "as"; alliteration would repeat an initial sound.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device: "The bees buzzed busily among the blossoms."
grade9-english.hint: Look at the first letter of each content word.
grade9-english.explanation: Alliteration is the repetition of the same initial consonant sound: b-ees, b-uzzed, b-usily, b-lossoms. It creates a musical effect.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device: "The thunder crashed and the rain hissed against the windows."
grade9-english.hint: "Crashed" and "hissed" — what is special about these words?
grade9-english.explanation: "Crashed" and "hissed" are onomatopoeic: their sounds imitate the sounds they describe. Onomatopoeia makes writing more vivid and physical.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device: "Her smile was as warm as sunlight after rain."
grade9-english.hint: "As warm as" — two words doing the comparing.
grade9-english.explanation: "As warm as sunlight" is a simile using "as…as". The warmth of the smile is compared to sunlight, with "as" making the comparison explicit.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device: "I have told you a million times to tidy your room."
grade9-english.hint: "A million times" is clearly not meant literally.
grade9-english.explanation: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for emphasis. "A million times" overstates the number to stress frustration, not to report a fact.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device: "The classroom fell silent; even the clock seemed to hold its breath."
grade9-english.hint: Can a clock really hold its breath?
grade9-english.explanation: Giving the clock the human ability to "hold its breath" is personification. It makes the silence feel living and suspenseful.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence uses a metaphor about time?
options: Time and tide wait for no man
Time is a thief that steals our years
The years went by very quickly
grade9-english.answer: Time is a thief that steals our years
acceptableAnswers: Time is a thief that steals our years
grade9-english.hint: Look for a direct equation without "like" or "as".
grade9-english.explanation: "Time is a thief" is a metaphor — it directly equates time with a thief. "Passes like a river" uses "like", making it a simile.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device: "Silently, softly, the snow settled on the sleeping city."
grade9-english.hint: Count how many words begin with the same sound.
grade9-english.explanation: Silently, softly, snow, sleeping, and city all begin with the s/s sound: this is alliteration. The repeated soft sound also mimics the quietness of falling snow.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device: "The wind howled and the door groaned on its hinges."
grade9-english.hint: "Howled" and "groaned" are the key words — what two things make them notable?
grade9-english.explanation: "Howled" (a human or animal action given to wind) is personification; "howled" and "groaned" also sound like what they describe, making them onomatopoeia. Both devices are present.

grade9-english.question: A poet writes: "Hope is the thing with feathers." What device is this?
grade9-english.hint: No "like" or "as" — it states directly that hope IS something.
grade9-english.explanation: "Hope is the thing with feathers" is a metaphor (from Emily Dickinson), directly equating hope with a bird. Without "like" or "as", the comparison is a metaphor.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device: "The engine spluttered and coughed before finally dying."
grade9-english.hint: "Spluttered", "coughed", and "dying" are human or animal qualities.
grade9-english.explanation: Giving the engine human actions — spluttering, coughing, dying — is personification. It makes the engine seem alive and struggling.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence uses irony?
options: The week began on a cheerful note
"Oh, wonderful — another Monday morning," she muttered
She was happy to see Monday arrive
grade9-english.answer: "Oh, wonderful — another Monday morning," she muttered
acceptableAnswers: "Oh, wonderful — another Monday morning," she muttered
grade9-english.hint: The words say one thing but the tone means the opposite.
grade9-english.explanation: The exclamation "wonderful" is ironic because the muttering and the word "another" signal she does not mean it. Irony says the opposite of what is meant, often to show displeasure or humour.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device in: "The roar of the engine tore through the silence."
grade9-english.hint: "Roar" — does the word sound like what it describes?
grade9-english.explanation: "Roar" imitates the loud, rough sound it names. Onomatopoeia makes the reader hear the sound through the word itself.

grade9-english.question: Identify the device: "Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers."
grade9-english.hint: Every content word begins with the same letter.
grade9-english.explanation: The repeated initial /p/ sound across "Peter", "Piper", "picked", "peck", "pickled", and "peppers" is alliteration — often used in tongue-twisters to foreground sound.

grade9-english.question: Which sentence uses a simile to describe speed?
options: The wind ran across the field
He was the wind across the field
He ran fast across the field
He ran like the wind across the field
grade9-english.answer: He ran like the wind across the field
acceptableAnswers: He ran like the wind across the field
grade9-english.hint: "Like" is the signal word.
grade9-english.explanation: "Ran like the wind" is a simile comparing speed to the wind using "like". "He was the wind" would be a metaphor.

grade9-english.question: A poet writes: "The waves clawed at the shore." What is the effect of using the verb "clawed"?
options: It makes the sea seem aggressive and dangerous
It suggests the sea is retreating
It makes the sea seem calm and gentle
It makes the shore seem threatening
grade9-english.answer: It makes the sea seem aggressive and dangerous
acceptableAnswers: It makes the sea seem aggressive and dangerous
grade9-english.hint: Claws are used to attack or grip — what does that suggest about the waves?
grade9-english.explanation: "Clawed" gives the waves the violent action of an animal attacking, making the sea seem aggressive. Naming the device is worth little; explaining what it creates is what earns marks.

grade9-english.question: A writer uses the simile: "Her eyes were like two dark pools." What is the effect?
options: It describes the colour of her eyes exactly
It suggests she is tired and ill
It suggests she is happy and bright
It creates a sense of depth and mystery
grade9-english.answer: It creates a sense of depth and mystery
acceptableAnswers: It creates a sense of depth and mystery
grade9-english.hint: A pool is deep and dark — you cannot see the bottom.
grade9-english.explanation: Dark pools are deep and unknowable, so comparing eyes to them creates a sense of mystery and depth. The simile tells us more about the feeling her eyes create than their literal appearance.

grade9-english.question: A poem uses alliteration: "The lazy, lapping lake." What is the effect?
options: The repeated "l" sound mimics the slow movement of gentle water
The repeated "l" suggests rapid violent movement
The alliteration shows the lake is dangerous
The sound emphasises the colour of the lake
grade9-english.answer: The repeated "l" sound mimics the slow movement of gentle water
acceptableAnswers: The repeated "l" sound mimics the slow movement of gentle water
grade9-english.hint: Say "lazy, lapping lake" slowly — what does it feel like?
grade9-english.explanation: The soft, slow /l/ sound, repeated three times, echoes the gentle, unhurried movement of lapping water. Alliteration here is both decorative and meaningful.

grade9-english.question: A poet personifies the moon: "The moon watched over the sleeping world." What is the effect?
options: It makes the moon seem threatening
It creates a feeling of comfort and protection
It shows the moon is scientifically described
It suggests the world is dangerous
grade9-english.answer: It creates a feeling of comfort and protection
acceptableAnswers: It creates a feeling of comfort and protection
grade9-english.hint: "Watched over" implies care and guardianship.
grade9-english.explanation: A guardian who watches over a sleeper is protective, so giving the moon this human role creates a feeling of safety and comfort. Personification makes the natural world feel benevolent here.

grade9-english.question: A story uses hyperbole: "He had waited an eternity for the bus." What is the effect?
options: It shows the man is unaware of time
It conveys how long and frustrating the wait felt
It tells the reader exactly how long the wait was
It suggests the bus never came
grade9-english.answer: It conveys how long and frustrating the wait felt
acceptableAnswers: It conveys how long and frustrating the wait felt
grade9-english.hint: "An eternity" is not a real measurement — what feeling does it create?
grade9-english.explanation: Hyperbole exaggerates to express emotion, not fact. "An eternity" conveys the subjective experience of a wait that felt endless and frustrating.

grade9-english.question: A poem uses onomatopoeia: "The brook babbled through the stones." What is the effect?
options: The word shows the brook is slow and silent
The word shows the brook is speaking a language
The word emphasises the coldness of the water
The sound of the word recreates the sound of the water
grade9-english.answer: The sound of the word recreates the sound of the water
acceptableAnswers: The sound of the word recreates the sound of the water
grade9-english.hint: Say "babbled" aloud — what does it remind you of?
grade9-english.explanation: "Babbled" imitates the light, repetitive sound of water moving over stones. Onomatopoeia makes the reader hear the scene as well as see it.

grade9-english.question: A writer uses a metaphor: "The mind is an ocean — sometimes still, sometimes stormy." What is the effect?
options: It suggests the mind is empty and vast
It captures how the mind can shift between calm and turmoil
It compares the mind to a weather forecast
It says the mind is actually under the sea
grade9-english.answer: It captures how the mind can shift between calm and turmoil
acceptableAnswers: It captures how the mind can shift between calm and turmoil
grade9-english.hint: An ocean has many states — what does each one suggest about the mind?
grade9-english.explanation: A still ocean suggests peace; a stormy one suggests distress. The metaphor captures the range of emotional states the mind can experience, more vividly than abstract language could.

grade9-english.question: A writer uses irony: "After six hours in the waiting room, he finally declared the service 'excellent'." What is the effect?
options: It suggests the wait was expected
It shows the writer agrees with the man
It shows the man was genuinely satisfied
It highlights the gap between the claim and the reality
grade9-english.answer: It highlights the gap between the claim and the reality
acceptableAnswers: It highlights the gap between the claim and the reality
grade9-english.hint: Six hours in a waiting room — is "excellent" a sincere word here?
grade9-english.explanation: "Excellent" after a six-hour wait creates irony: the word says one thing, but the reality contradicts it. The gap between the claim and the experience is the source of the criticism or humour.

grade9-english.question: A poem ends: "And silence was the loudest sound of all." What device is used and what is the effect?
options: Simile — it compares silence to sound
Alliteration — the s sounds are emphasised
Paradox — it makes the silence feel overwhelming
grade9-english.answer: Paradox — it makes the silence feel overwhelming
acceptableAnswers: Paradox — it makes the silence feel overwhelming
grade9-english.hint: The phrase contradicts itself — yet it makes a kind of sense.
grade9-english.explanation: "Silence" cannot literally be loud — it is a paradox. But the contradiction forces the reader to feel how overwhelming the silence was, more powerfully than a plain description could.

grade9-english.question: A poet personifies war: "War came like a hungry beast and swallowed the young." What is the effect of this choice?
options: It makes war seem predatory and destructive
It makes the young seem weak and foolish
It shows war can be controlled
grade9-english.answer: It makes war seem predatory and destructive
acceptableAnswers: It makes war seem predatory and destructive
grade9-english.hint: A hungry beast hunts — what does "swallowed the young" suggest?
grade9-english.explanation: A hungry beast that swallows its prey is violent and without mercy. Personifying war as such a creature makes its destructive, predatory nature vivid and disturbing.

grade9-english.question: A writer uses the simile: "The news hit him like a blow to the chest." What is the effect?
options: It conveys the physical shock of the news
It shows the news was not surprising
It says the news made him violent
It suggests the news was pleasant
grade9-english.answer: It conveys the physical shock of the news
acceptableAnswers: It conveys the physical shock of the news
grade9-english.hint: A blow to the chest is sudden, sharp, and physical.
grade9-english.explanation: Comparing the news to a physical blow makes the reader feel the sudden, winding shock it caused. The simile translates an emotional experience into a physical one.

grade9-english.question: A poem uses alliteration: "Dark drops of dread dripped through his dreams." What is the effect?
options: The sounds suggest happiness and joy
The "d" sounds create a light, cheerful mood
The alliteration speeds up the reading
The heavy "d" sounds create a dark, oppressive mood
grade9-english.answer: The heavy "d" sounds create a dark, oppressive mood
acceptableAnswers: The heavy "d" sounds create a dark, oppressive mood
grade9-english.hint: "D" is a hard, heavy consonant — what feeling do repeated heavy sounds create?
grade9-english.explanation: The hard, heavy /d/ sound, repeated across the line, creates a dark, oppressive mood that matches the content — dread dripping through dreams is not light or happy.

grade9-english.question: A writer uses a metaphor: "She was a rock — everyone leaned on her." What is the effect?
options: It suggests she is slow and heavy
It suggests she is hard-working but tired
It suggests she is cold and unfriendly
It suggests she is reliable and unchanging
grade9-english.answer: It suggests she is reliable and unchanging
acceptableAnswers: It suggests she is reliable and unchanging
grade9-english.hint: What qualities do we associate with a rock?
grade9-english.explanation: A rock is stable, solid, and dependable — it does not shift or break. The metaphor conveys that she is a source of strength and reliability for those around her.

grade9-english.question: A poet writes: "The clock ticked its heartless ticking." What is the effect of "heartless"?
options: It suggests the clock is broken
It suggests the clock is stopping
It makes the clock seem warm and comforting
It suggests the clock does not care that time passes
grade9-english.answer: It suggests the clock does not care that time passes
acceptableAnswers: It suggests the clock does not care that time passes
grade9-english.hint: "Heartless" means cruel or without feeling — what does the clock do regardless of human wishes?
grade9-english.explanation: "Heartless" personifies the clock as something that carries on without mercy, unconcerned whether its ticking brings joy or sorrow. It emphasises the indifference of time.

grade9-english.question: A story uses the phrase: "The city never sleeps." What is the effect?
options: It says the city has no night-time
It says the city is full of insomniacs
It suggests constant, non-stop activity at all hours
grade9-english.answer: It suggests constant, non-stop activity at all hours
acceptableAnswers: It suggests constant, non-stop activity at all hours
grade9-english.hint: Only living things sleep — what does it mean that the city does not?
grade9-english.explanation: Personifying the city with the ability to sleep (but refusing to) creates the image of a place that is alive and restless around the clock. It suggests energy and relentless activity.

grade9-english.question: A poem repeats the phrase "We will not forget" at the start of three stanzas. What device is this, and what is its effect?
options: Repetition — it reinforces the theme of memory and determination
Onomatopoeia — the words sound like what they mean
Simile — it compares memory to forgetting
grade9-english.answer: Repetition — it reinforces the theme of memory and determination
acceptableAnswers: Repetition — it reinforces the theme of memory and determination
grade9-english.hint: "At the start of three stanzas" is the key — that is a deliberate structural choice.
grade9-english.explanation: Repeating a phrase at the start of successive stanzas is called anaphora, a form of repetition. It hammers home the resolve not to forget, building emotional momentum.

grade9-english.question: A writer uses onomatopoeia: "The leaves rustled and whispered overhead." What is the effect?
options: It creates a gentle, natural atmosphere
It suggests the leaves are alive and angry
It creates a frightening, violent mood
It makes the scene feel artificial
grade9-english.answer: It creates a gentle, natural atmosphere
acceptableAnswers: It creates a gentle, natural atmosphere
grade9-english.hint: "Rustled" and "whispered" — both soft sounds.
grade9-english.explanation: "Rustled" and "whispered" are soft, gentle onomatopoeic words that create a quiet, peaceful natural atmosphere. The sounds of the words match the sounds of the scene.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "She wore her grief like a coat she could not take off." What does it mean?
options: She dressed in black every day
She felt cold because of her sadness
Her grief was always with her and impossible to escape
She refused to remove her coat in public
grade9-english.answer: Her grief was always with her and impossible to escape
acceptableAnswers: Her grief was always with her and impossible to escape
grade9-english.hint: A coat you cannot take off stays with you everywhere.
grade9-english.explanation: The simile compares grief to a coat that cannot be removed — always present, weighing her down. The line expresses that her sadness was constant and inescapable.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "The years behind him were a closed book." What does it most likely mean?
options: He had made peace with his past and was no longer troubled by it
He had written a book about his past
He had forgotten everything that had happened
He refused to read books about history
grade9-english.answer: He had made peace with his past and was no longer troubled by it
acceptableAnswers: He had made peace with his past and was no longer troubled by it
grade9-english.hint: A closed book has been finished — you do not need to re-read it.
grade9-english.explanation: A "closed book" is one that is done, finished, not being re-examined. The metaphor suggests he has come to terms with his past and moved on.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "Even in silence, her presence filled every room." What does this suggest?
options: She physically occupied a lot of space
She was very loud even when she was trying to be quiet
She had a powerful personality that others felt even without words
She spoke in a very quiet voice
grade9-english.answer: She had a powerful personality that others felt even without words
acceptableAnswers: She had a powerful personality that others felt even without words
grade9-english.hint: "In silence" rules out noise — what else could fill a room?
grade9-english.explanation: The line uses hyperbole and metaphor to convey that her personality and character made itself felt even without any action or speech. "Filled every room" suggests a commanding presence.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line from a war poem: "They gave everything, and no one came to collect the bill."
options: A bill was lost in the post
The soldiers were not paid for their service
The soldiers died without recognition or reward
The country saved money in the war
grade9-english.answer: The soldiers died without recognition or reward
acceptableAnswers: The soldiers died without recognition or reward
grade9-english.hint: "They gave everything" = they died; "collect the bill" = receive recognition.
grade9-english.explanation: "Gave everything" is a metaphor for giving one's life. "No one came to collect the bill" means no one honoured or repaid that sacrifice. The line expresses a sense of forgotten, unrewarded sacrifice.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "He was the last candle in a dark house."
options: He was afraid of the dark
He was the only source of hope or light in a desperate situation
He was the last person to leave
grade9-english.answer: He was the only source of hope or light in a desperate situation
acceptableAnswers: He was the only source of hope or light in a desperate situation
grade9-english.hint: A candle is a small but essential source of light.
grade9-english.explanation: The metaphor equates him with a candle — fragile, small, but essential. "Last candle in a dark house" means he was the only remaining source of hope in a hopeless situation.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "Words are loaded pistols." (Jean-Paul Sartre)
options: Words have power and can cause serious harm when used
Pistols are as useful as words
Words are dangerous only in wartime
grade9-english.answer: Words have power and can cause serious harm when used
acceptableAnswers: Words have power and can cause serious harm when used
grade9-english.hint: A loaded pistol is ready to fire — it can injure or kill.
grade9-english.explanation: The metaphor compares words to loaded weapons: ready for use, and capable of causing great harm. The line argues that language carries power and responsibility — it cannot be called back once fired.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "She built walls around herself so high that no one could reach her."
options: She isolated herself emotionally and refused connection
She moved to a gated community
She built a house with high walls for privacy
grade9-english.answer: She isolated herself emotionally and refused connection
acceptableAnswers: She isolated herself emotionally and refused connection
grade9-english.hint: "Walls" here are emotional barriers, not physical ones.
grade9-english.explanation: "Built walls" is a metaphor for emotional isolation. Very high walls keep others out — the line describes a person who has cut herself off from emotional connection.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line from a nature poem: "The tree held on to its last leaf like a secret."
options: The tree was growing new leaves in winter
The leaf was shaped like a secret note
The tree had only one branch left
Something small and precious was being kept, almost hidden
grade9-english.answer: Something small and precious was being kept, almost hidden
acceptableAnswers: Something small and precious was being kept, almost hidden
grade9-english.hint: A secret is held close and reluctantly shared.
grade9-english.explanation: The simile compares the last leaf to a secret — something precious and privately kept. The tree "holds on" suggests reluctance to let it go, as one holds on to something cherished.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "The empty chair at the table spoke louder than any words."
options: The absence of someone was felt more powerfully than speech
No one sat down for the meal
The family argued very loudly at dinner
grade9-english.answer: The absence of someone was felt more powerfully than speech
acceptableAnswers: The absence of someone was felt more powerfully than speech
grade9-english.hint: An empty chair means someone is missing — and it "spoke", which is personification.
grade9-english.explanation: The personification gives the chair a voice, but what it "says" is an absence — someone who should be there is gone. The line conveys that loss can be felt more keenly than it can be expressed in words.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "Her laugh was the only light in the room."
options: She carried a torch into the room
Her laughter brought joy and warmth to everyone present
She was the only one who was happy
grade9-english.answer: Her laughter brought joy and warmth to everyone present
acceptableAnswers: Her laughter brought joy and warmth to everyone present
grade9-english.hint: Light in a dark room is welcoming and warming.
grade9-english.explanation: The metaphor compares the laugh to light — something that brightens and warms the surrounding environment. Everyone benefited from it, as they would from light in darkness.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "He swallowed his pride and asked for help."
options: He was choking during the conversation
He was very hungry before the meeting
He overcame his reluctance and accepted he needed assistance
He ate food before calling for help
grade9-english.answer: He overcame his reluctance and accepted he needed assistance
acceptableAnswers: He overcame his reluctance and accepted he needed assistance
grade9-english.hint: "Swallowed" something unpleasant — what does that suggest?
grade9-english.explanation: "Swallowed his pride" is an idiom/metaphor meaning he suppressed his ego and admitted vulnerability. The verb "swallowed" implies the pride was hard to push down, like something bitter.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line from a poem about growing up: "Each birthday was a door closing behind me."
options: Birthdays made the poet sad about doors
The poet was afraid of celebrations
The poet always had parties in rooms with many doors
Each year taken away some part of childhood that could not be recovered
grade9-english.answer: Each year taken away some part of childhood that could not be recovered
acceptableAnswers: Each year taken away some part of childhood that could not be recovered
grade9-english.hint: A door closing behind you means you cannot go back through it.
grade9-english.explanation: The metaphor compares each birthday to a closed door — once passed, that stage of life cannot be re-entered. The line expresses the irreversible nature of growing up and the loss of childhood.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "He carried the weight of his family's expectations on his shoulders."
options: He worked as a porter for his family
He felt pressured by what his family wanted him to achieve
His family were physically very heavy
grade9-english.answer: He felt pressured by what his family wanted him to achieve
acceptableAnswers: He felt pressured by what his family wanted him to achieve
grade9-english.hint: "Carried on his shoulders" is a metaphor for a burden.
grade9-english.explanation: "Weight on his shoulders" is a metaphor for emotional or social pressure. Expectations are abstract, but the physical image of carrying weight makes the burden felt.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "The forest swallowed the path, leaving no trace of where we had come from."
options: The travellers deliberately hid the path
The forest was a dangerous place to walk
The vegetation had grown so densely that the path disappeared
grade9-english.answer: The vegetation had grown so densely that the path disappeared
acceptableAnswers: The vegetation had grown so densely that the path disappeared
grade9-english.hint: "Swallowed" means taken in entirely — what happens when a forest swallows something?
grade9-english.explanation: The personification of the forest "swallowing" the path creates the image of vegetation closing in and erasing the route. It also creates a sense of being lost and cut off from the past.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "Hope was a small fire we kept alive through the long night."
options: The poem is set during a power cut
Hope appeared at the end of the night
The campers kept a fire burning for warmth
Hope required constant effort to maintain during a difficult time
grade9-english.answer: Hope required constant effort to maintain during a difficult time
acceptableAnswers: Hope required constant effort to maintain during a difficult time
grade9-english.hint: A fire needs feeding or it goes out — what does that suggest about hope?
grade9-english.explanation: A fire must be tended or it dies — the metaphor suggests that hope in difficult times is fragile and requires active, constant effort to sustain. "Long night" suggests a prolonged period of suffering.

grade9-english.question: Explain the line: "The city was a machine that never rested."
options: The city was built from metal
The city operated continuously, without pause, like a mechanical system
grade9-english.answer: The city operated continuously, without pause, like a mechanical system
acceptableAnswers: The city operated continuously, without pause, like a mechanical system
grade9-english.hint: A machine is designed to work — and this one never rests.
grade9-english.explanation: The metaphor compares the city to a machine — impersonal, driven by function, relentlessly active. "Never rested" reinforces the idea of unstoppable, mechanical activity.

grade9-english.question: Which is the strongest supported statement about the mood of a poem describing an abandoned village?
options: "The poem is about an abandoned village which is sad"
"The poem has a melancholy mood: the phrase 'empty windows stared' personifies the village as hollow and abandoned"
grade9-english.answer: "The poem has a melancholy mood: the phrase 'empty windows stared' personifies the village as hollow and abandoned"
acceptableAnswers: "The poem has a melancholy mood: the phrase 'empty windows stared' personifies the village as hollow and abandoned"
grade9-english.hint: A strong response names the mood, quotes the text, and identifies the technique.
grade9-english.explanation: The best response states the mood, quotes the evidence, and explains the technique. The others assert the mood without any support from the text.

grade9-english.question: A student claims: "The narrator is afraid." Which quotation best supports this?
options: "She had lived there for thirty years"
"My hands shook and I could not turn the handle"
"It was a cold night in November"
grade9-english.answer: "My hands shook and I could not turn the handle"
