grade9-physics.hint: Think about who else has to be able to use it.
grade9-physics.explanation: A method is written so someone else can repeat the work and check the result. That is why measurements, apparatus and order all have to be there.

grade9-physics.question: In which order do the parts of a practical report normally come?
grade9-physics.hint: The report follows the order the work was actually done in.
grade9-physics.explanation: The report follows the investigation: what was asked, what was done, what was measured, what it shows.

grade9-physics.question: Which sentence is written in the style expected of a method?
options: You should raise the ramp to some height
The ramp was raised to a height of 20 cm
I raised my ramp up to about 20 cm high
We think the ramp was around 20 cm high
grade9-physics.answer: The ramp was raised to a height of 20 cm
acceptableAnswers: The ramp was raised to a height of 20 cm
grade9-physics.hint: Reports are impersonal and past tense, and they carry the number.
grade9-physics.explanation: A method reports what was done, not who did it, and states the actual measurement. "About" and "we think" leave the reader unable to repeat it.

grade9-physics.question: What must be included with every numerical result in a report?
options: The make of the instrument used
Its unit, written after the number
The time of day it was taken at
The name of the pupil who took it
grade9-physics.answer: Its unit, written after the number
acceptableAnswers: Its unit, written after the number
grade9-physics.hint: A number on its own does not say how much.
grade9-physics.explanation: "3" could be 3 m/s, 3 A or 3 s. Without the unit the reading means nothing and the mark is lost.

grade9-physics.question: How should the apparatus be shown in a physics report?
options: As a list of the items with their prices
As a paragraph naming each item in turn
As a photograph taken from the front
As a labelled diagram drawn with a ruler
grade9-physics.answer: As a labelled diagram drawn with a ruler
acceptableAnswers: As a labelled diagram drawn with a ruler
grade9-physics.hint: How does the exam paper itself show a set-up?
grade9-physics.explanation: A labelled line diagram shows how the parts were arranged in a way words cannot, and it is how every paper prints an experiment.

grade9-physics.question: A pupil found one anomalous reading. What should the report say about it?
options: That the apparatus must have been faulty
That it was found, and how it was dealt with
Nothing at all, because it was left out
That the experiment did not work at all
grade9-physics.answer: That it was found, and how it was dealt with
acceptableAnswers: That it was found, and how it was dealt with
grade9-physics.hint: A reader should be able to see the judgement that was made.
grade9-physics.explanation: The report names the anomaly, says it was repeated and excluded from the mean, and gives the reason. Silence hides a decision that affected the result.

grade9-physics.question: What belongs in the evaluation at the end of a report?
options: The list of every result that was measured
The names of everyone who was in the group
The aim of the whole investigation again
The errors met and how to improve the method
grade9-physics.answer: The errors met and how to improve the method
acceptableAnswers: The errors met and how to improve the method
grade9-physics.hint: It is the part that looks back at how well the work was done.
grade9-physics.explanation: An evaluation judges the quality of the evidence: what limited the accuracy, which readings were doubtful, and what would be done differently.

grade9-physics.question: Why should a graph in a report always carry a title and labelled axes?
options: So the points can be plotted much more quickly
So the graph fills more of the page than before
So the line can be drawn without using a ruler
So a reader knows what is plotted against what
grade9-physics.answer: So a reader knows what is plotted against what
acceptableAnswers: So a reader knows what is plotted against what
grade9-physics.hint: Imagine the graph on its own, away from the report.
grade9-physics.explanation: A graph should make sense on its own. Labels with units, and a title, tell a reader what the two quantities are and how they were measured.

grade9-physics.question: A pupil presents results to the class. Which is the most useful way to show the pattern?
options: A graph projected so everyone can see it
A description of the apparatus in words
A copy of the notes passed round slowly
A long list of readings read out aloud
grade9-physics.answer: A graph projected so everyone can see it
acceptableAnswers: A graph projected so everyone can see it
grade9-physics.hint: What shows a trend in a single glance?
grade9-physics.explanation: A graph shows the trend at once; a spoken list of numbers cannot be followed, and the apparatus is not the finding.

grade9-physics.question: Why should a report state the number of repeats that were taken?
options: It proves that the prediction had been right
It shows how long the practical lesson lasted
It fills out the method section of the report
It lets a reader judge how reliable the mean is
grade9-physics.answer: It lets a reader judge how reliable the mean is
acceptableAnswers: It lets a reader judge how reliable the mean is
grade9-physics.hint: A mean of two readings and a mean of five are not equally trustworthy.
grade9-physics.explanation: Knowing there were three repeats, and how closely they agreed, tells a reader how much confidence the mean deserves.

grade9-physics.question: Which conclusion is written well?
options: Speed rose from 1.4 to 3.2 m/s as height rose
The trolley went a lot faster down the ramp
The experiment worked and the results are good
The prediction that was made turned out right
grade9-physics.answer: Speed rose from 1.4 to 3.2 m/s as height rose
acceptableAnswers: Speed rose from 1.4 to 3.2 m/s as height rose
grade9-physics.hint: A conclusion carries the numbers, not just a direction.
grade9-physics.explanation: A good conclusion names the quantities, gives the figures with units and states the pattern. The others could describe almost any experiment.

grade9-physics.question: A pupil uses a spreadsheet to present the results. What is the main advantage?
options: The results are certain to be free of error
The graph is redrawn whenever a value changes
The spreadsheet works out the conclusion too
The readings do not have to be written down
grade9-physics.answer: The graph is redrawn whenever a value changes
acceptableAnswers: The graph is redrawn whenever a value changes
grade9-physics.hint: Think about what happens when one reading is corrected.
grade9-physics.explanation: A spreadsheet recalculates means and redraws the chart when a figure is corrected. It cannot decide what the results mean, and it cannot make a wrong reading right.

grade9-physics.question: Why should the source of any information copied into a report be given?
options: So the report is a little longer than before
So the teacher knows a book was opened
So the words do not have to be understood
So a reader can check where it came from
grade9-physics.answer: So a reader can check where it came from
acceptableAnswers: So a reader can check where it came from
grade9-physics.hint: It is the same reason a result needs a method.
grade9-physics.explanation: Naming the book or site lets a reader judge how trustworthy the claim is and find it again. Using someone else’s words as your own is not honest reporting.

grade9-physics.question: What should the title of a practical report tell a reader?
options: Which class carried out the practical
How many pupils were in the group
What was investigated in the practical
How long the whole practical lasted
grade9-physics.answer: What was investigated in the practical
acceptableAnswers: What was investigated in the practical
grade9-physics.hint: A title names the investigation, not the lesson.
grade9-physics.explanation: "How the height of a ramp affects the speed of a trolley" names both variables. "Physics practical 3" names nothing at all.

grade9-physics.question: A pupil is asked to report results to the class in two minutes. What should be left out?
options: The main conclusion that was drawn
The pattern that the results showed
The one anomaly that was found
Every individual reading from the table
grade9-physics.answer: Every individual reading from the table
acceptableAnswers: Every individual reading from the table
grade9-physics.hint: Two minutes is enough for the finding, not for the raw data.
grade9-physics.explanation: A short talk gives the aim, the pattern, the conclusion and any anomaly. Reading out forty numbers uses the time and communicates nothing.

grade9-physics.question: Why should a report avoid the word "it" when several things have been mentioned?
options: It makes the report look far too casual
A reader cannot tell which thing is meant
The word cannot be used in the past tense
The word is too short for a science report
grade9-physics.answer: A reader cannot tell which thing is meant
acceptableAnswers: A reader cannot tell which thing is meant
grade9-physics.hint: Think of "the trolley, the ramp and the timer — it was moved".
grade9-physics.explanation: Reports name things: "the trolley was released", not "it was released". Ambiguity in a method makes it impossible to repeat exactly.

grade9-physics.question: Two pupils get different results from the same experiment. What should each report do?
options: Choose whichever result looks the neater
Agree on one set of readings to write up
Leave the difference out of both reports
State the results honestly and compare methods
grade9-physics.answer: State the results honestly and compare methods
acceptableAnswers: State the results honestly and compare methods
grade9-physics.hint: The difference itself is evidence about the method.
grade9-physics.explanation: A disagreement points at something in the method — a different timing technique, a zero error. Reporting both and comparing is what finds it.

grade9-physics.question: Which of these belongs in the results section?
options: The list of apparatus set up on the bench
The reason the pattern came out that way
The prediction made before the experiment
The table of readings and the mean values
grade9-physics.answer: The table of readings and the mean values
acceptableAnswers: The table of readings and the mean values
grade9-physics.hint: Results are what the instruments said, and nothing else.
grade9-physics.explanation: The results section carries the table, the means and the graph. Predictions belong at the start and explanations belong in the conclusion.

grade9-physics.question: Why is a practical report normally written soon after the lesson?
options: The teacher will not accept it any later
The details are still remembered accurately
The apparatus is still out on the bench
The graph paper is easier to get hold of
grade9-physics.answer: The details are still remembered accurately
acceptableAnswers: The details are still remembered accurately
grade9-physics.hint: Which part of the report suffers most from a week’s delay?
grade9-physics.explanation: Small details of the method — the order, the settings, an odd reading — fade quickly, and they are exactly what makes a report repeatable.

grade9-physics.question: Name the variable that is deliberately changed in an investigation.
grade9-physics.hint: It is the one the pupil chooses.
grade9-physics.explanation: The independent variable is the one changed on purpose — the ramp height, the pendulum length, the number of cells.

grade9-physics.question: Name the variable that is measured in an investigation.
grade9-physics.hint: Its value depends on the one that was changed.
grade9-physics.explanation: The dependent variable is measured each time — the speed, the swing time, the current on the ammeter.

grade9-physics.question: Give the name for a variable that is kept the same throughout a fair test.
grade9-physics.hint: Keeping it the same is what makes the test fair.
grade9-physics.explanation: A controlled variable is held constant so that only one thing can explain the change in the measurement.

grade9-physics.question: What name is given to a testable statement made before an investigation?
grade9-physics.hint: One word, and it comes before the readings.
grade9-physics.explanation: A hypothesis is a prediction the experiment can support or contradict, written before any measurement is taken.

grade9-physics.question: Apart from the quantity, what else must a column heading in a results table give?
grade9-physics.hint: Think of "Current / A" and what the letter A is.
grade9-physics.explanation: A heading gives the quantity and its unit, written once, as in Time / s or Height / cm.

grade9-physics.question: Name the type of graph drawn when both quantities are measured on continuous scales.
grade9-physics.hint: Not the kind with separate bars.
grade9-physics.explanation: A line graph is used when both quantities vary continuously, such as current against voltage. Bar charts are for separate categories.

grade9-physics.question: Give the word for a result that does not fit the pattern of the others.
grade9-physics.hint: It is repeated and then left out of the mean.
grade9-physics.explanation: An anomalous result breaks the trend. It is recorded, repeated if possible, and excluded from the mean.

grade9-physics.question: State what the area under a speed–time graph represents.
grade9-physics.hint: Multiply a speed by a time and look at the unit.
grade9-physics.explanation: Speed × time gives the distance travelled, and that product is the area beneath the line.

grade9-physics.question: What is the SI unit of length?
grade9-physics.hint: The SI unit is the base one, not a multiple of it.
grade9-physics.explanation: The SI unit of length is the metre (m); centimetres and kilometres are multiples of it.

grade9-physics.question: What is the SI unit of mass?
grade9-physics.hint: It is the only base unit here with a prefix built in.
grade9-physics.explanation: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).

grade9-physics.question: What is the SI unit of time?
grade9-physics.hint: The base unit, not a multiple of it.
grade9-physics.explanation: The SI unit of time is the second (s).

grade9-physics.question: Which unit is used for volume in a school laboratory?
grade9-physics.hint: Volume is a measurement in three directions.
grade9-physics.explanation: Volume is measured in cubic centimetres (cm³); a square centimetre is an area and a centimetre is a length.

grade9-physics.question: Which quantity is measured in degrees Celsius?
grade9-physics.hint: It is read from a thermometer.
grade9-physics.explanation: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius in the laboratory (the SI unit is the kelvin).

grade9-physics.question: Which instrument is used to measure the volume of a liquid?
grade9-physics.hint: It is graduated in cubic centimetres.
grade9-physics.explanation: A measuring cylinder is graduated in cm³ and is used to measure the volume of a liquid.

grade9-physics.question: Which instrument is used to measure mass?
grade9-physics.hint: It compares or weighs the amount of matter.
grade9-physics.explanation: Mass is measured with a balance.

grade9-physics.question: Which instrument is used to measure a short interval of time?
grade9-physics.hint: It is started and stopped by hand.
grade9-physics.explanation: A stopwatch measures the time taken by an event.

grade9-physics.question: Which instrument would you choose to measure the thickness of a single sheet of paper most accurately?
grade9-physics.hint: The measurement is far smaller than one millimetre.
grade9-physics.explanation: A micrometer measures to a hundredth of a millimetre, which a metre rule cannot approach.

grade9-physics.question: How is the volume of a small stone found with a measuring cylinder?
options: By timing how long the stone takes to sink to the bottom
By the rise in the water level when the stone is lowered in
By measuring the stone from end to end with a ruler
By weighing the stone carefully on an accurate balance
grade9-physics.answer: By the rise in the water level when the stone is lowered in
acceptableAnswers: By the rise in the water level when the stone is lowered in
grade9-physics.hint: The stone pushes the water up.
grade9-physics.explanation: The stone displaces its own volume of water, so the rise in the level is the volume of the stone.

grade9-physics.question: Read the measuring cylinder shown. What is the volume of the liquid?
grade9-physics.hint: Read the mark at the bottom of the curved surface.
grade9-physics.explanation: The bottom of the meniscus sits on the 30 mark, so the volume is 30 cm³.

grade9-physics.question: Read the measuring cylinder shown. What is the volume of the liquid?
grade9-physics.hint: The small marks are every 5 cm³.
grade9-physics.explanation: The level is halfway between 20 and 30, on the 25 mark, so the volume is 25 cm³.

grade9-physics.question: Read the ruler shown. How long is the grey object?
grade9-physics.hint: Subtract the reading at one end from the reading at the other.
grade9-physics.explanation: The object runs from the 2 cm mark to the 7 cm mark, so its length is 7 - 2 = 5 cm.

grade9-physics.question: Read the ruler shown. How long is the grey object?
grade9-physics.hint: The small marks are every half centimetre.
grade9-physics.explanation: The object runs from 1 cm to 4.5 cm, so its length is 4.5 - 1 = 3.5 cm.

grade9-physics.question: Which instrument gives the more accurate measurement of a length of about 4 cm?
options: A metre rule marked in decimetres
A ruler marked in centimetres only
grade9-physics.hint: Smaller divisions give a more precise reading.
grade9-physics.explanation: The smaller the smallest division, the more precisely the length can be read - millimetre marks beat centimetre marks.

grade9-physics.question: Why is a measuring cylinder better than a beaker for measuring a volume?
options: It holds a much larger volume of liquid
It is made of a stronger glass
It can be heated more safely
Its scale has much smaller divisions
grade9-physics.answer: Its scale has much smaller divisions
acceptableAnswers: Its scale has much smaller divisions
grade9-physics.hint: Compare the two scales, not the two shapes.
grade9-physics.explanation: A beaker is marked roughly; a measuring cylinder has a fine scale, so the reading is far more accurate.

grade9-physics.question: A pupil measures the thickness of one page by measuring 100 pages and dividing by 100. Why?
options: One page is too thin for the ruler to measure accurately
It makes the answer a whole number
A ruler cannot measure paper at all
The pages become thicker when they are stacked up
grade9-physics.answer: One page is too thin for the ruler to measure accurately
acceptableAnswers: One page is too thin for the ruler to measure accurately
grade9-physics.hint: Think about the smallest division on the ruler.
grade9-physics.explanation: A single page is far thinner than the smallest division, so many are measured together and the total divided.

grade9-physics.question: In the figure the eye is placed as shown when the scale is read. What error does this cause?
options: An error in the units used
grade9-physics.hint: Look at where the eye is compared with the liquid level.
grade9-physics.explanation: The eye is not level with the mark, so the line of sight meets the scale at an angle and the reading is wrong - a parallax error.

grade9-physics.question: In the figure the eye is placed as shown when the scale is read. Is the reading affected?
options: Yes, because the eye is below the mark
Yes, because the eye is too close to the scale
No, because the eye is level with the mark
Yes, because the eye is above the mark
grade9-physics.answer: No, because the eye is level with the mark
acceptableAnswers: No, because the eye is level with the mark
grade9-physics.hint: Look at where the eye is compared with the liquid level.
grade9-physics.explanation: The eye is level with the mark being read, so there is no parallax error.

grade9-physics.question: How is a parallax error avoided?
options: By placing the eye level with the mark being read
By using a much larger measuring cylinder
grade9-physics.answer: By placing the eye level with the mark being read
acceptableAnswers: By placing the eye level with the mark being read
grade9-physics.hint: It is about where the eye is.
grade9-physics.explanation: A parallax error is avoided by looking at the scale square-on, with the eye level with the mark.

grade9-physics.question: A balance reads 0.4 g when there is nothing on it. What kind of error is this?
options: An error in the choice of unit
grade9-physics.hint: The instrument does not start at zero.
grade9-physics.explanation: An instrument that does not read zero when it should has a zero error, and every reading is out by that amount.

grade9-physics.question: A balance shows 0.4 g when empty. An object placed on it reads 12.7 g. What is the true mass?
grade9-physics.hint: Take the zero error off the reading.
grade9-physics.explanation: The zero error of +0.4 g must be subtracted: 12.7 - 0.4 = 12.3 g.

grade9-physics.question: Read the measuring cylinder shown. State the volume of the liquid, in cm³.
grade9-physics.hint: Read the mark at the bottom of the curved surface.
grade9-physics.explanation: The bottom of the meniscus is on the 40 mark, so the volume is 40 cm³.

grade9-physics.question: Read the ruler shown. State the length of the grey object, in cm.
grade9-physics.hint: Subtract the reading at one end from the reading at the other.
grade9-physics.explanation: The object runs from 3 cm to 8 cm, so it is 8 - 3 = 5 cm long.

grade9-physics.question: A stone is lowered into a measuring cylinder. The water level rises from 20 cm³ to 32 cm³. Calculate the volume of the stone, in cm³.
grade9-physics.hint: The stone pushes aside its own volume of water.

grade9-physics.question: A balance reads 0.2 g when empty. A sample reads 8.9 g on it. Calculate the true mass, in grams.
grade9-physics.hint: Subtract the zero error.

grade9-physics.question: 100 identical sheets of paper form a stack 12 mm thick. Calculate the thickness of one sheet, in mm.
grade9-physics.hint: Divide the total by the number of sheets.

grade9-physics.question: Give the SI unit of length.
grade9-physics.hint: Not the centimetre.
grade9-physics.explanation: The SI unit of length is the metre.

grade9-physics.question: Give the SI unit of mass.
grade9-physics.hint: Not the gram.
grade9-physics.explanation: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram.

grade9-physics.question: Name the error caused by reading a scale with the eye not level with the mark.
grade9-physics.hint: Two words.
grade9-physics.explanation: Reading a scale from an angle gives a parallax error.

grade9-physics.question: Name the error present when an instrument does not read zero before it is used.
grade9-physics.hint: Two words.
grade9-physics.explanation: A zero error offsets every reading the instrument gives.

grade9-physics.question: Name the instrument used to measure the volume of a liquid.
grade9-physics.hint: It is graduated in cm³.
grade9-physics.explanation: A measuring cylinder measures the volume of a liquid.

grade9-physics.question: How many centimetres are there in one metre?
grade9-physics.hint: The prefix centi- means one hundredth.
grade9-physics.explanation: One metre = 100 centimetres.

grade9-physics.question: How many grams are there in one kilogram?
grade9-physics.hint: The prefix kilo- means one thousand.
grade9-physics.explanation: One kilogram = 1 000 grams.

grade9-physics.question: A bench is 1.5 m long. What is this length in centimetres?
grade9-physics.hint: Multiply by 100 to convert metres to centimetres.

grade9-physics.question: A bag of rice has a mass of 2 500 g. What is this mass in kilograms?
grade9-physics.hint: Divide by 1 000 to convert grams to kilograms.

grade9-physics.question: Which is the correct symbol for the SI unit of mass?
grade9-physics.hint: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram.
grade9-physics.explanation: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram, symbol kg.

grade9-physics.question: What is the SI unit of temperature used in scientific work?
grade9-physics.hint: This unit is named after a Scottish physicist.
grade9-physics.explanation: The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K), though laboratory work commonly uses degrees Celsius.

grade9-physics.question: A stopwatch shows 3 minutes and 20 seconds. What is this time in seconds only?
grade9-physics.hint: 1 minute = 60 seconds.

grade9-physics.question: 45 mm is equal to which of these?
grade9-physics.hint: Divide by 10 to convert mm to cm.
grade9-physics.explanation: 45 ÷ 10 = 4.5 cm.

grade9-physics.question: A distance is measured as 3.6 km. What is this distance in metres?
grade9-physics.hint: Multiply by 1 000 to convert km to m.

grade9-physics.question: Which row correctly matches each quantity with its SI unit?
options: Length → cm, Mass → g, Time → min
Length → km, Mass → mg, Time → s
Length → m, Mass → kg, Time → s
Length → m, Mass → g, Time → s
grade9-physics.answer: Length → m, Mass → kg, Time → s
acceptableAnswers: Length → m, Mass → kg, Time → s
grade9-physics.hint: All three must be the base SI units.
grade9-physics.explanation: The SI base units are the metre (m), kilogram (kg) and second (s).

grade9-physics.question: How many millimetres are there in 5 cm?
grade9-physics.hint: Multiply by 10 to convert cm to mm.
grade9-physics.explanation: 5 × 10 = 50 mm.

grade9-physics.question: A wire has a diameter of 0.05 cm. What is this diameter in millimetres?
grade9-physics.hint: Multiply by 10 to convert cm to mm.

grade9-physics.question: Which instrument measures the temperature of a liquid?
grade9-physics.hint: Temperature is measured in degrees.
grade9-physics.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius.

grade9-physics.question: Which two instruments are needed to measure the mass and the volume of a liquid sample?
options: A thermometer and a measuring cylinder
A balance and a measuring cylinder
grade9-physics.answer: A balance and a measuring cylinder
acceptableAnswers: A balance and a measuring cylinder
grade9-physics.hint: You need one instrument for mass and one for volume.
grade9-physics.explanation: A balance measures mass; a measuring cylinder measures volume of a liquid.

grade9-physics.question: A vernier calliper can measure external diameters to which precision?
grade9-physics.hint: A vernier scale divides the millimetre into ten parts.
grade9-physics.explanation: A vernier calliper reads to 0.1 mm, which is ten times finer than a standard millimetre ruler.

grade9-physics.question: The smallest division on a measuring cylinder is 2 cm³. What is the smallest volume it can read reliably?
grade9-physics.hint: The smallest division sets the smallest readable quantity.
grade9-physics.explanation: You can read directly to the nearest division, which here is 2 cm³.

grade9-physics.question: A stone is added to a measuring cylinder that holds 20 cm³ of water. The level rises to 34 cm³. What is the volume of the stone?
grade9-physics.hint: The stone displaces its own volume of water.

grade9-physics.question: Which instrument is best for measuring the external diameter of a cylindrical rod?
grade9-physics.hint: It grips the object between its jaws.
grade9-physics.explanation: A vernier calliper grips the rod and gives its diameter to 0.1 mm.

grade9-physics.question: A student measures a 1.46 m table with a 100 cm ruler in one placement. What is the problem?
options: A ruler cannot be used horizontally
The ruler is shorter than the table, so it must be repositioned, adding error at each join
The ruler can only measure to the nearest centimetre
Metres cannot be measured with a centimetre ruler
grade9-physics.answer: The ruler is shorter than the table, so it must be repositioned, adding error at each join
acceptableAnswers: The ruler is shorter than the table, so it must be repositioned, adding error at each join
grade9-physics.hint: Compare the length of the ruler with the length to be measured.
grade9-physics.explanation: A 100 cm ruler covers only 1 m; measuring 1.46 m requires repositioning, which introduces additional error.

grade9-physics.question: Where on the meniscus should a student read the volume in a measuring cylinder?
options: At the top of the curved surface
At the bottom of the curved surface
At the midpoint of the liquid from outside
grade9-physics.answer: At the bottom of the curved surface
acceptableAnswers: At the bottom of the curved surface
grade9-physics.hint: Water curves downward in glass.
grade9-physics.explanation: The correct reading is at the lowest point of the meniscus, which is the bottom of the curve.

grade9-physics.question: Which instrument measures how long a race takes?
grade9-physics.hint: A race is a time interval.
grade9-physics.explanation: A stopwatch measures time intervals in seconds.

grade9-physics.question: A pebble is placed in a measuring cylinder. The water rises from 24 cm³ to 30 cm³. What is the volume of the pebble?
grade9-physics.hint: Subtract the first reading from the second.

grade9-physics.question: Why is a beaker not suitable for accurate volume measurements?
options: Its scale markings are too far apart for precision
It has no scale at all
It must not be used with hot liquids
grade9-physics.answer: Its scale markings are too far apart for precision
acceptableAnswers: Its scale markings are too far apart for precision
grade9-physics.hint: Compare the divisions on a beaker with those on a measuring cylinder.
grade9-physics.explanation: A beaker is marked roughly; a measuring cylinder has a much finer scale.

grade9-physics.question: A solid block cannot be dissolved. How would you find its volume in the laboratory?
options: Measure one edge and cube the result
Float it in a bowl and see how much it sinks
Submerge it in a measuring cylinder and read the rise in water level
Weigh it on a balance and divide by the density of water
grade9-physics.answer: Submerge it in a measuring cylinder and read the rise in water level
acceptableAnswers: Submerge it in a measuring cylinder and read the rise in water level
grade9-physics.hint: Any solid displaces its own volume of water.
grade9-physics.explanation: The rise in water level equals the volume of the solid, whatever its shape.

grade9-physics.question: Which thermometer gives the most precise reading near 37 °C?
grade9-physics.hint: Smaller divisions mean a more precise reading.
grade9-physics.explanation: A thermometer with 0.1 °C divisions gives ten times more detail than one with 1 °C divisions.

grade9-physics.question: One balance reads to the nearest 1 g; another reads to the nearest 0.1 g. Which has greater precision?
options: It depends on the mass being measured
grade9-physics.hint: Precision is set by the size of the smallest division.
grade9-physics.explanation: Smaller divisions give a finer reading and therefore greater precision.

grade9-physics.question: Student A uses a ruler marked every mm; Student B uses a ruler marked every 5 mm. Whose result is more precise?
grade9-physics.hint: Which scale can you read more finely?
grade9-physics.explanation: Student A’s ruler has smaller divisions, giving a more precise reading.

grade9-physics.question: A micrometer reads to 0.01 mm; a ruler reads to 1 mm. Which is more accurate?
grade9-physics.hint: Compare the smallest measurable quantity.
grade9-physics.explanation: The micrometer measures to 0.01 mm, which is 100 times finer than a ruler.

grade9-physics.question: A student measures a rod five times and gets: 12.3, 12.4, 12.3, 12.4, 12.3 cm. Which statement best describes these results?
options: Precise but may not be accurate
grade9-physics.answer: Precise but may not be accurate
acceptableAnswers: Precise but may not be accurate
grade9-physics.hint: Precision means the readings cluster together; accuracy means they are near the true value.
grade9-physics.explanation: The readings are consistent (precise) but without the true value we cannot confirm accuracy.

grade9-physics.question: Which instrument gives the most accurate reading of a mass near 500 g?
options: A digital balance reading to 0.01 g
A kitchen scale reading to 5 g
A spring balance reading to 10 g
A bathroom scale reading to 100 g
grade9-physics.answer: A digital balance reading to 0.01 g
acceptableAnswers: A digital balance reading to 0.01 g
grade9-physics.hint: Smaller divisions and a digital readout reduce reading error.
grade9-physics.explanation: A digital balance reading to 0.01 g has the finest resolution for this mass.

grade9-physics.question: A measuring cylinder is graduated every 2 cm³. To what precision can a careful student record a reading?
options: To the nearest 1 cm³ (by estimating between graduations)
grade9-physics.answer: To the nearest 1 cm³ (by estimating between graduations)
acceptableAnswers: To the nearest 1 cm³ (by estimating between graduations)
grade9-physics.hint: You can read the division; an experienced student estimates half a division.
grade9-physics.explanation: The scale reads to 2 cm³; a careful student can estimate to the nearest 1 cm³ but no finer.

grade9-physics.question: A ruler is marked at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 cm only. What is the maximum length it can measure in one placement?
grade9-physics.hint: The last mark gives the maximum range.
grade9-physics.explanation: The ruler extends to 20 cm, which is its maximum range in one placement.

grade9-physics.question: A student measures the boiling point of water three times: 99.1 °C, 99.0 °C, 99.2 °C. The true boiling point is 100.0 °C. Which statement best describes the measurements?
grade9-physics.hint: The readings cluster closely (precise) but are all about 1 °C below 100 °C (not accurate).
grade9-physics.explanation: The three readings agree well with each other (precise) but are consistently below the true value (not accurate).

grade9-physics.question: Why do scientists prefer digital instruments to analogue ones for reading a value?
options: Digital instruments do not require a power supply
Digital instruments are physically more accurate in all cases
Digital instruments cannot have a zero error
Digital instruments eliminate the reading error from scale interpolation
grade9-physics.answer: Digital instruments eliminate the reading error from scale interpolation
acceptableAnswers: Digital instruments eliminate the reading error from scale interpolation
grade9-physics.hint: Think about how the value is displayed.
grade9-physics.explanation: A digital display shows a number directly, removing the uncertainty of reading between scale divisions.

grade9-physics.question: A student measures the same mass three times and gets 45.2 g, 52.1 g and 38.9 g. What problem do these results reveal?
options: Poor repeatability — the readings are very scattered
The balance has a zero error
grade9-physics.answer: Poor repeatability — the readings are very scattered
acceptableAnswers: Poor repeatability — the readings are very scattered
grade9-physics.hint: Consistent measurements cluster together; a range of over 13 g is far too large.
grade9-physics.explanation: Good precision requires repeated readings to agree closely; these differ by more than 13 g.

grade9-physics.question: A 100 g standard mass is weighed on a balance. The reading is 102 g every time. What type of error is present?
options: A random error (the balance gives different readings each time)
A systematic error (the balance reads consistently too high)
No error — the mass has changed
A parallax error in reading the pointer
grade9-physics.answer: A systematic error (the balance reads consistently too high)
acceptableAnswers: A systematic error (the balance reads consistently too high)
grade9-physics.hint: It reads the same wrong value every time.
grade9-physics.explanation: A consistent offset in all readings is a systematic error; this is what a zero error produces.

grade9-physics.question: A student reads the volume on a measuring cylinder from above the liquid level. Will the reading be too high or too low?
grade9-physics.hint: Looking down from above shifts the apparent level upward.
grade9-physics.explanation: Looking from above makes the line of sight cut the scale higher than the actual meniscus level, giving a reading that is too high.

grade9-physics.question: A student reads the volume on a measuring cylinder from below the liquid level. Will the reading be too high or too low?
grade9-physics.hint: Looking from below shifts the apparent level downward.
grade9-physics.explanation: Looking from below makes the meniscus appear lower than it is, giving a reading that is too low.

grade9-physics.question: How can a student check whether a balance has a zero error?
options: Weigh a known standard mass and compare
Read the balance before placing anything on it
Reset the balance after every reading
Use a different balance each time
grade9-physics.answer: Read the balance before placing anything on it
acceptableAnswers: Read the balance before placing anything on it
grade9-physics.hint: The simplest check is to look at the reading before use.
grade9-physics.explanation: If the balance reads a non-zero value when empty, it has a zero error.

grade9-physics.question: A ruler has its zero mark 2 mm from the end. A student always places the end of the ruler at one edge of the object. Will measurements be too long or too short?
grade9-physics.hint: The real zero is 2 mm into the ruler, so every reading includes 2 mm of ruler before the object.
grade9-physics.explanation: Each reading includes the 2 mm before the zero mark, so the measured length is 2 mm greater than the true length.

grade9-physics.question: Which type of error affects every reading in the same direction and cannot be reduced by averaging?
grade9-physics.hint: It shifts all readings the same way.
grade9-physics.explanation: A systematic error biases every reading by the same amount; more readings do not cancel it.

grade9-physics.question: Which type of error can be reduced by repeating the measurement and averaging several results?
grade9-physics.hint: Random errors are scattered above and below the true value.
grade9-physics.explanation: Random errors are equally likely to be above or below the true value, so averaging several readings reduces their effect.

grade9-physics.question: A balance reads −0.3 g when empty (the pointer is 0.3 g below zero). An object reads 15.4 g. What is the true mass?
grade9-physics.hint: The balance reads 0.3 g too low, so add 0.3 g to correct.
grade9-physics.explanation: The zero error is −0.3 g (reads low), so true mass = 15.4 + 0.3 = 15.7 g.

grade9-physics.question: A thermometer records 38.2 °C, but later it is found to have a zero error of +0.5 °C. What was the true temperature?
grade9-physics.hint: Subtract the zero error from the reading.
grade9-physics.explanation: The thermometer reads 0.5 °C too high, so true temperature = 38.2 − 0.5 = 37.7 °C.

grade9-physics.question: What is the most common mistake when using a ruler to measure an object?
options: Pressing the ruler against the object
Not aligning the zero mark with one edge of the object
grade9-physics.answer: Not aligning the zero mark with one edge of the object
acceptableAnswers: Not aligning the zero mark with one edge of the object
grade9-physics.hint: The zero mark must start at one edge.
grade9-physics.explanation: If the zero mark is not at the edge, the reading includes a portion of ruler before the object, giving a wrong length.

grade9-physics.question: Two students measure the same string: Student A records 23.5 cm and Student B records 23.6 cm. What type of error is the 0.1 cm difference?
grade9-physics.hint: Small, unpredictable differences between independent readings are random.
grade9-physics.explanation: Random errors vary between measurements and are not consistently in one direction.

grade9-physics.question: A worn metre rule’s first readable mark is at 1 cm. A student measures from this mark and reads 17 cm. They record 17 cm. What is the actual length?
grade9-physics.hint: Subtract the starting position from the final reading.
grade9-physics.explanation: The object runs from 1 cm to 17 cm, so its length = 17 − 1 = 16 cm.

grade9-physics.question: Which of these is a luminous object?
grade9-physics.hint: A luminous object makes its own light.
grade9-physics.explanation: The Sun produces its own light, so it is luminous. The others are seen only by reflecting light.

grade9-physics.question: Which of these is a non-luminous object?
grade9-physics.hint: A non-luminous object only reflects light from elsewhere.
grade9-physics.explanation: The Moon makes no light of its own; we see it because it reflects sunlight.

grade9-physics.question: Why can a planet be seen from Earth even though it produces no light?
options: It produces its own light after all
It is heated by the Earth
It glows because it is very cold
It reflects light from the Sun
grade9-physics.answer: It reflects light from the Sun
acceptableAnswers: It reflects light from the Sun
grade9-physics.hint: Where does the light reaching us come from?
grade9-physics.explanation: Planets are non-luminous: they are visible because sunlight falls on them and is reflected to us.

grade9-physics.question: What has to happen before an object can be seen?
options: The object must be warmer than the air
The eye must send out light towards the object
The object must be making a sound
Light from the object must enter the eye
grade9-physics.answer: Light from the object must enter the eye
acceptableAnswers: Light from the object must enter the eye
grade9-physics.hint: Which way does the light travel?
grade9-physics.explanation: We see an object when light from it - made by it or reflected off it - enters the eye.

grade9-physics.question: Why can nothing be seen in a completely dark room?
options: The air becomes too cold to see through
The eye stops working in the dark
Objects disappear when it is dark
There is no light to enter the eye
grade9-physics.answer: There is no light to enter the eye
acceptableAnswers: There is no light to enter the eye
grade9-physics.hint: Seeing needs light reaching the eye.
grade9-physics.explanation: With no light in the room there is none to reflect off the objects into the eye, so nothing can be seen.

grade9-physics.question: Which of these gives out its own light?
grade9-physics.hint: Only one of these is luminous.
grade9-physics.explanation: A star produces its own light; planets, moons and clouds are seen by reflected light.

grade9-physics.question: The light from the lamp reaches the screen through the small hole, as shown. What does this demonstrate?
options: Light bends round the edges of the card
Light travels faster through a hole
Light is absorbed by the card
grade9-physics.hint: Look at the path drawn from the lamp to the screen.
grade9-physics.explanation: The light only reaches the screen along a straight path through the hole, which shows that light travels in straight lines.

grade9-physics.question: In the arrangement shown, the card is moved sideways so the hole is no longer in line with the lamp and the screen. What happens?
options: The light bends round the card and still reaches the screen
The screen becomes a great deal brighter than before
The screen goes dark, because the straight path is blocked
grade9-physics.answer: The screen goes dark, because the straight path is blocked
acceptableAnswers: The screen goes dark, because the straight path is blocked
grade9-physics.hint: Light cannot turn a corner on its own.
grade9-physics.explanation: Because light travels in straight lines, moving the hole out of line blocks the only path to the screen.

grade9-physics.question: A shadow forms behind an object placed in front of a lamp. What does the sharp edge of the shadow show?
options: Light changes colour at the edge
Light is reflected by the object
Light passes straight through the object
grade9-physics.hint: Think about why the edge is sharp rather than blurred.
grade9-physics.explanation: A sharp-edged shadow is formed because the light is blocked along straight paths from the source.

grade9-physics.question: What happens to light when it is reflected?
options: It is absorbed by the surface
grade9-physics.hint: Think about what a mirror does.
grade9-physics.explanation: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface rather than being absorbed or passing through.

grade9-physics.question: Why does a smooth mirror give a clear image while a sheet of white paper does not?
options: The mirror absorbs far more of the light than the paper does
The paper reflects no light at all, so no image can form
The mirror makes light of its own, while the paper does not
The mirror reflects the rays in one direction; the paper scatters them
grade9-physics.answer: The mirror reflects the rays in one direction; the paper scatters them
acceptableAnswers: The mirror reflects the rays in one direction; the paper scatters them
grade9-physics.hint: Think about what a rough surface does to parallel rays.
grade9-physics.explanation: A smooth surface reflects parallel rays together, forming an image; a rough surface scatters them in all directions.

grade9-physics.question: In the figure, which letter marks the incident ray?
grade9-physics.hint: The incident ray is the one arriving at the mirror.
grade9-physics.explanation: P is the ray travelling towards the mirror, so it is the incident ray; Q leaves the mirror and is the reflected ray.

grade9-physics.question: In the figure, which letter marks the reflected ray?
grade9-physics.hint: The reflected ray is the one leaving the mirror.
grade9-physics.explanation: Q travels away from the point where the light met the mirror, so it is the reflected ray.

grade9-physics.question: In the figure, what is the dashed line called?
grade9-physics.hint: It is drawn at right angles to the mirror.
grade9-physics.explanation: The dashed line drawn perpendicular to the mirror at the point where the ray strikes is called the normal.

grade9-physics.question: The first law of reflection states that the angle of incidence is:
options: Equal to the angle of reflection
grade9-physics.answer: Equal to the angle of reflection
acceptableAnswers: Equal to the angle of reflection
grade9-physics.hint: The two angles either side of the normal match.
grade9-physics.explanation: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

grade9-physics.question: From which line is the angle of incidence measured?
grade9-physics.hint: Not from the mirror itself.
grade9-physics.explanation: Both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface.

grade9-physics.question: A ray strikes a plane mirror so that the angle between the ray and the mirror surface is 30°. What is the angle of incidence?
grade9-physics.hint: The normal is at 90° to the mirror.
grade9-physics.explanation: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal: 90 - 30 = 60°.

grade9-physics.question: The second law of reflection states that the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal:
options: All lie in the same plane
Are always parallel to each other
grade9-physics.answer: All lie in the same plane
acceptableAnswers: All lie in the same plane
grade9-physics.hint: It is about them lying flat together, not about their sizes.
grade9-physics.explanation: The second law states that the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.

grade9-physics.question: In the figure, the angle marked x is 40°. What is the angle of reflection?
grade9-physics.hint: Apply the first law of reflection.
grade9-physics.explanation: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so it is also 40°.

grade9-physics.question: A ray hits a plane mirror along the normal, so the angle of incidence is 0°. What happens to it?
options: It travels along the mirror surface
It is reflected straight back along the same path
It is reflected at right angles to the normal
grade9-physics.answer: It is reflected straight back along the same path
acceptableAnswers: It is reflected straight back along the same path
grade9-physics.hint: The angle of reflection must equal 0° too.
grade9-physics.explanation: With an angle of incidence of 0° the angle of reflection is also 0°, so the ray returns along its own path.

grade9-physics.question: A ray strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 35°. State the angle of reflection, in degrees.
grade9-physics.hint: The two angles are equal.
grade9-physics.explanation: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence: 35°.

grade9-physics.question: The angle between an incident ray and the mirror surface is 25°. Calculate the angle of incidence, in degrees.
grade9-physics.hint: The normal is at 90° to the mirror.

grade9-physics.question: The angle of incidence is 30°. Calculate the total angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray, in degrees.
grade9-physics.hint: Each ray is 30° from the normal, on opposite sides.
grade9-physics.explanation: The two rays sit 30° either side of the normal, so the angle between them is 30 + 30 = 60°.

grade9-physics.question: A ray travels along the normal to a plane mirror. State the angle of reflection, in degrees.
grade9-physics.hint: The angle of incidence is zero here.
grade9-physics.explanation: The angle of incidence is 0°, so the angle of reflection is 0° and the ray returns along its path.

grade9-physics.question: Give the term for an object that produces its own light.
grade9-physics.hint: The Sun is one.
grade9-physics.explanation: A luminous object makes its own light.

grade9-physics.question: Name the line drawn at right angles to a mirror at the point where a ray strikes it.
grade9-physics.hint: It is drawn dashed in a ray diagram.
grade9-physics.explanation: The normal is perpendicular to the mirror at the point of incidence, and both angles are measured from it.

grade9-physics.question: Give the term for light bouncing off a surface.
grade9-physics.hint: It is what a mirror does.
grade9-physics.explanation: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface.

grade9-physics.question: State how light travels through a uniform medium such as air.
grade9-physics.hint: It is why shadows have sharp edges.
grade9-physics.explanation: Light travels in straight lines through a uniform medium, which is why shadows form.

grade9-physics.question: Give the term for an object that gives out no light of its own.
grade9-physics.hint: The Moon is one.
grade9-physics.explanation: A non-luminous object is seen only by the light it reflects.

grade9-physics.question: Which of the following is a luminous object?
grade9-physics.hint: A luminous object makes its own light.
grade9-physics.explanation: A candle flame produces light by burning; the Moon, mirror and paper only reflect light from other sources.

grade9-physics.question: The Moon is visible at night. Why is the Moon not a luminous object?
options: It is too far away to be luminous
It only produces light during a full moon
It emits infrared radiation rather than visible light
It does not produce its own light; it reflects sunlight
grade9-physics.answer: It does not produce its own light; it reflects sunlight
acceptableAnswers: It does not produce its own light; it reflects sunlight
grade9-physics.hint: A luminous object makes its own light.
grade9-physics.explanation: The Moon reflects light from the Sun; it does not generate light of its own.

grade9-physics.question: Which row correctly classifies the objects as luminous or non-luminous?
options: Sun: non-luminous; Moon: luminous; mirror: non-luminous
Sun: luminous; Moon: luminous; mirror: non-luminous
Sun: luminous; Moon: non-luminous; mirror: non-luminous
Sun: luminous; Moon: non-luminous; mirror: luminous
grade9-physics.answer: Sun: luminous; Moon: non-luminous; mirror: non-luminous
acceptableAnswers: Sun: luminous; Moon: non-luminous; mirror: non-luminous
grade9-physics.hint: Only objects that generate their own light are luminous.
grade9-physics.explanation: Only the Sun generates light. The Moon and a mirror both reflect light from other sources.

grade9-physics.question: A student says a neon sign is luminous. Is this correct?
options: Yes, but only when the surrounding area is dark
No, because it only reflects light from street lamps
No, because only natural objects can be luminous
Yes, because the gas inside emits light when electricity passes through it
grade9-physics.answer: Yes, because the gas inside emits light when electricity passes through it
acceptableAnswers: Yes, because the gas inside emits light when electricity passes through it
grade9-physics.hint: Think about where the light comes from.
grade9-physics.explanation: A neon sign produces its own light through electrical excitation of the gas, so it is luminous.

grade9-physics.question: Which of the following is non-luminous?
grade9-physics.hint: Planets reflect sunlight; stars generate their own light.
grade9-physics.explanation: Planets are non-luminous because they only reflect sunlight. Stars (including the Sun) are luminous.

grade9-physics.question: A torch is switched on in a dark room. Which object in the room becomes visible because of the torch?
options: The air in the room (which scatters light)
grade9-physics.hint: Non-luminous objects become visible when they reflect light from a luminous source.
grade9-physics.explanation: The chair reflects some of the torch’s light toward the observer’s eyes, making it visible.

grade9-physics.question: A planet is visible from Earth on a clear night. Explain why the planet can be seen even though it does not produce light.
options: It absorbs starlight and re-emits it
Its surface is hot enough to glow
It reflects sunlight toward the Earth
grade9-physics.answer: It reflects sunlight toward the Earth
acceptableAnswers: It reflects sunlight toward the Earth
grade9-physics.hint: Think about what travels from the planet to your eye.
grade9-physics.explanation: Planets reflect sunlight; some of that reflected light travels to Earth, where it enters the eye.

grade9-physics.question: Which statement is correct about a star?
options: A star is luminous because it produces its own light
A star is non-luminous because it reflects sunlight
A star is non-luminous because it is too far away
A star is luminous only when it is closer than the Moon
grade9-physics.answer: A star is luminous because it produces its own light
acceptableAnswers: A star is luminous because it produces its own light
grade9-physics.hint: Stars generate energy by nuclear fusion.
grade9-physics.explanation: Stars produce their own light through nuclear fusion, making them luminous objects.

grade9-physics.question: In terms of luminosity, how are the Sun and the Moon different?
options: The Sun is luminous; the Moon is non-luminous
The Moon is luminous; the Sun is non-luminous
grade9-physics.answer: The Sun is luminous; the Moon is non-luminous
acceptableAnswers: The Sun is luminous; the Moon is non-luminous
grade9-physics.hint: One generates light; the other reflects it.
grade9-physics.explanation: The Sun generates its own light (luminous); the Moon only reflects sunlight (non-luminous).

grade9-physics.question: A student lists: torch bulb, mirror, white paper, fire. Which are luminous?
grade9-physics.hint: Luminous objects produce their own light.
grade9-physics.explanation: A torch bulb (electrical) and fire (chemical) both produce their own light. The mirror and paper only reflect light.

grade9-physics.question: Why can we see non-luminous objects?
options: They are transparent so light passes through them
Our eyes can detect objects without light being present
They reflect light from luminous sources into our eyes
They emit a small amount of light of their own
grade9-physics.answer: They reflect light from luminous sources into our eyes
acceptableAnswers: They reflect light from luminous sources into our eyes
grade9-physics.hint: Non-luminous objects need a light source to be visible.
grade9-physics.explanation: Non-luminous objects reflect incident light from luminous sources; this reflected light enters the eye.

grade9-physics.question: A student claims that a fluorescent tube is non-luminous because it needs electricity from outside to work. Is the student correct?
options: Yes; any object needing an external energy source is non-luminous
No; all electrical devices are automatically luminous
Yes; only chemical sources like flames are luminous
No; the tube produces its own light when current flows, so it is luminous
grade9-physics.answer: No; the tube produces its own light when current flows, so it is luminous
acceptableAnswers: No; the tube produces its own light when current flows, so it is luminous
grade9-physics.hint: A luminous object produces light, regardless of its energy source.
grade9-physics.explanation: Luminosity is about producing light, not about the energy source. The tube produces light, so it is luminous.

grade9-physics.question: Which of these objects would be visible in a completely dark room with no external light source?
grade9-physics.hint: Only a luminous object is visible without an external light source.
grade9-physics.explanation: A glowing LED produces its own light; the mirror, wall and window all need an external source to be visible.

grade9-physics.question: The Sun, a candle and a neon sign have something in common. What is it?
options: They all produce heat but not light
grade9-physics.hint: What do all three produce by themselves?
grade9-physics.explanation: All three produce their own light, making them luminous objects.

grade9-physics.question: At night, a car’s headlights illuminate a road sign. The sign is clearly visible. Is the sign luminous or non-luminous, and why?
options: Luminous; it has reflective paint that produces light
Luminous; it generates electricity from the headlights
Non-luminous; it reflects the headlights toward the driver’s eyes
Non-luminous; it absorbs the headlights completely
grade9-physics.answer: Non-luminous; it reflects the headlights toward the driver’s eyes
acceptableAnswers: Non-luminous; it reflects the headlights toward the driver’s eyes
grade9-physics.hint: The sign does not generate light on its own.
grade9-physics.explanation: Road signs reflect light from headlights; they do not produce their own light, so they are non-luminous.

grade9-physics.question: How does light from a luminous object reach the eye so that we see it?
options: The brain creates an image without any light entering the eye
The eye sends out rays that detect the object
Light travels in straight lines from the object to the eye
Light curves around objects to reach the eye
grade9-physics.answer: Light travels in straight lines from the object to the eye
acceptableAnswers: Light travels in straight lines from the object to the eye
grade9-physics.hint: Light needs a clear path from the source to the eye.
grade9-physics.explanation: Vision requires light to travel in straight lines from the object (or source) directly into the eye.

grade9-physics.question: Why can we see a non-luminous object such as this page?
options: The page is transparent, allowing light to pass through it
Light from a luminous source reflects off the page and enters the eye
The page produces a small amount of light of its own
The eye can see objects without any light
grade9-physics.answer: Light from a luminous source reflects off the page and enters the eye
acceptableAnswers: Light from a luminous source reflects off the page and enters the eye
grade9-physics.hint: Non-luminous objects must reflect light to be visible.
grade9-physics.explanation: The page reflects light from the room’s light sources; some of this reflected light enters the eye.

grade9-physics.question: A person closes their eyes in a brightly lit room. They cannot see anything. What does this show?
options: Seeing requires light to enter the eye
The room is too bright for normal vision
The brain cannot work without signals from the eye
grade9-physics.answer: Seeing requires light to enter the eye
acceptableAnswers: Seeing requires light to enter the eye
grade9-physics.hint: Vision depends on light reaching the retina.
grade9-physics.explanation: No light enters a closed eye, so no vision is possible; this confirms that seeing requires light entering the eye.

grade9-physics.question: Which correctly describes how an observer sees the Moon?
options: Sunlight reflects off the Moon and travels to the observer’s eye
The observer’s eye sends out rays that detect the Moon
The Moon sends out its own light to the observer’s eye
Light from the Earth reflects off the Moon
grade9-physics.answer: Sunlight reflects off the Moon and travels to the observer’s eye
acceptableAnswers: Sunlight reflects off the Moon and travels to the observer’s eye
grade9-physics.hint: The Moon is non-luminous.
grade9-physics.explanation: Sunlight hits the Moon; some of this light is reflected toward Earth, enters the eye and creates the image of the Moon.

grade9-physics.question: In ancient times, some thinkers believed the eye emits rays that detect objects. Modern science rejects this. What is the correct explanation of vision?
options: Objects emit an invisible aura that the eye detects
The brain directly senses distant objects without light
The eye emits rays that bounce off objects and return
Light from external sources enters the eye and is detected by the retina
grade9-physics.answer: Light from external sources enters the eye and is detected by the retina
acceptableAnswers: Light from external sources enters the eye and is detected by the retina
grade9-physics.hint: Light must travel from the object to the eye, not the other way around.
grade9-physics.explanation: Modern science shows that light from external sources (luminous or reflected) enters the eye and is focused on the retina.

grade9-physics.question: In a completely dark room, a student holds up a mirror. Can they see their reflection?
options: No, because there is no light to reflect
Yes, because the eye can see without light in a mirror
Yes, because mirrors produce their own light
No, because mirrors do not work in dark rooms
grade9-physics.answer: No, because there is no light to reflect
acceptableAnswers: No, because there is no light to reflect
grade9-physics.hint: A mirror is non-luminous and needs an external light source.
grade9-physics.explanation: Without a light source, there is no light for the mirror to reflect, so no image is formed.

grade9-physics.question: Which of the following is needed for a human to see an object?
options: The object must be within 1 m of the observer
Light from the object (produced or reflected) entering the eye
The observer must be in a brightly lit room
grade9-physics.answer: Light from the object (produced or reflected) entering the eye
acceptableAnswers: Light from the object (produced or reflected) entering the eye
grade9-physics.hint: The key requirement is light reaching the eye.
grade9-physics.explanation: Seeing requires light to enter the eye; the light may come directly from a luminous object or be reflected from a non-luminous one.

grade9-physics.question: Which statement about stars and planets is correct?
options: Stars and planets are both luminous
Stars and planets are both non-luminous
Stars are luminous; planets are non-luminous
Planets are luminous; stars are non-luminous
grade9-physics.answer: Stars are luminous; planets are non-luminous
acceptableAnswers: Stars are luminous; planets are non-luminous
grade9-physics.hint: Stars produce light by nuclear fusion; planets only reflect starlight.
grade9-physics.explanation: Stars generate their own light (luminous); planets reflect light from their star (non-luminous).

grade9-physics.question: A student is in a sealed room with no windows or light sources. They have a mirror. What can they see?
options: Nothing at all, because no light is present
Their reflection, because the mirror creates light
Outlines of objects, because the eye adjusts to darkness
The mirror surface, because it is slightly luminous
grade9-physics.answer: Nothing at all, because no light is present
acceptableAnswers: Nothing at all, because no light is present
grade9-physics.hint: Vision always requires some light entering the eye.
grade9-physics.explanation: Without any light source, no light enters the eye and nothing can be seen, regardless of having a mirror.

grade9-physics.question: Which event must happen for a person to see an object that is not luminous?
options: The object must release stored light energy
Light from a luminous source must reflect off the object and enter the person’s eye
The person must focus their vision on the object
The surrounding air must scatter light toward the object
grade9-physics.answer: Light from a luminous source must reflect off the object and enter the person’s eye
acceptableAnswers: Light from a luminous source must reflect off the object and enter the person’s eye
grade9-physics.hint: Non-luminous objects can only be seen by reflected light.
grade9-physics.explanation: A non-luminous object needs a light source. Some of that light reflects off the object and travels to the eye.

grade9-physics.question: A teacher switches off all the lights in a laboratory. After a few minutes of total darkness, can a student see a white wall?
options: Yes, because white walls glow in the dark
No, because there is no light to reflect off the wall
Yes, because the eye adjusts completely to darkness
No, because white walls absorb all light
grade9-physics.answer: No, because there is no light to reflect off the wall
acceptableAnswers: No, because there is no light to reflect off the wall
grade9-physics.hint: A white wall is non-luminous and needs a light source.
grade9-physics.explanation: With no light source, there is no light to reflect; the wall is invisible in complete darkness.

grade9-physics.question: Jupiter can be seen from Earth on a clear night. Jupiter is not a star. How is it visible?
options: Jupiter produces a small amount of nuclear light
Jupiter’s strong magnetic field makes it glow
Jupiter reflects sunlight, which travels to Earth and enters the eye
grade9-physics.answer: Jupiter reflects sunlight, which travels to Earth and enters the eye
acceptableAnswers: Jupiter reflects sunlight, which travels to Earth and enters the eye
grade9-physics.hint: Jupiter is a planet, so it is non-luminous.
grade9-physics.explanation: Jupiter reflects sunlight; some of this reflected light travels across space to Earth and enters our eyes.

grade9-physics.question: An observer on the Moon (no atmosphere) looks toward Earth. Explain why they can see the Earth.
options: The Earth emits its own light like a star
The Earth glows because of its internal heat
Sunlight reflects off the Earth’s surface and atmosphere, and travels to the observer’s eye
The observer’s eye sends out rays that detect the Earth
grade9-physics.answer: Sunlight reflects off the Earth’s surface and atmosphere, and travels to the observer’s eye
acceptableAnswers: Sunlight reflects off the Earth’s surface and atmosphere, and travels to the observer’s eye
grade9-physics.hint: The Earth is non-luminous; it reflects sunlight.
grade9-physics.explanation: From the Moon, an observer sees the Earth lit by reflected sunlight, just as we see the Moon from Earth.

grade9-physics.question: A firefly produces its own light. How should it be classified?
options: Luminous, but only when it is flying
Non-luminous, because it is a living organism, not a manufactured source
Luminous, because it generates light through a chemical reaction
Non-luminous, because it only glows intermittently
grade9-physics.answer: Luminous, because it generates light through a chemical reaction
acceptableAnswers: Luminous, because it generates light through a chemical reaction
grade9-physics.hint: Luminosity depends on producing light, not on the type of source.
grade9-physics.explanation: A firefly produces its own light through bioluminescence; it is a luminous object.

grade9-physics.question: Which of the following is the correct path of light when a person reads a book under a lamp?
grade9-physics.hint: Light travels from the source to the object and then to the eye.
grade9-physics.explanation: The lamp (luminous) sends light to the book; the book reflects some light into the reader’s eye.

grade9-physics.question: In what direction does light normally travel?
grade9-physics.hint: The Latin phrase “rectilinear propagation” describes this.
grade9-physics.explanation: Light travels in straight lines through a uniform medium; this is called rectilinear propagation.

grade9-physics.question: What is the evidence that light travels in straight lines?
options: Light always takes the longest path to reach a surface
A sharp shadow is formed behind an opaque object
Light bends around corners without a shadow
grade9-physics.answer: A sharp shadow is formed behind an opaque object
acceptableAnswers: A sharp shadow is formed behind an opaque object
grade9-physics.hint: Straight-line travel means nothing gets around the object.
grade9-physics.explanation: If light could bend, shadows would be blurred or absent. Sharp shadows prove light travels in straight lines.

grade9-physics.question: A student places three cards with small holes in a line between a lamp and a screen. Light passes through all three holes and reaches the screen. What does this demonstrate?
options: Light can pass through any solid material
Light bends around each card to reach the next hole
Light waves require a medium to travel through
grade9-physics.hint: If light were not straight, it could not pass through all three holes in line.
grade9-physics.explanation: Light only passes through all three holes if they are perfectly aligned, proving light travels in a straight line.

grade9-physics.question: An opaque ball is placed in front of a small lamp. What kind of shadow does the ball cast on the screen behind it?
options: A blurred shadow larger than the ball
A coloured shadow due to refraction
No shadow, because light bends around the ball
A sharp-edged shadow the same shape as the ball
grade9-physics.answer: A sharp-edged shadow the same shape as the ball
acceptableAnswers: A sharp-edged shadow the same shape as the ball
grade9-physics.hint: Straight rays produce sharp shadows.
grade9-physics.explanation: Because light travels in straight lines and cannot get around the opaque ball, a sharp-edged shadow is cast.

grade9-physics.question: A point source of light is 20 cm from an opaque disc. The disc casts a shadow on a screen 60 cm from the disc. The shadow diameter is 12 cm. What is the disc diameter?
grade9-physics.hint: The shadow is 3 times as far from the disc as the disc is from the lamp: scale by the ratio.
grade9-physics.explanation: Total distance from source to screen = 80 cm. The disc is 20 cm from the source. Shadow is 80/20 = 4 times bigger. Disc diameter = 12/3 = 4 cm.

grade9-physics.question: A small lamp is moved further from an opaque object. What happens to the shadow on the screen?
options: The shadow stays the same size
grade9-physics.hint: Moving the source further away makes the rays more nearly parallel.
grade9-physics.explanation: As the lamp moves further away, the cone of light that forms the shadow narrows and the shadow shrinks.

grade9-physics.question: A large light source (not a point source) produces two regions behind an opaque object. What are these regions called?
grade9-physics.hint: A large source creates a full shadow and a partial shadow.
grade9-physics.explanation: The umbra is the region of total shadow (no light from any part of the source); the penumbra is the region of partial shadow.

grade9-physics.question: Why can you not see around a corner without a mirror or other aid?
options: The corner absorbs all the light
Light is too weak to reach around a corner
Light travels in curves but is too slow to reach the corner
Light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around the corner
grade9-physics.answer: Light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around the corner
acceptableAnswers: Light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around the corner
grade9-physics.hint: Straight rays cannot change direction without reflection or refraction.
grade9-physics.explanation: Because light travels in straight lines, it does not bend around corners; you need a mirror to redirect it.

grade9-physics.question: A ray of light shines through a small hole in a screen into a dark room. What shape does the beam form?
options: A straight line from the hole to where it hits the wall
A curved path that bends downward
A fan-shaped cone that expands in all directions
A circle on the wall directly in front of the hole
grade9-physics.answer: A straight line from the hole to where it hits the wall
acceptableAnswers: A straight line from the hole to where it hits the wall
grade9-physics.hint: Light travels in straight lines through a uniform medium.
grade9-physics.explanation: The beam travels in a straight line from the hole to the opposite wall; no bending occurs.

grade9-physics.question: A pinhole camera produces an image that is upside down. Why?
options: The film inside the camera is placed upside down
The lens inside the camera inverts the image
Rays from the top of the object pass through the hole and hit the bottom of the screen
The pinhole reverses the direction of light
grade9-physics.answer: Rays from the top of the object pass through the hole and hit the bottom of the screen
acceptableAnswers: Rays from the top of the object pass through the hole and hit the bottom of the screen
grade9-physics.hint: Draw the straight rays from top and bottom of the object through the pinhole.
grade9-physics.explanation: Because light travels in straight lines, a ray from the top of the object passes through the pinhole and hits the bottom of the screen, inverting the image.

grade9-physics.question: An eclipse of the Sun occurs when the Moon is directly between the Earth and the Sun. Which property of light explains why a shadow forms on part of the Earth?
options: Light can be refracted by the atmosphere
grade9-physics.hint: A shadow forms only because light cannot bend around the Moon.
grade9-physics.explanation: Because light travels in straight lines, the Moon blocks sunlight completely in the umbra and partially in the penumbra.

grade9-physics.question: Which of these is a direct application of rectilinear propagation of light?
options: A mirror creating a virtual image
A prism splitting white light into colours
A pinhole camera forming an image
grade9-physics.answer: A pinhole camera forming an image
acceptableAnswers: A pinhole camera forming an image
grade9-physics.hint: A pinhole camera works purely because light travels straight.
grade9-physics.explanation: The inverted image in a pinhole camera is formed because rays from each part of the object travel in straight lines through the pinhole to opposite parts of the screen.

grade9-physics.question: A student uses three cards with holes and lines them up. The lamp is visible through all three. The middle card is then moved sideways. What happens?
options: The lamp is still visible because light bends
The lamp is no longer visible through the holes
The lamp is dimmer but still visible
The lamp is still visible because the other two holes are aligned
grade9-physics.answer: The lamp is no longer visible through the holes
acceptableAnswers: The lamp is no longer visible through the holes
grade9-physics.hint: All three holes must be in a straight line for light to pass through all of them.
grade9-physics.explanation: If the middle card is moved, the three holes are no longer in a straight line; light cannot turn the corner so the lamp is blocked.

grade9-physics.question: A lamp is placed 10 cm from a 4 cm opaque disc. A screen is placed 40 cm beyond the disc (50 cm from the lamp). How wide is the shadow on the screen?
grade9-physics.hint: Use similar triangles: shadow width / disc width = screen distance from source / disc distance from source.
grade9-physics.explanation: Shadow width = disc width × (screen distance from source ÷ disc distance from source) = 4 × (50 ÷ 10) = 20 cm.

grade9-physics.question: Why do astronomers use straight cylindrical telescope tubes rather than curved ones?
options: Light from distant stars travels in straight lines into the telescope
Straight tubes are easier to manufacture
Curved tubes would absorb more light
Curved tubes would cause light to speed up
grade9-physics.answer: Light from distant stars travels in straight lines into the telescope
acceptableAnswers: Light from distant stars travels in straight lines into the telescope
grade9-physics.hint: Light from very distant sources arrives as nearly parallel straight rays.
grade9-physics.explanation: Because starlight travels in straight lines, a straight tube correctly collects and directs it to the eyepiece or detector.

grade9-physics.question: A student holds a cardboard tube to their eye and sees a light source at the far end. When the tube is bent, the source disappears. What does this show about light?
options: Light travels in straight lines and cannot go around a bend
Light cannot travel through any tube
Light cannot go around a bend
Light only travels in a vacuum
grade9-physics.answer: Light cannot go around a bend
acceptableAnswers: Light cannot go around a bend
grade9-physics.hint: Straight-line travel means no path around a corner.
grade9-physics.explanation: When the tube is bent, there is no straight-line path from the source to the eye; since light cannot bend, nothing is seen.

grade9-physics.question: What is reflection of light?
options: Light splitting into a spectrum of colours
Light slowing down when it hits a surface
Light bending as it passes from air into glass
Light bouncing off a surface and changing direction
grade9-physics.answer: Light bouncing off a surface and changing direction
acceptableAnswers: Light bouncing off a surface and changing direction
grade9-physics.hint: Think about what happens when light hits a mirror.
grade9-physics.explanation: Reflection is the bouncing of light off a surface; the direction changes but the speed and wavelength do not (in the same medium).

grade9-physics.question: What type of surface gives regular (specular) reflection?
options: A rough, dull surface such as paper
A smooth, polished surface such as a mirror
A transparent surface such as glass
A black surface such as a chalkboard
grade9-physics.answer: A smooth, polished surface such as a mirror
acceptableAnswers: A smooth, polished surface such as a mirror
grade9-physics.hint: A mirror gives a clear image; rough surfaces scatter light.
grade9-physics.explanation: Regular reflection occurs at smooth surfaces; all reflected rays are parallel and a clear image is formed.

grade9-physics.question: Why does a rough surface produce diffuse (irregular) reflection?
options: The surface absorbs most of the light and reflects very little
Diffuse reflection only occurs in a liquid surface
Rough surfaces have gaps between atoms through which light escapes
The tiny bumps on the surface reflect rays in many different directions
grade9-physics.answer: The tiny bumps on the surface reflect rays in many different directions
acceptableAnswers: The tiny bumps on the surface reflect rays in many different directions
grade9-physics.hint: Each part of a rough surface acts like a tiny tilted mirror.
